Reckon on the pass being under snow into July in a normal year and later after a heavy winter; the north-facing ground above it holds much longer. Weather comes across from the west with no warning here and there is no shelter for hours in any direction, so this is a camp to be conservative about.
bivy.water: Seasonal snowmelt only, and not to be relied on late in the summer. The dependable sources are down in Mill Creek on the west side and in the Brush Creek drainage on the east. Fill low and carry it up; a party that arrives here dry in September has a problem.
bivy.permit: None. National forest, dispersed camping, no permit and no quota. Camp on gravel or scree rather than the meadow. No fires — there is nothing to burn and a ban is likely in force anyway.
bivy.capacity: Open ground at and just below the pass, at around six thousand seven hundred feet — mapping and reports put it anywhere between about 6,680 and 6,750, so take the figure loosely. Room for a couple of small tents. Exposed, with no shelter and no windbreak worth the name.

wa_azurite_peak_southeast.notes: From the Canyon Creek trailhead on SR-20, follow Canyon Creek to the Mill Creek trail and up past the old Azurite Mine to the west slopes of the peak or on to Azurite Pass. The Mill Creek trail is badly overgrown in places and route-finding through alder is slow, so most parties prefer the east-side starts.

wa_bear_mountain_chilliwack_north_buttre.name: Hannegan Pass and the Chilliwack River Trail to Bear Creek
camps: Meadow basin below the northwest-ridge saddle
wa_bear_mountain_chilliwack_north_buttre.notes:
From the road end at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 runs nearly level for the first mile and then climbs at a steady grade to Hannegan Pass at about 5,100 ft. Drop off the east side and continue down into the Chilliwack valley, bearing right at the park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail proper. The tread loses height past a backcountry camp to the Chilliwack River crossing - historically a hand-pulled cable car, and a serious ford if it is not running, so check its status before you plan around it - then runs down-valley past further camps to the Bear Creek confluence. The camp at that confluence has been closed since fire came through the drainage, so confirm it is open rather than assuming a bed there.

At Bear Creek the maintained trail ends. Ford the creek, which can be a genuinely committing crossing in snowmelt, and climb steep brushy timber eastward; higher the brush turns to huckleberry and slide alder before opening into meadows above Ruta Lake. Traverse the divide from there, skirting the loose south-facing slopes below two unnamed points and crossing a rock rib, to a broad saddle at about 6,480 ft with running water and heather tent sites. Most parties split this over two days.
wa_bear_mountain_chilliwack_north_buttre.season: Late July through September, once the Chilliwack crossing has dropped and the buttress is dry
hazards: a river crossing that depends on a cable car being in service
the Bear Creek ford in snowmelt
steep brushy timber and slide alder with no tread
loose south-facing traverse slopes below the divide points
rockfall and icefall out of the shrinking glacier in the couloir
a moat between neve and slab that worsens through the season
a position days from any road, on either side of the border
wa_bear_mountain_chilliwack_north_buttre.baseFinding:
The route begins by losing height, and that is the single most important thing to know at camp. From the 6,480 ft saddle you drop down steep scree, trending climber's right, and cross several minor gullies to reach the toe of the small glacier remnant spilling out of the couloir below the buttress. Any line that climbs upward from the saddle toward rock is the wrong one.

Identify the saddle first: it is broad, it has running water on it and flat heather sites, and it sits on the north-west ridge with the wall around the corner rather than above you. A saddle with no water and no camping is not it.

At the ice, the positive test is which side of the buttress you go up. This route climbs the glacier or neve on the climber's-left side of the buttress and then works into slabs that lead to a corner system - the corner is where the technical climbing starts. The toe of the buttress itself, where the rock meets the ice on the right-hand side, is the start of the direct and not of this route. If you are roping up at the very bottom of the rock rather than walking past it on snow, you are on the harder line.

Watch the join between snow and rock. A moat opens where the neve pulls away from the slabs and it deepens through the season; getting out of it onto the slabs is often the awkward move of the approach and it is worth an axe and crampons even in high summer.

A cross-check once committed: the climbing above the corner runs up to about 5.10 with the hardest move an offwidth part-way up, and it finishes on the buttress top, from where a scramble gains the true summit. If your first pitch off the ice is already at your limit, you have started too low and too far right.

wa_bear_mountain_chilliwack_north_buttre.name: From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side

bivy.name: Meadow basin below the northwest-ridge saddle
bivy.notes: The standard and effectively the only high camp for the buttress, in heather meadow a little below the notch on the northwest ridge, where scattered trees give some wind shelter and flat grassy ground. Reached by climbing roughly 3,000 ft out of the Bear Creek valley to treeline on a rough climbers' path through open forest that gives way to blueberry brush. Around nine hours from the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side; the American approach over Hannegan Pass and down the Chilliwack River is far longer, on the order of seventeen miles, but is the one that keeps the permit straightforward. Expect mosquitoes.
bivy.water: Running water at the camp, fed by semi-permanent snowfields just above; those patches are described as holding meltwater well into the later part of the season.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, Bear Mountain cross-country zone: maximum party of six and six permits per night. This zone cannot be reserved in advance — it is walk-up only, from the Wilderness Information Center. Cross-country camping is restricted to durable ground.
bivy.capacity: No published tent count. The binding number is the permit: six people per party, six parties a night in the zone.

approachLogistics.trailhead: Chilliwack Lake road, south end (British Columbia)

wa_bear_mountain_chilliwack_north_buttre.notes: There is a far shorter line to the same camp from the road on the Canadian side of the border - a fraction of the distance the Hannegan approach covers. It crosses the border on foot where there is no port of entry, and this page cannot say that crossing is lawful, so confirm it with the border authorities before planning on it; and the tread turns unmaintained and badly overgrown after the first mile or two, so the miles it saves are not all easy ones. Most parties starting in the United States take the long way rather than deal with it; parties already north of the border have the opposite calculation.
wa_bear_mountain_chilliwack_north_buttre.season: Same window, and only if the border crossing is confirmed lawful
hazards: an international border crossing on foot, with the documents and permissions that implies
unmaintained and heavily overgrown tread for most of the distance
the same loose divide traverse and the same glacier remnant beneath the buttress
a rescue that may involve two countries
wa_bear_mountain_chilliwack_north_buttre.baseFinding:
The approach variant changes only how you arrive at the 6,480 ft saddle. Once there, everything is as for the long approach: the camp is the broad saddle with running water and heather sites on the north-west ridge, and the route starts by dropping off it on steep scree, trending climber's right, across several minor gullies to the toe of the glacier remnant beneath the couloir.

The same two tests apply at the ice. Go up the snow on the climber's-left side of the buttress into the slabs and the corner system. If you are tying in at the very toe of the rock where it meets the ice on the right, you are under the Direct.

And the same negative marker: gaining height straight from the saddle toward rock means you have not gone far enough down. The wall is below and around the corner from camp, not above it.

wa_blackcap_mountain_scramble.name: Shellrock Basin camp and the traverse to the east-face col
camps: Doris Lake and Freds Lake basins
Shellrock Pass, Shellrock Basin and the Eureka Creek meadows
wa_blackcap_mountain_scramble.notes: Blackcap is a leg of a multi-day traverse rather than an objective on its own, and the walk in is measured in days, not hours. The usual staging is a camp in Shellrock Basin just below and east of Shellrock Pass, reached over Rolo Pass from Fred's Lake after a long valley approach up the Middle Fork Pasayten. From camp the peak is a half-day round trip on easy ground. Water is at the basin and in upper Eureka Creek and there is none on the mountain. An eastern line exists off the Monument Creek trail into the open Monument-Blackcap basin, but the Shellrock side is the travelled one and the one with a recognisable start.
hazards: Loose scree and talus on the east face, worse descending than ascending
Exposure and loose blocks near the top of the northeast ridge
A steep snowfield below Shellrock Pass that can persist into early summer
High, cold fords of Eureka Creek and the Middle Fork Pasayten during runoff
Days from the nearest road with no cell coverage
wa_blackcap_mountain_scramble.baseFinding: The base is a col, and getting to it is the only route-finding on the day. Leave the trail at Shellrock Pass itself and traverse south-southwest across the open grassy and rocky basin, keeping below the cliff bands the whole way. That traverse ends at the foot of a talus slope. Work the left, eastern edge of that talus southward until the cliff band above you finally runs out; the saddle at the end of it, directly beneath Blackcap's east face, is where the climbing starts. The confirmation is the rock itself and it is the clearest single marker on this peak: Blackcap's summit cap is near-black hornfels and shale sitting abruptly on top of much paler rock, and the colour boundary is visible from the col and is under your hands within a few minutes of leaving it. If everything around you is still light-coloured after several hundred feet of scree, you are on the wrong flank. Two ways to know you have overshot. Following the trail over Shellrock Pass and down its far side takes you away from the peak altogether. Continuing south past the end of the cliff band instead of turning up drops you toward the Monument basin. In early season a steep snowfield sits below the pass on this traverse and is normally bypassed on its left; carry an axe if it is still there.

wa_blackcap_mountain_scramble.name: Robinson Creek over Robinson Pass

bivy.name: Doris Lake and Freds Lake basins
bivy.notes: This is the working climbers' camp for Osceola Peak and Blackcap Mountain and the first night of the long traverse that links them with Carru and Lago. The line in starts high, which is the point: from Slate Pass at about 6,900 feet a short connector drops to the Middle Fork Pasayten trail, five miles of valley walking leads to the Ferguson Lake spur, and three more miles of climbing reaches Doris Lake at just under 7,000 feet. Osceola is then a short cross-country scramble northeast through open forest from camp, which is as close as anything in the Pasayten comes to convenient. Blackcap is further along the ridge system and is usually taken on the second or third day. Freds Lake sits on the parallel line toward Rolo Pass and serves the same purpose for parties heading for Shellrock. Reckon on three to four days for anything based here and remember that the return from a high camp means regaining Slate Pass at the end. Larches turn in the last week of September and the first of October, which is also when the nights get genuinely cold at this elevation.
bivy.water: Both lakes hold through the season and are the dependable supply for this whole group of peaks. Between them and the Middle Fork river flats a party can plan a multi-day traverse without rationing, which is not true of most of this wilderness.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Slate Pass or Harts Pass, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Camp at least a hundred feet back from either shoreline — the ground close to the water is thin and already worn. Weed-free feed for stock, and no tying animals to trees overnight.
bivy.capacity: Informal sites on benches and ridge shoulders back from the water, room for two or three small parties without crowding. Nothing developed, no tables, no toilets.

bivy.name: Shellrock Pass, Shellrock Basin and the Eureka Creek meadows
bivy.notes: Shellrock is the camp for Ptarmigan Peak and Dot Mountain, both of which are otherwise out of reach. The standard line leaves Slate Pass, follows the Middle Fork Pasayten to Berk Creek, climbs to Freds Pass and crosses the head of Eureka Creek to Shellrock Pass, which puts a party in position to scramble Ptarmigan the following day; Dot is taken from the same country on the way through, usually in combination with the Lago and Carru group. This is genuinely remote — thirty-five miles and thirteen thousand feet of gain over four days is a fair description of a trip that collects three or four summits here — and there is no short version. The meadow ground is soft and holds a footprint for years, so pitch on the timber edge or on gravel rather than in the open grass. Snow lingers on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the single biggest constraint on when this is worth attempting.
bivy.water: Reliable at the creek camp and in the Eureka meadows, and the pond in Shellrock Basin usually holds. The passes themselves are dry, so fill in the basin or the meadows before going up rather than expecting to find snowmelt on the crest late in the season.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Slate Pass or Robinson Creek. Stock use is significant through here — weed-free feed is required and animals may not be tied to trees overnight. Fires are legal outside a ban but the meadows are fragile and most parties cook on a stove and leave it at that.
bivy.capacity: Dispersed rather than designated. There is a forested site by the creek at about 5,800 feet where the old Eureka Creek trail joins, a broad spread of good ground in the Eureka Creek meadows near 6,300 feet, and open camping around the pond in Shellrock Basin. Several parties can spread out through this country without seeing each other.

wa_blackcap_mountain_scramble.notes: From the Robinson Creek trailhead on the Lost River road, climb over Robinson Pass and descend into the Middle Fork Pasayten, joining the standard line up to Freds Lake and over Rolo Pass into Shellrock Basin. It starts much lower than Slate Pass but works when the upper Harts Pass road is not an option, and suits loop trips.

wa_blackcap_mountain_scramble.name: Monument Creek and the Monument-Blackcap basin
wa_blackcap_mountain_scramble.notes: Follow the Monument Creek trail toward Butte Pass, and a few miles short of the pass leave it where Monument Creek bends west into the basin between Monument Peak and Blackcap. The lower basin is slow going, but its upper part is open and pleasant, and the peak is climbed from there.

wa_booker_mountain_northeast_face.name: Head of Park Creek: easier cliffs to the small glacier, then right through the icefall
wa_booker_mountain_northeast_face.notes:
A multi-day backpack toward Park Creek Pass and the head of Park Creek — from the Thunder Creek trail out of Colonial Creek Campground, or as part of a Buckner-area traverse — then camp near the base of the face for an alpine start.

From camp the sequence is: climb easier cliffs to a small glacier at the base of the face, ascend left up that glacier to an icefall, then traverse right through the icefall to reach the main rock wall. The first-ascent party described that crossing as genuinely exposed and frightening.

The face averages about 70 degrees and is over 3,000 ft high, on generally sound Cascade granodiorite and orthogneiss, apart from one band that is not. The first ascent was made in August 1964.

The descent is not the face: from the summit, take the ordinary route down to the Booker-Buckner col and back toward a Park Creek camp — which is what the first-ascent party did, reaching their camp just before dark.
wa_booker_mountain_northeast_face.season: Climbed historically in early-to-mid August; the window is narrow because it depends on a stable, well-bridged icefall and on residual snow and ice in the summit gully
hazards: An icefall traversed on the approach, with crevasse and serac fall the standing hazard and the crossing itself described as frightening
A crumbly red rock stratum crossing the whole face at mid-height, which is where the rockfall comes from
Extreme remoteness — an incident on a 3,000 ft face this rarely climbed would be very hard to get help for
Heavy packs on class 4-5 ground, which the first-ascent account flags as compounding the difficulty
wa_booker_mountain_northeast_face.baseFinding: The sequence is countable from bottom to top and it is the best thing this route has: easier cliffs, then a small glacier, then left up it to an icefall, then right through the icefall to the rock. The direction reverses — left to reach the icefall, right to get through it — and that reversal is what tells you the crossing you are making is the intended one. The rope-up point is a ledge system near the second prominent tree, where the ledge makes its first descent. An oddly specific marker, and a genuinely countable one if the trees are visible. The mid-route confirmation is a colour and it crosses the whole face: a prominent, crumbly red stratum at roughly half height. You cannot go round it — it spans the face — so meeting a red band of bad rock at mid-height is proof you are on the line and not beside it. It is also the crux and the rockfall source, so it is worth expecting. Between those two, follow the prominent central rib essentially straight up. Near the top a 100-ft notch is passed on steep snow or ice through a narrow gully angling across the rib, and then it is easier ground to the summit. And the negative test is the whole peak: Booker's other two routes are walks. If the ground you are on is class 2-3 talus, you are on the Northwest Route or the South Ridge — this is the only technical line on the mountain, and the first ascent said so in as many words.

wa_booker_mountain_northeast_face.name: Park Creek trail from the Stehekin valley

bivy.name: Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail
bivy.notes: The eastern counterpart to Thunder Basin: the last practical night before crossing Park Creek Pass from the Stehekin side, and the staging point for Buckner and Booker approached from the east. The trail above climbs through hanging meadows to the pass with good views of Goode, Buckner and Booker on the way. Coming in from Stehekin turns a very long one-way walk into a shorter approach than the roughly nineteen miles from Colonial Creek, at the cost of a lake crossing and road transport. Which side is faster depends entirely on whether the shuttle is running to the upper valley that season.
bivy.water: Park Creek is immediately adjacent and reliable.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required, covering Lake Chelan National Recreation Area as well as the park proper. Permits for an approach started from Stehekin still come through the same park system. Plan around Lake Chelan boat and shuttle schedules, since a missed connection can put you a day off your permitted itinerary.
bivy.capacity: Creekside stock camp on the Park Creek trail. Small; the neighbouring Two Mile camp downvalley was reduced to a single site by past flooding, so do not count on it as overflow.

wa_booker_mountain_northeast_face.notes: Reach the Stehekin valley by boat and the valley shuttle, or on foot over Cascade Pass, then walk or bike the washed-out upper valley road to the Park Creek trailhead. The Park Creek trail climbs toward Park Creek Pass, and the face sits at the head of the valley below the pass. Much less walking than Thunder Creek once you are in the valley.

wa_boving_christensen.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, then a hundred feet right of the left-flank classic
camps: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
wa_boving_christensen.notes:
The shared Core Enchantments approach: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek and up to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, then the boulder field at the south end and Aasgard Pass — 2,000 ft in 1.25 miles of loose scree, the crux of the walk in, dangerous under snow into early July and avalanche-prone in shoulder season.

From the pass, cross-country north past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn and the base of the south face — roughly 7.5 to 8 miles and 4,600 ft one way, the last stretch unmarked over slabs and talus.

Four pitches, about 450 ft: a short crack and slab to a corner, a long exposed and somewhat dirty face-crack pitch, a corner with a bouldery move, and a finishing fingers-to-hands pitch to the ridge.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose scree with a hidden creek and moat under early-season snow
A long, exposed and dirty second pitch
Natural non-bolted rappel anchors on the north side, periodically rebuilt as old tat accumulates
Unmarked cross-country approach over slabs and talus
Afternoon thunderstorms with a long walk back over the pass
wa_boving_christensen.baseFinding:
Pace it off from the left-flank classic: this route starts about 100 feet to the right of it, on the west side of the south face. That is a measurable distance rather than a description, and it is what makes the start findable — everything else on this end of the face is identified relative to the same outside corner.

So the procedure in poor visibility is two steps. First find the outside corner where the south face turns onto the west side. The classic left-flank line starts just right of that corner. Then walk right roughly a hundred feet along the base. That is where you are.

What tells you you have overshot: keep walking right along the base and the ground under the middle of the face is where the summit route starts, and beyond that the two large V-features of the next line along. Reaching either means you have gone several hundred feet too far.

What tells you you are short: a large roof at the base means you have crossed the corner onto the west face entirely and are two routes left.

First-pitch confirmation: a short crack and slab leading to a corner. It is not a long lead and it is not hard. The long, exposed, somewhat dirty face crack is the second pitch. If your first pitch is long and dirty you have started one pitch too high or on the wrong line.

And the top-out check: this route finishes on the West Ridge, not the summit — the same as its two neighbours on this flank. That shared finish is why they share one rappel descent on the north side.

wa_boving_christensen.name: Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments

bivy.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
bivy.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.
bivy.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
bivy.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

bivy.name: Gnome Tarn
bivy.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. Getting there means leaving the main basin route and scrambling up from around Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass on a faint, easily lost path over granite. It is exposed and high, so a night here can be considerably colder and windier than the lakes below. The camping is on rock, which is both the right surface to use and the reason a level spot takes some hunting.
bivy.water: The tarn itself, though it is small and can drop low or silty late in a dry season; the lakes below are the fallback
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded

wa_boving_christensen.notes: The longer, more gradual way in from Icicle Creek Road: the Snow Lakes trail climbs past Nada and Snow lakes to Lake Vivianne, about ten miles with well over 5,000 ft of gain, looking straight at Prusik's south face. From Vivianne continue past the upper lakes to the base of the face below Prusik Pass. It avoids the loose grind of Aasgard Pass at the cost of roughly two more miles and a thousand more feet.

wa_boving_roofs.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Y-shaped larch at the base of the Southwest Rib, then three pitches up before this route starts
wa_boving_roofs.notes:
Same start as the Southwest Rib: Blue Lake Trailhead, Blue Lake Trail about 1.25 miles to the northwest clearing, then the climber's path up into the basin.

Three pitches at 5.10b as counted here, but understand what the route is: it is pitch 5 of a combined line, about 100 ft of sustained climbing under and through a pair of roofs.
hazards: No ground start; three pitches of another route must be climbed first
A loose block right at the start of the roof pitch
Rappelling back through an overhanging roof is awkward and undocumented, so bailing here means natural gear anchors
No water in the basin
wa_boving_roofs.baseFinding:
This route has no ground start, and that is the most important fact about finding it. You reach it by climbing the first three pitches of the southwest rib, or alternatively by the Northwest Face Boving-Pollock line, and then going left at a ledge where the two roofs come into view.

So the base of the day is the base of the southwest rib, and that has a landmark you can stand under: the Y-shaped larch tree at the base of the southwest rib, left of the southwest couloir. A larch with a forked trunk, at the foot of a rib, with a couloir to its right. That is the aiming point from the basin.

The in-route test is visual and binary: go left at the ledge where the two roofs come into view. Two roofs, stacked. If you can see only one overhang, or none, you have not reached the ledge. If you have climbed more than three pitches of the rib you have gone past it.

A hazard right at the start of the pitch, recorded because it is exactly where a party is committing: there is a loose block right at the start of the roof pitch.

What nobody does here, which answers the obvious question: parties do not reverse this pitch. Rappelling back through an overhanging roof is awkward and is not the documented practice. Most continue up the remaining Southwest Rib pitches to the true summit and take the standard South Arete descent, downclimbing the arete to the rabbit ears then three single-rope 60 m rappels from bolted stations climber's right of the gully, which land at the foot of the South Arete rather than back at the larch.

wa_bread_loaf.name: Silver Falls loop from the Ohanapecosh side
wa_bread_loaf.notes:
This is a single roadside boulder at about 1,900 ft in old forest, not an alpine objective, and the approach is a walk on maintained trail with essentially no gain.

From the Ohanapecosh day-use area, follow the Silver Falls Loop about a mile. The loop can also be picked up from the Grove of the Patriarchs end via the Eastside Trail, which is the alternative when work on the campground side has closed the near entrance — that corridor has been under reconstruction in recent seasons, so check which end of the loop is open rather than assuming either.

The road serving this corner of the park is seasonal: normally open from late spring through fall and gated in winter.

No climbing permit is involved. The park's climbing permit and its blue-bag rules apply to parties travelling on glaciers or above 10,000 ft, which this is not; the park entrance fee still applies.
wa_bread_loaf.season: Roughly late spring through fall, whenever the southeast corner of the park is open to vehicles
hazards: Nothing alpine — the real risks are trail closures and construction in this corner of the park
Landing on forest floor with roots and uneven ground
Seasonal road closure to the southeast entrance in winter
wa_bread_loaf.baseFinding:
The test is that you never leave the trail. The boulder sits a few feet off the Silver Falls Loop, roughly a mile round from the Ohanapecosh day-use area. If you have stepped off maintained tread, started bushwhacking, or gained more than about a hundred feet, you have walked past it — go back rather than searching uphill.

The shape is the name: a low boulder with a loaf-shaped top hold, climbed on its left side. One problem, a couple of moves.

The strongest negative is about the whole outing rather than the last hundred yards, and it is worth stating because this route is filed under the mountain: if you are on snow, on a glacier, or anywhere above a few thousand feet, you are not near this boulder and never will be. It is in low forest in the southeast corner of the park, tens of miles and twelve thousand feet from the summit routes filed beside it.

Water and escape are non-problems here — the loop has running water nearby and you can walk out either way round it. That is the honest description; do not carry mountain planning onto it.

wa_bread_loaf.name: Eastside Trail from the Grove of the Patriarchs lot

approachLogistics.trailhead: Grove of the Patriarchs parking lot (Stevens Canyon Road)

wa_bread_loaf.notes: Park at the Grove of the Patriarchs lot on the Stevens Canyon Road, cross the road to the Eastside Trail and follow it about half a mile to the Silver Falls Trail, then continue south toward the falls; the boulder is a few feet off the trail. This is the way in whenever the campground end of the loop is closed, and during that closure the loop cannot be walked through, so come back the way you went. The Grove itself stays closed behind its damaged bridge, but the lot and the Eastside Trail are open in season.

wa_bryant_peak_southeast_slopes.name: Denny Creek Trail to Hemlock Pass, then the ridge
wa_bryant_peak_southeast_slopes.notes: The standard summer approach. From the Denny Creek trailhead (~2,300 ft), reached from I-90 Exit 47 by Denny Creek Road and FR 5830, follow the Denny Creek Trail #1014 toward Melakwa Lake past waterfalls and up steeper switchbacks to Hemlock Pass, about 4 miles and roughly 2,300 ft of gain. Leave the trail at the pass for the ridge on the right.
wa_bryant_peak_southeast_slopes.season: Late July to September for a dry scramble; earlier the ridge and talus hold snow and an axe is needed
hazards: Loose rock and rockfall on the summit block
Lingering snow on the ridge and talus early in the season
Brush in the notch below the talus once the snow has gone
Exposure on the north side of the summit block
wa_bryant_peak_southeast_slopes.baseFinding: Hemlock Pass is where the trail stops climbing. At its crest, before the trail drops toward Melakwa Lake, turn right onto the ridge and hold a bearing of about 33°, skirting the cliff bands mainly on their left. The check that you are on line is a plateau and meadow on the ridge, then a talus field wrapping most of the peak's base with the summit block above. Negative marker: if you are descending toward a lake, you stayed on the trail past the pass.

wa_bryant_peak_southeast_slopes.name: Alpental, Source Lake and Great Scott Basin to the Bryant-Chair gully
wa_bryant_peak_southeast_slopes.notes: A steeper alternative from the Alpental side, better known as a winter and spring snow climb than as a summer scramble. From the Alpental day-use trailhead at about 3,120 ft, take the Snow Lake Trail #1013 through old avalanche brush and second growth. At roughly 1.8 miles and 720 ft of gain, a boot path splits left (southwest) toward Source Lake while the main trail continues right toward Snow Lake Col. Drop briefly to cross Source Lake's outlet creek — the last dependable water — and follow the use trail along the lake's north and east shore into the open basin below The Tooth and Chair Peak. From there the tread becomes intermittent boot-track over boulders and heather benches, climbing southwest into Great Scott Basin under The Tooth's east face. Contour left (south) beneath the broken cliff bands on Bryant's east side and cross a talus field to the foot of the gully.
wa_bryant_peak_southeast_slopes.season: Roughly July to September once the gully has melted out; earlier the gully holds snow and needs an axe and crampons
hazards: The gully is an active avalanche path in winter and spring; avoid it in unstable snow or soon after a storm
Loose scree, with the centre and left of the gully markedly worse than the right
The gully funnels rockfall from parties above
Lingering early-season snow, requiring axe and crampons
Exposed and loose class 3 on the north side of the summit block when the block is dry
wa_bryant_peak_southeast_slopes.baseFinding:
The thumbtack is the landmark you walk past, and the gully is the one immediately beyond it. Contouring south beneath Bryant's east side you cross a talus field below the rock spire known locally as the Thumbtack. The mouth of the route's gully is at the far side of that talus. Spire behind you, steep scree-and-talus gully splitting the face in front of you.

What the gully is, in other words: this is the same drainage backcountry skiers call the Bryant Couloir or the wonder gully. If your winter partner knows the ski line, they know the route.

The footing test tells you where to be within it: climb favouring the far climbers' right side of the gully, which is noticeably firmer than the loose centre and left. A party grinding up loose ground in the middle is in the correct gully and in the wrong part of it.

Where it delivers you: the gully tops out on the Bryant-Chair connecting ridge, not on a summit. From there you work south over blocky ridge and talus to the base of the summit block. A gully that finishes on a summit is not this one.

And the last step changes character with the snow, which is worth knowing before you commit: with snow on the block the final scramble is easy class 3 with little real exposure. Dry, the only reasonable line goes round the north — climbers' left — side on exposed and distinctly loose class 3. Test every hold.

wa_buck_mountain_south_ridge.name: Trinity to Buck Creek Pass, then the High Pass high route around the west side
camps: Buck Creek Pass and the High Pass camps
wa_buck_mountain_south_ridge.notes:
Start at Trinity at the end of the Chiwawa River Road, FR 62, at about 2,800 ft. Take the Buck Creek trail #1513, which splits off the Chiwawa River trail within the first mile and climbs steadily to Buck Creek Pass — roughly six hours and about 3,100 ft of gain.

Why this way round at all is worth understanding before you commit: Buck sits only about three miles from Trinity as the crow flies and is Class 2-3 from the south-west, but a long rugged ridge runs north and south of it and there is no road or trail up the Napeequa on the west, so the normal route is a very long way round. The two documented ways to reach that west side are the high route north from Buck Creek Pass and Little Giant Pass from the south.

At the pass there is a large established camp with toilets just before the switchbacks up toward Liberty Cap. Fill up with water there — there is none for the next four miles and the ridge walk is fully sun-exposed.

Follow the old High Pass trail as it winds high around the side of Liberty Cap, then south for several miles until the tread dies out in talus and hard snowfields at High Pass; crampons are worth having for that. Contour through the pass and under Mount Berge, then angle up to the ridge crest just south of Point 7839. A short section of Class 3 reaches a faint saddle from which there is an easy walk-off down into Louis Creek Basin.
wa_buck_mountain_south_ridge.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the traverse from the Berge saddle crosses steep heather that is nasty when wet, and holds snow into summer
hazards: No water for four miles beyond Buck Creek Pass on an exposed ridge
Steep heather ledges at the Berge saddle, very sketchy when wet
Waterfall slabs below the traverse line if you lose too much height
Hard snowfields at High Pass wanting crampons
Loose rubbly schist on the summit crest, with a fatal fall on record on this peak
Burn scar on the lower Buck Creek trail — hot, and blowdown
wa_buck_mountain_south_ridge.baseFinding:
The critical instruction on the traverse is about height, and it comes with a stated consequence: from the saddle south of Berge, curving right around the bowl toward the mountain, stay high. Drop too low and you end up in steep waterfall slabs. If you are looking at running water over slabby ground, you have lost too much elevation and should climb back.

The arrival is unmistakable and it is not rock: you reach a beautiful forested bench with larches — good enough that parties note it as a campsite — and cross a river. Once across that river you are at the base of Buck.

Above there the ground is broad pumice, talus and low-angle snowfield up to the south ridge around 7,400 ft, and then rubbly slabby schist along the crest with a short step up to Class 3-4 near a horn close to the top.

Summit warning, and it is a genuine unresolved disagreement rather than a caution: parties do not agree how many summits Buck has or which is highest. One party climbed the middle of the long crest, found the register there, and judged it higher than both the north point and the south by twenty feet or more. Another says the south is the true one. A third found the register — dated 1967 — on the north horn and reported the two tops as roughly equal. Only one of those parties actually measured anything. The summit crest holds several bumps within a few feet of each other, so expect to walk the crest rather than to arrive at an obvious high point, and do not treat a register as proof.

A useful sighting cue from a party approaching by a different line: the summit does not come into view until you reach the flat ground around 8,000 ft, in an upper cirque one climber described as looking like the flying bridge of a boat.

This mountain has killed someone — a climber fell fifty feet scrambling on a route on the east side, direct from Trinity, in 2018. The direct east line involves a river ford and a savage brushy bushwhack and is generally recommended as a descent rather than an ascent.

wa_buck_mountain_south_ridge.name: Little Giant Pass and the Napeequa valley

approachLogistics.trailhead: Little Giant Trailhead (Chiwawa River Road, Trail #1518)

wa_buck_mountain_south_ridge.notes: Ford the Chiwawa River at the Little Giant trailhead, climb steeply over Little Giant Pass and drop into the Napeequa valley. Go upvalley, then leave the trail at Louis Creek and climb its brushy left side past a waterfall into the basin around 6,400 ft on the peak's southwest side. The river ford can be deep and swift in early summer.

wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.name: Snow Lakes trail to Perfection Lake, Prusik Pass and the Druid Plateau
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.notes:
Start at the Snow Lakes trailhead, about four miles up Icicle Creek Road from Leavenworth. Follow Snow Lakes Trail #1553 through burn-scarred forest and switchbacks above Icicle Creek, past Nada and Snow Lakes at roughly six to seven miles, and on into the core basin — Lake Viviane, Leprechaun, Sprite, then Perfection Lake, by which point you have covered ten or eleven miles and about 6,000 ft.

At the north side of Perfection Lake, leave the main trail on the scramblers' path that switchbacks up to Prusik Pass at about 7,460-7,500 ft. That junction is easy to miss and the pass is the last reliable water.

From the pass everything is cross-country. Contour northwest across talus and heather benches at roughly 7,300-7,400 ft, keeping to the west side of the Lorelei Lakelets, then north to a broad rib at about 7,900-8,000 ft. From just below 8,000 ft turn northwest and climb steep talus and scree onto the Druid Plateau at about 8,350 ft.

There are no cairns and no tread above Prusik Pass. Round trip is 30-plus miles with 7,300-plus ft of gain, so essentially everyone camps.
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the cross-country section above Prusik Pass frequently holds snow into July
hazards: No cairns and no tread above Prusik Pass — serious route-finding on talus and heather
Snow frequently lingering on the cross-country section into July
An exposed, holdless friction slab for the final fifteen feet, harder to downclimb than to climb
Verglas on shaded ground into July, adding real exposure to otherwise easy terrain
No bail-out shelter: sun, lightning and afternoon storms on open high ground
Core Zone overnight permits are competitive and effectively required
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.baseFinding:
The summit block is a separate object and the plateau is not the top. This is the failure mode on Cannon: parties gain the Druid Plateau at about 8,350 ft, find themselves on broad high ground, and treat arriving there as arriving. The actual climbing is a distinct block that only comes into view once you are on the plateau, across it to the west.

So the test is: can you see a discrete block of rock standing above the plateau surface? If you are on flat or gently rolling ground with nothing obviously above you, you have not crossed the plateau yet. Cross it and take the western slopes to the foot of the block.

Which side of the block, and this is the part that matters in cloud: the way up is a ramp on the block's south side. It is the last fifteen feet or so to the true summit, low-angle friction slab with almost no positive holds. If you have walked round the block and found only steep unfriendly rock, you are on the wrong aspect — keep going round to the south.

What the right ground feels like: this is a friction problem, not a hold problem. Approach shoes with good rubber, or rock shoes, make a real difference, and the downclimb of the same ramp is the psychological crux of the day for most parties because low-angle slab is harder to read going down.

Staging check below the plateau: from Prusik Pass you should pass the Lorelei Lakelets on their west side and reach a broad rib around 7,900-8,000 ft before turning northwest. If you passed the lakelets on their east, you are drifting toward the wrong drainage.

wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.name: Stuart Lake trailhead and the Cannon Creek basin — the shorter, rougher side
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.notes:
The documented alternative reaches the same staging ground near the Druid Plateau from the north instead, out of the Stuart Lake trailhead: up the Mountaineer Creek valley and then cross-country into the Cannon Creek basin.

This is much shorter than the Snow Lakes walk, and that is the whole of its appeal. It is also markedly rougher: the lower section is brushy and there are cliff bands to negotiate, and there is no trail for any of it.

Cannon has no maintained trail to its summit by any line, so both approaches end in the same cross-country problem. What differs is how much of the day is spent on tread before that starts — nearly all of it on the Snow Lakes side, very little on this one.

No reliable published time or distance exists for this variant and none is given. Treat it as a full day of navigation rather than a walk with a scramble at the end.
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the lower cross-country section is brushy and holds snow later than the trail does
hazards: Brushy lower cross-country with cliff bands to negotiate and no trail
No cairns or tread anywhere on the upper mountain
An exposed holdless friction ramp on the summit block
Snow and verglas on shaded ground into July
No published timing for this variant — plan conservatively
No bail-out shelter on the high ground
wa_cannon_mountain_south_slopes.baseFinding:
Both approaches converge on the Druid Plateau, so the base test is identical and the arrival test is not. Coming from the north you reach the plateau area from the Cannon Creek basin rather than from Prusik Pass, so the Lorelei Lakelets and the broad rib are not on your route and cannot be used to confirm position — do not try to apply the southern approach's landmarks here.

What still holds: the summit block is a distinct object standing above the plateau, reached across the plateau on its western slopes, and the way up it is a low-angle friction ramp on its south side, roughly the last fifteen feet to the true summit. Almost no positive holds. That is the base, and it is the same base for anyone who gets here.

The north-side-specific warning: the ground below the basin has cliff bands in it. Unlike the southern route, where the navigation problem is featureless open talus, here it is possible to be cliffed out and to have to lose height to get round. If you are on steepening ground with the basin still above you, come down and traverse rather than pushing on.

And a route-choice note: the northeast ridge is a separate line on this mountain and is described as an ascent route only, with most parties descending the Prusik Pass side. If you have come up from the north expecting to reverse it, check which line you are actually on before committing to that plan.

wa_castle_peak_pasayten_scramble.name: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek trail and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_scramble.notes:
This is the way in that stays entirely inside the United States, and it is the reason the peak costs three or four days.

From the highway pullout above the dam, a short spur trail drops to the lake shore. Cross the lake by water taxi, or paddle a private or inflatable boat portaged down that spur, and land near the head of the lake where the Lightning Creek trail starts at about 1,500 ft. Parties with their own boat commonly start walking around four in the morning to leave daylight for the day above; the water taxi runs only in the daytime, 8am to 5pm.

After a couple of hours watch for the junction with the old, no-longer-maintained Freezeout Creek trail. The stretch immediately above that junction is the hardest navigation of the entire approach: steep rock and alder slopes that want a rising, diagonal line before you regain forest and real tread. Intermittent orange flagging marks it and is worth hunting for.

Back in the trees the tread improves up to a cabin at about 3,600 ft, sited just after a creek crossing — bunks, a wood stove and a logbook, and a useful emergency shelter. About a quarter mile past it, cross the creek again and pass through an old burn. Tread mostly disappears around 4,200 ft.

The lower part of this corridor is national recreation area and needs a park backcountry permit for camping; above the boundary it is wilderness with a free self-issue permit.
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_scramble.season: Late July through September in a normal year; the creek is hard to ford until the snowmelt drops
hazards: Several similar-looking gullies in the upper basin; the wrong one cliffs out above the creek
The steep rock-and-alder section above the trail junction is the hardest navigation of the approach
Krummholz and vegetation-covered rock on the crux band
Teetering blocks near the summit
Days long enough that parties routinely finish the descent in the dark, with a boat pickup to make
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_scramble.baseFinding:
There is no rock start to find on this route. What you are finding is the right gully out of a basin that offers several, and getting that wrong is how parties get cliffed out.

Above where the tread dies, climb the Freezeout drainage and work up steep heather, talus and scree toward the notch on the ridge at about 7,600 ft. That notch is the target and it is the only feature in the upper basin worth navigating to. Cross to the east side of the creek at roughly 5,000 ft on the way up.

The physical tests on the climb itself are rock quality and terrain grade, in that order. This is granite and the rock is genuinely good — clean, coarse and solid, the sort people compare to the best cragging ranges. It is mostly class 2 with short class 3 steps, and the crux is a steeper band with krummholz and bluffs where you are pulling on vegetation-covered rock. If you are roping up, you are off route.

The negative marker is enormous and unmistakable. This peak's north side is a fourteen-hundred-foot wall of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs holding ice or the remains of it, with a glacier at its foot. If you are looking up at that, you are on the wrong side of the mountain entirely and you are under the technical routes. The scramble never sees the north face.

Mark your exact ascent gully before you leave it, and this is the single most important sentence here. The upper basin holds several gullies and chutes that look alike from above, and dropping into the wrong one on descent risks cliffing out on bluffs well above the creek. Do not improvise a shortcut down. Reverse exactly what you came up.

Near the summit, watch teetering blocks, and expect the final ground to be exposed and windy.

wa_castle_peak_pasayten_scramble.name: The crest trail north from Harts Pass to Castle Pass
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_scramble.notes:
The third way in, and the one that trades a boat for a great deal of walking. The high pass road climbs roughly twenty miles of unpaved single lane from Mazama with pullouts rather than passing room, a rock wall on one side and an unguarded drop on the other, and grades approaching seventeen percent on the upper ramps. Trailers are prohibited and wide vehicles are strongly discouraged. It opens with the snowmelt, typically early to mid July, and closes with the first serious autumn storms.

From the pass, the crest trail runs north through country that starts near 6,200 ft and barely drops below 5,000 ft, over a high pass and on to Castle Pass, where it meets the Boundary Trail running east across the Pasayten and west toward the lake. Camps along the way are open and windy; pitch behind timber rather than in the meadow.

This stays inside the United States throughout, and it needs no boat.
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_scramble.season: Late July through September, once the high road is open and the traverse is clear of snow
hazards: A long unpaved mountain road with 17 percent grades, no passing room and an unguarded drop
The road opens late and closes with the first autumn storms
Very long approach on foot with exposed, windy high camps
The international boundary lies about a mile north of the summit and crossing it here is unlawful
Similar-looking descent gullies that cliff out above the creek
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_scramble.baseFinding:
From Castle Pass the peak lies roughly four miles to the west-northwest, and what you are looking for is the head of the drainage on its southern flank rather than a base of rock.

Drop off the pass into the head of the creek basin on the peak's south side and work up it. The scramble ground is the same ground the eastern approach reaches from the other direction: heather, talus and scree leading to the notch on the ridge at about 7,600 ft, then class 2 granite with short class 3 steps to the summit.

The confirming test is the rock. Once you are on it, the granite is clean, coarse and solid, and the difficulty stays at scrambling grade with one steeper krummholz-and-bluff band as the crux. Roped climbing means you are not on the standard route.

Negative marker, and it is the whole mountain: the north side is a fourteen-hundred-foot granite wall above a glacier. From anywhere on this approach you should be looking at broken scrambling ground, not at a wall. If a wall is above you, you have gone round the mountain.

Second negative marker, and it is a legal one rather than a navigational one. The summit sits about a mile south of the international boundary and the boundary clearing is visible from high on the peak. Do not follow ground north from the summit or from the basin. Crossing on foot away from a port of entry is not a lawful crossing, the corridor is patrolled, and this is the one mistake here that ends with more than a long walk.

On descent, mark your ascent gully. The basin holds several that look alike from above and the wrong one cliffs out.

wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.name: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail to the north-face glacier
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.notes:
This is the approach that stays inside the United States, and it is a multi-day trudge rather than a walk.

From the highway pullout above the dam a short spur trail drops to the lake shore. Cross by water taxi or by a boat you portage down that spur, and land near the head of the lake where the Lightning Creek trail begins. Follow it, then pick up the abandoned and increasingly brushy Freezeout Creek trail, whose worst navigation is the steep rock-and-alder diagonal immediately above the junction — intermittent orange flagging marks it. The cabin at about 3,600 ft is a good waypoint and an emergency shelter; tread mostly dies around 4,200 ft.

The lower corridor is national recreation area and camping there needs a park backcountry permit; the upper part is wilderness with a free self-issue permit.

From the upper basin, cross round to the north side and onto the glacier at the foot of the wall. The glacier itself is mellow and allows easy travel.
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.season: Roughly late June through September, once the approach glacier and moraine are passable
hazards: Several unmarked routes on one fourteen-hundred-foot wall; position under the summit is the only identifier
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the start of the climbing
Rockfall on the lower wall; the first pitch exists mainly to escape the fall line
Dirt and moss-filled cracks through the middle section and teetering blocks near the top
Multi-day approach with no cell coverage and an extremely slow retreat
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.baseFinding:
The north face is a wall of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs about fourteen hundred feet high, holding ice or the remnants of it, with a glacier at its foot. It carries several routes and they are not marked, so identification is by position against the summit and nothing else.

The test is simple and it is the whole identification: this route takes the central buttress, and that buttress sits directly below the summit. Stand back on the glacier, find the summit on the skyline, and drop a plumb line from it. The buttress under that line is this route. If the summit is off to one side from where you are standing, you are under a different climb.

Getting onto it is the second problem. Expect an awkward bergschrund or moat where the glacier meets the rock, and start with easy fifth-class ground whose purpose is to get out of the rockfall line rather than to climb anything — that first pitch is a position move, not a feature.

Confirm on pitch two, because it arrives fast and it is unmistakable: the crux comes almost immediately, mid-fifth-class face climbing hard enough that the first ascent used a short aid move to pass it. A wall this size whose hardest pitch is the second one is unusual, and it is the strongest evidence you are on line.

The middle of the route then traverses out of a dihedral on a tricky flake and takes a roof on the left via cracks and stemming, over slabs that needed heavy cleaning of dirt and moss. After about five pitches the route gains the ridge proper and the rock quality improves markedly, with one short harder hand-and-fist crack. The final technical pitch picks its way around teetering blocks, and then moderate snow slopes run the last four hundred feet to the top.

Negative marker: if your line starts in a blocky set of face holds beside a gully or chimney at the left edge of the buttress, you are on the neighbouring route at the buttress's left margin, and higher up it follows a distinctive yellow quartz dyke that this route does not touch.

Descent is not the climb reversed. Walk off the south side and the east ridge back toward camp.

wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.name: Provincial park approach from the north over Frosty Mountain to Crow Creek

approachLogistics.trailhead: Lightning Lake, E.C. Manning Provincial Park (British Columbia)

wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.notes:
Read the legal point first. This line walks in from the provincial park on the northern side and then crosses the international boundary cross-country. That is not a lawful crossing. Away from a port of entry it requires prior arrangement with the border authority, the corridor is patrolled, and casual parties cannot simply walk over. It is the first-ascent line, not a recommendation.

It starts from the lake in the provincial park, climbs up and over Frosty Mountain, descends into the next creek basin to the south, traverses to the divide, and drops into the Crow Creek drainage below the peak's north face. The first ascent camped on the only dry spot on the ridge, roughly two-thirds of the way down toward the glacier.

The wholly lawful alternatives are the boat crossing and abandoned creek trail from the east, or the crest trail from the west.
hazards: The described approach crosses the international boundary cross-country and is not a lawful crossing
Cross-country travel over a mountain and two drainage divides with one dry camp on the ridge
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the base of the wall
Rockfall on the lower face
Retreat from anywhere on this trip is measured in days
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.baseFinding:
However you reach it, the glacier at the foot of the wall is the same and the identification is the same.

Come down the ridge from camp to the glacier, which is mellow enough to walk. Then stand back far enough to see the whole face at once — this is the step the approach itself makes easy from this side, because you descend toward the wall rather than arriving under it, and a descending approach gives you the one view that settles the route.

From that view, drop a plumb line from the summit. The buttress under it is this route. The face carries several other lines and none is marked; being under the summit is the identification.

Watch for an awkward bergschrund or moat where the glacier meets the rock. The first pitch is easy fifth-class ground taken to escape the rockfall line rather than for the climbing, and the crux arrives at once on pitch two — face climbing hard enough that a short aid move was used on the first ascent.

Negative marker: a start in blocky face holds beside a gully or chimney at the left edge of the buttress is the neighbouring route, which follows a yellow quartz dyke higher up.

Second negative marker, and it applies from the moment you leave camp: the boundary clearing is a visible cut line on this ground and it is not a route. The summit sits about a mile south of it.

Descent is the south side and the east ridge, unroped third and fourth-class ground from the top of the technical climbing, back toward camp.

wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.name: Pacific Crest Trail north from Harts Pass
wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge.notes: Follow the Pacific Crest Trail north from Harts Pass along the crest, about 27 miles to Castle Pass, then go cross-country onto the peak and around to the north side. It needs no boat and stays in the United States, but it is a very long high walk and the Harts Pass road usually opens only in July.

wa_cathedral_peak_last_rites.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 from the Chewuch River road
wa_cathedral_peak_last_rites.notes:
Drive north from Winthrop up the Chewuch River road to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,050 ft. This is the shortest drive of the three ways in and it is paved the whole way.

Walk Andrews Creek trail #504 up the drainage. The lower miles cross an old burn, so there is almost no shade, the tread is overgrown and soaks you after rain, and blowdown is normal. Andrews Creek runs beside the trail for that whole stretch and is reliable water. The trail tops out at Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, where the burn gives way to open parkland.

From the pass continue on the Boundary Trail #533 and drop on the Cathedral Lakes side trail to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft. Bear off near the old wilderness guard-station cabin. Strong parties walk it in one long day with heavy packs; others split it with a camp partway up the drainage.

One thing to leave alone: there is a shorter-looking way in from the Canadian side. Crossing into the United States here is illegal, the border is patrolled, and the penalties are severe.
wa_cathedral_peak_last_rites.season: Roughly mid-July through September, once the trails and the face have shed snow
hazards: No climbers' trail and no marked start; the base is identified by landform and by what is above you
Rockfall from parties above and from loose blocks on the featured lower face
Afternoon storms on a summit that is the local high point
A walk-off descent whose crux is a no-fall step across a gap near the summit
Remote enough that any injury becomes a multi-day evacuation
wa_cathedral_peak_last_rites.baseFinding:
There is no climbers' trail to the base. Cross the parkland and talus from camp toward the deep gully that divides Cathedral Peak from The Monk, the semi-detached tower leaning against the lower right side of the wall. Thirty to sixty minutes from camp.

The first test is the tower, and it is a negative one. This route is on the main wall, not on the tower and not on the buttress behind it. If a separate tower stands between you and the rock you are about to climb, walk further left along the base — you are under the Southeast Buttress. If you are looking up at an open thousand-foot face with nothing standing in front of it, you are in the right place.

Now place yourself across that face. This line takes the right-hand portion of the open wall, between the central line and the line further right. There is no start ledge, no cairn and no fixed gear to find; the ground low down is heavily featured and the first ascent treated it as choose-your-own, so the start is a zone rather than a point. Pick the most featured rock in that right-hand third and go up.

Confirm it above you before you commit, because the low ground will accept almost any line. Look for a long ramp slashing rightward across the middle of the face, and above the ramp a steep, clean crack splitting a headwall. Those two features in that order are this route. If the ramp is not there and instead you find a big curving chimney above you, you have drifted into the centre of the wall and you are on the original central line — several number grades easier, and a different day.

Second negative marker, at the top: this route joins the buttress route for its final hand crack to the summit. Arriving at that shared pitch is correct. Arriving at it early, without having crossed a rightward ramp and pulled a thin headwall, means you traversed off.

wa_cathedral_peak_last_rites.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
wa_cathedral_peak_last_rites.notes:
This is a trail, #510A, not a four-wheel-drive road, despite a persistent claim to the contrary — the high-clearance warning in circulation belongs to a different spur road. Access is from Loomis by Toats Coulee Road, then a Y junction, then the forest roads up to the trailhead at about 5,570 ft.

Be careful with the trailhead name. It appears in print under three or four spellings, and one of those names also belongs to a completely different trailhead near Winthrop. Navigate to the road, not to the name.

The trail descends from its high trailhead to join the valley trail below, and from there it is the valley to the Cathedral Lakes basin. This is the shortest walk and the least climbing of the ways in.

The catch sits at both ends. The drive is about two hours longer than from Winthrop, and because the trailhead is high and the trail drops to meet the valley, you finish the trip with roughly 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out, at the point when you least want it.
hazards: 1,300 ft of climbing at the very end of the trip, on the way out
A trailhead published under several different names
Same lack of any climbers' trail to the base
Beta headed South Face may describe the small tower rather than the mountain
wa_cathedral_peak_last_rites.baseFinding:
The way in changes; the base does not. From Upper Cathedral Lake it is the same walk toward the deep gully dividing Cathedral Peak from The Monk, and the same question at the bottom: is there a tower standing between you and the rock? If yes you are under the buttress, not this face.

What this approach genuinely changes is your first sighting of the wall. Coming up the valley you arrive in the basin from below rather than over the pass, so the whole south side presents itself at once from across the water. Use that. Standing at the lake, pick out three things before you walk up: the tower at the lower right of the wall, the open thousand-foot face left of it, and the long ramp that slashes rightward across the middle of that face. This route is the right-hand third of the open face, working up to that ramp and to the steep crack in the headwall above it.

That identification is far easier from across the lake than from underneath, where the face foreshortens and the ramp disappears into the general featuring. Photograph it or draw it before you leave camp.

Negative marker: if from the lake you cannot see a ramp at all on the face you are looking at, you are looking at the wrong wall. The tower has its own south face with its own short routes on it, and beta written about that tower will also say South Face. The tower is small and stands clear of the mountain; the main face runs the full height of the peak behind it.

wa_cathedral_peak_last_rites.name: Thirtymile Trailhead and the Chewuch River trail toward Remmel Lake

approachLogistics.trailhead: Thirtymile Trailhead (end of the Chewuch River Road)

wa_cathedral_peak_last_rites.notes: Follow the Chewuch River trail north from the Thirtymile Trailhead nearly to Remmel Lake, then climb to the Cathedral Lakes basin. A longer way round than Andrews Creek, used when combining the Remmel Lake country with the climb.

wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 from the Chewuch River road
camps: Cathedral Pass benches and the tarn slabs
wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.notes:
Drive north from Winthrop up the Chewuch River road to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,080 ft, roughly a five-hour drive from Seattle and the shortest drive of the three ways in.

Walk Andrews Creek trail #504 up the drainage. The lower miles pass through an old burn, so there is little shade and the tread can be overgrown and wet after rain, but the creek is beside you and reliable. The trail tops out at Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, where the burn gives way to open parkland.

Continue on the Boundary Trail #533 and drop on the Cathedral Lakes side trail to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft. Published figures for the whole walk from this trailhead are about nineteen miles with 5,550 ft of gain, and everyone splits it over at least two days.

Of the three trailheads this one has the shortest drive and the most walking gain; the Thirtymile trailhead is only about five and a half miles further along the same road, which makes a car shuttle between them easy.

One thing to leave alone: there is a shorter-looking approach from the Canadian side. Crossing into the United States here is illegal, the border is patrolled, and the fines are severe.
wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; snow lingers at Andrews Pass into early July
hazards: No climbers' trail to the base; navigation is off the landform and photographs
Long approach through burn with little shade and overgrown tread
A no-fall step-across or hop on the walk-off descent
Remote enough that a two- to four-day trip is the norm, so a retreat is slow
wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.baseFinding: There is no climbers' trail to the base. A party who got there reported finding none and navigating purely off photographs, so stop looking for tread and navigate by the landform. The landform is the deep gully that separates Cathedral Peak from The Monk, the semi-detached tower on the lower right side of the south face. One published account leaves the maintained trail at the first switchback after Cathedral Pass and heads for the gully from there; others come across the parkland between Upper Cathedral Lake and the pass. Both end up in the same place, thirty to sixty minutes from camp. Go up into the gully — do not stop at its mouth. Three accounts put the start of the first pitch about 150 feet up the Cathedral–Monk gully, on the left wall, which is the Cathedral side. Scramble onto a tall pedestal there; it gives a decent belay stance to start from. Pedestal, left wall, about 150 feet in: that is the whole identification. How to tell this from the South Face routes, and it is a simple physical test: is there a semi-detached tower standing between you and the wall? If yes, you are at the SE Buttress, which follows the ridge behind The Monk on the right-hand edge of the south face. If you are walking up to an open face with nothing in front of it, that is the South Face route, a different and much harder climb. A related trap in the naming rather than on the ground: The Monk has its own south face with its own routes on it. Beta headed South Face may be describing the tower, not the mountain. Coming down, the descent is the walk-off to the west and then south-west back toward Upper Cathedral Lake, and its crux is a gap the route description tells you to hop across. It can be avoided by downclimbing the exposed nose beside it and stepping over — easy when dry, but no-fall ground.

wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee

bivy.name: Upper Cathedral Lake basin
bivy.notes: The working climbers' camp for both the Southeast Buttress and Amphitheater's ridges, sitting directly under the peaks with short walks to either. The basin has taken heavy use for decades and the Forest Service has posted revegetation closures on damaged ground here in the past, so treat the shoreline as off limits and camp on rock or bare dirt well back from the water. Check the posted signs on arrival rather than assuming last year's layout still applies — which sites are open has changed between seasons. Nights are cold and exposed at this elevation even in August.
bivy.water: The most dependable water anywhere on this approach — the lake holds through the season and needs no rationing. The one place on the route where you can plan on filling without checking a report first.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at the Andrews Creek trailhead. No quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day fee to park.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites on slabs and benches back from the water; realistically three or four small parties before it feels crowded, and it does fill on midsummer weekends and during larch season

wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.notes:
This is a trail, #510A, and not a four-wheel-drive road, despite a persistent claim to the contrary — the high-clearance warning in circulation belongs to the Iron Gate spur, a different road. Access is from Loomis by Toats Coulee Road, then a Y junction, then NF-39 and NF-300 to the trailhead at about 5,570 ft.

Be careful with the trailhead name. It appears in print as Cathedral Driveway, Chewuch, and Chewack Driveway, and the Chewuch name also belongs to a completely different trailhead near Winthrop. Navigate to the road, not the name.

The Cathedral Driveway descends from its trailhead to join the Chewuch trail #510 around mile 4.8 at about 4,300 ft, and from there it is the Chewuch valley to the Cathedral Lakes basin. Total is about seventeen and a half miles with roughly 3,700 ft of gain — the shortest walk and the least climbing of the three approaches.

The catch is at both ends. The drive is about two hours longer than from Winthrop, and because the trailhead sits high and the trail drops to meet the Chewuch, you finish the trip with roughly 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out, at the point when you least want it.
hazards: 1,300 ft of climbing at the very end of the trip on the way out
A trailhead with four different published names
Same lack of any climbers' trail to the base
wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.baseFinding:
The approach changes but the base does not. From camp at Upper Cathedral Lake it is the same thirty to sixty minutes: cross toward the deep gully dividing Cathedral Peak from The Monk, go about 150 feet up into the gully, and start on the left wall from a tall pedestal.

What this approach does affect is your first sighting. Coming down the Chewuch you arrive in the basin from below rather than over Andrews Pass, so take the time at the lake to pick out The Monk as a separate tower leaning against the peak's flank before walking up. The tower in front of the wall is the whole discriminator between this route and the South Face, and it is far easier to identify from across the water than from underneath.
