approachLogistics.trailhead: Thirtymile Trailhead (end of the Chewuch River Road)

wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.notes: Follow the Chewuch River trail north from the Thirtymile Trailhead nearly to Remmel Lake, then climb to the Cathedral Lakes basin. A longer way round than Andrews Creek, used when combining the Remmel Lake country with the climb.

wa_cathedral_peak_southwest_route.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 to Upper Cathedral Lake, then the trail toward Cathedral Pass
wa_cathedral_peak_southwest_route.notes:
Drive north from Winthrop up the Chewuch River road to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,050 ft and walk trail #504 up the drainage to Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft. The lower half is an old burn with no shade and brushy tread. From the pass, drop into the next drainage and take the Cathedral Lakes trail up to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft. That is the base camp and it is a full long day of walking, usually two.

One early-season bonus is worth planning around: the chasm that splits the summit rocks is often snow-filled early, which makes the first step-across easy or trivial. Late season means a bare hole and the pure version of the move. It can snow here in any month, so carry layers whatever the forecast says.

The alternatives are the valley trail from the Thirtymile trailhead, gentle but longer, and the Cathedral Driveway trail from the high trailhead above Loomis (not the longer Iron Gate route), which walks least but drives longest and leaves you 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out.
wa_cathedral_peak_southwest_route.season: July to mid-September; the sunny south-west aspect melts out first
hazards: The step-across onto the chockstone is easy climbing over serious exposure and is harder in descent than in ascent
The second step-across never has snow in the hole, whatever the season
Ducks and cairns are the only route markers on the granite section
Loose blocks and sandy slopes that plunge-step well going down and slide going up
This is also the descent for every technical route here, so parties meet it tired and often late in the day
wa_cathedral_peak_southwest_route.baseFinding:
This route has no rock start to find. It begins where you leave the trail, and that spot is defined by the pass, not by a cairn: walk about 0.6 mile of trail from Upper Cathedral Lake toward Cathedral Pass and step off just short of the pass at roughly 7,600 ft. If you have crested the pass and started descending the far side, you have gone too far — turn round.

Above that, the route confirms itself by texture, in a fixed order. First several hundred vertical feet of easy sandy slopes with no rock scrambling at all. Then ducks and cairns over coarse granite blocks and slabs, solid rock, class 2 to 3, with two minor steps that need a hand and one place where a friction push gets you over a block. If you are pulling on anything harder than that, you have wandered off the ducks.

The route then enters a hidden cleft running parallel to and just below the west ridge crest. That cleft is the strongest confirmation on the whole climb, because it cannot be seen from below and you either find yourself in it or you do not.

The last feature is the crux and it is unmistakable: a long chasm cleaving the summit rocks into a north and a south half, with a big chockstone jammed in the slot. Step onto the chockstone and mantle onto the bulge on the far side. The move is easy; the exposure is not, and most parties rig a handline with prusiks for the return. Lower down there is a cannonhole giving an easier alternative to one vertical step.

Negative marker: if at any point you are standing under a thousand-foot wall with a detached tower leaning against its lower right side, you have walked round to the south side of the mountain and you are below the technical routes, not on the walk-up.

wa_cathedral_peak_southwest_route.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
wa_cathedral_peak_southwest_route.notes: From the Cathedral Driveway Trailhead on the Toats Coulee road out of Loomis, the trail drops to join the Chewuch trail and then climbs the valley to the Cathedral Lakes basin. The eastern way in, with less climbing than Andrews Creek.

wa_cathedral_peak_southwest_route.name: Thirtymile Trailhead and the Chewuch River trail toward Remmel Lake

approachLogistics.trailhead: Thirtymile Trailhead (end of the Chewuch River Road)

wa_cathedral_peak_southwest_route.notes: Follow the Chewuch River trail north from the Thirtymile Trailhead nearly to Remmel Lake, then climb to the Cathedral Lakes basin. A longer way round than Andrews Creek, used when combining the Remmel Lake country with the climb.

wa_chikamin_peak_southeast_slopes.name: PCT from Snoqualmie Pass, leaving the trail half a mile short of Chikamin Pass
camps: Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake, PCT beyond Kendall Katwalk
Ridge Lake / Gravel Lake saddle camps
wa_chikamin_peak_southeast_slopes.notes:
From the PCT North trailhead, Trail #2000, off I-90 exit 52, the trail switchbacks through timber and avalanche paths, crosses beneath Kendall Peak, and reaches the Kendall Katwalk around mile 5 at about 5,400 ft — a good checkpoint, though not reliable water late in the season.

Continue north past Ridge Lake at about mile 6.5, which has reliable camping and water, and the Alaska Lake and Joe Lake junctions, then along the rolling rocky PCT beneath Alaska and Huckleberry Mountains to the Huckleberry-Chikamin saddle around mile 10.25. The trail then contours below the Four Brothers and Chikamin's south face, passing the Park Lakes Trail junction.

About 13.5 miles one way to the base of the gullies with roughly 4,600 ft of gain, so most parties camp at Ridge Lake or the pack camp near the turnoff and make it a two or three day trip.
hazards: An unmarked gully turnoff near Chikamin Pass — overshooting puts you in the cliffy Four Brothers
Loose scree and rockfall in the upper gully system
A steep, snow-filled and rubble-choked gully in early season
Short but exposed class 3 moves on the summit horn
A long trail approach with camps well short of the peak
wa_chikamin_peak_southeast_slopes.baseFinding:
The test is to leave the trail before you reach the pass, and that is counter-intuitive enough that it is the whole finding. At roughly mile 13.5 — about half a mile short of Chikamin Pass, near an established pack camp where the trail dips to about 5,500 ft — leave the PCT and climb steep grassy and heather slopes into the gully systems on the south and southeast face.

The negative is explicit and expensive: do not continue to Chikamin Pass before cutting uphill. Doing so puts you in the middle of the Four Brothers, a band of cliffy towers that force technical terrain on a route that is otherwise a scramble. If you are standing at Chikamin Pass, you have overshot the turn.

So use the pack camp as the marker: an established camp on the trail, with the peak's south face above and the pass still ahead of you. Turn uphill there.

What the ground should do, in order: class 2 hiking low on grass and heather, then loose scree and dirt-and-heather slots in the upper gully, sustained class 3 as you gain Chikamin Ridge with some exposure near the crest, and finally a short, well-protected class 3-4 chimney or slot of about 10 ft right below the summit block, with roughly 75 more feet of easy scrambling above it to the top. A 10 ft chimney immediately below the summit horn is the confirming feature.

Snow changes the character of the gully entirely: early in the season it is a steep, rubble-choked chute and an axe is needed.

wa_chikamin_peak_southeast_slopes.name: Mineral Creek and Park Lakes, then the gullies above Glacier Lake

bivy.name: Park Lakes basin
bivy.notes: The standard camp for Chikamin Peak's southeast slopes, and the reason Chikamin is the peak in this group least honestly described as a Snoqualmie Pass objective. Most parties reach it from Mineral Creek on the far eastern side, walking up from a trailhead at around 2,375 ft — an approach that begins nowhere near I-90 exit 52. From the pass it is reachable instead by the PCT north over Chikamin Pass, which is a long day in itself. Upper Park Lake sits at about 4,700 ft in open meadow and rolling ground with roomy sites, and a short side trail drops around 550 ft to Glacier Lake where there are more sites on the north shore among boulders and heather. From the basin the southeast slopes rise directly toward the summit. Note the campfire ban is specific to this basin rather than an elevation rule, and it is enforced — the meadows are fragile and the ground here recovers slowly.
bivy.water: The lakes and the basin outlets run all season. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at whichever trailhead you start from. Campfires are prohibited in the Park Lakes basin outright, and above 5,000 ft generally on this side of the crest. Party size capped at 12. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. The eastern approaches were inside the 2026 wildfire closure area; confirm before driving out.
bivy.capacity: Large established sites among trees and meadow at Upper Park Lake, comfortable for a group; more sites at Glacier Lake below

approachLogistics.trailhead: Mineral Creek Trailhead (Trail #1331, end of FR-46)

wa_chikamin_peak_southeast_slopes.notes:
From the Mineral Creek trailhead, Trail #1331, at the end of FR-46 / Cooper Pass Road at about 2,400 ft, the trail is brushy low down but well trodden. It climbs steadily beside Mineral Creek to Park Lakes at 4.3 to 5.4 miles and about 2,570 ft of gain, and ties into the PCT.

From the PCT / Park Lakes junction, head north toward the Spectacle Point saddle overlooking Spectacle Lake, then drop about a mile to Glacier Lake, a common camp, before climbing the southeast-slope gullies above it.

This is the shortest line in — day-trip feasible for a strong party at roughly 14 to 16.5 miles round trip — but the tread is rougher and there are creek crossings low down.
hazards: Brushy lower trail and creek crossings on the Mineral Creek approach
Loose scree and rockfall in the upper gullies
Exposure near the final ridge crest
Snow-filled gullies in early season
wa_chikamin_peak_southeast_slopes.baseFinding:
From this side the arrival is a lake, not a trail junction: you climb the gullies directly above Glacier Lake. Standing at the lake with the southeast slopes rising in front of you is the arrival, and the lake is a hard landmark that cloud does not remove.

What the ground below the gullies looks like, as confirmation: brooks, waterfalls, tarns, heather benches, sandstone slabs and blocky breccia low down. Running water and heather benches are right for this side; if you are on bare scree from the lake upward, you have started too high.

The two approaches meet on the same upper mountain, so the finding from there is identical: loose scree and dirt-and-heather slots in the upper gully, sustained class 3 to the crest of Chikamin Ridge, and a short well-protected 10 ft class 3-4 chimney below the summit block with about 75 ft of easy scrambling above it.

And the same negative applies once you are on the PCT: do not wander south toward Chikamin Pass looking for a way up. The Four Brothers sit between the pass and the route.

wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.name: Phelps Creek and Spider Gap (standard)
camps: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.notes: From the Phelps Creek Trailhead (~3,500 ft), Trail #1511 climbs the valley about 6.5 miles to Spider Meadows, then into upper Phelps Basin and up the Spider Glacier snowfield to Spider Gap at 7,100 ft. Descend the north side — the steepest 100 vertical feet first, softer snow tends to be climber's-left — then scree and easing snowfield past the Lyman Glacier to Lower Lyman Lake, and back up about 1.8 miles of open meadow to Cloudy Pass at 6,438 ft. This is the line the recorded distance matches.
hazards: Spider Gap is the crux of the approach — a permanent snow/glacier slope that is a straightforward boot-pack in summer but can hold open crevasses and firm icy snow early season. Carry an axe and know how to use it.
A whiteout or an early-morning refreeze moves crampons from optional to necessary.
wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.baseFinding: Cloudy Pass is the staging point, not the base: the climbing starts where the boot path leaves the meadows and gains the southwest ridge, with the summit about 1,500 ft above the pass.

wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.name: Buck Creek Trail from Trinity, over Buck Creek Pass

bivy.name: Lyman Lakes and Cloudy Pass
bivy.notes: This basin is the reason North Star Mountain, Cloudy Peak and Chiwawa Mountain sit in the same zone as Bonanza — it is reachable from both sides and belongs to neither. From the west it is roughly two miles and 1,700 ft above Spider Meadow over Spider Gap, crossing the permanent snowfield below the gap and dropping onto the Lyman Glacier, which puts an ice axe and traction on the packing list even in August. From the east it is a long valley walk up Railroad Creek from Holden, with intermediate camps at Hart Lake and at Rebel Camp about a mile beyond it that break the approach in two. North Star and Cloudy are scrambles off the Cloudy Pass trail from here; Chiwawa is reached by traversing the Lyman Glacier to its east ridge, which is a roped glacier objective rather than a walk. Cloudy Pass itself is scenic and thoroughly exposed to wind and lightning. With the Holden road closed and the Chiwawa road under its own closures, both ends of this corridor have been unreachable at times through 2026.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lakes, the Lyman Glacier outflow and creeks all through the basin
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. Camping and campfires are prohibited within 200 feet of Lyman Lake's shoreline, so pitch back from the water; carry a stove rather than planning on a fire. Reached from the west, no recreation pass is needed at the Phelps Creek trailhead, which the Forest Service lists as a no-fee site; reached from the east it needs the ferry and bus booking instead.
bivy.capacity: Established sites at Lower Lyman Lake, more scattered ground toward the upper lakes, and a small number of exposed camps at Cloudy Pass; a popular corridor, so plan on sharing

approachLogistics.trailhead: Trinity Trailhead (end of Chiwawa River Road)

wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.notes: A longer alternative reaching Cloudy Pass from the Trinity Trailhead by way of Buck Creek Pass. One of the three ways in; it is a multi-day trip rather than a variation on the standard day.

wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.name: Railroad Creek from Holden Village

wa_cloudy_peak_southwest_slopes.notes: Reaches Lower Lyman Lake and Cloudy Pass from Holden Village, which is itself reached by the Lake Chelan boat and a vehicle shuttle. The longest of the three and the one with the most fixed logistics.

wa_copper_peak_south_route.name: Holden Village and the Copper Creek boot trail to the Copper Basin bench
wa_copper_peak_south_route.notes:
There is no drivable trailhead. Ferry from Chelan or Field's Point to Lucerne, shuttle up to Holden Village near 3,300 ft. Both have been closed since the December 2025 flood and landslide.

From the village, walk the old mine road and Railroad Creek Trail about half a mile east to a large tailings pile around 3,320 ft, where the Copper Creek Trail branches off on the far side of the creek. A footbridge is the normal crossing; if it is out this becomes a ford and it runs highest in early season.

Above the tailings the boot trail turns steep at once, climbing about 0.7 mile of open burned hillside — loose footing in standing dead timber, unmaintained, slower than its half-mile suggests — before dropping into the Copper Creek drainage. It then parallels the creek south about three miles to an open bench at roughly 5,600 ft, which is the standard camp. Maps show maintained tread ending near 4,750 ft but the boot path continues; do not read the end of the mapped trail as the end of the path.

From camp, ford Copper Creek to its west side and climb into the upper basin on talus and slabs, following the outlet stream that drains the glacier remnant on the peak's east face.
wa_copper_peak_south_route.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, best in August; the snowfield below the ridge often still wants crampons and an axe into July
hazards: Several notches in the spur ridge, most of them Class 5 from below — picking the wrong one is the route's real crux
Crevasses and rock-margin moats on the diminished glacier remnant, worst late summer
A short exposed Class 4 step below the summit ridge with no fixed protection
Standing dead timber and loose footing in the burn above the tailings pile
Two creek crossings that both run high in early-season melt, one of them dependent on a footbridge that may be out
wa_copper_peak_south_route.baseFinding: The arrival test is a notch, and it is the best negative marker on this peak: several notches cut the spur ridge and most of them are class 5 from below. The one you want is the highest notch you can reach easily, gained by a loose Class 3-4 gully on climber's right — the north side — near the top of the glacier. Picking it is the route. If the notch in front of you needs fifth-class moves to enter, it is the wrong notch and there is a better one further up and right. How you know you are under it: you have crossed the glacier remnant on the east face, roped, and you are near its top. The glacier is a fraction of its mapped size and crevasses are usually minor and walkable around, but the moats along the rock margins are what show themselves late in the summer. The stream is the handrail from camp: leave the trail at the bench, ford to the west side, and follow the outlet stream that drains the glacier. It comes from the thing you are walking to, so in cloud it is a line you can follow uphill without seeing anything. What happens immediately after the notch, so you can confirm you took the right one: turn left and traverse a short, steep snowfield — roughly a hundred feet of exposed side-hilling that usually wants crampons and is worth a belay if the surface has gone hard. Once on the crest, blocky Class 3 leads up the ridge to the summit. Notch, then a hundred feet of side-hill snow, then the crest. If there is no snow traverse beyond the notch, you are in a different one. The last obstacle is one move, not a pitch. A single short, exposed Class 3+ or 4 step sits just below the top, and some parties carry a short handline for one airy notch there — a fixed handline, not a rappel. If you are looking for rappel anchors on this route you will not find any; nothing on it is rappelled. A note on the route's name: the south-east in this route's aspect is the glacier remnant itself, which faces south-east from under the spur ridge on the peak's east side; the finish is on the upper north-east ridge. Navigate by the glacier and the notch, not by the compass point in the name.

wa_copper_peak_south_route.name: Phelps Creek over Spider Gap
wa_copper_peak_south_route.notes: From the Phelps Creek trailhead, walk up through Spider Meadow and the Spider Glacier to Spider Gap, drop past the Lyman Glacier to Lyman Lake, then follow the Railroad Creek trail down the valley to Copper Creek. It avoids the boat and shuttle but is far longer, with a steep snow climb to the gap.

wa_crooked_thumb_peak_south_route.name: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack cable car and Whatcom Pass to Perfect Pass, then over the Challenger Glacier and through West Challenger Notch
camps: Ledge at 7,800 ft on the peak's ridge
West Challenger Notch / Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine camp
wa_crooked_thumb_peak_south_route.notes:
From the Hannegan Trailhead at 3,100 ft at the end of Ruth Creek Road, the Hannegan Pass Trail runs about 4 miles and 2,500 ft to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft, then drops off the north side into the Chilliwack River valley and loses most of the gain again.

The valley traverse passes Copper Creek Camp around mile 9 and U.S. Cabin Camp around mile 12; expect brushy tread near U.S. Cabin and, in blowdown years, real timber. One party logged roughly two hours to move 1.5 miles through fallen trunks beyond the cable-car crossing. The Chilliwack is crossed on a hand-pulled cable car, which is mandatory and somewhat exposed; the river is not reliably fordable.

Beyond it the Brush Creek Trail climbs to Whatcom Pass at 5,206 ft, roughly 17 miles in. From Whatcom Camp, leave trail and traverse below Whatcom Peak's northeast flank on the Whatcom Glacier to Perfect Pass, about 4.5 hours and 1,750 ft. Perfect Pass has reliable running water and is a common high camp. From there rope up, climb the Challenger Glacier to a high bench near 8,100 ft, and descend through West Challenger Notch onto the Crooked Thumb Glacier. Round trip is on the order of 40 miles.
wa_crooked_thumb_peak_south_route.season: Jun-Sep. The Crooked Thumb Glacier itself can be severely crevassed with open moats late in the season
hazards: A mandatory, somewhat exposed hand-pulled cable-car crossing of the Chilliwack River; the river is not reliably fordable
Blowdown on the Chilliwack River Trail, measured at roughly two hours per 1.5 miles in bad years
Crevasses and open moats on the Whatcom, Challenger and Crooked Thumb Glaciers
Loose class 4-5 rock throughout the upper route, described in trip reports as horribly loose
Weathered fixed tat on the north-ridge horn that should not be trusted without backing up
A 40-45 degree snow couloir that wants pickets or flukes when firm
wa_crooked_thumb_peak_south_route.baseFinding:
The route starts at the foot of a snow couloir on the northwest side, and the couloir is the only thing on the peak you can identify in cloud. From the moraine camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier, the line goes up a 40-45 degree northwest-facing snow couloir to the saddle just north of the peak. In fog, do not navigate by the summit; navigate by the fact that you are in a confined snow gully with rock walls on both sides, steepening steadily to about 45 degrees. If the ground opens out and flattens, you are on the glacier, not in the couloir.

Arrival at camp, which is the harder find: the camp is a lateral moraine, i.e. a ridge of rubble sitting on the ice, reached by descending through West Challenger Notch off the Challenger Glacier bench at about 8,100 ft. The notch is the crux of the navigation, not the couloir. You are through it when the ground stops dropping and you are standing on loose rock with ice on both sides.

Confirm on the climb: above the couloir the route works along loose class 4-5 ledges around the north ridge's pinnacles, and the crux is a single roughly 10 ft near-vertical crack, 5.8+ or 5.2 with a point of aid, taken at the top of a headwall. A rock horn draped with old slings sits below those pinnacles. If you have climbed the couloir and are on clean, moderate rock with good stances, you are not on this route; everything here is described as horribly loose.

What going too far looks like: continuing up the Challenger Glacier past the 8,100 ft bench instead of dropping through the notch takes you toward Challenger's own summit rocks, which is a different peak.

wa_crooked_thumb_peak_south_route.name: Big Beaver valley and Wiley Ridge

bivy.name: Crooked Thumb Glacier lateral moraine
bivy.notes: Planned camp and the base for the climb itself, on the narrow lateral moraine at the southern edge of the glacier after crossing the high bench near 8,100 ft and dropping through the West Challenger notch. Fully exposed alpine ground with no shelter and long views out to the volcanoes. The moraine is loose and the glacier below it is heavily crevassed with big moats late in the season — rope up leaving camp, not after.
bivy.water: glacier meltwater
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.capacity: tight — a narrow strip, enough for a small party

bivy.name: Ledge at 7,800 ft on the peak's ridge
bivy.notes: Emergency ledge, not a camp — a small stair-stepped shelf on the descent ridge overlooking the precipitous east face, where a party spent an unplanned full night out. No water, no shelter, cold, and highly exposed. On a peak this far in, a benightment is a realistic outcome rather than a remote one, so it is worth knowing this ledge is there and worth carrying enough to survive it.
bivy.water: none
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.capacity: three at a squeeze

bivy.name: West Challenger Notch / Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine camp

wa_crooked_thumb_peak_south_route.notes: Take the water taxi from Ross Lake Resort to the Big Beaver landing and follow the Big Beaver trail up the valley toward Luna Camp. Leave the trail and climb Wiley Ridge off-trail to the basin on its south side, then continue to the Challenger Arm and cross to West Challenger Notch above the Crooked Thumb Glacier. Expect several days and serious bushwhacking.

wa_direct_north_buttress.name: Hannegan Pass and the Chilliwack River Trail to Bear Creek
camps: Basin below the Bear Mountain saddle
wa_direct_north_buttress.notes:
From the road end at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 climbs to Hannegan Pass near 5,100 ft, then drops off the east side into the Chilliwack valley, bearing right at the park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail. Past a backcountry camp the trail reaches the Chilliwack River crossing, where a hand-pulled cable car carries hikers over in high water (by late July and August the river is often below knee deep and can be forded), then continues down-valley to the Bear Creek confluence, where the maintained trail ends. The camp there has been closed since the 2021 fire.

Ford Bear Creek, climb steep brushy timber east through huckleberry and slide alder into meadows above Ruta Lake, then traverse the divide - loose south-facing slopes below two unnamed points, and a rock rib - to the broad 6,480 ft saddle with running water and heather tent sites. Two days for most parties.
wa_direct_north_buttress.season: Late July through September, for dry rock and a river crossing that is passable
hazards: the Chilliwack River crossing in high water
the Bear Creek ford in snowmelt
steep brushy timber, slide alder, and a loose divide traverse
rockfall and icefall from the glacier remnant in the couloir
a deep moat at the toe of the buttress late in the season
sustained hard climbing days from the nearest road, with a descent onto the other side of the peak
wa_direct_north_buttress.baseFinding:
The Direct starts at the very bottom of the rock, and that is what separates it from the route it shares a camp with. From the saddle you first go down: steep scree trending climber's right, across several minor gullies, to the small glacier remnant filling the couloir below the wall.

The toe of the buttress lies on the right-hand side of that ice, where the rock runs down into the snow. That junction is the start. You should be tying in with the whole buttress rising above you and no snow left to climb.

The negative marker is unambiguous and it is the common mistake: the regular North Buttress walks past this toe and continues up the glacier on the buttress's climber's-left side, then moves onto slabs leading into a corner system well above the bottom of the rock. If you are still walking on snow with the buttress rising to your right, you have walked past the Direct and are heading for the regular start. Turn round and go back to where rock meets ice.

A second check is how soon it gets hard. The Direct gives sustained climbing from low down, with an offwidth, thin cracks and steep crest pitches; the regular line gives a snow climb and slabs first. A long easy start means you are not on the Direct.

Watch the moat at the junction. Where the neve has pulled away from the rock the gap deepens through the season and can be the hardest move of the day before any climbing has started.

wa_direct_north_buttress.name: From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side

bivy.name: Basin below the Bear Mountain saddle
bivy.notes: The launching point for the north side of Bear Mountain, reached by leaving the Chilliwack valley trail and following a lightly marked line up the ridge toward treeline and then over into the basin. It is a long way in — most parties treat it as a second or third night rather than something reachable from the road — and the ground above the trail is faint enough that route-finding matters. The alternative approach from Chilliwack Lake in British Columbia is shorter, but the cross-border stretch can be heavy bushwhacking, so the long trail-based approach from Hannegan Pass is the price of certainty.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and tarns in the basin, reliable in early summer and can fail entirely by late season — carry water up if the year has been dry
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for a cross-country zone rather than a designated camp, arranged at Marblemount. Zones are quota-limited with their own siting rules, so ask for the zone by name rather than assuming a valley camp reservation covers you.
bivy.capacity: Informal boulder-and-heather sites for a small party; no facilities of any kind

approachLogistics.trailhead: Chilliwack Lake road, south end (British Columbia)

wa_direct_north_buttress.notes: A much shorter walk to the same saddle camp exists from the road on the Canadian side, but it crosses the border on foot where there is no port of entry, and follows an unmaintained, heavily overgrown tread after the first stretch. It is the natural choice for parties already north of the border and the awkward one for parties starting south of it.
wa_direct_north_buttress.season: Same window, and only if the border crossing is confirmed lawful
hazards: an international border crossing on foot
overgrown unmaintained tread
the same glacier remnant, moat and rockfall beneath the buttress
a cross-border rescue picture
wa_direct_north_buttress.baseFinding:
Arrival differs, the start does not. From the 6,480 ft saddle drop down steep scree trending climber's right, cross the minor gullies, and reach the glacier remnant under the couloir.

Tie in at the toe of the rock on the right-hand side of the ice, where the buttress runs down into the snow and there is no more snow above you. If you find yourself climbing neve with the buttress on your right, you have passed the Direct's start and are on the regular route's line toward the slabs and corner.

Expect the moat where snow has pulled back from the rock to be the first real obstacle, and expect the climbing to be hard immediately rather than after a snow lead.

wa_dome_peak_dome_glacier.name: Downey Creek Trail #768 and the Bachelor Creek route
wa_dome_peak_dome_glacier.notes:
From the Suiattle River Road, take the Downey Creek Trail on the east bank through old growth — about six and a half miles to the Six Mile campsite at roughly 2,440 ft. The maintained trail effectively ends there.

The Bachelor Creek route continues on the north side of the creek and crosses to the south at about 4,000 ft on a log; some parties cross higher, nearer 4,400. Between roughly 3,800 and 4,400 ft the tread is genuinely overgrown — parties describe swimming through brush without being able to see their feet — but the important point is that the trail IS still there under it, so do not abandon it and start making your own line. At about 4,500 ft an old avalanche swath from 2002 wiped out the trail and this is the hardest stretch to get through.

Above that, cross the pass at about 5,900 ft north-west of Cub Lake and descend to the lake at 5,338 ft, around fourteen miles in. Good camping. A well-established trail then crosses flats and climbs heather beside a cascade to Itswoot Ridge at about 6,200 ft, which is the better-placed camp for summit day. Reported car-to-camp times have been nine to eleven hours; this is a multi-day approach, not a hike-in.
hazards: brush so dense between roughly 3,800 and 4,400 ft that the trail is invisible underfoot
the 2002 avalanche swath at about 4,500 ft where the trail is destroyed
Bachelor Creek crossing on a log
open avalanche paths below Spire Point in early-season snow
crevasses on the Dome Glacier
unmarked cross-country traverse if the cairns are lost
wa_dome_peak_dome_glacier.baseFinding:
From Itswoot Ridge the traverse north-east toward the Dome Glacier goes through a basin that is well marked with cairns and is followable even with reduced visibility — so in cloud, look for cairns rather than trying to hold a bearing. Losing the cairns is the sign you have drifted.

The climbing starts where you rope up at the glacier's edge. The upper Dome Glacier is mellow, so the arrival is undramatic; the feature you are climbing to is the notch or col at 8,560 ft immediately north of the summit block. It is confirmed by what happens on the far side: from the col a snow slope of about three hundred feet and then a rock arete of about five hundred feet lead to the summit at 8,920 ft.

The useful cross-check in poor visibility is that the col also gives onto the Chickamin Glacier beyond — a much larger icefield than the one you came up. So a very big glacier appearing on the far side is correct and not a sign you are in the wrong place; the thing to verify is that the summit block is immediately to your south. If the ground on the far side does not drop away onto a large icefield, you are at a different notch.

wa_dome_peak_dome_glacier.name: Ptarmigan Traverse from Cascade Pass

bivy.name: Dome-Dana col
bivy.notes: A high perch around 7,300 ft used by parties who want to shorten summit day or who are linking the Ptarmigan Traverse. It puts you above the traverse and its route-finding, with the upper Dome Glacier — which parties describe as mellow — immediately above. The trade is no running water and full exposure; the ridge camp lower down is the more common choice, and pushing this high is generally judged not to save enough time to be worth it.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only
bivy.permit: No permit or quota in Glacier Peak Wilderness
bivy.capacity: Small; two parties have camped there at once

approachLogistics.trailhead: Cascade Pass Trailhead (end of Cascade River Road)

wa_dome_peak_dome_glacier.notes: Dome Peak is the far end of the Ptarmigan Traverse, so it is also reached from the Cascade Pass trailhead by travelling the whole traverse south. This is the long way in by a wide margin and is undertaken as part of the traverse rather than as an approach to the peak; parties heading only for Dome use the Downey Creek side.
hazards: multi-day committing traverse with several glacier crossings before Dome is reached
crevasses on the Dome Glacier
wa_dome_peak_dome_glacier.baseFinding: Arriving from the north along the traverse, the reference points are the same: the cairned basin traverse toward the Dome Glacier, and the 8,560 ft col north of the summit block with the Chickamin Glacier beyond it and the summit rock arete immediately to the south.

wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.name: Bean Creek Trail to Earl Pass
camps: Teanaway Community Forest campgrounds — 29 Pines, Teanaway Campground and Indian Camp
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.notes: From the road-end trailhead start north on the Beverly Turnpike Trail #1391, a mellow stretch of old roadbed beside Beverly Creek, and at the signed junction bear right and east onto the Bean Creek Trail; the Turnpike Trail carries straight on up the wrong valley for this peak. The Bean Creek tread climbs through forest into a tight, steep-sided valley, drops to a ford of Bean Creek, then keeps climbing until the forest breaks open into a broad flower meadow with old-growth stands and several informal camping flats. That basin is the last dependable water. At the meadow fork bear right and east rather than left into the upper basin; tread goes intermittent through the upper meadows before switchbacking to a broad saddle on the divide.
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.season: Class 2 on dry ground from July into October, and a popular spring snow climb before that, when an axe and sometimes crampons are wanted on the steep south-facing summit slopes.
hazards: The Bean Creek ford runs cold and pushy in May and June and is the real decision point of the day
Old avalanche debris crosses the trail just above the ford
Sustained loose scree, sand and broken rock on the final ridge, easy to kick down onto a party below
No dependable water above the meadows
Steep, icy south-facing snow on a spring ascent
wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.baseFinding: At the saddle, straight on goes somewhere else and the peak is left and straight up. Above the flower basin the tread goes intermittent through upper meadows and switchbacks to a broad, largely treeless saddle on the divide between the two drainages, around 6,200 ft, with scattered flat tent sites on it. The climbers' track up the peak is obvious underfoot but carries no marker of any kind — no cairn, no post, no blazed tree — so the test is the fork rather than a landmark: carrying straight on to the east takes you toward the far creek and away from the mountain, while the summit line turns left, to the north, and goes straight up the ridge. If you are still among flower meadow and old-growth stands you are in the basin below and have not reached the saddle at all. The upper ridge is roughly 800 vertical feet of unrelenting loose scree, sand and broken rock with the track fading in and out. Accounts disagree about whether there is one false top or several undulating bumps below the summit, so treat any high point with more ridge rising beyond it as another bump rather than the end.

wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.name: Standup Creek trail

bivy.name: Teanaway Community Forest campgrounds — 29 Pines, Teanaway Campground and Indian Camp
bivy.notes: The low-valley drive-in option, on the paved and lower gravel stretches of the Teanaway River Road below the national forest boundary, and the practical answer for a party arriving late from the west side the night before a climb. It is a longer morning drive to the trailheads than the small Forest Service campgrounds higher up — 29 Pines sits at the point where the road turns to dirt, with the Stafford Creek fork about a mile beyond it, Beverly Creek several miles further and the Esmeralda road end roughly ten — but these have far more capacity, they are free, and they do not fill in the same way. The state ownership is the thing to internalise: the boundary between Community Forest rules and national forest rules falls partway up this road, camping law changes at it, and the change is not signed as clearly as it should be. Above the boundary the gravel road washboards badly by August, holds snow into early summer, and was subject to closure orders following the 2025 fire.
bivy.water: No potable water. Bring what you need or filter from the Teanaway River, which runs beside all three and is dependable year round at this elevation — a useful contrast with everything higher in the valley, which is snowmelt-fed and unreliable after July.
bivy.permit: This is state Community Forest land, not national forest, and the rules are genuinely different from the Forest Service ground further up the road. The campgrounds are free but a Discover Pass is required to park. Dispersed camping is prohibited anywhere in the Community Forest — camping is confined to these designated campgrounds, and this is actively enforced, so the roadside pullout habit that works on the national forest above does not work down here. Stays are capped at seven days in any thirty. Rubbish is not collected, so everything packs out, and cutting firewood is not permitted. Fire restrictions arrive early and are strict.
bivy.capacity: Large by the standards of this valley: roughly fifty-nine sites at 29 Pines, about fifty-five at the Teanaway camping area, and eleven plus two group sites at Indian Camp. All first come, first served, no reservations. Equestrian camping is confined to Indian Camp and the Teanaway camping area.

wa_earl_peak_southwest_ridge.notes: From the Standup Creek trailhead, the trail runs up a gentle valley, then steepens through open hillside to the southwest ridge of Earl Peak, where a boot path leads to the summit. Quieter and gentler at first than the Bean Creek side, with the hard climbing saved for the upper slopes.

wa_east_face.name: Downey Creek, Bachelor Creek and Itswoot Ridge
camps: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
wa_east_face.notes: From the Suiattle River Road, follow the Downey Creek trail up the valley, then turn up Bachelor Creek on a faint, brushy path toward Cub Lake and Itswoot Ridge. From the ridge, cross the glaciers east toward the Gunsight Range. Plan on a long two-day approach.

wa_east_face.name: From Stehekin up Agnes and Spruce Creeks
wa_east_face.notes: From High Bridge on the Stehekin Valley Road, follow the Pacific Crest Trail south up Agnes Creek about ten miles to the Spruce Creek confluence, crossing both creeks on logs. Then go cross-country, through dense brush, up toward the Icy-Spruce col for a high camp facing the Gunsights. Reaching Stehekin takes a boat or floatplane, so this is a multi-day trip.

wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.name: North Fork Entiat to the Pyramid Mountain junction, then the basin between Saska and Emerald
camps: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
Fox Camp, North Fork Entiat trail
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.notes:
From the North Fork Entiat River Trailhead near 3,940 ft at the end of FR-5606, take Trail #1437 upstream on a gentle grade — only about 1,300 ft of gain over six miles. The lower miles run through old burn and blowdown, so plan on working over and around deadfall rather than walking clean tread. Grouse Creek has been crossed on a logjam roughly 100 ft upstream of the trail crossing, or on a deteriorating footbridge, depending on the year.

Bear right at the Fern Lake fork and stay on #1437. Around mile 7 the trail swings sharply east and switchbacks half a mile to its end at the Pyramid Mountain Trail junction. In early season the tread gets hard to follow once snow patches start above roughly 4,800 ft.

Leave the maintained trail at the junction and head west; the timber opens into a clearing within about a quarter mile. Fill and treat water there — the valley bottom is the last easy water and there is little of it above.

From the clearing the travel is cross-country: angle west then south-west, contouring below Cardinal Peak's west side toward the basin system south of Emerald. Expect to give back 200-300 ft to skirt cliff bands before regaining the open basin floor around 6,900 ft. A camp flat sits near 7,000-7,100 ft.
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.season: Mid-Jul-Sep for snow-free scrambling; late May and June need an axe and crampons for neve in the summit gullies. October is popular for larch colour and brings short days
hazards: Loose rock and choss in the summit gullies, with several similar-looking gully and bench variations that do not all go
A small summit area with a steeply inclined south slab whose slip line runs down the east face
Lingering snow and possible cornices in the summit gullies through June
A dry approach above the valley bottom, with the last easy water a quarter mile past the trail's end
Unmaintained, log-choked trail sections from past wildfire damage on the lower six miles
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.baseFinding:
The start of the climbing is the upper basin wedged between Saska and Emerald, and the thing that leads you into it is running water. From the 6,900 ft basin, cross a shoulder near 7,100 ft and climb a gully system into that upper basin. The slabby watercourse draining it gives the most continuous line and holds snow well into early summer — so in cloud, follow the drainage uphill rather than picking a gully by eye.

The arrival is a bench at about 7,800 ft beneath the south-east side of the summit ridge. From there several scramble lines look much alike and none is obviously better than the rest. That is the honest state of this route and it is why the rule below is a direction rather than a description.

The rule is: work up and to climbers' right to stay on the standard line. Right, from the bench. If you have drifted left you are on one of the variations that this face is full of, and they do not all go.

What the correct gully does at its top, which is the confirmation: it tops out at a notch in the summit ridge, and from that notch it is only a short Class 2-3 scramble to the top — one described account calls it a very short Class 3 scramble near the top. So the test is proportion: if you have topped out of a gully and there is a great deal of climbing still above you, you are in the wrong gully.

The summit is two points about 100 ft apart and the north one is the true, marginally higher top. The south point is a noticeably steeper inclined slab and a slip off it runs down the east face. The whole summit area is small and drops away within a few paces in most directions, and several nearby lower rock points can be mistaken for the summit — so the exposure, not the difficulty, is what deserves attention at the top.

What this route is not: it is not a ridge climb despite the name. The name describes the ridge and notch it gains relative to Cardinal Peak, which sits just to the south-east. The climbing is a gully and a short scramble.

wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.name: Emerald Park and Milham Pass from Lucerne

bivy.name: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
bivy.notes: The high camp for the crest traverse, about a mile and a half beyond Fox Camp on the Pyramid trail, in the basin that separates Emerald Peak from Saska Peak. This is where a party stages to link Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain in a single push over Milham Pass at about 6,663 ft, which is the classic way to do these four and much the most efficient. From the basin you climb to the upper shelf just below the ridge between Emerald and Saska and pick up the broad gully to the summit. Cardinal is the highest of the group and the furthest, and it is the one that turns a two-day plan into three. The setting is superb and the ground is loose — expect scree and blocky scrambling rather than clean rock, and expect the descents to take longer than the ascents. Season is short at this height in a heavy year, realistically mid-July to early October, and the reason to come late is the larch and the reason not to is the water. Weigh that honestly: an August party that finds the tarns dry has a long, hot walk back down to fix it. Weather moves in from the west with little warning here and the basin is fully exposed.
bivy.water: Snowmelt tarns and rivulets in the basin, and these are the crux of the whole plan. They are dependable in early and mid summer, unreliable by mid-August, and in a dry year they are gone entirely by late August, at which point the nearest certain water is back down at Fox Camp. Do not commit to a high camp here in late season without either confirming water or carrying it up. Milham Pass itself has none.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue, party limit of twelve. Camp on durable ground and well back from the tarns. No campfires — forest-wide restrictions aside, there is no fuel at this elevation and the ground is fragile. Reached only through trails inside the Little Giant Fire closure area (Okanogan-Wenatchee order 06-17-07-2026-40), in effect September 3 through October 31, 2026 unless lifted sooner.
bivy.capacity: A small number of tent-sized spots on benches and moraine in the upper basin; two or three parties at most, and less if you want flat ground

wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.notes: Take the boat up Lake Chelan to Lucerne, follow the Domke Lake trail and fork onto the Emerald Park trail, climbing along Emerald Park Creek to the Emerald Park meadows. Continue about two miles to Milham Pass and drop into the basin between Emerald and Saska, where the ridge begins. It depends on the boat schedule, but it is the natural choice when coming from the Lake Chelan side or linking peaks along the crest.

wa_emerald_peak_west_route.name: North Fork Entiat Trail #1437 to the meadow camp
camps: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
Fox Camp, North Fork Entiat trail
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.notes: Drive the Entiat River Road and then the switchbacking forest-road spur to the North Fork Entiat Trailhead, and follow North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437 up-valley. Almost all of the distance to the peak is on trail. The usual staging point is the trail camp in the meadow below the summit around 6,700 ft, and the climb starts from the tread a short way north of it. A boat-access alternative exists on the far side, reaching the peak from Emerald Park via Trail #1230 out of the lakeshore settlement; it is a genuine second way in, but where that line joins the climbing is unclear, so the base-finding below is written for the trail camp side.
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.season: Mid-July into early October. Snow can hold in the gullies well into the season, and an axe is worth carrying early and mid-season.
hazards: Deep loose scree with a boot path dug into it in places — kicked rock runs straight onto anyone below, so spread out and wear a helmet
Several gullies present themselves and the correct one is hidden until you round a buttress
The whole summit area is small and becomes exposed within a few paces of its centre
The south point is a steeply inclined slab and a slip off it runs down the East Face
Sub-summits nearby are convincing enough that parties have tagged them by mistake
No water once you leave the meadow
wa_emerald_peak_west_route.baseFinding: The small boggy meadow where the trail turns sharply left is the departure. From the meadow camp, follow the tread north until it turns sharply left at a small boggy meadow around 6,900 ft — past that turn the trail carries on around the south shoulder of the neighbouring peak, which is not where you are going. Leave it there and climb north, or slightly east of due north, over open ground almost to the ridge crest between the two peaks. Just before the crest, look for a scree and talus slope leading up and to the right to a notch on the northwest ridge. Take that about halfway, then cut right and south into the adjacent gully, and climb it to the depression between the two summits. Expect to see several gullies on the way in and not the one you want: it stays hidden until you round a buttress, and cairns only start marking the way once you are past that corner. The true summit is the north point, to the left of the depression as you arrive. Do not use a register to settle which point you are on — parties have found none on either.

wa_emerald_peak_west_route.name: Emerald Park trail from Lucerne

bivy.name: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
bivy.notes: The high camp for the crest traverse, about a mile and a half beyond Fox Camp on the Pyramid trail, in the basin that separates Emerald Peak from Saska Peak. This is where a party stages to link Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain in a single push over Milham Pass at about 6,663 ft, which is the classic way to do these four and much the most efficient. The setting is superb and the ground is loose — expect scree and blocky scrambling rather than clean rock, and expect the descents to take longer than the ascents. Weigh that honestly: an August party that finds the tarns dry has a long, hot walk back down to fix it. Weather moves in from the west with little warning here and the basin is fully exposed.

They are dependable in early and mid summer, unreliable by mid-August, and in a dry year they are gone entirely by late August, at which point the nearest certain water is back down at Fox Camp. Do not commit to a high camp here in late season without either confirming water or carrying it up. Milham Pass itself has none.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue, party limit of twelve. Camp on durable ground and well back from the tarns. No campfires — forest-wide restrictions aside, there is no fuel at this elevation and the ground is fragile. The trails in have been closed by the Little Giant Fire closure; check the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest for current closures before you go.
bivy.capacity: A small number of tent-sized spots on benches and moraine in the upper basin; two or three parties at most, and less if you want flat ground

wa_emerald_peak_west_route.notes: Take the boat up Lake Chelan to Lucerne, follow the Domke Lake trail to the Emerald Park trail, and climb up Emerald Park to Milham Pass, which drops into the basin between Emerald and Saska. A boat-dependent alternative to the Entiat side, and the natural choice when coming from Lake Chelan.

wa_energizer_bunny.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, to the left side of the south face
camps: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
wa_energizer_bunny.notes:
The shared Core Enchantments approach: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, the boulder field at the south end, and Aasgard Pass — 2,000 ft of loose scree in 1.25 miles, hazardous under snow into early July.

From the pass, cross-country north past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn, roughly 7.5 to 8 miles and 4,600 ft one way from the trailhead.

Five pitches, about 450 ft: a burly and somewhat dirty roof pitch straight off the deck, an exposed corner to a good ledge, a short aid section through steep ground, a fingery crack between two features, and then the final corner crack shared with the neighbouring line to finish.

Because it joins that neighbour near the top, it shares its descent: a single full-length rappel on the north side and about thirty minutes of scrambling back round to the base.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose scree with a hidden creek and moat under early-season snow
A burly, dirty roof pitch immediately off the ground
A short aid section through steep terrain at mid-height
Shared natural rappel anchors on the north side that have been rebuilt and relocated over the years
Afternoon weather arriving unseen from behind the peak
wa_energizer_bunny.baseFinding:
The roof at ground level is the marker, and it is the only one you need. This route starts underneath a large roof formation at the very base — climbing it is the first pitch, straight off the deck. No other line at this end of the peak starts under a roof. Standing under a big overhang means you are here.

It is on the left side of the south face, just left of Solid Gold. If you have turned the corner onto the west side of the peak, you have gone too far left.

Mid-route confirmation: there is a pair of rock features partway up that the route is named for, with a steep fingery crack running between them. If you never pass between two distinct features, you are not on this line.

And the top: this route joins its neighbour's final corner crack, so the last pitch is shared and the summit is not reached directly — you finish on the West Ridge. That shared finish is also why the rappel descent is the same one.

wa_energizer_bunny.name: Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments

bivy.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
bivy.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.
bivy.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
bivy.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

bivy.name: Gnome Tarn
bivy.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. Getting there means leaving the main basin route and scrambling up from around Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass on a faint, easily lost path over granite. It is exposed and high, so a night here can be considerably colder and windier than the lakes below. The camping is on rock, which is both the right surface to use and the reason a level spot takes some hunting.
bivy.water: The tarn itself, though it is small and can drop low or silty late in a dry season; the lakes below are the fallback
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded

wa_energizer_bunny.notes: The longer, more gradual way in from Icicle Creek Road: the Snow Lakes trail climbs past Nada and Snow lakes to Lake Vivianne, about ten miles with well over 5,000 ft of gain, looking straight at Prusik's south face. From Vivianne continue past the upper lakes to Prusik Pass and round onto the west face. It avoids the loose grind of Aasgard Pass at the cost of roughly two more miles and a thousand more feet.

wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.name: Basalt Ridge crest to Fifth of July Pass
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.notes: This is the shorter alternative to the Entiat River approach. From the Basalt Pass trailhead, climb to the pass — the small stream in the gully below it is the last water, and there is none at all beyond — then follow the ridge north. The trail bypasses the first high point about 300 ft below it, and beyond the trail fork the tread fades into slick pumice. Continue north past the neighbouring tower's saddle, then through a col around 7,480 ft on the next peak's southwest ridge, dropping through a scree gully into the basin west of it. Hop the massive boulders in that basin, cross a small larch meadow, and regain the ridge. The peak can also be reached from the Entiat River side by way of Myrtle Lake, the Larch Lakes and Cow Creek Pass — that is the line the main approach and waypoints describe; the marks below are written for this Basalt Ridge side.
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.season: Mid-July through early October, and popular in early autumn for the larch.
hazards: No water at all beyond the stream in the gully below Basalt Pass
Slick pumice where the ridge trail fades out
A scree gully to descend off the col, and a 500 ft loss into the boulder basin that must be regained
Loose rock and tree debris on the south ridge
The ridge is long, open and fully exposed to afternoon weather
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.baseFinding: A larch forest and then Fifth of July Pass is the gateway to the south ridge. After the boulder basin and the small larch meadow put you back on the ridge, the ground drops gradually and you walk through a larch forest immediately before arriving at Fifth of July Pass — that named saddle is where the south ridge begins, and the larch immediately below it is the confirmation. From the pass the south ridge is straightforward, with tree debris to avoid, and a short traverse along a long, broken ridgetop reaches the high point. The negative marker is the neighbouring tower: Devils Smoke Stack is a separate and harder summit with a sheer north side, climbed by steep gullies on its south with two tall steps of choss, and it lies on the far side of the intervening peak. You cannot arrive at one thinking it is the other without crossing that peak in between — so if the ground ahead rears into a tower with sheer cliffs on its north and no walkable line, you are back at the Smoke Stack rather than on this mountain's long broken crest.

wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.name: Entiat River and Larch Lakes
camps: Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
wa_fifth_of_july_mountain_scramble.notes: From the trailhead at the end of the Entiat River road, follow the Entiat River trail up the valley and climb the side trail to the Larch Lakes meadows. From a camp between the lakes the summit is a modest day out along the ridge. Longer than the Basalt Ridge line, but on maintained trail with water, so it suits multi-day trips and loops.

wa_flora_mountain_southwest_slope.name: Devore Creek Trail from Bird Creek Camp over the Enigma saddle
camps: Purple Point and Harlequin — the landing camps, and the boat that decides the trip
wa_flora_mountain_southwest_slope.notes: Come up the lake by passenger ferry or floatplane, ride the shuttle up the valley road to the bridge, cross it and follow the road past the camp and the airstrip to pick up the river trail. Follow that mostly flat trail southeast to the signed Devore Creek Trail junction, then climb steeply through rock bluffs and open forest into the wilderness and traverse brushy, dry hillside to Bird Creek Camp — the only designated camp in that stretch of trail, sitting about fifty yards before the creek crossing, with room for about three tents and a cook area. From camp the peak is a long day of its own; it does not combine with the neighbouring summit above the same camp, and every account allows a full day for each.
wa_flora_mountain_southwest_slope.season: Midsummer into early autumn, and tied to the boat and shuttle timetable at both ends.
hazards: Off-trail navigation with no tread and no user path through the woods
Two distinct ways to end up in the wrong basin, both described below
A 600 ft descent off the divide into the creek that must be reclimbed on the return
Talus that starts as large solid boulders and degrades into fist- to football-sized rock that moves underfoot
The rock throughout is loose rubbly gneiss on lower-angle slopes
The north side of the true summit is craggy enough to block a traverse to the lower north point
wa_flora_mountain_southwest_slope.baseFinding: Two elevations tell you you are in the wrong place, and both are worth memorising. Leave the trail at about 5,000 ft, cross the creek and bear east-southeast; if you have climbed to 5,200 ft you have gone too far along the trail and risk dropping into the wrong basin when you turn off. Then, if you find yourself heading cross-country into a narrow basin as early as 6,200 ft, you are too far south — contour northward at once, round the corner below the steeper ground, and get into the next basin over. The correct basin leads to a divide at about 7,460 ft on the south ridge of the neighbouring peak, reached up an increasingly steep and unstable talus slope to an obvious saddle on climber's left, the rock starting as large solid boulders and degrading into loose softball- and football-sized stuff. From the divide, descend about 600 ft off its east side toward the creek, contouring around at roughly 6,800 ft to avoid steeper ground, then aim for the high southwest basin, from which a simple talus scramble reaches the top. The true summit is the south end of the massif; the north point is about a hundred feet lower.

wa_flora_mountain_southwest_slope.name: Holden Village over Tenmile Pass
wa_flora_mountain_southwest_slope.notes: From Holden, climb to Tenmile Pass, descend the shoulder into upper Riddle Creek, then traverse northeast into the Castle Creek basin to join the standard line around 6,500 ft. Longer and more involved than Devore Creek; mostly used to combine Flora with Riddle Peak, or by parties exiting to Holden after climbing from Stehekin.

wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.name: White Chuck River and Kennedy Ridge to the 7,200 ft camp

bivy.name: Kennedy Ridge high camp
bivy.notes: Planned camp and the standard high camp for the route, on an open ridge crest of snow and pumice reached by a climbers' path leaving the PCT. Pumice takes stakes poorly — bring something to anchor to snow or rock. Fully open to weather in every direction, with a straight view up at the mountain. Everything above this is snow and glacier, so this is the last comfortable ground.
bivy.water: snowmelt; last running water is the creek crossings on the approach below
bivy.capacity: several parties spread along the ridge crest

bivy.name: Vista-Kennedy saddle
bivy.notes: Planned intermediate camp on the saddle where the route rounds Kennedy Peak and steps onto the Kennedy Glacier. Bivy sites exist here and it is used to shorten summit day, but it puts you above the last easy ground with nothing to hide behind.
bivy.water: snowmelt only
bivy.capacity: a couple of bivy-scale sites

bivy.name: 8,800 ft saddle at the foot of Frostbite Ridge
bivy.notes: Planned high camp and the last dependable bivy before the crater. Rocky ridge ground at the top of the Kennedy Glacier's loose moraine, and it is exposed enough to cost you the night — one party was battered by wind here until dawn and concluded afterwards that a platform cut into the lee snow would have been the right call. Site low and downwind of the crest, not on it.
bivy.water: snowmelt only; a documented trick is bagging snow on sun-warmed rock
bivy.capacity: a small tent or two on rock, better platforms cut into lee snow

bivy.name: Ledge near 9,900 ft below the ridge crux
bivy.notes: Emergency only. A spot has been reported at about this height below the steep sections, and the party who found it said plainly they would not count on it being there. No shelter, extreme exposure, and immediately below the loose rock of the Rabbit Ears where warm dry conditions turn the ground overhead into a rockfall hazard. Use it if you must, never plan on it.
bivy.water: snowmelt only

wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.notes:
The White Chuck River Trail was destroyed by a 2003 flood and has no road or trail access, so this approach is no longer usable; reach Kennedy Ridge from White Pass on the PCT instead. The old line ran from the White Chuck River trailhead at about 2,300 ft. Follow the White Chuck River Trail (FST 643) about six miles to the Kennedy Ridge Trail (FST 639) junction, then Kennedy Ridge Trail about a mile and three quarters to the PCT.

Head north on the PCT past the Glacier Creek crossing, which is your water, to an unmarked climbers' path leaving the trail on Glacier Ridge about two thirds of a mile beyond the creek. That path climbs snow and pumice to the standard high camp near 7,200 ft on the Kennedy Ridge shoulder.
hazards: long-running road access problems on the White Chuck side
unmarked climbers' path leaving the PCT
loose moraine and boulders low on the Kennedy Glacier
very loose rock around the Rabbit Ears, worst in warm dry conditions
crevasses on the Ptarmigan, Vista and Kennedy glaciers
wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.baseFinding:
The high camp at about 7,200 ft on snow and pumice is the staging point, not the route. From there the approach continues across the upper south-west slopes of the Ptarmigan Glacier just below the ridgeline to about 8,000 ft, rounding Kennedy Peak to a saddle at 8,000 ft between the Vista and Kennedy Glaciers, then up the Kennedy Glacier — loose moraine and boulders low down — to a saddle at about 8,800 ft. That saddle is where Frostbite Ridge proper begins, and it is the last bivy site before the crater.

The critical navigation warning is about the Rabbit Ears. They are the route's famous feature, a pair of eroded lava pinnacles, and they are not visible until you are immediately below them, slightly east of the ridge crest. Do not try to navigate toward them from a distance and do not conclude you are off route because you cannot see them — get to the 8,800 ft saddle and follow the crest, and they will appear.

Above the Ears the ridge steepens into alpine ice, reported anywhere from a single short step to a couple of hundred feet, before the crater rim.

wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.name: Suiattle River Road and the PCT via Milk Creek

bivy.name: Kennedy Ridge high camp
bivy.notes: Planned camp and the standard high camp for the route, on an open ridge crest of snow and pumice reached by a climbers' path leaving the PCT. Pumice takes stakes poorly — bring something to anchor to snow or rock. Fully open to weather in every direction, with a straight view up at the mountain. Everything above this is snow and glacier, so this is the last comfortable ground.
bivy.water: snowmelt; last running water is the creek crossings on the approach below
bivy.capacity: several parties spread along the ridge crest

bivy.name: Vista-Kennedy saddle
bivy.notes: Planned intermediate camp on the saddle where the route rounds Kennedy Peak and steps onto the Kennedy Glacier. Bivy sites exist here and it is used to shorten summit day, but it puts you above the last easy ground with nothing to hide behind.
bivy.water: snowmelt only
bivy.capacity: a couple of bivy-scale sites

bivy.name: 8,800 ft saddle at the foot of Frostbite Ridge
bivy.notes: Planned high camp and the last dependable bivy before the crater. Rocky ridge ground at the top of the Kennedy Glacier's loose moraine, and it is exposed enough to cost you the night — one party was battered by wind here until dawn and concluded afterwards that a platform cut into the lee snow would have been the right call. Site low and downwind of the crest, not on it.
