bivy.capacity: a small tent or two on rock, better platforms cut into lee snow

bivy.name: Ledge near 9,900 ft below the ridge crux
bivy.notes: Emergency only. A spot has been reported at about this height below the steep sections, and the party who found it said plainly they would not count on it being there. No shelter, extreme exposure, and immediately below the loose rock of the Rabbit Ears where warm dry conditions turn the ground overhead into a rockfall hazard. Use it if you must, never plan on it.
bivy.water: snowmelt only

wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.notes:
Drive the Suiattle River Road (FR 26) from Darrington to its end at Sulphur Creek Campground. Follow the Suiattle River trail about seven miles to the bridge over the river, then the PCT southbound about nine miles to a camp in the East Fork Milk Creek basin at about 5,600 ft. From there continue up the ridge on snow and pumice to the same standard high camp near 7,200 ft.

The Suiattle River Road has a long history of flood damage and multi-year closures, so its status is worth confirming rather than assuming.
hazards: repeated flood damage and long closures on the Suiattle River Road
very long PCT approach day
same upper-mountain hazards as the Kennedy Ridge variation
wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.baseFinding: Identical above the 7,200 ft camp: traverse the upper south-west Ptarmigan slopes to about 8,000 ft, round Kennedy Peak to the 8,000 ft saddle between the Vista and Kennedy glaciers, up the Kennedy to the 8,800 ft saddle where the ridge begins. Remember that the Rabbit Ears stay hidden until you are directly beneath them slightly east of the crest.

wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.name: North Fork Sauk to White Pass, then north
camps: 8,800 ft saddle at the foot of Frostbite Ridge
Ledge near 9,900 ft below the ridge crux
wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.notes: Some parties use the North Fork Sauk trail to White Pass — about nine miles and 5,900 ft — and then make a long traverse north on or near the PCT to the same Kennedy Ridge camp area. It is a twenty-mile-plus approach day and is chosen when the other two roads are out.
hazards: twenty-mile-plus approach day
same upper-mountain hazards as the other variations
wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.baseFinding: Same as the other variations: the 8,800 ft saddle above the Kennedy Glacier is where the ridge starts, and the Rabbit Ears do not become visible until you are immediately below them.

wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.name: White Chuck River and Kennedy Ridge to the Glacier Creek camps

bivy.name: Kennedy Ridge and the Glacier Creek camps, Suiattle side
bivy.notes: This is the base for Glacier Peak's Kennedy Glacier and for the Frostbite Ridge line above it, and it is also reached from the Suiattle side. The walk in from there is long even when the road is open — the Suiattle River trail runs about seven miles to the river bridge and the crest trail then carries you south toward Kennedy Ridge, so this is a full day before the climbing camp is even in sight. Kennedy Creek has no bridge and will not get one; the standard tactic is to camp short of it and cross in the morning when the flow is at its lowest, using whatever logs are in place rather than wading the main channel. Above the forest the route climbs the ridge and the glacier toward the saddle between the Kennedy and Vista glaciers at around 8,000 feet, where bivouac sites exist for parties willing to sleep on snow and rock with no shelter and no clean water. With the road washed out the trailhead is normally reachable on foot or by bike from the closure point, which adds roughly eighteen miles each way to an approach that was already the longest on the mountain, and a fire closure has also shut the upper Suiattle River Road, the Suiattle River Trail and the PCT from Mica Lake north; check with the Darrington Ranger District before planning this way in.
bivy.water: Glacier Creek and Kennedy Creek are both right there and both silty with glacial flour — let it settle or filter accordingly. Higher on the ridge water disappears entirely by late season and has to be carried or melted.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Suiattle road end. Stove only above the forest. Check the road order before driving: the Suiattle River road washed out about four and a half miles in during the December 2025 storms and is closed to vehicles at that point under a closure order that runs into 2028 unless lifted sooner, with the campgrounds and trailheads up the road closed.
bivy.capacity: Forested sites in ones and twos scattered along the crest trail near the creek crossings, plus rougher bivouac ground higher on the ridge; nothing organised, and no single site takes a large party

wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.notes:
The historic line starts at the White Chuck River Trailhead at the end of FR-23 and follows Trail #643 about four miles, then Kennedy Ridge Trail #639 for 1.7 miles to the Pacific Crest Trail near 5,000 ft. Turn north on the PCT and follow it about two miles to the Glacier Creek crossing, where there are established camps with reliable water near 5,300 ft. Four to five hours is the usual pack-in.

FR-23 has been closed from milepost 3.7 to its end, so the reliably open option in recent seasons has been the North Fork Sauk Trail and the PCT over Red Pass to the same Glacier Creek camps. That is a much longer walk to the same place, and it changes nothing above camp.

From the Glacier Creek camp a climbers' trail runs up a gully to the crest of Kennedy Ridge. Everything above is glacier, and the character of the day is set by how well you read the upper glacier rather than by any technical difficulty — the headwall at the top is about 40 degrees and short, while the crevasse field below it is the part parties spend hours on.
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.season: Roughly Jun-Aug, and it is one of the shorter windows on the mountain — the upper Kennedy is a small, steep glacier that opens into a maze of 5-15 ft crevasses as the season runs on
hazards: An upper glacier described by parties as a maze of 5-15 ft crevasses that needs deliberate, slow routefinding
Seracs on climber's left beneath the Kennedy Peak wall, where some parties have had to belay off bare glacier ice
Trading crevasse navigation for rockfall by hugging the left wall — the simplification is real and so is the cost
A bergschrund at the head of the glacier whose only crossing may be a single bridge found from the snow dome above it
8,200 ft of gain from a trailhead served by a road that has been closed at milepost 3.7, so the walk in may be far longer than the mileage
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.baseFinding:
The start of the climb is below you, not above you, and that is the whole test. From the Glacier Creek camp the climbers' trail climbs a gully to the crest of Kennedy Ridge — and then you go down off the far side, to climber's right, to the foot of the Kennedy Glacier. A party that tops the ridge and keeps climbing has left the route. If you have not lost height since the ridge crest, you have not reached the base.

Arrival: the foot of the glacier, where ridge ground runs out into ice. Rope up there. On the lower glacier keep right; on the upper glacier take the centre. That right-then-centre sequence is worth memorising before you leave camp, because the upper Kennedy is a maze and there is nothing to sight on inside it.

The discriminator against Frostbite Ridge, which shares this mountain flank and this camp: Frostbite rounds Kennedy Peak to the saddle between the Vista and Kennedy glaciers at about 8,000 ft, climbs the Kennedy to a saddle at about 8,800 ft, and then leaves the ice for the ridge. This route never leaves the ice. If you are standing on a saddle looking for a rock crest to follow, you are on Frostbite. If you are still roped on glacier at 9,500 ft heading for a bergschrund, you are on this one.

The top end, and it is a real decision point: the bergschrund sits at the head of the glacier. Reach it by climbing left to the top of a snow dome and looking for a bridge from there — do not walk the schrund's length hunting for a gap at its lowest point. Above it the headwall runs about 40 degrees; stay left of, but close to, the prominent rock outcrops, and that puts you on the crater rim.

What hugging the left wall costs: parties commonly move under the Kennedy Peak wall on climber's left to simplify the crevasse problem. It works, and it buys the simplification with rockfall and serac exposure. That is a trade to make deliberately, not one to drift into.

wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.name: North Fork Sauk and the crest trail north
camps: Kennedy Ridge and the Glacier Creek camps, Suiattle side
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.notes: Walk the North Fork Sauk trail up the valley and climb to the crest trail near White Pass, then follow it north past Red Pass, across the White Chuck basin and on toward Kennedy Creek, descending to the bench below the glacier. Long, with real elevation loss on the way, but this is how most parties now reach the Kennedy side.

wa_golden_age.name: Up the gully to its own ledge
wa_golden_age.notes: From the pullout near milepost 166, hike the gully below the wall for about an hour and follow a narrow ledge back right to the start, a prominent left-arching wide corner. The direct way, and the most practical when the gully is in shape.

wa_golden_age.name: Via the centre route's lower pitches
wa_golden_age.notes: You can scramble on up the gully to this climb's own ledge, but many parties add pitches instead: do the usual gully approach from the pullout near milepost 166 to the wall's upper ledge, then climb the lower pitches of the centre eleven-pitch line to the shared midway ledge system and traverse left from there. Rack for the pitches you are climbing to get there as well as for this route.
wa_golden_age.season: Summer, once the wall has dried; the pitches used to reach it are the same ones that seep into early summer in wet years.
hazards: From the lower pitches, a retreat means reversing or rappelling somebody else's route
Loose and deteriorating rock on the lowest pitches and again high on the line
Belays are bolted but not all of them are rigged for rappel, so find the rappel stations before you need them
Everything below you is occupied ground; manage rockfall onto parties on the route you climbed in on
wa_golden_age.baseFinding: You are looking for a two-bolt anchor sitting on the midway ledge, and the trees are what place it: the anchor is on the ledge below a stand of trees, not level with them and not above them. Traverse left along the ledge until the trees are above you and the two bolts are at your feet. Confirm it from the rock: the first pitch off this anchor is a technical corner with loose chockstones at its hardest moves, so if what rises from your anchor is a clean face or a slab you are at the wrong station. Negative markers: if the anchor you have clipped is one of the bolted rappel stations belonging to the route you just climbed, you have not traversed at all; if the trees are still off to your left, you have not traversed far enough.

wa_golden_age.name: Via the right-hand cave route's lower pitches
wa_golden_age.notes: The same idea from the other side: climb the lower pitches of the right-hand cave line off the upper ledge to reach the shared midway ledge system, then traverse left. This is the longer leftward traverse of the two, so allow for it.
wa_golden_age.season: Summer, once the wall has dried.
hazards: From the lower pitches, escape means rappelling a neighbouring line
Loose and deteriorating rock low and high on the route
Not all belays are rappel-rigged, so plan the descent before you leave the ledge
Long leftward traverse on a ledge with loose material on it
wa_golden_age.baseFinding: From the midway ledge, traverse left — further than from the centre line — until you find the two-bolt anchor set on the ledge directly below a stand of trees. The trees are the test: below them, not beside them. The first pitch above the anchor is a technical corner holding loose chockstones at the crux, which distinguishes it from the clean faces either side. Negative markers: if you are still passing bolted rappel stations that belong to the route you climbed up, keep traversing; if you have reached ground where the ledge system ends and the wall closes down, you have gone past it.

wa_gunrunner.name: Downey Creek, Bachelor Creek and Itswoot Ridge
camps: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
wa_gunrunner.notes: From the Downey Creek trailhead follow the trail to the Bachelor Creek crossing, then the climbers' path to Cub Lake and Itswoot Ridge. Rope up for the Dome Glacier to the high bivouacs that put the Gunsight peaks within reach.

wa_gunrunner.name: Stehekin, Agnes Creek and the Blue Glacier
wa_gunrunner.notes: Boat to Stehekin and the shuttle to High Bridge, then about ten miles south on the Agnes Creek trail. Cross Agnes Creek on a log and bushwhack roughly 5,000 ft up into the Blue Glacier basin on the east side of the peaks. It is a two-day approach.

wa_gunsight_peak_standard.name: Chickamin Glacier to the snow finger between the main and south spires
camps: Chikamin Glacier bench below the west face
wa_gunsight_peak_standard.notes: From the Chikamin-Dome col, a descending traverse of roughly ninety minutes drops onto the Chickamin Glacier and reaches a snow dome and rock outcrop at about 7,000 ft, closely below the peak; many parties move camp here or day-climb from the col. From that outcrop, boot up to the snow finger running between the main spire and the south spire. On the snow approach, take the first col south of the south peak — the long-standing published advice to use the second col south of it has been corrected by parties who followed it, and the first is the right one. Descent reverses the line by rappel: from the top of the chimney, traverse to the notch, downclimb to a second station, rappel to the ledge above the glacier, then one more onto the snow.
hazards: Crevasse hazard on the Dome and Chickamin Glaciers — rope, and crevasse rescue gear
Loose rock in the basalt dike section
Wild exposure on the narrow summit ridge
A summit horn only one party member can stand on at a time
wa_gunsight_peak_standard.baseFinding: A reddish-black basalt dike is the line, and it is softer than everything around it. From the 7,000 ft snow dome and rock outcrop, boot up the snow finger between the main and south spires; from a breach in that finger, a short wall leads to a broad ledge, then leftward to a steep dihedral of black rock whose top fifteen feet is the exposed 5.6 crux on solid granite. Above it, traverse left on Class 3 granite into a distinctive dike of reddish-black basalt — this is the feature that carved the gunsight notch in the first place, eroding faster than the granite either side, so if the rock you are on is the same colour as its neighbours you are not in the dike. It scrambles easily, if loosely, to the high notch between the main and north spires. There a vertical headwall blocks a direct exit: descend about twenty feet and traverse right across steep, solid, well-broken rock into a shallow parallel gully. Short chimneys and cracks to 5.5 end at the crest beside a large horn slung with old rappel tat — that horn is not the summit; the summit is a separate horn about the size of a barstool further along the ridge.

wa_gunsight_peak_standard.name: Stehekin, Agnes Creek and Spruce Creek

bivy.name: Chikamin Glacier bench below the west face
bivy.notes: Planned advanced camp, about ninety minutes of descending traverse below the col and directly under Gunsight's west face. Parties move here to shorten summit day rather than day-climbing from the col. It is a glacier bench: rope up moving to and from it, site the tent clear of the fall line off the face, and expect a cold, fully exposed pitch.
bivy.water: snowmelt only
bivy.capacity: small — a snow dome and rock outcrop, a tent or two

wa_gunsight_peak_standard.notes: Take the boat to Stehekin and the shuttle to High Bridge, then hike south on the Pacific Crest Trail up Agnes Creek about ten miles to the Spruce Creek confluence. Cross Agnes Creek and Spruce Creek on logs and scramble northwest to a high camp near Icy-Spruce Creek pass, then cross onto the Chickamin Glacier for the standard line. Expect a long off-trail day with real bushwhacking.

wa_hagan_mountain_south.name: Bacon-Hagan saddle and the southwest couloir

bivy.name: Hidden Lake, below the Blum-Hagan divide
bivy.notes: A small lake in the saddle country between Hagan and Bacon, reached from the Blum Lakes by crossing the ridge southeast of them and dropping to it. It matters here as the reliable water on Hagan's far side and as the standard second night for parties traversing east. It is a considerable drop below the Hagan bench, so it is a poor choice if Hagan is your only objective — you give back four hundred feet you will re-climb in the morning. Reaching it involves snow into midsummer and steep heather afterwards. Do not treat this as an approach camp for Bacon Peak from the Baker River side; the practical way to Bacon is from a different road entirely.
bivy.water: The lake. Treat it. Reliable all season, which is not true of the benches above
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit. This lake sits toward the Bacon Peak side of the divide, so check which cross-country zone the ranger writes your permit for. No fires, six-person limit, camp a hundred feet back from the water
bivy.capacity: Two or three tents on the flats near the shore

wa_hagan_mountain_south.notes: This is the line used by parties arriving on the traverse from the Watson and Bacon side: descend north off the glacier and past several tarns, then follow a heathered ridge to the saddle between Hagan Mountain and Bacon Peak, where a small tarn sits with reliable water. From the tarn, bushwhack north up steep forest, working through two distinct rock cliffbands — the sustained route-finding crux of the whole approach — picking brushy ramps and weaknesses through each band to keep the ground climbable. Above them the timber breaks out onto open heather and grass on Hagan's south flank around 6,000 to 6,400 ft, with seasonal snowmelt water and rough camps. Mark your line through the cliffbands with photos, cairns or a track before going higher: the weaknesses you threaded are hard to spot from above, and the descent is consistently slower and more error-prone than the climb.
hazards: Two cliffbands in steep timber with no marked line through them
Loose rock the whole length of the scree-and-talus couloir — helmets, and a tight party
Crevasses and moats on the Hagan Glacier ice apron even in summer
The descent reverses ground that reads very differently from above
wa_hagan_mountain_south.baseFinding: A broad scree-and-talus couloir, topping out at a col at the southwest end of the crags. From the open heather and grass benches on Hagan's south flank, one broad couloir of loose scree and talus leads up to a col near the southwest end of the line of Hagan summit crags, around 7,000 ft. That col is the base of the climbing, and the slabs above it on the south side go at Class 3 to the top. Hagan is a massif of several crags rather than a single peak, so which col you reach matters: if the notch you have gained sits in the middle of the crags with towers rising on both sides of you, it is not this one — keep working to the southwest end of the line. Note carefully where the couloir meets the heather benches before you leave them, because it is also the way down and it is far harder to identify from above.

wa_hagan_mountain_south.name: Lower Blum Lake and the 6,831 ft pass
camps: Hidden Lake, below the Blum-Hagan divide
Sulphide Camp, end of the Baker River trail
wa_hagan_mountain_south.notes: The approach from the north, out of the Blum Lakes basin rather than off the Bacon side. From lower Blum Lake, traverse south and rope up for glacier travel to a pass at 6,831 ft that sits between the south and middle Hagan peaks. This is glacier ground and the rope goes on before the traverse, not at the pass. Parties reaching the Blum Lakes come up the climbers' path off the Baker River Trail near Blum Creek, a faint path in brush marked with flagging tape that climbs the ridge to about 4,000 ft before veering south and traversing toward the lakes.
hazards: Glacier travel with crevasse hazard between lower Blum Lake and the pass
The Blum climbers' path is faint, brushy and marked only with flagging tape
Loose rock and exposure on the spur and summit ridge above the notch
Several named crags on one massif — easy to commit to the wrong summit
wa_hagan_mountain_south.baseFinding: The pass sits between the south and middle peaks, and it is the south peak you climb. Arriving at 6,831 ft, you should have a summit on either hand: this is a pass between two of Hagan's own peaks, not a col on the outside of the massif, and if only one side of you rises to rock you are in the wrong gap. The climbing then goes up the south peak's north side to a notch on its upper east side — that notch is high on the peak, not at the pass, and it is on the east flank, so a notch you can walk into from the west is the wrong one. From the notch, traverse onto the south face and gain the summit ridge, work up a spur on the east, then bear around to the south, where slabs lead to the summit at Class 3. The finish is south-facing slab, not a gully: if you are grovelling up a loose gully at the top you have missed the traverse around to the south side.

wa_hozomeen_mountain_northeast_buttress.name: The long way: the ridge trail from the north to a camp near the boundary high point
wa_hozomeen_mountain_northeast_buttress.notes:
There is no road to this peak from the south. From the highway on the north side of the boundary, follow the valley road south on gravel through the provincial park to the trailhead - a slow drive of well over an hour. Confirm the boundary gate's status before planning: the crossing at Hozomeen has been closed to both vehicle and foot traffic.

From the trailhead, climb roughly four thousand feet on trail to the ridge junction, then turn south along the ridge over rolling ground to a camp near the boundary high point at about 6,345 ft. Take water from the three creeks in the forest below the ridge, because there is none again until you are well south of the boundary.
wa_hozomeen_mountain_northeast_buttress.season: July through September; the gravel road governs the season at its own end
hazards: a boundary crossing that has been closed to vehicles and to walkers
a long gravel drive with no services
no water south of the creeks below the ridge junction
an exposed ridge camp
a 545 ft descent from camp that must be re-climbed at the end of the day
loose rock on the buttress
wa_hozomeen_mountain_northeast_buttress.baseFinding:
From camp the route starts by losing height - about 545 ft down to the 5,800 ft saddle at the head of the north cirque. Any line that climbs from the camp is the wrong way. The saddle is the low point at the head of a bowl, with the cirque falling away in front of you and the buttress rising on its far side.

Recognise the cirque by its shape: it is an enclosed bowl beneath the north side of the peak, not an open flank. If the ground ahead of you drops away into a valley rather than into a bowl with walls around it, you have gone off the ridge too early or too late.

The buttress is on the north-east side, so from the saddle it should stand between you and the sun in the middle of the day rather than in it. A wall you approach in full afternoon sun is on the wrong aspect.

Check the peak: this is the north summit, the higher and broader of the two. The other main summit should lie to the south, connected by a rotten ridge that is not a usable link between them.

Water is the other fixed point. The last of it is the creeks in the forest below the ridge junction, well before camp. If you have passed those without filling, the correct move is to go back for water rather than to press on to a dry camp above a dry cirque.

wa_hozomeen_mountain_northeast_buttress.name: The short way: the border swath from the ranger station

approachLogistics.trailhead: Hozomeen ranger station and campground (head of Ross Lake)

wa_hozomeen_mountain_northeast_buttress.notes: A much shorter start leaves from the ranger station at the head of the lake, follows the short interpretive loop, and then bushwhacks east up the overgrown boundary swath, past a swamp, gaining about three thousand feet to a col near 6,300 ft where it joins the ridge. It saves miles and costs hours - the swath is overgrown rather than cleared, and the ground is steep and brushy. Reaching the ranger station itself means either the water taxi up the lake or the gated road from the north.
wa_hozomeen_mountain_northeast_buttress.season: July through September, and slower than its distance suggests
hazards: an overgrown boundary swath that is steep, brushy and slow
a swamp low on the line
three thousand feet of unrelenting bushwhacking with no tread
no water on the upper half
reaching the ranger station depends on a boat schedule or a closed border gate
wa_hozomeen_mountain_northeast_buttress.baseFinding:
The swath is the handrail - it is a cleared line through forest that runs east, and if you are not on it you are not on the approach. It is overgrown, so it looks like brush rather than like a corridor from inside it; the tell is that it is straight, and it does not wander with the terrain the way a game trail does.

A swamp is passed low down. Reaching it confirms the line; never reaching it means you have drifted off the swath into ordinary forest.

The join is a col near 6,300 ft, roughly three thousand feet above the start, where the swath's climbing ends against the ridge. From there the route is the same as the long approach: work along to the saddle at the head of the north cirque near 5,800 ft, which means losing height again, and the buttress stands on the far side of the bowl.

If you arrive on a ridge and the ground beyond is an open valley rather than an enclosed bowl, you are at the wrong col. The cirque is walled; the valley is not.

wa_jack_mountain_nohokomeen_headwall.name: East Bank Trail on foot from milepost 138, leaving it at May Creek
camps: High camp below the Nohokomeen Glacier
wa_jack_mountain_nohokomeen_headwall.notes: Park at the East Bank Trailhead near milepost 138 at about 1,800 ft. The trail drops immediately to the bridge over Ruby Creek and then runs north along Ross Lake, mostly flat and fast, to the May Creek camp. This is the whole of the easy walking. At May Creek leave the trail and climb east, staying loosely between the creeks on the mountain's west side. Cliff bands start around 3,200 ft and are threaded on boot and game trails rather than climbed; snow generally begins around 4,800 to 5,000 ft. Three miles or so of that work reaches a flat camp just over 5,200 ft below the toe of the ice. Strong parties carry a second camp onto the upper glacier near 7,400 ft, which shortens summit day considerably.
wa_jack_mountain_nohokomeen_headwall.season: Late May through July while the headwall is still a snow climb; the highway gate closes the season at both ends
hazards: steep brushy timber with cliff bands from about 3,200 ft, far worse to reverse than to ascend
crevasses on the Nohokomeen Glacier, thinly bridged late in the season
sustained steep snow on the headwall itself, with a long runout onto the glacier below
rockfall and icefall off the wall once the sun reaches it
a two to four day commitment with no quick way off the mountain
wa_jack_mountain_nohokomeen_headwall.baseFinding:
The timber belt is the navigation, the glacier toe is the arrival. Leaving May Creek you are looking for weaknesses, not a line: the cliff bands from about 3,200 ft up are passed on boot and game trails that thread left and right, so a section that forces you to climb rock means you have pushed into the band rather than around it. The reliable signal that you are through is underfoot rather than overhead - continuous snow starting somewhere near 4,800 to 5,000 ft, and above that the timber gives out onto open ground.

The camp is a flat bench, not a viewpoint. Just over 5,200 ft the ground levels into a flat bench in the upper May Creek basin, still well below the toe of the ice; if it does not suit, flat ground appears again from about 6,100 ft. If you are already on the ice you have walked past both.

The headwall is above the glacier, not at its toe. From the bench the glacier runs up in front of you at an easy angle for a long way before anything steepens. The route's steep ground is the wall at the head of that ice, directly beneath the summit. If you are roping up and swinging tools within minutes of leaving camp, you are on a serac or a crevasse wall low on the glacier, not on the headwall. The headwall is only reached after the whole gentle bowl has been crossed and the ground ahead of you rears up as one continuous face rather than a series of rolls.

A cross-check at the top of the ice: the summit should be directly above the headwall, not off to one side. If the wall in front of you tops out on a shoulder with more mountain visible beyond it, you have drifted around the bowl.

wa_jack_mountain_nohokomeen_headwall.name: Water taxi up Ross Lake to the eastern shore, cutting out most of the trail

bivy.name: High camp below the Nohokomeen Glacier
bivy.notes: Most parties climb straight up from the lake trail on day one and camp high on the ridge below the toe of the Nohokomeen Glacier, roughly 5,200 ft, to leave a manageable summit day. Some camp higher on the ridge.
bivy.water: Snowmelt; early-season trips camp on snow
bivy.permit: Ross Lake NRA backcountry permit for a cross-country camp
bivy.capacity: Open slopes and ridge snow; room for a few tents

bivy.name: May Creek Camp, Ross Lake
bivy.notes: Designated camp on the East Bank Trail about 8 miles from the East Bank trailhead, where climbers leave the trail for the north side of Jack Mountain. It can also be reached by water taxi. Used as a first night or as the camp on the way out.
bivy.water: Ross Lake and May Creek; treat
bivy.permit: Ross Lake NRA backcountry permit
bivy.capacity: Designated lakeshore camp with several tent sites

wa_jack_mountain_nohokomeen_headwall.notes: The resort at the south end of Ross Lake runs a water taxi that will drop parties on the eastern shore, which removes most of the flat trail miles and turns the approach into the off-trail climb alone. It has to be booked ahead and the schedule and drop points change, so confirm directly before building a trip around it. The trade is that you are committed to a pickup time on a lake with no road out, so build slack into the plan rather than into the summit day.
wa_jack_mountain_nohokomeen_headwall.season: Same window as the trail approach, but only once the boat service is running for the year
hazards: fixed pickup times on a lake with no road out
the same steep brushy cliff-banded timber belt above the shore
arriving late enough that the timber belt is done in the dark
crevasses on the glacier above
no reliable communication once off the lake
wa_jack_mountain_nohokomeen_headwall.baseFinding:
From the landing the first task is to get onto the trail and find may creek - the East Bank Trail runs along this shore and the departure point is the creek, not a bearing. Once you leave the trail at May Creek every marker is identical to the walk-in variant: cliff bands from around 3,200 ft passed on game trails, continuous snow near 4,800 to 5,000 ft, and the flat bench just over 5,200 ft below the toe of the ice.

The one thing the boat changes is your margin, not your route. Parties dropped late in the day have started the timber belt in fading light, which is where the cliff bands become genuinely dangerous, because the passages through them are found by eye. If you cannot reach open ground above the bands in daylight, camp low rather than commit to the belt.

The negative marker is the same: if the ground ahead of you steepens into rock rather than easing onto snow, you are in a cliff band and should traverse to find the boot track rather than force it.

wa_jack_mountain_nohokomeen_headwall.name: Before the highway opens: the gate at milepost 134
wa_jack_mountain_nohokomeen_headwall.notes: The highway closes each winter between the gate west of the trailhead and a second gate far to the east, and reopens somewhere between mid-April and early summer depending on the year's damage and snowpack. Parties wanting the headwall in condition have started at the closed gate and covered the road on bikes or skis to the trailhead before starting the walk in. Everything above that is unchanged, except that the snow line is far lower and the timber belt may go faster on skis than it does on foot in summer.
wa_jack_mountain_nohokomeen_headwall.season: Late winter and early spring, before the highway is cleared, when the headwall holds its best snow
hazards: avalanche terrain through the timber belt and on the glacier approach in early season
a long road section on bike or ski before the trip proper starts
short daylight and cold, with a committing position
cornices on the upper mountain
the road gate opening date moves year to year and can strand a plan
wa_jack_mountain_nohokomeen_headwall.baseFinding:
The road section is navigation-free; the approach still starts at may creek. Ride or ski the closed highway to the trailhead near milepost 138 and pick up the East Bank Trail there. The departure from the trail is the creek, as in summer.

What changes is where the snow starts. In this window continuous snow is likely to begin well below the 4,800 to 5,000 ft line that summer parties describe, which means the cliff bands between roughly 3,200 ft and there are being crossed on snow rather than on game trails. A band that would be walked around in August may be a loaded slope in April. If the passage you would normally take through a band is a smooth, wind-loaded ramp rather than a boot track, treat it as avalanche terrain and not as a route.

The flat bench just over 5,200 ft below the glacier toe may be buried and unrecognisable as a bench; in that case camp where the angle eases, or carry on to the toe of the ice near 6,100 ft, where the ground stops climbing and the glacier begins running away ahead of you toward the wall.

wa_jack_mountain_north_ridge.name: Ross Lake to May Creek and the Nohokomeen Glacier
wa_jack_mountain_north_ridge.notes: A genuinely remote three-day outing on a mountain that sees almost no traffic, and the approach is the hard part of it. Parties reach May Creek Camp on the east shore of Ross Lake at about 1,600 ft either by walking seven or eight flat miles of the East Bank Trail from SR 20 or, far more often, by taking the resort water taxi, which removes nearly all of that. From the lake it is a few thousand feet of steep forest, and the trick is finding the open timber rather than fighting brush: parties who get it right leave the trail in open forest a couple of hundred yards from the junction, angle left of the fall line, and follow game trails through the rock bands between roughly 3,500 and 4,100 ft, where a short cliff step sometimes carries webbing left behind by earlier parties. Reaching the ridge crest around 5,000 ft, traverse to the top of the moraine, pass under the toe of the Nohokomeen Glacier and climb slabs on its left side to camp at about 6,700 ft. Some parties push on and camp higher on the glacier near 7,400 ft. The glacier above is usually straightforward and largely crack-free to its top at about 8,000 ft. Most parties climb this ridge and descend the East Ridge, which turns the trip into a traverse and puts the exit out to Jerry Lakes and the Crater Mountain trail rather than back down the timber.
hazards: Serac fall off the Nohokomeen Glacier onto the ground below its toe
Loose, fractured chert throughout, with little that will hold protection
Steep forest with cliff bands on the approach, far worse to descend than to climb
Wet slabs and a pitch of low fifth class where the glacier meets the ridge
Big exposure on the knife-edge crest and on the snow traverse below the summit tower
Crevasses low on the glacier, and a moat where snow meets rock late in the season
Very remote, several days from a road in any direction, with no realistic quick rescue
wa_jack_mountain_north_ridge.baseFinding: Nobody climbs this ridge from its toe; you meet it partway up off the Nohokomeen Glacier, and exactly where to leave the ice is unsettled, so treat the aiming points below as the frame and read the ground. Climb the glacier up its centre, passing just to the right of the large rock that stands out on the ice, and head for the crest to the left of the summit tower rather than for the tower itself. The glacier runs out against rock at about 8,000 ft. The one unmistakable feature on the route is there: a hole clean through the rock, a keyhole big enough to squirm through, and that hole is how the crest is gained. Parties travelling in both directions have used it as their marker. Taken from the very top of the glacier the exit costs a pitch of wet, junky low fifth class and a scramble over greasy slabs, and the party who did it that way came away convinced an easier line onto the crest exists a little lower down, short of the glacier's top edge, so it is worth traversing under the rock and looking rather than forcing the highest weakness. Above the keyhole the confirmation is instant and unlike anything below it: a knife-edged crest of genuinely solid rock, which is rare on this mountain. If what is under your hands is fractured and rotten, you are not on the crest yet. One decoy matters. The north side's other line, the headwall, rises off the same glacier and tops out within minutes of the summit, so if the snow you are on runs straight to the top with no ridge left to travel, you are on the headwall and not this route. The North Ridge leaves the ice well below the summit and still has a long way to go: knife edge, then an exposed snow traverse south across and below the summit tower with occasional protection along the upper moat, and a final pitch of low fifth class up the East Ridge to the top at 9,066 ft.

wa_jack_mountain_north_ridge.name: East Bank Trail on foot to May Creek

bivy.name: May Creek Camp, Ross Lake
bivy.notes: Designated camp on the East Bank Trail about 8 miles from the East Bank trailhead, where climbers leave the trail for the north side of Jack Mountain. It can also be reached by water taxi. Used as a first night or as the camp on the way out.
bivy.water: Ross Lake and May Creek; treat
bivy.permit: Ross Lake NRA backcountry permit
bivy.capacity: Designated lakeshore camp with several tent sites

wa_jack_mountain_north_ridge.notes: Walk the East Bank Trail from SR-20 north along the east shore of Ross Lake to May Creek Camp, where climbers leave the trail. Several hours of flat walking each way, but it needs no booking and works whenever the highway is open.

wa_kololo_peaks_standard.name: North Fork Sauk Trail #649 to White Pass, then the Foam Basin traverse and the White Chuck Glacier
camps: White Chuck Glacier basin, under Kololo Peaks
Sloan Creek Campground and the North Fork Sauk road end
wa_kololo_peaks_standard.notes: From the North Fork Sauk Trailhead near 2,050 ft at the end of FR-49, Trail #649 runs about 5.5 miles up the valley on an easy grade through old growth, fording several tributaries. Red Creek is the first crossing that can actually stop you: manageable at normal flow, considerably higher during snowmelt or after rain, and worth a pole. Mackinaw Shelter at 2,950 ft is a possible camp but tight for a big party, and it is where the trail leaves the river — fill water there. Above the shelter the trail climbs about 3.2 miles of sustained switchbacks to a meadow junction with the Pacific Crest Trail near 6,000 ft, then a quarter mile north on the PCT to White Pass at 5,900 ft. That is roughly nine miles and 4,800 ft from the car and the last easy water before the high traverse. Maintained trail ends at the pass. Traverse north below the White Mountain ridge into Foam Basin and White River Meadows around 6,300-6,500 ft — the usual base camp — either by way of Red Pass or by crossing snowfields to the notch west of Point 6770 and dropping into the White Chuck basin. Almost nobody does this from the car in a day, and the round trip is long enough that the two published distances for it disagree.
wa_kololo_peaks_standard.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Late summer opens the crevasses so you can see and weave them; early season covers them with bridges you cannot read, and puts Red Creek and Lightning Creek in flood
hazards: Open crevasses and a roughly 200-yard band of exposed blue ice on the White River Glacier, worse late season
Red Creek and Lightning Creek run high and fast in snowmelt — the first is an ordinary ford at normal flow and a stopper at high water
Twelve-plus miles one way with the last several off any maintained trail, so a navigation error is measured in hours
Snow bridges over the White Chuck Glacier that are unreadable under early-season cover
Road closures on FR-49 and the Mountain Loop Highway that can shut the west approach entirely, turning this into a much longer trip from the east
wa_kololo_peaks_standard.baseFinding: This route has two arrivals and they are different kinds of thing. The first is where glacier travel starts, and the second is where the scrambling starts. Confusing them is how a party ends up unroped in the wrong place. Glacier starts at foam pass. From camp climb to Foam Pass and step onto the White Chuck Glacier. Rope, axe and crampons go on here, not later — the crossing to Glacier Gap and then onto the White River Glacier is the whole of the day's crevasse exposure. Scrambling starts at the top of the snow. From Glacier Gap, drop a short way onto the White River Glacier and come at the peak from the south, up the snow headwall to the summit ridge; above the snow it is an easy talus-and-ledge scramble. Of the twin tops on the summit ridge the eastern one is the true high point by only 10-15 ft, so bag both. One thing to expect on the ice rather than look for: a roughly 200-yard band of exposed blue ice, a shallow icefall, on the White River Glacier. It is a crampon problem, not a navigation one, but it is the reason the descent takes longer than the map suggests.

wa_kololo_peaks_standard.name: White River trail from the east
wa_kololo_peaks_standard.notes: From the White River trailhead beyond Lake Wenatchee, walk the White River trail about 10 miles up the valley to the Lightning Creek crossing, then go cross-country up into the high basin east of the peaks. About as far on foot as the Sauk side, with less trail and more off-trail travel.

wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.name: Lake of the Woods camp and the east ridge
camps: Lake of the Woods and the Eureka Falls camp
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.notes: There is no trail on the mountain itself; the whole climb is talus, scree and boulder-field walking off a high camp. The usual staging is a camp around 6,600 ft near Lake of the Woods, reached over Pistol Pass on the long-abandoned Pistol Ridge tread out of the Monument Creek valley. That approach has been unmaintained for decades and involves an unbridged ford of Eureka Creek that runs thigh to waist deep during snowmelt. A longer alternative from the Slate Pass road end reaches the same country by way of the Ferguson Lake trail and avoids that ford, at the cost of tread that is harder still to follow. From camp the peak is a couple of hours each way for a fit party, and most parties pair it with Monument Peak.
hazards: Loose talus near the summit
Short exposed sections of blocky granite on the ridge
Unbridged ford of Eureka Creek, dangerous during snowmelt
Abandoned, brushy, deadfall-choked approach tread navigated by cairns
Steep north wall and northeast face immediately off the standard line
No cell service and multi-day self-rescue distance
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.baseFinding: From camp near Lake of the Woods, head uphill out of the lake basin toward the peak, which rises directly above camp. The base is where the open slope steepens toward the summit, and the mountain tells you where that is by refusing the obvious line. A subsidiary rock knob blocks a direct ascent from the south, and a cliff band bars a straight finish near 8,000 ft, so if you are looking up at a clean unbroken slope from the south side you are not below the standard start and pushing on will cliff you out. Bend instead onto the mountain's lower east ridge. That ridge is identifiable at its foot by larch: the lower slopes are studded with scattered larch groves, and the climbing proper begins where the larches thin out around 7,800 ft and the ground turns to boulder-hopping and coarse scree. Several gullies of much the same difficulty run up from there and any of them will go; take the one where hands come out only occasionally and the footing stays blocky rather than sliding. Early sections often feel like a staircase of granite blocks, which is a good sign you are on the ridge rather than in a scree runnel beside it. Two warnings on where not to be. The north wall and the northeast face are appreciably steeper and are not part of this route, so if the ground ahead drops away rather than rising, move back south. And the last few hundred feet hold snow late; footprints in it are a reasonable line but not proof of a good one.

wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.name: Slate Pass and the Pasayten side
wa_lake_mountain_pasayten_scramble.notes: Start high at Slate Pass on the Harts Pass road and drop toward the Middle Fork Pasayten, then work east by Eureka Creek and around into the basin below the peak. Longer and more cross-country than Pistol Pass, but it starts thousands of feet higher.

wa_liberty_cap_liberty_ridge_finish.name: White River, St. Elmo Pass and the Carbon Glacier
camps: Curtis Ridge / Carbon Glacier access bivy
Lower Curtis Ridge / Carbon Glacier camp
wa_liberty_cap_liberty_ridge_finish.notes: Everyone walks in from White River Campground, and the walking is over quickly. The Glacier Basin Trail is maintained for about three and a half miles to the basin at roughly 5,900 ft, which holds the last running water you will see until the descent brings you down to Camp Schurman. Above the basin there is no trail: a boot track climbs snow and scree to St. Elmo Pass at about 7,400 ft, and from the far side of the pass you drop onto the Winthrop Glacier and stay roped for the rest of the trip. The counter-clockwise traverse under Mount Ruth and around the toe of Curtis Ridge is the part that decides the day, because it runs directly beneath Willis Wall and both walls shed rock and ice more freely once the sun is on them. Most parties split the approach with a bivy on lower Curtis Ridge somewhere between about 7,200 and 7,600 ft, right beside the ramp that drops onto the Carbon Glacier, and it is the only place on the whole approach where you get a head-on look at the route to pick your line. Curtis Ridge is broad and deceptive in cloud and parties repeatedly think they have arrived when they have not; the rule everyone repeats is to stay low and, when in doubt, angle down and right. If what you are looking over is not a mellow fifty-foot talus slope, you are too high, and climbing further only cliffs you out. A climbing permit is required and this line carries its own briefing, so sort both before driving up rather than on the morning you want to leave.
hazards: Rockfall and icefall off Willis Wall onto the Carbon Glacier traverse, worsening through the day
Serac collapse off the Liberty Cap Glacier onto the west side of the Carbon basin
Crevasses and thin snow bridges on the Winthrop and Carbon crossings
The moat between glacier and rock at the foot of the ridge, which turns parties around outright
Rockfall into Thumb Rock camp, which has been swept out by slides off the tower opposite
Sustained steep ice to around 60 degrees above the Black Pyramid
Altitude, and no retreat down the route once above Thumb Rock
wa_liberty_cap_liberty_ridge_finish.baseFinding: Coming off Curtis Ridge everything underfoot is glacier, so the ridge has to be picked out by shape and by what stands either side of it. Where Liberty Ridge meets the Carbon it is a rock nose, a prow of broken volcanic rock at roughly 8,450 to 8,600 ft rather than a snow slope, and often the place you can watch rocks peeling off. Memorise the compass check, because it holds everywhere on the climb. Facing uphill, Willis Wall is on your left, to the east, and the Liberty Wall is on your right, to the west. If the big wall is on your right hand as you look up, you are on the wrong feature. Cross the Carbon up climber's right of the main icefall and aim for the nose. The real crux of the approach is the moat where the glacier pulls away from the rock, and parties are stopped here more often than anywhere else on the climb — not because the ridge is hard to see, but because there is no way across the gap that day. You can gain the crest from either flank or straight up the toe, at roughly 8,600 to 8,800 ft. The east flank is steeper and carries more rock bands, so most parties cross onto the west flank as soon as they are on the crest and stay there up to camp. Which side actually goes is decided by the moat and the crevasses rather than by preference, so scout instead of committing to the first weakness. In poor visibility the confirmation is not at the toe at all, it is above it: Thumb Rock, a 300 ft gendarme of broken volcanic rock at somewhere around 10,500 ft, with a second loose tower opposite it and barely room for two small tents in the saddle between. Parties fogged out at the base have started to retreat and turned around again only when Thumb Rock showed through a break in the cloud, so if you are unsure, wait for a window and look up rather than along. You have gone too far west if the ground opens into the Carbon basin beneath the Liberty Wall's hanging ice; crevasses routinely push parties that way, and the next spine past that wall is Ptarmigan Ridge, a different climb off a different camp.

wa_liberty_cap_liberty_ridge_finish.name: Carbon River and the Wonderland Trail to Curtis Ridge

bivy.name: Thumb Rock
bivy.notes: Planned high camp and the standard one — flat, partly wind-sheltered tent sites tucked behind the rock buttress, reached by moderate snow and loose rock bands. Reports place the platforms anywhere from about 10,400 to 10,700 ft depending on which bench and how much snow is in; the ground above the rock is more exposed and takes the full wind. There is no liquid water at any point. The approach ramps immediately below turn loose and unpleasant once they melt out, so late-season parties arrive slower than they plan.
bivy.water: none — melt snow or ice
bivy.permit: climbing permit required above 10,000 ft in addition to the camping permit
bivy.capacity: a handful of existing snow platforms; can be crowded in season, and late parties dig their own

bivy.name: Curtis Ridge / Carbon Glacier access bivy
bivy.notes: Planned intermediate camp, and the usual way to split what is otherwise a 7-10 hour push from the car to Thumb Rock. Established sites sit in the ramp that gains the Carbon at about 7,300 ft, with more ground on the ridge crest above. Parties camp here specifically so they can cross the exposed ground under Willis Wall early and cold. Do not pitch out on the open Carbon under the wall to shorten the morning — that is the fall line for serac collapse off the summit icecap.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.capacity: a few small sites in the access gully and on the ridge

bivy.name: Camp Schurman
bivy.notes: Descent camp. Liberty Ridge tops out near Liberty Cap and most parties come down the Emmons-Winthrop, so this is where a slow summit day ends rather than a forced night out high on the ice. Ranger hut and solar toilet, both potentially buried in snow — carry blue bags and pack them out. Reserve well ahead.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.permit: wilderness camping permit required; separate climbing permit for glacier travel
bivy.capacity: limited designated tent sites; fills early in season

bivy.name: Lower Curtis Ridge / Carbon Glacier camp

wa_liberty_cap_liberty_ridge_finish.notes: The older way in, used mainly early in the season when the White River road is still closed. From the Carbon River entrance, walk or bike the old road to Ipsut Creek, then follow the Wonderland Trail up the Carbon River to the snout of the Carbon Glacier and onto the ice toward Curtis Ridge. It starts lower and is noticeably longer than the White River approach, and the Carbon River crossing on the Wonderland Trail can be a problem.

wa_liberty_cap_ptarmigan_ridge_finish.name: Mowich Lake, Spray Park and the Ptarmigan crest
wa_liberty_cap_ptarmigan_ridge_finish.notes: The prettier of the two ways in, and the one that puts you on the route's own ridge from the bottom. Mowich Lake sits at about 4,929 ft at the end of a road that has had no public access since the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge closed in April 2025 (before that it was often snowed shut into early or mid July), and that single fact decides whether this approach is available at all. From the lake it is three to four miles of trail up through Spray Park; at about 6,400 ft a beaten path breaks off right toward the permanent snow. Cross the Flett Glacier in the gap between Echo Rock, 7,870 ft, and Observation Rock, 8,364 ft, at somewhere around 7,500 ft, climb to the saddle immediately east of Observation Rock, and cross onto the Russell Glacier near 7,800 ft. From there the crest runs south, sometimes on rock but mostly on easy snow just left of the crest line, with the Russell falling away east. This stretch is uncrevassed and is genuinely a walk. The last few hundred yards to camp are not: the crest narrows to a knife edge with an overhanging rock step on it, and most parties bypass that by dropping about 200 ft onto 40 degree snow on the east side and traversing back. Well above the base, the exit gully through the rock buttress is the one identification climbers argue about — whether it is the first or the second break in the cliffs is genuinely unsettled, so climb to the fixed pin rather than to a count. The descent is the Emmons route out to White River, so coming in this way needs a car shuttle or a very long road walk.
hazards: Ice avalanche off the Liberty Cap Glacier's ice cliffs onto the traverse between camp and the bergschrund
Bare rock at the crux chimney in lean years, which raises both the grade and the rockfall
Bergschrund and crevasses at the start of the technical ground, around 9,800 ft
Sustained 45 to 60 degree snow and ice, with a long exposed rising traverse
Rockfall off decomposing volcanic cliffs on everything below about 12,200 ft
Overhanging rock step on the knife edge into high camp
No road access to Mowich Lake since the April 2025 bridge closure, and a descent that finishes at a different trailhead
wa_liberty_cap_ptarmigan_ridge_finish.baseFinding: The walking and the climbing are cleanly separated here and the boundary is a flat spot, but the climb does not start above camp — it starts several hundred feet below it and on the far side of the ridge, and that is what parties get wrong. Follow the crest south from the saddle beside Observation Rock until the ridge stops rising and levels out at about 10,200 to 10,300 ft. You will know the place without being told, because four things sit together there and nowhere else: room for a couple of small tents on flat ground, a steep 2,000 ft drop to the Carbon Glacier immediately east of you, huge banded ice cliffs standing directly south above you where the Liberty Cap Glacier ends, and a clean view straight across at Liberty Ridge. From that camp the route drops west off the crest a few hundred feet onto the upper Mowich Glacier and crosses the bergschrund at about 9,800 ft, aiming for a bridge just left of a rock outcropping near the middle of the face. Look that crossing over from camp the evening before, because it is in plain sight from up there and its condition changes year to year. The traverse down to it passes under the run-out of the ice cliffs and is usually walked across old avalanche debris and stray boulders sitting on the ice, so it is done in the dark and fast. Two ways to know you are wrong. If you have descended onto the Mowich Glacier and kept going west or south, you are wandering out onto Mowich Face ground rather than to the schrund. And if you cross a bergschrund with no ice cliffs above and to your left, stop: from the schrund the route rises back east, climber's left, toward those cliffs, not away from them. The route finishes on Liberty Cap; Columbia Crest is a separate trip across the summit plateau and is not part of this climb.

wa_liberty_cap_ptarmigan_ridge_finish.name: White River, St. Elmo Pass and across the Carbon

bivy.name: Ptarmigan Ridge high camp
bivy.notes: The high camp the route is climbed from, on the crest of Ptarmigan Ridge near 10,000 ft. Exposed to wind; no running water.
bivy.water: Melt snow
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier wilderness permit and climbing registration
bivy.capacity: A few tent sites on the ridge crest

bivy.name: White River Campground
bivy.notes: The roadhead camp for the Emmons-Winthrop, five miles up White River Road off Highway 410, and the Glacier Basin trail to Camp Schurman starts here. Being the highest of the park's drive-in campgrounds it is normally the last to open, around late June, and the first to close in September, so early-season parties often sleep outside the park. Its availability is not guaranteed year to year — it has been listed closed for fire activity — so confirm status before driving in. A reasonable place to sort gear and get a short night before an early start up the Inter Glacier.
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground when it is open for the season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed, but this is inside Mount Rainier National Park so park entrance applies, and the park has operated timed-entry reservations for corridor access in recent summers. Recent NPS listings show it as first-come rather than reservable, which contradicts several third-party campground sites still advertising reservations, so check the current NPS page before relying on either. A camping permit here does not cover the mountain: the wilderness permit and the climbing fee are separate.
bivy.capacity: 88 individual drive-in sites with flush toilets and fire grates; RV length is limited to about 27 ft

bivy.name: Camp Schurman
bivy.notes: The high camp for the Emmons-Winthrop, the standard north-side route, approached from the White River Campground through Glacier Basin and up the Inter Glacier. There is an NPS ranger hut with an emergency radio on its exterior and toilet facilities, but the hut is staff quarters and not a shelter climbers can sleep in, so a tent is mandatory. Access is gated by the White River Road, which typically does not open until late June, and by the Inter Glacier, which is small but crevassed enough that roping up is a judgement call that changes through the season. Late in a dry summer the Inter Glacier turns to bare ice and rubble.
bivy.water: Snow to melt in most conditions, and the camp generally has adequate clean snow through the season. Some parties find running meltwater near camp late in summer, but it is seasonal and should not be counted on when planning fuel
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit required, same reservation and walk-up split as the rest of the park's climbing camps, with in-person registration before the climb. The climbing cost recovery fee applies to anyone continuing onto the Emmons or Winthrop glaciers or attempting the summit; walking to Camp Schurman as a day trip without going higher does not trigger it.
bivy.capacity: Considerably smaller than Camp Muir, on the order of a dozen tent sites on the snow and rock around Steamboat Prow; the quota fills quickly on good-weather weekends

wa_liberty_cap_ptarmigan_ridge_finish.notes: The way in that is actually available during the ice season, because the White River road opens in late spring while Mowich Lake has had no road access since the 2025 bridge closure, and it puts you back at your own car after the Emmons descent instead of on the far side of the mountain. It is the Liberty Ridge approach as far as the Carbon: Glacier Basin, then a boot track up snow and scree to St. Elmo Pass, given variously as 7,400 or 7,600 ft, then onto the Winthrop Glacier and a roped traverse at roughly 7,200 to 7,400 ft around to Curtis Ridge, where there are good bivy sites near 7,500 ft. Next morning drop and cross the Carbon around 7,000 ft, staying clear of its seracs and north of the ice cliffs where the Russell calves onto it, then take snowfields up onto the Ptarmigan crest at about its 9,000 ft point and follow the ridge to high camp. It is longer than the Mowich walk, it crosses three glaciers, and it spends hours under actively shedding walls, so it wants to be done cold and early. One thing to fix in your head before the descent: parties coming off Liberty Cap routes routinely wander onto the busy Disappointment Cleaver at Columbia Crest instead of the faint Emmons track, which is the wrong side of the mountain if your car is at White River.
hazards: Hours of exposure to rockfall and icefall crossing beneath Willis Wall and the Liberty Wall
Ice avalanche off the Liberty Cap Glacier's cliffs onto the traverse into the route
Crevasses on the Winthrop and the Carbon, thin bridges early and open cracks late
Committing traverse with no quick exit once past Curtis Ridge
Sustained 45 to 60 degree ice and a rock or mixed crux around 12,000 ft
Very little traffic, so no established track above the Carbon and a slow rescue
Losing the faint Emmons descent to the well-trodden Disappointment Cleaver at the summit
wa_liberty_cap_ptarmigan_ridge_finish.baseFinding: This is the approach on which Rainier's two Liberty Cap routes actually get confused, and the trap is a physical one: there is usually a bootpack running from St. Elmo Pass to the Carbon Glacier, and it was stamped in by parties going to Liberty Ridge. It is the right track as far as the Carbon and the wrong one after that. Working west you cross under Willis Wall and meet a narrow rock and snow ridge dropping straight to the glacier. That first spine is Liberty Ridge. Keep going. Past it the ground opens beneath a big pale cirque wall capped by hanging ice, and the next crest beyond that wall, roughly a mile and a half further west, is Ptarmigan Ridge. Put it the simple way and it is hard to get wrong: on Liberty Ridge the Liberty Wall is on your right, and on Ptarmigan Ridge it is on your left. Cross the Carbon below the seracs, gain the Ptarmigan crest at about its 9,000 ft point and follow the ridge up to the flat high camp at 10,200 to 10,300 ft. That flat is the base of the climb, and four things fix it together: room for a couple of small tents, a steep 2,000 ft drop to the Carbon immediately east, banded ice cliffs standing directly south above you where the Liberty Cap Glacier ends, and Liberty Ridge in full view straight across. From camp the route drops west off the crest onto the upper Mowich Glacier and crosses the bergschrund at about 9,800 ft, near a rock outcropping about the middle of the face — study that crossing from camp the evening before, because it is in plain sight from up there. Above the schrund the line rises back east, climber's left, toward the ice cliffs. If you have crossed a schrund with no ice cliff up and left of you, you are on the wrong part of the mountain.

wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.name: Smithbrook Trail and the crest trail to Lake Valhalla
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.notes: From the Smithbrook Trailhead on the gravel spur off the highway, climb the signed Smithbrook Trail through nearly twenty short switchbacks to Union Gap, where it meets the crest trail; the summit is in view to the south for much of that stretch once the forest opens. Turn left and follow the crest trail south, contouring below the mountain's east flank through a mix of forest and open heather meadow and crossing Smith Brook, which is a reliable place to filter before leaving the trail. Where the trail bends away from Lake Valhalla, drop off it down a steep dirt path to the water and follow the rocky shoreline round to the lake's south tip.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.season: Snow-free ground roughly July through October; the same slopes are skinned or snowshoed as a separate winter tour. The access road is unplowed in winter and typically melts out by early to mid summer.
hazards: There is no trail of any kind beyond the lake outlet — real tread only reappears on the summit ridge itself
More than one gully runs up this side of the mountain and only one of them is the route
The peak visible from the lake is a lower sub-summit, and parties have climbed it by mistake onto slick class 4 and 5 ground
Short cliff bands that force minor backtracking
Loose talus with rockfall onto anyone below
The gully often holds snow into early summer, so an axe and light traction are worth carrying outside peak summer
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.baseFinding: When faced with a choice of gullies, take the middle one — and know that the peak you can see is not the summit. From the southeast area of the lake begin a slight ascent to the southeast, looking for the obvious rock-filled gully. Be careful here: there is more than one gully on this side of the mountain, and the middle of them is the route. Ascend it to where it terminates, then work around the first small cliff band to the left, on its north side. Above that, climb right toward a gentle saddle; from the saddle a traverse northeast is the easier finish, while going northwest is the exposed option and is not the ordinary line. The wrong-place marker is the thing you have been looking at all along: from the lake the true summit is hidden, and what stands in front of it is a smaller unnamed peak that looks steep and sketchy. Parties have climbed toward it by mistake and turned back a few metres short on slick class 4 and 5 rock. There is no trail at all beyond the lake outlet, so finding none is expected; real tread reappears only on the summit ridge.

wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.name: Crest trail north from Stevens Pass

bivy.name: Lake Valhalla
bivy.notes: The natural base for both Lichtenberg Mountain and Mount McCausland, which stand on opposite sides of the bowl the lake fills. Lichtenberg's broad face rises straight out of the water on the south side and is the peak everyone photographs from camp; McCausland is the gentler summit to the northeast, gained by a signed spur off the Pacific Crest Trail a little under three miles from the Smithbrook trailhead and reachable from camp in about an hour. The short way in is Smithbrook Road to the trailhead, then a mile or so of switchbacks to Union Gap and a traverse south on the Pacific Crest Trail, roughly five miles each way. The long way is the Pacific Crest Trail north from the pass itself, about five and a half miles with less climbing but more distance. Thru-hiker traffic through July and August adds real pressure on a small number of sites, so arrive early or plan to camp away from the water. Season is roughly mid-July through October; snow lingers in this bowl and the trail is muddy for weeks after it goes. In winter Smithbrook Road is unplowed and the approach lengthens considerably, which is why the winter ascents of Lichtenberg come at it from the road rather than from the lake.
bivy.water: The lake itself, and a small inlet at the south end. Wash and rinse well back from the shore — this is a small basin carrying a lot of traffic.
bivy.permit: Henry M. Jackson Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the trailhead register. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Smithbrook trailhead; the Pacific Crest Trail lot at Stevens Pass needs no pass but does need the self-registration. Campfires are prohibited at the lake — carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites scattered around the lake, mostly in the trees on the north and east shores, plus a couple of backcountry toilets. First come, first served, and genuinely full on summer weekends.

approachLogistics.trailhead: Stevens Pass North Lot (crest trail northbound)

wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.notes: Park in the north lot at Stevens Pass and pick up the crest trail heading north from behind the maintenance buildings. It contours the slopes above Nason Creek and reaches Lake Valhalla from the west, where you leave the trail and work around the lake to the scramble. It is a few miles longer than the Smithbrook start but needs no gravel road, and it is the usual start when Smith Brook road is under snow.

wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.name: Smith Brook road trailhead via Union Gap
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.notes: From the trailhead on Smith Brook road, climb to Union Gap on the crest trail and follow it toward Lake Valhalla and Lichtenberg Pass, then leave the trail for the base of the west face.

wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.name: Crest trail north from Stevens Pass

A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Smithbrook trailhead; the Pacific Crest Trail lot at Stevens Pass needs no pass but does need the self-registration.
