approachLogistics.trailhead: Stevens Pass North Lot (crest trail northbound)

wa_lichtenberg_mountain_west_face_west_r.notes: Park in the north lot at Stevens Pass and follow the crest trail north to Lake Valhalla, arriving from the west below the face. It is a few miles longer than the Smith Brook start but needs no gravel road, and it is the usual start when Smith Brook road is under snow.

wa_lincoln_peak_standard.name: Middle Fork Nooksack Road (FR-38) and Rankin Creek to the treeline camp, then the southwest basin
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.notes:
This is the more direct way to the X Couloir: from the south via the Middle Fork Nooksack River Road (FR-38). The southwest face can also be reached from Heliotrope Ridge through the Thunder Glacier cirque, a less direct line with more glacier travel; do not confuse either with the north-facing Coleman side, which leads to the other route on this mountain.

Drive FR-38 toward its mile-12.5 switchback and start walking the old decommissioned road around Point 4481 toward Rankin Creek. Snow travel — often by bike or snowshoe on the lower stretch — leads past East Rankin Lake near 5,120 ft and up into the basin to a sheltered camp at treeline around 6,100 ft, by the highest trees in the basin below Seward Peak. Roughly seven miles and 3,350 ft of gain to camp.

Access: FR-38, damaged in the December 2025 floods, has been closed to vehicles at milepost 7 by a washout since July 27, 2026, with no end date given on the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest alert still posted on September 26, 2026, and a separate gate at Wallace Creek near mile 10 closes the road 1 December to 15 June for elk calving. Confirm the drivable road-end with the Mount Baker Ranger District before the trip; the length of the approach varies year to year.
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.season: Roughly Apr-Jun. A spring snow climb; essentially never done in summer, because what makes it climbable is continuous snow rather than the rubble underneath
hazards: A bergschrund crossing that must be done cold and early
1,500 ft of 30-40 degree snow with a steep serac step, all of it above a long runout
FR-38 flood damage with no repair timeline, plus an elk-calving gate closed 1 Dec - 15 Jun
A gully that funnels rockfall and spindrift after storms
A descent that is a real rappel sequence off pickets and slung horns, not a walk-off
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.baseFinding:
The highest trees in the basin are the camp, and the camp is the last thing you can navigate to. Above treeline the southwest side of Lincoln is open snow and there is nothing to hold on to in cloud. So the arrival marker is vegetative rather than topographic: climb until the trees stop, and camp at the last of them, below Seward Peak, around 6,100 ft.

The bergschrund is the base of the climb. From camp an alpine start takes you into the southwest basin and to the schrund while the snow is still cold and firm. Above it is roughly 1,500 ft of 30-40 degree snow with a steep serac step in it.

Do not expect one clean couloir — this is the trap the name sets. Parties who have climbed and skied it describe it as less a couloir and more a series of steep chutes and faces, and the line drops from the high point to the highest notch, then down a narrow chute, and trends right out of view. So 'find the obvious couloir' is the wrong instruction and will have you standing in the basin looking for something that is not there. Work from the notch downward: the correct line is the one that connects to the highest notch on the skyline, and it is narrow where it leaves the basin.

The serac step is the confirmation. Somewhere in that 1,500 ft you meet a steep serac step. A line with no ice step in it is not the X Couloir.

And the aspect settles the coarse error: this route faces southwest and this approach reaches it from Rankin Creek. If you are standing on the Coleman Glacier looking at a shaded north-facing cirque, you are under the other route on this mountain.

wa_lincoln_peak_standard.name: Heliotrope Ridge and the Thunder Glacier cirque
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.notes: Start at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead and follow the trail toward the old cabin site, then rope up and cross the lower glaciers south into the Thunder Glacier cirque to reach the southwest side of the peak. It is less direct than the Rankin Creek line, with much more glacier travel, but it starts from a paved-to-gravel road that is usually open when the Middle Fork road is not.

wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie to Dutch Miller Gap
camps: Williams Lake and the upper Middle Fork meadows below Dutch Miller Gap
Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.notes: The standard way. From the Middle Fork Snoqualmie road end, follow the Dutch Miller Gap trail up the valley for a long day — roughly fourteen to fifteen miles — passing the horse camp and the Williams Lake trail junction on the way to the gap. Most parties break this over two days and camp near Williams Lake or at the gap. There is no cross-country detour for this route: stay on the trail to the top.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.season: July to September; recorded ascents cluster in August and September. The upper cirque holds snow well into summer, so carry an axe.
hazards: Snow lingering in the approach cirque well into summer, with variable soft, icy or moat-riddled conditions
Loose rock on the heather and rock steps, on the ridge and on the face
No cell coverage, and a remote position that makes rescue difficult
The gap is a trail high point with several ways off it — confirm you are on the southwest side before committing
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.baseFinding: The climbing starts directly above the gap. From the low point of Dutch Miller Gap, turn onto the peak immediately southwest of it — the first ground above the trail that needs hands is the start, roughly five hundred feet of heather and rock steps rising onto the northeast ridge. The physical test is the sequence: heather steps give way to an open bench, and above the bench you cross a snowfield into a cirque below the east face; if you have not crossed snow you have not reached the cirque, and the two short belayed pitches to the summit start from it. At the top of the first of those pitches, move climber's left for the direct finish. Negative markers: if you left the trail at a small steel bridge well below the gap and dropped south into a side valley, you are heading for the long gully-and-crack route on the far side of the mountain; if you are looking up nine hundred feet of talus at a prominent left-trending gully, you are under that route and not this one.

wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.name: Necklace Valley and La Bohn Gap from the north
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.notes: A longer alternative from the other side of the divide: the Necklace Valley trail off the Foss River road, over La Bohn Gap, then down to Dutch Miller Gap. It joins the standard line at the gap, so everything above is identical. Worth knowing about mainly as a through-trip option or if the Middle Fork road end is not usable.
hazards: Long approach over a second pass, with snow on La Bohn Gap into summer
Loose rock above the gap
Remote, rescue-difficult terrain with no cell coverage
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.baseFinding: You are aiming for the same point as the standard approach: the low saddle of Dutch Miller Gap, with the peak on its southwest side. Coming from the north you drop TO the gap rather than climbing to it, so the check is that you have finished descending and the peak is now above you on the left. The climbing begins at the first hands-on heather-and-rock steps above the gap, leading to an open bench and then a snowfield crossing into the cirque below the east face. Negative marker: if you are still descending and the ground ahead keeps dropping into a valley, you have passed the gap and are heading down the Middle Fork.

wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.name: Pete Lake and Summit Chief camp from the east
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.notes: The eastern option, from a camp near Pete Lake and Summit Chief. It does not reach Dutch Miller Gap at all — it comes at the peak's northeast basin from the other side and joins the route higher up. It is the approach that puts the ridge notch in your path, which the trail-to-the-gap line avoids.
hazards: Exposed low-fifth-class crux move at the ridge notch, which most parties belay
Route-finding through the northeast basin's cliff bands
Loose rock throughout
Remote with no cell coverage
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.baseFinding: From camp, work into the peak's northeast basin. The route is guarded by a ridge notch, and the notch is identified by a single feature: a large vertical crack forming a low-fifth-class step that most parties rope up for. If the notch you have reached can be walked through, it is not this one. Above the notch the ground eases and joins the snowfield and cirque used by the trail approach. Negative marker: if you are standing in a broad trail saddle with tread underfoot, you are at Dutch Miller Gap and on the standard line, where no such crack step exists.

wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.name: Waptus River and Lake Ivanhoe from Salmon La Sac

bivy.name: Waptus Lake, with Spade Lake above it
bivy.notes: Waptus is roughly nine miles of easy river trail from Salmon la Sac with only about 800 ft of gain, which makes it the least strenuous long approach in the zone and a genuinely pleasant first night. For climbers here it is the eastern gateway to Little Big Chief Mountain, which sits immediately southwest of Dutch Miller Gap. The useful camps for that peak are not at the lake but a couple of miles further up the valley, near the bridge over the Waptus River above the lake and near the ford of Chief Creek — call it twelve miles in — and from there the Dutch Miller Gap trail climbs past Lake Ivanhoe to the gap, where the northeast face scramble starts. Spade Lake is the other well-known destination above Waptus and it is worth being clear about what it is and is not: the spur trail gains nearly 3,000 ft in about three miles of steep, downed-timber forest with scrambly and overgrown sections, and it lands in a rocky cirque on the flank of Mount Daniel. It is a superb, lonely camp and it is not a base for Chimney Rock, which lies across the valley on the other side of the crest. Snow lingers in the Spade cirque into July. Wildfire closures on the Cle Elum Ranger District have shut the Waptus and Spade trails for whole seasons — check for a current closure order before driving to Salmon la Sac.
bivy.water: Waptus Lake, the Waptus River and Chief Creek at the lower camps; the lake and small inlet streams at Spade
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Salmon la Sac trailhead. Group limit twelve including stock — this is horse country and the trail is shared. Campfires are permitted at Waptus but banned at Spade and everywhere else above 5,000 ft. Camp at least a hundred feet back from water and off the meadows.
bivy.capacity: Large — Waptus has upwards of two dozen established sites strung along the shore and near the outlet, first come first served. Spade Lake above is the opposite: scattered bluff sites for a party or two.

approachLogistics.trailhead: Salmon La Sac / Waptus River Trailhead

wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.notes: The long southeastern way in, usually spread over two or three days. From the Salmon La Sac road end north of Cle Elum, follow the Waptus River trail up its gentle valley to Waptus Lake, roughly nine miles. The old hiker bridge over the river below the lake is gone, so this is a real ford, about knee deep at normal summer flow. Past the lake the trail follows the southeast shore, which can hold steep snow into early summer, to a ford of Chief Creek near the head of the lake, about twelve miles from the car. From Chief Creek the Dutch Miller Gap trail switchbacks up the forested slope, passes Lake Ivanhoe and reaches the gap, roughly five more miles and about 2,000 ft higher. At the gap it meets the standard approach, and the climbing above is the same.
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.season: July to September. The river ford and the lakeshore snow are both much more serious during snowmelt.
hazards: Unbridged Waptus River ford below the lake: cold and swift, and serious in snowmelt
Chief Creek ford near the head of Waptus Lake
Steep snowfields on the lake's southeast shore into early summer
Very long approach far from help, with no cell coverage
wa_little_big_chief_mountain_northeast_f.baseFinding: You are aiming for the same point as the standard approach: the low saddle of Dutch Miller Gap, with the peak on its southwest side. Coming up from Lake Ivanhoe you climb to the gap from the east, so the check is that the trail has stopped climbing and starts to drop west toward the Middle Fork, with the peak above you on the left. The climbing starts at the first heather and rock steps above the gap and leads to an open bench, then a snowfield crossing into the cirque below the east face. Negative marker: if you are still beside Lake Ivanhoe or below it, you have not reached the gap yet.

wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder.name: Fryingpan Creek, Summerland and Meany Crest to Whitman Notch
wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder.notes:
Start at the Fryingpan Creek Trailhead near 3,800-3,900 ft on the Sunrise and White River Road, a few miles past the White River entrance station. Follow the signed trail up through old-growth beside Fryingpan Creek.

At roughly 3.2 miles and about 1,400 ft of gain there is an established footlog crossing of Fryingpan Creek — the main water and a spot that needs care in high runoff. Continue to Summerland at about 4.5 miles and roughly 5,900 ft: patrol cabin, pit toilet, bear wires, and the last reliable running water.

From Summerland leave maintained trail and take the climbers' path northwest of the campground knoll, up steep tundra and snow on the Meany Snowfield to Meany Crest, a rock outcrop at roughly 7,350-7,500 ft with flat sites and stone wind breaks. This is the standard high camp.

Above Meany Crest gain the toe of the Fryingpan Glacier and rope up. Climb south and southwest across the lower apron to the broad notch between the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers at about 9,000-9,100 ft, then traverse and climb the upper Whitman across a bergschrund to about 10,500-11,000 ft, where snow gives way to rock.

The basin holds heavy snow and the approach slopes can be avalanche terrain in soft early-season conditions. Afternoon whiteout and thunderstorm activity is common on Rainier's flanks.
wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder.season: Roughly Jun through Aug, best early July to early August — firm morning snow, drier rock, and bridges not yet melted out
hazards: Loose volcanic rock and rockfall on the summit gully and crest, worsening through the day
Crevasses and weakening bridges on the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers, worst in August and September
A bergschrund that is a step-across early season and a problem late
Cliff-out potential between Summerland and Meany Crest if the line drifts climber's right
Avalanche potential on the Meany Snowfield in soft or early-season conditions
Major exposure on the final crest, with about 2,000 ft to the Emmons on the north side
wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder.baseFinding:
Whitman Notch at about 9,100 ft is the arrival, and you know it by what becomes visible rather than by the altimeter: it is the first place the Whitman Glacier comes into view. Until you can see a second glacier on the far side, you have not reached the notch.

The base of the climbing proper is higher still, and it is a change of surface: at about 10,500-11,000 ft the snow ends and a loose rock-and-scree gully begins. That transition is the base. The sequence above it is countable and in this order: gully, a short step of about 6 ft, a gully-chimney, the summit notch, then an exposed scramble along the crest.

The route-finding trap is low, not high, and it is the one thing on this climb that regularly commits parties to bad ground: between Summerland and Meany Crest, if you find yourself contouring climber's right into a bowl under rock bands, you are cliffed out and off the line. The cairned and boot-packed line stays left of that bowl. Fix this by going back to the last cairn, not by traversing further.

The summit-crest test is a negative and it is unambiguous: the last 30 to 100 ft is a narrow crumbling andesite crest with roughly 2,000 ft dropping away to the Emmons Glacier on the north side. If the ground is not falling away on both sides of you, you have not reached the true summit — you are on the notch or a subsidiary block below it.

Timing as a finding: the andesite loosens as the sun works on it, and the crevasse bridges soften through the day. Being at the notch early is not tidiness, it is the whole plan.

wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder.name: White River Campground and the Wonderland Trail to Summerland

bivy.name: Meany Crest
bivy.notes: The standard high camp for Little Tahoma, and the one that makes the climb reasonable. It is a large flat area within the cliff band directly above Summerland, gained by the climbers' path and scrambling out of the basin, and it also serves Whitman Crest and the spires on that shoulder. From here the Fryingpan Glacier lies immediately ahead and the summit is a manageable morning rather than an epic. It is exposed — the shelf catches wind off the mountain and there is nothing to hide behind — so build walls if the forecast is doubtful and site the tent where a rockfall from the band above cannot reach it. Getting a permit for the zone is generally far easier than getting one of Summerland's few designated sites, which is a second, practical reason to camp high.
bivy.water: Meltwater runnels and small falls at the edge of the snow through most of the season — parties routinely find running water a short walk from camp. Late in a dry summer it thins out, so carry a stove and be prepared to melt
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit issued for the cross-country zone rather than a named site, obtained the same way and at the same per-person nightly rate as an established camp. Zone rules govern the pitch: well back from trails, at least a hundred feet from water, and on snow, rock or bare durable ground — never on the meadow. The climbing cost-recovery fee applies to this trip regardless of where you sleep, since the route crosses glaciers. There is no toilet, so human waste must be packed out; the park's blue bag system exists for exactly this and is the expected practice on any glaciated route here.
bivy.capacity: A broad, flat rock and snow shelf with room for several tents; no designated sites, no numbers, and no facilities

bivy.name: Summerland Camp
bivy.notes: The subalpine meadow basin that everything on this side of the mountain stages from, a little over four miles up the Wonderland Trail from the Fryingpan Creek bridge. For Little Tahoma it is the lower of the two realistic camps and much the more comfortable one — running water, a toilet, a stone shelter to cook under in bad weather, and a designated pitch. The catch is the site count and the competition: these are among the most sought-after backcountry sites in the park and they book out for midsummer weekends, with Wonderland Trail through-hikers taking most of them. Early season, before the Wonderland traffic builds, is when a climbing party can most easily get in. Camping here rather than higher costs you roughly 1,600 feet and a cliff band on summit morning, which turns Little Tahoma into a genuinely long day, so most parties treat Summerland as a staging night rather than a high camp.
bivy.water: Fryingpan Creek runs through the meadow just below the shelter and is reliable all season; treat it
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit, required for every overnight. In 2026 that is roughly twelve dollars per person per night for anyone sixteen and over, plus a per-trip application fee, booked through the federal reservation system with about two thirds of capacity reservable in advance and the rest held for walk-ups; walk-up permits are issued in person at the White River Wilderness Information Center on this side of the park, or at Longmire or Carbon River. The park's separate climbing cost-recovery fee — about eighty-two dollars a head — is NOT triggered by camping here, but IS triggered the moment you step onto the Fryingpan or Whitman Glacier, or go above 10,000 feet, which every route on Little Tahoma does. Pay it online before you arrive and bring proof; a climbing permit will not be issued to a team until every member has paid.
bivy.capacity: A handful of designated individual sites — around five — plus a stone shelter built by the Civilian Conservation Corps a little below them, and a backcountry toilet

bivy.name: Toe of the Fryingpan Glacier
bivy.notes: A slightly higher and more committed alternative to Meany Crest, on the moraine and snow where the Fryingpan Glacier begins. It shaves a little more off summit morning and puts you on the ice within minutes of leaving the tent, which is worth something on a route where the Whitman Glacier softens badly through the day and the descent is best done before it does. The ground is rubble and old ice rather than a shelf, so expect to build a platform, and expect the good spots to have moved since whatever description you read. The glacier here has been retreating steadily, which is the honest caveat: this camp is described differently in accounts a decade apart, and its condition should be treated as a current-season question rather than settled.
bivy.water: Glacial meltwater at the snout in warm weather, silty and worth settling before filtering, or snow to melt. Carry fuel on the assumption you will be melting
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone wilderness permit, same as Meany Crest. The climbing cost-recovery fee is unavoidable at this point — you are camping at the edge of a glacier. Pack out all human waste; there are no facilities above Summerland at all.
bivy.capacity: A small number of parties on moraine and snow at the glacier's lower edge; informal, and the usable ground shifts as the ice recedes

bivy.name: Whitman Glacier notch camp
bivy.notes: The highest of the three camps, in the prominent gap on the crest between the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers, just under the base of the peak itself. It reduces summit day to a short glacier walk and the East Shoulder scramble, which is its whole justification. Everything else about it is a cost: it is cold, wind-hammered, waterless, and small enough that a third party arriving has nowhere to go. Little Tahoma's summit block is notoriously loose volcanic rock and the peak is the site of one of the largest rockfalls recorded in the range, so where you site a tent relative to the slopes above matters more here than anywhere lower on the route. Sound judgement is to camp high only if the freezing level is low enough to keep the mountain frozen overnight.
bivy.water: Snow only. No running water at this elevation — carry all fuel for the bivouac and for summit day
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone wilderness permit, plus the climbing cost-recovery fee, which is mandatory here in every sense. Registration for the climb is completed in person at a wilderness information center before you start, and the climbing rangers' account of current glacier and rockfall conditions is worth treating as part of the plan rather than a formality. Blue bags for all waste.
bivy.capacity: Two or three tents in the gap, dug into snow; very limited and fully exposed

wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder.notes: The Fryingpan Creek trailhead and its spur trail are closed for the bridge replacement, planned to last into 2029. Park at White River Campground, where parking is limited, and follow the Wonderland Trail to Summerland. From Summerland the climb is unchanged: the climbers' path to Meany Crest, the Fryingpan Glacier and Whitman Notch.

wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder.name: From Paradise across the Cowlitz and Ingraham glaciers
wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder.notes:
From the Paradise parking lot, climb the standard Camp Muir route to about 8,600 ft. Leave it there and traverse east onto the Paradise Glacier and across the Cowlitz, holding elevation to stay above the cliff and serac band below, then through a notch in the Cathedral Rocks cleaver and across the Ingraham Glacier to a snow or rock ramp at the base of Little Tahoma's south and east face near 8,900 ft.

Camps are made on the Cowlitz or Ingraham glaciers, or on the more exposed Cathedral Rocks cleaver.

Above the ramp the route climbs the Whitman Glacier and exits its upper left-hand corner into a gully, climbs about two-thirds of it to a short step, continues up a gully-chimney to the summit notch, and finishes with a short loose scramble along the crest.

The Paradise road stays open far later into winter than the roads on the north and east sides, which is the whole reason this variant exists.
wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder.season: Nov-May, while the White River road to Summerland is shut
hazards: Serac fall and crevasse hazard across an extended Cowlitz and Ingraham traverse
A cliff and serac band immediately below the traverse line, which is why elevation must be held
Wind-slab avalanche potential on the ramp gaining the face in early season
Loose rock in the summit gully-chimney and on the final crest scramble
A long committing traverse with the same ground to reverse on the way out
wa_little_tahoma_east_shoulder.baseFinding:
The decision is at 8,600 ft and it is a leaving, not an arriving. You step off the Camp Muir track while still about 1,500 ft below Camp Muir. If you reach Camp Muir you have gone too far — by a vertical quarter of a mile, on the busiest bootpack on the mountain, which is exactly why it happens.

Count what you cross: three glaciers and one rock cleaver, in this order — Paradise, Cowlitz, then a notch in Cathedral Rocks, then the Ingraham. If you have crossed the Cowlitz and walked into rock without finding a notch, you are below the notch and need to regain height. The traverse deliberately holds elevation to stay above a serac and cliff band; drifting down is the error that feels easy at the time.

The base is a ramp, and it is the only ramp: a snow or rock ramp at about 8,900 ft leading onto the south and east face. Arriving at the foot of a face with no ramp means you are round the wrong side of it.

The negative that separates this from the peak's other route: the standard line on Little Tahoma comes from the Fryingpan side, over Whitman Notch, from the east. This one comes from Paradise, from the southwest, and never goes near Summerland or Meany Crest.

Why this route exists and when it stops working: it is the winter line, done before the Cowlitz and Ingraham become too broken to cross safely. Once those glaciers open up, the traverse is the hazard rather than the climb.

wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.name: From the north — Cascade Pass and the glacier corridor
camps: Crest bivouacs above the South Cascade and Chickamin glaciers
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.notes: Lizard has no trailhead of its own and is normally met partway through the high traverse rather than approached. From the Cascade River Road end, the maintained trail switchbacks up a forested rib and then traverses meadow and talus to Cascade Pass, which is the last built tread of the trip. Leave it there and work south and east across the Mixup flank on boot path, talus and snow to the Cache Glacier and Cache Col, then drop the steep snow on the far side to the tarn at Kool-Aid Lake. Beyond, the Red Ledge cuts the cliff band west of Art's Knoll, then the Middle Cascade Glacier leads to the Spider-Formidable col and down to Yang Yang Lakes. From there the line climbs past Le Conte Mountain, crosses the Le Conte Glacier to the gap north of Sentinel Peak, and crosses the South Cascade Glacier to the col at its head before dropping into the White Rock Lakes basin. Lizard is the side trip from that camp: climb back out of the basin northeast to the broad notch on the peak's south ridge.
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.season: Mid-July through September, once the Cache Col snow has consolidated and the Red Ledge is clear of verglas; the whole corridor has to be in condition, not just the peak.
hazards: roped glacier travel on the Cache, Middle Cascade, Le Conte and South Cascade Glaciers, with crevasses opening through late season
steep heather above the Cache Col descent, where a slip runs out onto rock
the Red Ledge can hold an open moat, verglas or fresh snow well into summer
whiteout navigation at the Spider-Formidable col, with no bail once past Cache Col
loose blocks on the summit ridge itself
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.baseFinding: The col is the reference, and it is the only place on this mountain where you can see both basins at once. The notch you want is the broad pass in the south ridge at a little over 6,800 ft, roughly two thousand feet of horizontal distance west of the summit. Standing in it, White Rock Lakes should be below you to the southwest and South Cascade Glacier ice below you to the northeast; the ground rising off the col toward the high point is a single broad, blocky, loose ridge of only about six hundred vertical feet, and the top of it is visible from where you stand. If you cannot see both the lakes and the glacier from the notch, or if what rises above you is far more than six hundred feet, or if you have to step back onto glacier ice to keep going up, you are at the wrong gap in the ridge. Nothing on the correct line is harder than hands-on scrambling on loose blocks — if you meet a step that makes you want a rope, you have drifted off the crest onto the flanks, where the rubble is worst. Stay near the crest and keep the party out of each other's fall line rather than strung out directly below.

wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.name: From the south — Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek (road closed at milepost 4)

bivy.name: Crest bivouacs above the South Cascade and Chickamin glaciers
bivy.notes: Say it plainly: these are not sites, they are wherever a party gets to. Elephant Head is the southernmost peak, standing on the divide above the lakes at the south end of the crest with big cliffs dropping east into the head of the west fork of Agnes Creek, between the ice on either side. It gets a handful of ascents in a decade and there is no established camp for it, so parties climbing it either work out from the lake basin below or level a spot on the divide and accept a dry, exposed night. The same is true of anyone caught out on the South Cascade side by weather or by a slower day than planned. The season is short and matters more here than anywhere else: July into August has the glaciers covered and the bivouac snow usable, while September brings open crevasses, bare ice and no water at all. Anyone planning a night on this ground should carry the fuel to melt snow and treat the whole thing as an unplanned shelter that happens to be foreseeable.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and unreliable after midsummer. The last certain water on this stretch is the lakes below, and everything east of the divide is snow, ice and bare rock.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or ice, never on the heather benches. Pack out human waste. No fires; there is nothing to burn and nothing that would recover.
bivy.capacity: Whatever the party can level. Rock rings, gravel benches and snow platforms for one party at a time, scattered along the divide. No toilet and no established sites of any kind.

approachLogistics.trailhead: Downey Creek Trailhead (Trail #768, Suiattle River Road)

wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.notes: Not usable while the Suiattle River Road stays closed at milepost 4 under a Forest Service order in effect April 2, 2026 through January 1, 2028 unless rescinded sooner; washouts cut off the Downey Creek Trailhead, and the Forest Service's Miner's Fire order (06-05-26-17) also closes the trailhead and the Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek trails from August 15 through December 31, 2026. Before the closure this was the other end of the same corridor. From the Downey Creek Trailhead on the Suiattle River Road, Downey Creek Trail #768 enters wilderness within the first half mile and climbs gently through old growth, crossing tributary creeks that run high in early season, to the Bachelor Creek junction. The Bachelor Creek path is unmaintained, steadily steeper, and notorious for blowdown, with an alder and slide-alder band around 3,800 to 4,400 ft that becomes a genuine bushwhack when snow has not flattened it. It fords Bachelor Creek itself, which runs fast and cold with snowmelt. Above treeline the tread breaks into meadows near Bachelor Meadows and reaches Cub Lake, reliable water and a common first camp. A steep, often snow-covered pitch gains Itswoot Ridge; from there the route climbs to Spire Col, descends the Dana Glacier to White Rock Lakes, and regains the col on Lizard's south ridge from the lakes.
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.season: Late July through September. The Bachelor Creek brush is worst before the snow has settled it and the Bachelor Creek ford is worst during peak melt.
hazards: road and trailhead cut off by washouts on the Suiattle River Road; check status
sustained blowdown and slide-alder bushwhacking on the Bachelor Creek path
the Bachelor Creek ford during snowmelt
crevasse hazard on the Dana Glacier below Spire Col
multi-day evacuation distance with no cell coverage
loose blocks near the summit crest
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route.baseFinding: The col is the reference, and it is the only place on this mountain where you can see both basins at once. Climbing out of the White Rock Lakes basin you reach a broad pass in the south ridge at a little over 6,800 ft, roughly two thousand feet of horizontal distance west of the summit. From it, White Rock Lakes lie below to the southwest and South Cascade Glacier ice lies below to the northeast; the ground rising toward the high point is one broad, blocky, loose ridge of only about six hundred vertical feet, with its top visible from where you stand. If you cannot see both the lakes and the glacier from the notch, or if what rises above you is far more than six hundred feet, or if you have to step back onto glacier ice to keep gaining height, you are at the wrong gap. Nothing on the correct line is harder than hands-on scrambling — a step that makes you want a rope means you have drifted off the crest onto the flanks, which carry the worst of the rubble. Stay near the crest, and keep the party abreast rather than strung out directly below one another.

wa_lundin_peak_west_ridge.name: Commonwealth Basin and Lundin Basin

bivy.name: Commonwealth Basin and Red Pond
bivy.notes: This is the natural overnight for Lundin Peak and for Red Mountain, and it is the only site here that sits directly beneath its objectives rather than across a ridge from them. From the pass the PCT runs north about two and a half miles before the Commonwealth Basin trail branches left and climbs the basin; spur paths reach Red Pond at around three and a half to four miles, with Red Pass another half mile above at roughly 5,400 ft. Red Mountain's scramble leaves from near the pass, and Lundin's west ridge is gained by traversing the ridge crest west from the same ground, so a camp at the pond removes the entire approach from the summit day. Be honest about the trade: both peaks are comfortable day climbs car-to-car and most parties do them that way, so this is a way to buy a relaxed morning or to rescue a late finish rather than a necessity. The basin is snowbound and avalanche-prone well into spring, and the old trail below the pond is steep and eroded in places.
bivy.water: The creek through Commonwealth Basin runs all summer and Red Pond holds water into autumn. Treat everything. The upper basin melts out late and can be entirely snow-covered into early July.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the PCT trailhead, required for day and overnight use roughly May 15 to October 31. Party size capped at 12. Unlike Melakwa, Snow and Gravel Lakes, this basin is NOT on the designated-sites-only list, so dispersed camping is legal here — which puts the whole burden on siting well, on durable ground and away from the water. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft, which covers the pond and the upper basin. Parking at the exit 52 trailhead takes a Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass; in winter the lot becomes a Sno-Park and needs the state permit instead. No drones anywhere in the wilderness.
bivy.capacity: Informal established sites scattered through the basin and a small amount of level ground by the pond; a handful of parties rather than a large camp

approachLogistics.trailhead: PCT North Trailhead (Snoqualmie Pass, I-90 Exit 52)

wa_lundin_peak_west_ridge.notes:
From the PCT-North / Commonwealth Basin trailhead off the Alpental road (about 3,000 ft), follow the Pacific Crest Trail northbound; within roughly half a mile bear left onto the Commonwealth Basin use trail, which climbs gently along Commonwealth Creek through old-growth for about 1.7 miles as the valley opens out.

Near 4,200 ft leave the main Red Pass tread and cut west, contouring into Lundin Basin below Red Mountain's south face. From there climb a broad couloir — snow in early season, scree and talus by late summer — up the steep south side of Lundin to gain the West Ridge at its notch.

This is much the better line while snow still covers the basin: it buries the brush and the boulders, and parties report a long glissade on the way out. Once melted out the lower basin is brushy with steep scree and talus, and that is the reason many parties switch to the Cave Ridge approach late in the season.

Commonwealth Creek is reliable water low down; nothing above is dependable, so fill up in the basin.
wa_lundin_peak_west_ridge.season: Jun-Jul on snow is the good window; brushy and slow once melted out
hazards: wet-slide and sluffing in the south-face couloir under afternoon sun - axe, crampons if firm, early season
heavy brush and steep loose scree in the basin once the snow is gone
no reliable water above Commonwealth Creek
the ridge is unsafe wet and unsafe without rock gear
wa_lundin_peak_west_ridge.baseFinding:
Both approaches converge at the low notch on the West Ridge, near 5,800 ft, and that notch is where the technical climbing starts — nothing below it needs a rope.

Coming up from the basin, aim for a depression in the face beneath the notch. Climb easy class 3 ground up to that depression, then the slabby depression itself is the crux of the entry, class 4 to low fifth, and you bear right at the top of it to arrive in the notch. If you are climbing slab and it does not lead to a col within a rope length or two, you picked the wrong depression.

Negative markers. If you gained the crest somewhere that walks easily on both sides, you are on the ridge but past the notch and the climbing above will not match any description. And if you find yourself scrambling straight at the summit block instead of setting out along a ridge, you came up the south face rather than to the west ridge notch.

The ridge involves class 4 to mid fifth moves and wants rock gear. Do not attempt it wet.

wa_lundin_peak_west_ridge.name: Cave Ridge traverse from Alpental
wa_lundin_peak_west_ridge.notes:
Park at the Alpental day-use lot and find the unmarked, unmaintained Snoqualmie Mountain climbers' trail that starts about 50 ft south of the signed Snow Lake trailhead. It crosses below a small waterfall and climbs steeply through forest and slide alder.

At an unsigned split around 4,600 ft, paths fork toward Snoqualmie Mountain, Cave Ridge and Lundin. Take the Cave Ridge / Lundin fork, cross over Cave Ridge near its low notch, then follow an ascending climbers'-trail traverse below the ridge crest — staying on the Commonwealth Basin, north, side — to the West Ridge notch.

This skirts the brushy lower basin entirely, which is why parties prefer it once the snow has gone. There is no reliable water past the trailhead.
hazards: exposed and sometimes loose climbers'-trail traverse beneath Cave Ridge
early-season snow traverse on the crossing that can warrant an axe
unsigned trail split around 4,600 ft with three destinations
slide alder low down
no reliable water past the trailhead
wa_lundin_peak_west_ridge.baseFinding:
You arrive directly at the low notch on the West Ridge, around 5,800 ft, which is where the technical climbing begins. Arriving by this line you should be traversing beneath the crest on the north (Commonwealth) side and then step up into a col with the ridge rising to your right toward the summit.

If the traverse has you on the south side looking down into Lundin Basin, you have crossed the crest too early. If you top out on a walkable ridge with no notch, you have gone past.

As with the basin approach, the entry from below the notch goes class 3 to a slabby depression, then class 4 to low fifth up the depression, bearing right into the notch.

wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.name: Lower Monument Basin and the left-angling ramp
camps: Lake of the Woods and the Eureka Falls camp
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.notes: Monument is the most rugged thing in this group and sits nearly as an island, with Eureka Creek wrapping three sides of it. The travelled approach is the Monument Creek trail from the Lost River road: well maintained through old growth for about four miles to the Eureka Creek confluence, then unmaintained, brushy and deadfall-choked, with a ford of Eureka Creek that can run thigh to waist deep in early summer. From there the abandoned tread climbs onto Pistol Ridge and over Pistol Pass, and most parties camp near Lake of the Woods. Three other approaches exist off Slate Pass and Buckskin Ridge by way of the Ferguson Lake trail and reach the same basin from the north. Summit day is long enough that finishing the last talus by headlamp is common.
hazards: Loose blocky talus on the whole upper mountain
Exposed scrambling on the final summit block
A snowfield below the summit that can hold firm or icy into midsummer
Eureka Creek ford, cold and high with early-season snowmelt
Faint, unmaintained tread beyond Pistol Pass, worse on the return
Long, remote, multi-day approach with no cell service
wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.baseFinding: The base of the climb is marked by water, which is convenient because you should be stopping there anyway. From high camp, traverse northwest to the saddle below Lake Mountain around 7,400 ft, then drop into Lower Monument Basin at roughly 6,100 ft. The outlet creek running from the lake in that basin is the last dependable water on the peak and it sits directly beneath the route; late in the season it can shrink to a trickle but the drainage is still obvious. Fill bottles, then look up and to the left for a ramp system that angles left across the face above you. That ramp is the start of the climbing and it is the feature to identify: it is a continuous weakness slanting up and left, not a gully, and it delivers you onto the south ridge crest at about 6,900 ft. Once you are on the crest the ground flattens into a broad talus highway that runs for well over a mile toward the summit, and that flatness is itself the confirmation that you gained the ridge in the right place rather than on a side rib. Two things mislead near the top. A false summit around 8,000 ft takes a short scramble and looks convincing; the true top is a distinctive leaning horn of granite, so if what you are standing on is not leaning you are not finished. And a steep snowfield sits just below the true summit well into midsummer, which can be crossed with an axe or turned on rock to its left, but should not be glissaded on the way down because it stays firm.

wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.name: From Slate Pass by Robinson Creek and the Ferguson Lake trail

bivy.name: Lake of the Woods and the Eureka Falls camp
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Monument Peak and Lake Mountain and it is worth being clear that they are approached from a completely different point on the Harts Pass road than the crest peaks — the Monument Creek trailhead at about 2,400 feet, roughly seven miles up from Mazama, thirteen miles short of the pass. The route runs up the Lost River valley, crosses Eureka Creek where the bridge has been out in the past, then climbs the abandoned Pistol Ridge trail to Pistol Pass at 7,100 feet before dropping to the lake. Expect around thirty miles and thirteen thousand feet over three to four days for both summits — Monument at 8,592 feet by its south ridge, Lake Mountain at 8,371 by its east ridge, each a short steep scramble from the basin. The Pistol Ridge trail is unmaintained and route-finding through it is part of the work. An alternative for parties coming from the north is to drop off Lake Mountain into Eureka Creek and camp near the south fork, which shortens things considerably if the traverse is already underway. Late September brings the larches and cold clear nights; earlier in the summer the long dry climb to the pass is punishing.
bivy.water: The lake is dependable and so is Eureka Creek down in the valley. Between them, though, is the crux: the creek crossing about four miles in is the last certain water before an eight-mile climb gaining five thousand feet to the pass, and in a hot late-summer spell that carry is what makes or breaks the day. Fill completely at the creek.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Monument Creek trailhead kiosk, no quota. No parking pass or fee is needed at this trailhead. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of the lake shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock, and the usual prohibition on tying animals to trees overnight.
bivy.capacity: Lake of the Woods is a small alpine basin with room for a couple of tents on the benches below Lake Mountain. The Eureka Falls site down in the valley near the confluence of the Lost River and Eureka Creek is a forested camp taking a party or two. Neither is developed.

wa_monument_peak_pasayten_scramble.notes: Gentler, though not shorter. Drop north from Slate Pass to the Robinson Creek trail along the Middle Fork Pasayten, then near the big meadow horse camp take the Ferguson Lake trail, which descends about seven miles to Eureka Creek just south of the peak. From there, pick a line up the south side or into the basin between Monument and Lake Mountain.

wa_mount_adams_mazama_glacier_headwall.name: Bird Creek Meadows and Sunrise Camp, on the Yakama Reservation side
wa_mount_adams_mazama_glacier_headwall.notes:
This is the southeast side of the mountain and the approach crosses Yakama Nation land, which makes it an access problem before it is a climbing problem. A tribal-use permit for Tract D is required, bought at the fee station on entry at the Mirror Lake gate — it cannot be obtained in advance — and it is only available when the area is open to non-tribal use. The Yakama Nation sets that window for non-members each year, somewhere between July and early autumn. The area has also been closed outright in some years, so confirm with the Yakama Nation before building a trip around this approach; there is no alternative way in from this side.

From the Bird Creek Meadows parking area (about 5,576–5,700 ft), the trail is easy to follow to roughly 6,700 ft. Above that it is route-finding: any number of lines through moraine, scree and glacier remnants lead up to Sunrise Camp at about 8,300 ft. Carry a map — locating the camp is the part people get wrong. Trailhead to camp is about 3–4 hours.

Sunrise Camp sits at the base of the Mazama Glacier, tucked between the glacier and a small rock hill, with hand-built rock shelters. It is a fine fair-weather camp and a poor one otherwise: it is exposed to winds that can reach hurricane strength, and to rockfall off the glacier. The rock walls help, but only somewhat.

From camp to summit is about 5 hours.
wa_mount_adams_mazama_glacier_headwall.season: Summer; non-tribal access to this side has historically been limited to a mid-summer to early-autumn window
hazards: Tribal-use permit required and only sold at the gate, in a limited seasonal window — no advance purchase, and the area has been closed in some years
Route-finding through moraine and scree above 6,700 ft to locate Sunrise Camp
Rockfall off the glacier onto Sunrise Camp
Extreme wind exposure at camp
Bergschrunds around 9,500 ft
Mistaking Piker's Peak, where the route tops out, for the true summit
wa_mount_adams_mazama_glacier_headwall.baseFinding:
The climbing starts directly above camp — the first ground you cross after leaving Sunrise Camp is the glacier itself, so the recognition problem here is finding camp, not finding the base.

Sunrise Camp: at roughly 8,300 ft, a flat with rock wind shelters, wedged between the toe of the Mazama Glacier on one side and a small rock hill on the other. If you are on open moraine with no rock hill beside you, you are short of it or off to one side; the terrain between 6,700 and 8,300 ft has many plausible lines and only some of them end at the camp.

Above camp the sequence is legible. Long stretches of glacier at about 40 degrees, then bear right onto the headwall proper, which runs about 45 degrees and is where pickets earn their place. Bergschrunds appear around 9,500 ft. The glacier narrows as it climbs.

The top is where the route makes you choose. Nearing Piker's Peak — the south summit at 11,644 ft — you can exit left onto easy 25–30 degree ground, or stay right for a short technical finish: roughly 40 ft of 60–70 degree snow and ice on the southeast corner, worth two or three screws.

Critical negative marker at the top: Piker's Peak is not the summit of Mount Adams. When the ground flattens out you have reached the south summit; the true summit is a further dome across the plateau to the north, with the geographic high point to the east. This route tops out on the false summit by design, so treat the flattening as a halfway signal rather than an arrival.

wa_mount_adams_mazama_glacier_headwall.name: Cold Springs and the Round the Mountain trail
wa_mount_adams_mazama_glacier_headwall.notes: From the Cold Springs trailhead, climb the South Climb trail to the Round the Mountain trail and follow it east across the lava flows to the reservation boundary and the edge of Bird Creek Meadows, then turn uphill onto the moraine toward the Mazama Glacier and Sunrise Camp. The turnoff is farther along the Round the Mountain trail than many descriptions suggest. A Recreation Pass is needed at Cold Springs.

wa_mount_adams_mount_adams_circumnavigat.name: Start and finish at Killen Creek
wa_mount_adams_mount_adams_circumnavigat.notes: Climb the Killen Creek trail to the crest trail and the Highline trail, then go around the east side of the mountain off trail, cross the untrailed gap on the Yakama side, and return along the Round the Mountain trail and the crest trail. The gap is open only a few weeks a year and needs glacier skills and route finding.

wa_mount_adams_mount_adams_circumnavigat.name: Start and finish at Cold Springs
wa_mount_adams_mount_adams_circumnavigat.notes: Start on the South Climb trail from Cold Springs and climb steeply toward Sunrise Camp, then circle the mountain mostly between 7,000 and 8,000 ft across many glaciers and moraines, picking up the Round the Mountain trail east of Horseshoe Meadows to return. It is a little shorter than the Killen Creek start.

wa_mount_anderson_eel_glacier.name: Dosewallips road walk, West Fork to Anderson Pass and the tarn camp
camps: Camp Siberia / Anderson Pass shelter area
wa_mount_anderson_eel_glacier.notes:
From US-101 at Brinnon, drive Dosewallips Road about 8.5 miles to the road-end parking and leave the car there; the road beyond has been closed to vehicles since the 2002 flood, and the washout itself is about a mile farther on. A mountain bike genuinely saves hours on the road miles. A short bypass trail with a few switchbacks gets round the washout, then the abandoned roadbed resumes for roughly 5.6 miles to the Dosewallips Ranger Station at about 1,600 ft.

From the ranger station take the Dosewallips River Trail 1.4 miles to the West Fork junction, then the West Fork Trail upstream past Dose Forks, Big Timber and Diamond Meadows to Honeymoon Meadows at 3,527 ft, roughly 8 trail miles on. Expect at least one calf-to-knee ford of the West Fork depending on snowmelt, and substantial blowdown — maintenance has lagged since the road closed. Beyond Honeymoon Meadows the trail climbs past Camp Siberia to Anderson Pass at 4,464 ft.

Leave the maintained trail at the pass and follow the climbers' path up the moraine to a camp on the snowy saddle above a small tarn at about 5,100 ft (Anderson or Valkyrie Lake). Most parties take 7-9 hours trailhead to camp. Fill up at the tarn; there is nothing above it.
wa_mount_anderson_eel_glacier.season: Best spring to early summer, while the snow finger below Flypaper Pass is still continuous. By late summer that finger has thinned and steepened and the bergschrund above it has opened
hazards: Crevasses on the upper Eel Glacier, including large ones on its eastern slopes
A bergschrund at the head of the Eel that is hardest to cross late in the season, with a short steep step above it
The Flypaper Pass snow finger at 40-45 degrees, firm or icy, steeper than older descriptions state
Glide avalanches and cornice-triggered slides off the cliffs above the glacier terminus
Loose, crumbly meta-sedimentary rock on the final summit scramble
Unbridged fords and heavy blowdown on the West Fork trail, plus roughly 6.5 miles of closed road at each end
wa_mount_anderson_eel_glacier.baseFinding:
The base of the climb is Flypaper Pass, and the test is which things are on which side of it. Flypaper Pass at about 6,500 ft is the notch between Mount Anderson on the east and Echo Rock (7,033 ft) on the west. Standing in the notch, Anderson is on your right and Echo Rock on your left when you are facing north through it. If both walls beside you are the same mountain, you are in a gully on a flank rather than in the pass.

The approach test, done before you can see the notch, is the tarn. From the camp saddle, traverse above the tarn — often still frozen — and take the single steep snow finger that runs up from the far side of it. There is one finger and it goes to one notch. If you are walking round the tarn at its level rather than above it, you have dropped too low and will meet cliffs.

Second test, and it is the one that says the pass is in the condition you planned for: the finger's steepest section now runs 40 degrees or more. Glacier recession has steepened it well beyond the older published figure of about 30 degrees over 300 vertical feet, so a party that finds it far steeper than the book has not gone the wrong way — those descriptions are old. If it has melted out to bare scree and ice, that is the season telling you to come back earlier, not a route-finding error.

What going too far looks like: over the pass the ground drops onto the Eel Glacier and a bergschrund cuts across below the headwall, forcing an end-around to one side. If you are on glacier and looking for a way past a schrund, you are past the base and onto the climb.

wa_mount_anderson_eel_glacier.name: East Fork Quinault and Enchanted Valley to Anderson Pass from the west

bivy.name: Tarn camp above Anderson Pass
bivy.notes: Planned high camp and the one worth reaching — open slopes above Anderson/Valkyrie Lake, roughly a mile past the pass up the climbers' path and moraine, and preferred by parties specifically to avoid sleeping in the forest at or below the pass. Budget 7-9 hours from the road closure to here. This is the last water on the route: the snow finger to Flypaper Pass and everything on the Eel above it has none, so fill here or plan to melt. Exposed to wind, with no built shelter.
bivy.water: the tarn when melted out; often still frozen in spring, so melt snow
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required year-round for all overnight stays
bivy.capacity: a few tents on open ground near the tarn

wa_mount_anderson_eel_glacier.notes:
Anderson Pass is a divide, and the Quinault side of it is a maintained trail too. From the Graves Creek trailhead at the end of the South Shore Quinault road, the East Fork Quinault Trail runs up the valley through Enchanted Valley to the pass. It is a longer valley walk than the Dosewallips side but it is a trail the whole way, with no closed road at the start and no West Fork fords, which in a wet year is the difference between the two.

At Anderson Pass the two approaches become one: leave the maintained trail and follow the climbers' path up the moraine to the tarn camp at about 5,100 ft, then the snow finger to Flypaper Pass.

Mileages published for the Quinault side vary widely with where the count starts and with the current state of the road, so none is quoted here.
wa_mount_anderson_eel_glacier.season: Same window as the standard side — the pass and the snow finger above it decide the season, not the valley
hazards: Everything above the pass is the same: the 40-45 degree snow finger, the Eel Glacier crevasses and bergschrund, and loose summit rock
A long valley walk with river crossings and blowdown of its own
Arriving at the pass from the west means the shelter and the climbers' path are both below and behind you as you crest it
No cell coverage anywhere on either side
wa_mount_anderson_eel_glacier.baseFinding:
Identical to the Dosewallips variant above, because both arrive at Anderson Pass and everything above the pass is shared: traverse above the tarn, take the one steep snow finger from its far side, and know you are at Flypaper Pass when Mount Anderson is on one side of the notch and Echo Rock on the other.

The extra test this side needs is at the pass itself, because you arrive there from the opposite direction. Anderson Pass is a signed trail junction — the West Fork Dosewallips and East Fork Quinault trails meet there, with the Anderson Pass shelter (Camp Siberia) just below on the Dosewallips side at roughly 4,180 ft. The climbers' path leaves north off the pass and up the moraine. If you have walked over the pass and begun descending the other valley, you have missed the turn; it is a boot path, not a signed one.

wa_mount_angeles_standard.name: Klahhane Ridge climbers' trail from Hurricane Ridge
wa_mount_angeles_standard.notes: Paved path off the east end of the visitor centre lot, then open subalpine ridge for about two and a half miles to an unsigned split. A shorter, steeper start climbs from the Switchback Trail on the road below and joins higher up. Nothing dependable to drink past the visitor centre — carry it all.
hazards: Fractured, rotten rock on the summit block with holds that break
Rockfall funnelling down the crux gully onto anyone below
Rotten snow choking the summit notch into July and August
Exposed Class 3 moves with a fall of well over a hundred feet
Fast-building afternoon storms on a fully exposed ridge
wa_mount_angeles_standard.baseFinding: The climbers' path leaves the maintained Klahhane Ridge Trail at an unsigned fork roughly 2.3 miles out: bear left and uphill to the north, where the maintained tread carries on right along the ridge toward Victor Pass and Lake Angeles. From the fork the primitive path climbs rocky meadow on the peak's west side and does about eight hundred of the day's feet in a little over half a mile, topping out near 6,000 ft in a scree bowl beneath the summit block. The identification that matters here is which notch, and it catches people every season: do not scramble the first notch you reach. The boot path keeps traversing higher and the gully that goes is further along, directly beneath the true summit. Stay on the worn tread climber's-left of the open scree fan rather than going straight up the fan itself, which is the rockfall funnel. You are at the base when the meadow ends and you are standing on dirty, fractured ledges with a roughly forty-foot exposed step above you. If the ground has levelled off or you are back on maintained tread heading toward Lake Angeles, you have overshot.

wa_mount_angeles_standard.name: Switchback Trail up to Klahhane Ridge

bivy.name: Heart o' the Hills campground
bivy.notes: This is the staging base for Mount Angeles and it is a staging base only — it is a few miles up the Hurricane Ridge road from Port Angeles, and no part of the climb passes through it. The scramble itself starts from a pull-out around mile 15 on that road, where the Switchback trail gains about 700 ft in six-tenths of a mile to its junction with the trail from Hurricane Ridge, then about half a mile west along that trail and a spur onto the unmaintained final ridge — exposed walking and class 3 on loose fractured rock to the 6,454 ft summit. It is a day trip for a fit party, so this camp exists for the group that starts late, gets weathered off, or wants to be at the trailhead at first light. Read the road before you count on it: in winter the Hurricane Ridge road is plowed and open only Friday through Sunday plus a few holiday dates, with uphill traffic released from mid-morning, and it closes without notice in bad weather. Recent seasons have also brought midweek closures for utility work in the weeks after Memorial Day, so check the current schedule rather than assuming summer means open. Because there are no reservations, arrive early on a summer weekend.
bivy.water: Drinking water on tap, flush toilets and rubbish collection through the season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — frontcountry campground, nightly fee paid on site, park entrance fee applies. Fires permitted in the provided rings unless a seasonal ban is in force, which happens most late summers on this peninsula.
bivy.capacity: Around 105 single-family sites in old growth, taking tents and rigs up to about 24 ft with a few longer; first-come, first-served with no reservations

wa_mount_angeles_standard.notes: A steep, short trail from the Hurricane Ridge Road up to the Klahhane Ridge trail, then the same climbers' path to the summit.

wa_mount_angeles_standard.name: Heather Park trail from Heart O' the Hills

bivy.name: Heart o' the Hills campground
bivy.notes: This is the staging base for Mount Angeles and it is a staging base only — it is a few miles up the Hurricane Ridge road from Port Angeles, and no part of the climb passes through it. The scramble itself starts from a pull-out around mile 15 on that road, where the Switchback trail gains about 700 ft in six-tenths of a mile to its junction with the trail from Hurricane Ridge, then about half a mile west along that trail and a spur onto the unmaintained final ridge — exposed walking and class 3 on loose fractured rock to the 6,454 ft summit. approachLogistics.trailhead: Heather Park Trailhead (Heart O' the Hills)

wa_mount_angeles_standard.notes: The long way from low on the Hurricane Ridge Road: the Heather Park trail climbs around the west side of the peak to join the climbers' path.

wa_mount_appleton_standard.name: Sol Duc River Trail to Appleton Pass
camps: Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort campground
wa_mount_appleton_standard.notes: Just under five miles upriver, crossing Crystal Creek on a suspension bridge, to the signed pass junction, then a couple of miles and roughly two thousand feet through forest and meadow to the gap. The Boulder Creek side reaches the same pass but is far longer now that the road below it is walked or ridden.
hazards: Exposed Class 3 through a heathery gully where several holds are vegetation
A narrow goat ramp on the final approach to the true summit
Loose rock and talus on the upper ridge and basin slopes
Snow near the pass and in the basin below the summit into July
Braided, unmarked climbers' path that wanders onto steeper ground in fog
wa_mount_appleton_standard.baseFinding: Appleton Pass is a true gap with scattered tent pads just below it and maintained trail running on north toward Boulder Lake and east toward Oyster Lake. Leave the tread at the gap and take the climbers' path north along the ridge crest. The base of the real scrambling is a rock step at about 5,800 ft, and the way you know it is a distinct rock horn standing on its south, or left, side — that horn is the marker, and there is nothing else like it on the crest. Below the step you have been on easy heather with a talus basin crossed on the north flank near 5,400 ft; above it you are on exposed Class 3 through a heathery gully and ledge system. Minor outcrops lower on the crest can be turned on either side and are not the step, so do not stop at the first thing that makes you use hands. The narrow goat ramp people talk about comes after the horn, not before it. If you are still traversing level ground with the basin below and no horn in view, you are too low; the notch below the true summit sits near 6,000 ft between the peak's two rocky humps.

wa_mount_appleton_standard.name: Boulder Creek from the Elwha

bivy.name: Appleton Pass
bivy.notes: The direct base for Mount Appleton, a class 3 scramble of just over 6,000 ft sitting northwest of the pass on a ridge with a couple of genuinely exposed moves. From the Sol Duc trailhead it is about seven and a bit miles: roughly five easy miles up the river before the trail breaks north and climbs hard, gaining around 2,000 ft in the last two and a bit. This used to be a short outing from the Elwha side, but that road is washed out and closed to cars at the park boundary, so unless you are willing to ride a bike in and add many miles, Sol Duc is the approach. The meadows above the pass are open and windy, so the sheltered sites go first. Snow lingers on the final climb to the pass well into early summer.
bivy.water: Oyster Lake just above the pass, and closer snowmelt earlier in the summer; late in a dry season the snowfields go and the lake is the only option
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and the high camps in this area are quota-controlled, reserved for a specific night on the federal booking site. Bear canisters mandatory. No campfires — the pass is well above the 3,500 ft line and the meadow vegetation here is exactly what that rule protects.
bivy.capacity: Several tent sites spread between the pass and Oyster Lake, some fully exposed on the crest and some tucked into trees; a small nightly cap

approachLogistics.trailhead: Boulder Creek Trailhead (Olympic Hot Springs Road)

wa_mount_appleton_standard.notes: From the Elwha side, follow the Boulder Creek trail past the old hot springs and climb to Appleton Pass, where it meets the Sol Duc line. It is the longer way, since the road below the trailhead may have to be walked or biked. Boulder Lake makes a good side camp.

wa_mount_baker_cockscomb_ridge.name: Heliotrope Ridge, the Hogsback and the Coleman-Roosevelt crossing
wa_mount_baker_cockscomb_ridge.notes:
Glacier Creek Road (FR 39) to the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead, then Trail 677 through old growth to the fork at about two miles. Take the right-hand climbers' path up the crest of the Hogsback moraine to the camps near 6,000 ft beside the Coleman Glacier, the same camp used for the Coleman-Deming and the North Ridge.

From camp the route ropes up and heads northeast, crossing the Coleman and then the Roosevelt Glacier. Expect two to three hours of glacier travel through a crevasse field before low-to-moderate snow ramps lead to the foot of the ridge.
hazards: crevasses and thin snow bridges on the Coleman and Roosevelt Glaciers
bergschrunds below and on the ridge
loose rock on the ridge, worse as the snow melts out
icefall on the ramps that skirt the towers
wa_mount_baker_cockscomb_ridge.baseFinding:
The ridge is reached by traversing northeast from the Hogsback camps across the Coleman and then the Roosevelt Glacier. Aim for the foot of the ridge at about 7,500-7,800 ft, where low-angle snow ramps lead up onto the crest.

The Cockscomb Tower, about 300 ft high, stands well above the base and is passed on its east side by steep snow; if you are already beside it, you are far above the start. If you have crossed only the Coleman and are still west of the Roosevelt, you have not reached this ridge yet.

wa_mount_baker_cockscomb_ridge.name: Artist Point and Ptarmigan Ridge to the Park Glacier

bivy.name: Park Glacier camp near the Portals
bivy.notes: Beyond Camp Kiser, across the Rainbow Glacier and onto the Park Glacier. This is where most parties sleep before the Park Glacier Headwall or the Cockscomb.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only
bivy.permit: No overnight permit required
bivy.capacity: Snow or rock platforms for a few tents

bivy.name: Camp Kiser, Ptarmigan Ridge
bivy.notes: About five miles out Ptarmigan Ridge where the maintained trail ends. A good first night, with the glaciers still to cross.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only; can be dry late in summer
bivy.permit: No overnight permit required
bivy.capacity: Dispersed sites among rock wind walls

wa_mount_baker_cockscomb_ridge.notes: From Artist Point at the end of the Mount Baker Highway, take the Chain Lakes trail to the Ptarmigan Ridge junction and follow Ptarmigan Ridge west to Camp Kiser where the trail ends. Cross the Rainbow Glacier onto the Park Glacier and camp near the Portals, the usual base for the Cockscomb from this side. It is a much longer approach than Heliotrope Ridge.

wa_mount_ballard_south.name: Mill Creek and the Azurite Pass side
wa_mount_ballard_south.notes: This is the approach the peak is normally catalogued under and the one that pairs naturally with Azurite. It runs from Highway 20 up Canyon Creek and then Mill Creek on tread that has seen little maintenance since the mine closed, where slide alder and downed timber are the recurring complaint and parties routinely lose the path entirely for stretches. A longer alternative from the West Fork Methow trailhead reaches the same country by way of the Pacific Crest Trail and Horse Heaven Camp and is often preferred for combined trips despite the extra mileage. Camp is usually made near the old mine or in the basin above it. Note that the point long marked on maps as Mount Ballard is a lower north sub-summit; the true high point lies about 1,100 ft further south and is slightly higher.
hazards: Slide alder and downed timber on an unmaintained approach trail
Route-finding through brush pockets and broken gullies on the flank
Loose, rotten rock and exposure near the summit ridge
Snowfields into July that can require an ice axe
Open upper mountain with full lightning exposure
Very remote, with a long and difficult evacuation if injured
wa_mount_ballard_south.baseFinding: On this side the walking ends at the old Azurite Mine site around 4,440 ft and the brush begins immediately. The base of the climb is the open basin at roughly 6,600 ft above and east of the mine, sitting between Ballard and the ridge running out toward Azurite. You know you are in it when the timber gives out and you can see the peak's flank in one piece above you rather than through trees. That flank is the difficulty: it is not a single clean face but a patchwork of brush pockets, rock ribs and short gullies, and parties consistently find that the hard part of the day is not the scrambling but picking which gully continues, a decision that comes to a head around 7,400 ft. Read the ground rather than committing early, because a gully that closes out costs a long reversal. The obvious-looking answer is a trap: the south ridge presents as a clean continuous line from below and is blocked higher by a notch with a gendarme in it, so a party that racks up the ridge crest on sight will be turned around. The other check is on which summit you are heading for. There are two high points on this mountain, and the northern one, the one carrying the old survey mark, is the lower; keep working south along the crest until the ground stops rising. If you find yourself on the connecting ridge with Azurite you have gone north and are on the wrong end of the massif.

wa_mount_ballard_south.name: South Fork Slate Creek and the east ridge

approachLogistics.trailhead: South Fork Slate Creek road end (over Harts Pass)

wa_mount_ballard_south.notes: The other side of the mountain, approached from the Slate Creek road system rather than from Mill Creek, and the line most parties who climb this peak actually use. It is shorter, the forest below camp is comparatively brush-free, and the route-finding above camp is far more legible than on the Mill Creek side, at the cost of one genuinely steep step low down and some exposed ledge work near the top. Snow conditions change this route's character completely: a filled-in slot low down and firm snow in the upper cirque make for fast travel, while dry late-season conditions leave loose rock and slippery vegetation. Camp is normally made in a scree basin below the east ridge.
hazards: A steep vegetated step through the lowest cliff band, the hardest ground on the route
Exposed ledge traverse above the high saddle
Loose rock in the summit gully with a party stacked below
Steep snow in the east cirque into midsummer
Full lightning exposure on the open upper mountain
Very remote, with a long and difficult evacuation if injured
wa_mount_ballard_south.baseFinding: The approach has one unmistakable marker and the climb has another. Start at the locked gate on the Slate Creek road at about 3,800 ft and walk the South Fork road for roughly a mile and a half to an old vehicle bridge at about 4,000 ft; that bridge is the single positive check on the whole road walk, and if you have not crossed it you are still on the main branch. From the bridge, head south through open, brush-free forest for another mile and a half or so to a scree basin around 4,800 ft, the usual camp. From camp the route climbs through tight forest and then open scree to a shoulder on the east ridge at roughly 6,200 ft. The base of the real climbing is right there and it is easy to identify because it is the wrong colour: a steep slot of heather and grass cutting through the lowest cliff band, green vegetation in an otherwise rocky wall, and the only weakness in that band. It is the steepest ground on the route and it is the crux. Bare rock gullies to either side look more like a climb and are harder and looser, so the vegetated slot is the line. Above it stay on the rib and follow the ridge crest, then the scree slope and east cirque, to a high saddle north of the summit. From that saddle do not go straight up; traverse ledges, some of them exposed, to a narrow gully that gains the summit block.

wa_mount_ballard_south.name: West Fork Methow and the PCT
wa_mount_ballard_south.notes: Up the West Fork Methow to the Pacific Crest Trail and over to the Mill Creek side. Longer, and usually chosen for combined trips.

wa_mount_barnes_scramble.name: Bailey Range crest to Bear Pass
camps: Elwha Basin, Queets Basin and the upper cross-country bivy zones
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.notes: This peak has two genuinely different journeys to it: the western one from the Sol Duc over the High Divide and along the Bailey crest through Cat Basin, Ferry Basin and Stephen Peak, and the eastern one up the Elwha with a long road walk or ride added at the start. Both take days. Almost every ascent is a side-summit off a traverse rather than a trip in its own right.
hazards: Days of off-trail travel with no quick bail-out and no cell coverage
Dense slide-alder bushwhacking between the Elwha and Elwha Basin
Loose, fragmented sedimentary rock with few solid cracks
Firm snow on the small glacier below Bear Pass — axe and traction
Long stretches with no maintained trail and no dependable water
wa_mount_barnes_scramble.baseFinding: Bear Pass is a broad saddle marking the southeastern end of the Bailey Range proper, and from it the ground drops into a flat meadow before the mountain itself. Cross the meadow and contour southeast over scree and lingering snow patches until you are southwest of the summit. That position is the base, and you will know it from the change underfoot: the sidehill traversing stops and the slope above turns into a straight fall-line of moderate, evenly sized scree with a boot track curling left, to the north, onto it. Aside from one brief patch of brush the terrain here is open and the top is in view, so the navigation problem is behind you once you are on that track. Decoys: the ridge running east off Bear Pass is not the summit ridge, and the first obvious scree fan you meet while still traversing leads onto broken ground short of the peak. If the boot track has stopped curling north and you are dropping toward the Queets side, you have gone past the turn.

wa_mount_barnes_scramble.name: Up the Elwha to Elwha Basin

bivy.name: Elwha Basin, Queets Basin and the upper cross-country bivy zones
bivy.notes: This is the working base for the Elwha Basin peaks and the only sensible way to reach the Bailey Range from the south. From Chicago Camp the route into Elwha Basin is a notorious bushwhack in low snow years, then the Elwha Snowfinger leads to Dodwell-Rixon Pass at 4,763 ft and over into Queets Basin. From a basin camp, Mount Barnes, Mount Noyes and Mount Queets are all short days, Mount Meany is usually taken from Seattle Basin or over the Noyes-Meany col, and a further push west from Queets Basin puts Mount Ferry and Mount Pulitzer within reach. Season is everything: the snowfinger in good condition is fast and pleasant, and the same ground in September is loose talus and alder. There is no shelter, no toilet and no established site, so pick ground that will not be flooded and leave nothing. If your party is not comfortable making its own camp on unimproved terrain, this zone is not the right objective.
bivy.water: Meltwater and snow. Abundant early, and increasingly a question by late summer once the snowfinger and the basin streams shrink — carry capacity rather than assuming the next creek is running.
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and cross-country zones cannot be booked online — you must telephone the wilderness information centre, and the rangers will ask about your experience before issuing. Name every zone you intend to sleep in; one permit follows you between zones on a multi-day route. Bear canister mandatory. No campfires above 3,500 ft, so this is a stove-only zone. Human waste should be buried well away from meltwater or packed out on snow and rock.
bivy.capacity: No designated sites — these are cross-country zones and parties camp on whatever flat gravel, heather bench or moraine they reach; groups are small by necessity

bivy.name: Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
bivy.notes: The whole Elwha approach now begins with a road walk, and it is the single biggest change to planning in this valley. Vehicles stop at the Madison Falls parking area; the Olympic Hot Springs Road and then the Whiskey Bend Road are closed by a washout that has stood for years with no repair date, which puts the old Whiskey Bend trailhead about six to seven miles away on foot. The park's own figure is seven. Bicycles are allowed on the closed road and cut that leg to well under an hour each way, and most parties heading deep now ride it and stash a bike.
