Lillian River is around four and a half miles past Whiskey Bend and Mary's Falls a little further, so either one turns a brutal first day into a civilised one when you are carrying enough food for a week in the interior. Going higher on day one is possible but you gain nothing except a shorter second day; the elevation profile of the Elwha barely rises for the first fifteen miles.
bivy.water: Reliable at both — the Lillian River at one, the Elwha at the other; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance on the federal recreation site. These lower Elwha camps are not inside a quota area, so they are usually obtainable late, but no sites anywhere in this park are held back as same-day walk-ups. Bear canister mandatory. Fires are allowed at this elevation but the Elwha and every tributary are closed to fishing.
bivy.capacity: Lillian River has roughly six roomy riverside sites; Mary's Falls is smaller and set in maple and grass with the river some way off

bivy.name: Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
bivy.notes: Elkhorn sits about eleven miles up the Elwha from Whiskey Bend and Hayes River about sixteen, both on level ground and both far more pleasant than Canyon Camp between them, which has been badly hit by treefall and is worth walking past. Hayes River is the camp for Mount Norton: the peak's east side rises roughly 3,200 ft straight out of the Hayes River drainage in under a mile, and the ascent is a steep off-trail slog rather than a climb. It is also the last comfortable place to sleep before the valley narrows, so parties bound for Chicago Camp and the Elwha Basin peaks routinely take it as night two. Going further the same day is a real option in long daylight but the trail past Camp Wilder deteriorates and the camps beyond are rougher. Bugs are heavy in the meadows from late June into July.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha at Elkhorn, the Hayes River at Hayes; both run all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not a quota area, so these are among the easier permits in the park to obtain at short notice. Bear canister mandatory.
bivy.capacity: Both are spacious grassy flats with several sites each, alongside old guard stations that are usually empty; they are the least contested camps in the valley

bivy.name: Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
bivy.notes: Chicago Camp is where the trail effectively ends and the cross-country begins, roughly twenty-five miles from Whiskey Bend at the confluence of the Elwha and Delabarre Creek. It is the standard last-trail-camp for Mount Barnes, Mount Meany, Mount Noyes, Mount Queets and Mount Wilder, all of which are reached by pushing on into the Elwha Basin above. The ford at the camp can be genuinely hazardous in high water and is the crux of the walk in for many parties. A short way beyond, the upper Elwha has a cave-like recess under an overhanging wall that has served as emergency shelter for generations, but it is a bolthole and not a camp. Camping here rather than in the basin costs you three miles and a couple of thousand feet on summit day; the trade is a sheltered site with running water and a defined trail underfoot, which matters more than it sounds after four days of walking.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha and Delabarre Creek meet here
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. It is more than fifteen miles from any road, and the booking system does not always surface camps that far in, so ring the wilderness information centre rather than assuming it is unavailable. Bear canister mandatory. No fires above 3,500 ft, which applies once you climb out of here.
bivy.capacity: Small, and it has been battered by fallen timber — expect only a couple of usable sites near the river

wa_mount_barnes_scramble.notes: The eastern way: follow the Elwha River trail up the full length of the valley past Hayes River and Chicago Camp to Elwha Basin, then climb onto the peak from the basin. It takes several days, and a road walk or bike ride may be needed to reach the trailhead.

wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.name: Little Giant Trail #1518 over the pass and down into the Napeequa
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.notes:
The Little Giant Trailhead sits at about 2,600 ft roughly mile 19 of Chiwawa River Road, three miles down-valley of Trinity. The trail begins with an unbridged ford of the Chiwawa River, right at the start — there is no way around it and it is the gate on the whole approach.

Trail #1518 then climbs steeply and badly-eroded to Little Giant Pass at 6,463 ft, with a small spring a few hundred feet below the pass at about 6,250 ft that is the last dependable water before the high basins. Maintained tread effectively ends at the pass.

From the pass the route drops toward the Louis Creek and Napeequa basin, then follows a climbers' path upstream to the end of tread at the creek draining Berge's south-west side. A steep, intermittent boot track climbs through timber to treeline and opens into the south-west basin. A narrow notch at about 7,840 ft in the ridge crest links the Louis Creek basin to the Buck Creek and High Pass side beneath the south-west face, and gaining it is exposed scrambling.

All options to this peak are 15-plus miles round trip and are multi-day trips.
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.season: Jul-Sep, August most reliable. The Chiwawa ford at the very start of this trail is waist-deep and swift in early season and is only reliably safe in late-summer and autumn low water
hazards: An unbridged ford of the Chiwawa River at the very start of Little Giant Trail, waist-deep and swift outside late-season low water
Berge's north and west faces are cliffy and the direct line from High Pass does not go
A steep, badly eroded trail to Little Giant Pass and no maintained tread beyond it
An exposed gully of slanted slabs near 7,800 ft where a slip has serious consequences
A short fourth-class step to the true north summit, harder than the rest of the route
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.baseFinding:
The base is a broad saddle on the south side at about 7,650 ft, and the way you get to it is a snow finger rather than a slope. Near a snowfield around 7,000 ft the line uses a snow finger and its moat, plus steep heather, to reach that saddle below the final summit block. Looking for a walkable slope will not find it; looking for the place where snow runs up into a narrowing tongue against rock will.

The saddle is where the route leaves the basin. Below it you are traversing basins; above it you are climbing rock bands and steep heather toward the summit ridge. If you are still contouring, you are below it.

The negative marker is the most important thing on this peak and it is about aspect: Berge's north and west faces are cliffy. Parties must stay on the south-west side. Do not try to go straight up from High Pass — the direct line from the north does not go. If the ground above you is steepening into walls rather than rock bands and heather, you are on the wrong side of the mountain.

The route-finding rule lower down is a descending traverse, which feels wrong and is right: near 5,400 ft the described line drops across into meadows, and it is from those meadows that several scrambling lines reach the top. Losing height on an approach to a summit is expected here.

The last obstacle has an elevation and a character: an exposed gully near 7,800 ft with slanted slabs and real exposure near its top. Holds and ledges are solid and the passage is straightforward, and a slip there would be consequential — helmet.

The summit is not one point. The true, north summit needs a short fourth-class step, harder than the third-class south summit. Standing on the easier top is not standing on the mountain.

wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.name: Trinity and Buck Creek, or the High Pass high route from Buck Creek Pass

bivy.name: Buck Creek Pass and the High Pass camps
bivy.notes: Buck Creek Pass at about 5,800 feet is the base for three peaks in this zone that have nothing to do with Glacier Peak's own approaches. Helmet Butte sits half a mile northeast of the pass and is the shortest objective from here. Buck Mountain rises directly south across the valley and is normally taken by leaving the Buck Creek trail lower down for the east ridge of Cleator and the Buck–Berge col, which also gives Mount Berge. From the pass a way trail continues north over Flower Dome to High Pass, which is both a fine high camp in its own right and the link over into the Napeequa, tying this side of the zone to Clark and Luahna. Getting here is around ten miles and three thousand feet of steady forest walking up Buck Creek from Trinity, so it is a full first day. It is a scenic and genuinely popular pass, which for a climbing party means arriving early enough to get a site. When the Chiwawa road is shut at Atkinson Flat the trailhead itself is roughly eleven road miles further on, which turns a two-day trip into a four-day one or a long bike shuttle.
bivy.water: A stream at the pass is the main supply and is reliable through the season; the higher camps toward High Pass run on snowmelt only and can be dry by September
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Trinity trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Fires are prohibited where posted and the meadow ground here is exactly the kind of place that gets posted — carry a stove. Camp on the bare established sites rather than in the heather. The road is the real permit question: the Chiwawa River road is closed from Atkinson Flat north to Trinity under a storm order running through the end of 2027, with no reopening estimate, and a large 2026 fire closure covered the same road on top of it.
bivy.capacity: Several established forested and meadow-edge sites at the pass itself, enough for a few parties, with rougher and more exposed ground higher toward Flower Dome and High Pass

approachLogistics.trailhead: Trinity Trailhead (end of Chiwawa River Road)

wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.notes:
Two other ways reach the same mountain from the Trinity side.

The east approach: from Trinity, follow Chiwawa River Trail #1550 about two miles to the Buck Creek Trail #1513 junction, then Buck Creek Trail roughly four to five miles into the basin Berge shares with Mount Cleator and Buck Mountain on its east side.

The north approach: continue past the Buck Creek junction to Buck Creek Pass, then take the climbers' path over High Pass and contour south under Berge's north side near Point 7839. This is the longest by mileage and has the least off-trail travel, which is the trade it offers.

Both involve unbridged or damaged creek crossings and both are multi-day. FR-6200 has been closed beyond Atkinson Flat under a storm-damage order, which affects the drive to Trinity.
hazards: Berge's north face is cliffy — the direct line from High Pass does not go, and this approach puts you underneath it
Unbridged or damaged creek crossings on both the Buck Creek and Napeequa approaches
Brush and blowdown on unmaintained climbers' paths above the end of tread
An exposed 7,840 ft notch linking the two sides of the ridge
FR-6200 closed beyond Atkinson Flat, affecting the drive to Trinity
wa_mount_berge_southwest_route.baseFinding:
The High Pass approach delivers you to the wrong side of the mountain on purpose, and the rule is that you must keep going around. Contouring south under Berge's north side puts a cliffy face above you. The climb is on the south-west side. Carry on around until the ground above you is rock bands and steep heather rather than wall, and only then start up.

The arrival is the same place for every approach to this peak: the broad saddle on Berge's south side at about 7,650 ft, where the south-west slopes route leaves the basin. Whichever valley you came up, that saddle is what you are walking to.

The approach-specific marker on the High Pass line is a numbered point rather than a shape: you contour beneath Point 7839. If you are still north of it you have not gone far enough around.

The 7,840 ft notch is the link between the two sides and it is worth knowing exists whichever way you came: a narrow notch in the ridge crest connects the Louis Creek basin on the Napeequa side to the Buck Creek and High Pass side beneath the south-west face. Gaining it is exposed scrambling, and it is the reason the two approaches meet at all.

And the same summit warning applies: the true summit is the north one and it takes a short fourth-class step. The south summit is third class and is not the top.

wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.name: Kindy Ridge from the Kindy Creek road
camps: Head of Kindy Creek and the Kindy-Buck Creek pass
wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.notes: Up Kindy Ridge from the Kindy Creek road off the Cascade River Road, then south through the Buckindy high country to below the north side. A longer two-to-three-day approach.

wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.name: Green Mountain trail and the Horse Lake saddle

bivy.name: Horse Lake saddle camp
bivy.notes: First-night camp on the Green Mountain approach, past the south shoulder of Green Mountain. Beyond it the traverse toward Misch and Buckindy is slow sidehill travel.
bivy.water: Horse Lake and snowmelt nearby; treat it
bivy.permit: No overnight permit required
bivy.capacity: A few tent sites just above the saddle

approachLogistics.trailhead: Green Mountain Trailhead (FR-2680 off Suiattle River Road)

wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.notes: The usual way: up the Green Mountain trail off the Suiattle River Road, then cross-country east and southeast along the ridges past Misch to Buckindy's north side. Check the Suiattle River Road before you go; it has been closed to vehicles for long stretches.

wa_mount_cameron_standard.name: Obstruction Point Road, Grand Pass and the Cameron Pass Trail
wa_mount_cameron_standard.notes: Read the name on this route with care — it says Southeast Slopes, and Cameron Pass lies west of the summit. The climb is a west-ridge walk gained at the pass. A party that reads the title and heads southeast off the pass is walking into the Dosewallips headwaters. Drive the narrow one-lane gravel Obstruction Point Road — Olympic National Park's highest road, topping out at 6,135 ft — 8 miles east from the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center to the Obstruction Point trailhead. Hike the Grand Pass Trail roughly 6 miles to Grand Pass at about 6,450 ft; the drop off the far side toward Cameron is steep and slick in wet weather or lingering snow. The trail then crosses several unbridged branches of Cameron Creek in a wet meadow — reliable water, and tread that is easy to lose in fog or high brush — to the Cameron Basin camps at about 6,000 ft near 8.3 miles, and on up to Cameron Pass at roughly 6,450-6,500 ft near 9.3 miles. Bear canister required in the basin; there are no trees to hang food. Steep snow can persist on the pass into late July or August and the climbers' path is frequently buried there.
wa_mount_cameron_standard.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and gated by the road: Obstruction Point Road is usually open only early-to-mid July through mid-October
hazards: Route-finding on open off-trail slopes above Cameron Basin, and faint brushy tread on the Cameron Pass Trail beyond the basin
Steep lingering snow on Cameron Pass into late July or August, over a buried climbers' path
Loose rock, scree and talus on the summit slopes and along the ridge connecting the three summits
No reliable water above Cameron Basin and minimal to no cell coverage
Obstruction Point Road closes for most of the year and is not a route you can count on before July
wa_mount_cameron_standard.baseFinding: The base is Cameron Pass and the test is the direction you turn out of it: the ridge you climb rises to the east. The pass is west of the summit. From it, leave the trail and follow the broad ridge crest east and up. If the ground under you is falling away, or you are contouring around a slope rather than walking a crest, you are not on the route — the correct line is a ridge, and a ridge in cloud is identifiable by the fact that the ground drops on both sides of you. Second test, and it is the one that matters most here: the ridge is a sequence of false summits. It is mostly Class 1-2 and it crosses many bumps before the true summit. So a high point that arrives sooner and more easily than you expected is a false one. Do not stop on the first thing that stops going up; keep the crest under you and keep going: the true top is still easy Class 1-2 ground, and steps of Class 3-4 mean you have passed it and are on the traverse. Third test, for the far end: Cameron is a triple summit and the crest continues past the true top toward the Middle Peak, which has spots of Class 3-4, and then to the East Peak. If you have started descending steeply and then re-climbing on harder ground, you have gone past the true summit and are onto the traverse. That is a legitimate outing; it is not this route. Carry a map and count your summits.

wa_mount_cameron_standard.name: Deer Park and the Cameron Creek Trail

bivy.name: Cameron Basin
bivy.notes: This is the working base for Mount Cameron, which is climbed from Cameron Pass just above the basin, and it is the western end of this zone rather than part of the Needles group at all. Two ways in and they are very different. From Obstruction Point it is a high, scenic and long day over Grand Pass and down into the basin, and it depends entirely on the Obstruction Point road, a rough high-elevation dirt road that typically does not open until well into July and closes with the first snow of autumn; if that road is shut, this approach does not exist. From the south it is reached from Dose Meadows over Lost Pass, which is short in distance and brutally steep, but getting to Dose Meadows means the whole washed-out Dosewallips walk first. Nothing about this camp helps you on The Needles, and a party trying to combine Cameron with Deception in one trip is really planning two trips. Snow lies late in the basin and on Cameron Pass, and the descent off Grand Pass wants a dry day.
bivy.water: Cameron Creek and its feeders through the basin. Reliable through the climbing season.
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; Cameron Basin itself is not a quota area, so it books readily. The catch is the approach: if you come the sensible way from Obstruction Point you pass through Grand and Badger Valleys, which ARE a quota area with reservations in effect through the high summer, so a night at Grand or Moose Lake on the way in has to be booked separately and early. Bear canisters are required throughout. Everything is reserved through the federal recreation booking system with the standard per-permit charge and per-adult nightly fee.
bivy.capacity: Several backcountry sites in the basin below Cameron Pass. Modest but usually adequate; the basin is on a well-travelled loop, so summer weekends can be busier than the remoteness suggests.

wa_mount_cameron_standard.notes:
The other trail-based way into Cameron Basin, and the one worth knowing when Obstruction Point Road is still closed. From Deer Park, the Grand Ridge and Cameron Creek trail system leads into the Cameron Creek drainage and up to Cameron Basin and Cameron Pass from the northeast.

It is longer than the Obstruction Point line and much of the Cameron Creek tread receives little to no maintenance — parties describe bushwhacking through dense growth, chest-high berry bushes, and log crossings barricaded by jams. Long sleeves and trousers are universally recommended.

Once at Cameron Pass the climb is identical to the Obstruction Point variant.
wa_mount_cameron_standard.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and it opens earlier than Obstruction Point in some years because Deer Park Road is a different road on a different aspect
hazards: Long stretches of unmaintained, brushy tread with log jams at creek crossings
Route-finding in wet meadow where the tread disappears
All the summit-ridge hazards of the standard variant, reached after a longer approach
Bear canister required; no reliable water above the basin
wa_mount_cameron_standard.baseFinding: Identical once you are at Cameron Pass: leave the trail and follow the broad ridge crest east and up, over many false summits, on Class 1-2 ground all the way to the top. The pass is west of the summit whatever the route title says. The extra test this side needs is in Cameron Basin, because you arrive up the creek rather than over Grand Pass. The Cameron Creek tread crosses several unbridged branches of the creek in wet meadow and is genuinely easy to lose in brush or fog. The handrail is the creek: stay with the drainage and keep climbing it toward the basin at about 6,000 ft. The established camps in the upper basin are the confirmation that you are in the right cirque, and the pass is above them. What going too far looks like: if you crest a pass and the ground beyond drops steeply into a large river valley to the south, you are looking at the Dosewallips headwaters and you have crossed Cameron Pass rather than turning up the ridge at it.

wa_mount_cameron_standard.name: Dosewallips road walk and the long push up-valley into Cameron Basin

bivy.name: Cameron Basin
bivy.notes: This is the working base for Mount Cameron, which is climbed from Cameron Pass just above the basin, and it is the western end of this zone rather than part of the Needles group at all. Two ways in and they are very different. From Obstruction Point it is a high, scenic and long day over Grand Pass and down into the basin, and it depends entirely on the Obstruction Point road, a rough high-elevation dirt road that typically does not open until well into July and closes with the first snow of autumn; if that road is shut, this approach does not exist. From the south it is reached from Dose Meadows over Lost Pass, which is short in distance and brutally steep, but getting to Dose Meadows means the whole washed-out Dosewallips walk first. Nothing about this camp helps you on The Needles, and a party trying to combine Cameron with Deception in one trip is really planning two trips. Snow lies late in the basin and on Cameron Pass, and the descent off Grand Pass wants a dry day.
bivy.water: Cameron Creek and its feeders through the basin. Reliable through the climbing season.
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required; Cameron Basin itself is not a quota area, so it books readily. The catch is the approach: if you come the sensible way from Obstruction Point you pass through Grand and Badger Valleys, which ARE a quota area with reservations in effect through the high summer, so a night at Grand or Moose Lake on the way in has to be booked separately and early. Bear canisters are required throughout. Everything is reserved through the federal recreation booking system with the standard per-permit charge and per-adult nightly fee.
bivy.capacity: Several backcountry sites in the basin below Cameron Pass. Modest but usually adequate; the basin is on a well-travelled loop, so summer weekends can be busier than the remoteness suggests.

wa_mount_cameron_standard.notes: Recorded because it is a real historical approach — but it is rarely chosen today and is not the recommended way in. From Brinnon, the Dosewallips River Road has been closed to vehicles since 2002 at a washout about a mile past the road-end parking. That forces a long walk or bike up the old roadbed before you even reach the Dosewallips River Trail, and then a multi-day push up-valley into Cameron Basin. It adds many miles over either northern approach. If you take it, the climb from Cameron Pass is unchanged.
hazards: Many extra miles including a long closed-road walk at each end
A multi-day valley approach with fords and blowdown
The southeast face of Cameron is not a route and the approach passes beneath it
All the summit-ridge hazards of the standard variant
wa_mount_cameron_standard.baseFinding: Identical at the pass: the ridge rises east out of Cameron Pass, over many false summits, on Class 1-2 ground to the true top. The test this side needs is about which valley you are in, because approaching from the south you come up beneath the peak's southeast face — the aspect the route's title wrongly names — and it does not go. Cameron's southeast side rises over 3,300 ft above the Dosewallips River in about one horizontal mile. If you are standing under that and looking for a line up it, you are on the wrong side of the mountain: the route is the west ridge, gained at the pass, and getting there from this side means continuing up-valley and round into Cameron Basin first.

wa_mount_carru_scramble.name: The south gully below the Carru-Lago col
camps: The high bench southwest of Shellrock Pass
The Berk Creek junction and the Middle Fork Pasayten river camps
wa_mount_carru_scramble.notes: Carru sits between Osceola and the higher Mount Lago and is almost always climbed as one summit of several on a multi-day trip out of the Harts Pass road end. Two lines reach the country below it: the shorter drops from Slate Pass and Buckskin Ridge into the Middle Fork Pasayten, then goes by Fred's Lake and over the ridge crest into upper Eureka Creek and Shellrock Basin; the Monument Creek trail is longer with more up and down. Tread through this wilderness is lightly maintained, with blowdown on the valley trail and stretches where the path is fainter on the ground than it looks on a map. The climb itself is short, well under two hours from the base, and unremarkable, essentially a heap of scree and talus with parallel ribs running up it.
hazards: Avalanche debris choking the lower gully
Loose scree and talus on the ascent and worse on the descent
Short rock steps and cliff bands within the gully
Steep cliffed north face immediately off the summit crest
Difficult creek crossings during snowmelt
Limited water on the high traverses between the peaks
wa_mount_carru_scramble.baseFinding: The base is a gully, and it identifies itself by being a mess. A scree-and-talus gully drops south off the Carru-Lago col and runs down to meet the trail; where it meets the trail it is typically choked with avalanche debris, meaning snapped timber, jammed branches and rubble piled in the bed. That debris is both the marker and the reason not to start there. Instead, climb the open forest on the right-hand, western side of the gully and step into the bed higher up, at about 6,600 ft, above the worst of the wreckage. Once in the gully the route is contained and hard to lose: scramble up it, weaving round a couple of short rock steps and small cliff bands, until the walls fall back and the ground opens out near the col. That opening-out is the second checkpoint. At that point turn left, to the west, onto the broad southeast ridge and follow the parallel scree ribs to the summit; the ribs run in the direction of travel and any of them will do. The single thing to watch on the upper mountain is which side of the crest you are on. Carru's north side is a steep, cliffed face and is not part of any route here, so if the ground in front of you falls away as a wall rather than a slope you have crossed the crest and should step back south.

wa_mount_carru_scramble.name: From Slate Pass down the Middle Fork Pasayten

bivy.name: The high bench southwest of Shellrock Pass
bivy.notes: This is the staging camp that makes Mount Carru and Mount Lago short days instead of enormous ones, and it is deliberately not the same ground as the Shellrock Basin and Eureka Creek meadow camps lower down. It is a bench at around 7,500 ft immediately southwest of the pass, high enough that every summit in the group is within reach from it. For Carru the line runs west along the east fork of Eureka Creek, leaves the trail at a creek crossing and takes a red talus gully east of the Carru-Lago saddle for a few hundred feet — under two hours from camp to the 8,595 ft summit. Lago at 8,745 ft is the highest thing in this part of the wilderness and goes from the same saddle. What you pay for the position is water and weather. There is no tree cover, the pass funnels wind, and a party that has not carried enough will be walking back down for it. Snow holds on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the real constraint on when this is worth doing. Larches turn in the last days of September and the nights at this height are properly cold by then.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and a small tarn below the pass, both of them seasonal. By late summer there may be nothing at all up here and the passes on either side are reliably dry. Carry water up from the Eureka Creek meadows or the river; this is the single most common mistake made on these summits.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass to park. The bench is thin alpine ground that holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the turf alone. Assume no fires — there is nothing to burn at this elevation and the meadows below are fragile.
bivy.capacity: Roughly half an acre of usable bench, so realistically two or three small parties. No established sites, no facilities and no shelter of any kind.

bivy.name: The Berk Creek junction and the Middle Fork Pasayten river camps
bivy.notes: This is the hinge of the whole Middle Fork approach and it is where a party bound for Mount Carru, Mount Lago or Lost Peak actually sleeps on the first night. Two roads reach it: the high start from Slate Pass at nearly 6,900 ft with a short connector down to the Middle Fork trail, or the low start from the Robinson Creek trailhead at about 2,560 ft over Robinson Pass at 6,220 ft, which is nine and a half miles before the valley walking even begins. The high start is shorter by a long way and is what most parties use. From the junction the climb to Freds Pass and the crossing of the upper Eureka Creek country puts you in position for the summits; the whole approach from a road is around fifteen miles. Being on the river rather than up at the lakes costs you height on the second day and buys you shelter, running water and a warmer night — a real trade when the high camps are exposed and dry. The forest here is patchy burn in places and blowdown varies. This is remote country by any standard and there is no mobile service anywhere in the valley.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Middle Fork Pasayten and Berk Creek meet here and both run all season. This is the last easy water before the long climb to the passes, and the country above lives on tarns and snowmelt, so fill completely.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Slate Pass or Robinson Creek, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, though the valley is dry and bans are common by August.
bivy.capacity: A single established site at the junction where the trail up to Freds Lake and Doris Lake leaves the Middle Fork, plus scattered ground along the river flats above and below it. One or two parties each, nothing developed.

wa_mount_carru_scramble.notes: The shorter and more common start. From Slate Pass the trail drops north to the Middle Fork Pasayten; follow it up-valley past the Berk Creek junction, then climb toward Fred's Lake and Shellrock Basin below Carru. Most parties combine Carru with Osceola and Lago over two or three days.

wa_mount_christie_west.name: North Fork Quinault to Low Divide, then Martins Park and the north couloir
camps: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
wa_mount_christie_west.notes: Every published account climbs the north couloir out of Martins Park to a north-ridge saddle, crosses the Christie Glacier to a col east of the summit, and finishes up the southeast ridge. From the North Fork Quinault Ranger Station at roughly 500 ft, at the end of the North Fork Quinault River Road about 17 miles east of US-101 at Lake Quinault, follow the North Fork Quinault River Trail upstream past Wolf Bar at about 2.5 miles, Halfway House Camp near 5 miles, Elip Creek near 6.5 miles, Trapper Shelter near 8.1 miles (day and emergency use only), a ford of the North Fork at Sixteen Mile Camp near 13.2 miles that can run thigh-deep in high water, and Low Divide near 16 miles, which sits on the actual Quinault-Elwha drainage divide. From Low Divide take the rough fisherman's path into Martins Park and the Martin Lakes basin and camp there.
wa_mount_christie_west.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Firm morning snow in the couloir is what makes this line reasonable; late season it thins to loose rock
hazards: A loose, chossy, poorly protected Class 4 step above the high col that has changed between seasons — treat published descriptions of it as provisional
Glacier travel on the Christie Glacier with a moat at its top whose width varies year to year and by time of day
Steep snow in the entry couloir with runout risk, and refreezing snow in it on a late return
Dense subalpine krummholz above the col
A thigh-deep ford of the North Fork Quinault at Sixteen Mile Camp in high water
Extreme remoteness — an injury near the summit means a multi-day self-extraction or a helicopter
wa_mount_christie_west.baseFinding:
From lower Martins Park there is one broad snow-and-rock couloir and it runs south toward the peak. That is the whole arrival test and it is why parties consistently report finding it easily: you walk out of the lower meadows and over to the base of the snowfield. You are at the base when the meadow ends and continuous snow begins, with the couloir running away from you south — not west. If the drainage you are looking up runs any other direction, it is not this one.

The confirming test is a number and a duration: the couloir gains about 2,100 ft and tops out at a saddle on the north ridge near 5,600 ft, and parties consistently report about three and a half hours for it. If you have climbed far more than 2,100 ft without reaching a saddle, you are in the wrong gully.

Second test, past the saddle, and it is the one that catches the real trap on this peak: from the saddle you drop down loose gravelly slopes to the lower edge of the Christie Glacier. A route that only ever climbs is not this one. Rope up — reports describe few or no open crevasses but the angle is enough that parties treat it as glacier ground anyway. At the top of the glacier a moat forms where ice meets rock; in a good year it is a single easy step across to the high col. Check it before committing, because it is the thing that changes year to year.

What waits at the col, so it is not a surprise: the barrier above it is a chossy eroded cliff band, very steep to locally overhanging, and it is the crux of the peak, not a formality. It has changed between recent seasons — one party found the expected weakness gone and had to force a line to the right across an extremely loose, essentially unprotectable ledge on a tight rope. Expect dense krummholz above it before the rock improves and the Class 2-3 southeast ridge leads to the summit.

wa_mount_christie_west.name: Elwha side to Low Divide, from Whiskey Bend

bivy.name: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
bivy.notes: Low Divide is the saddle between Mount Seattle and Mount Christie and the obvious base for both, and by all accounts it is the most comfortable camp in the interior — flat, watered, with a toilet and a bear hang. Mount Seattle has three established scramble lines from here, by Noyes Basin, by Seattle Creek Basin and by the south slopes, and the upper meadows above camp are open walking. Mount Christie is usually taken by dropping to Martins Park, a boulder garden about three miles below the Christie Glacier, and climbing the north couloir from there. The honest planning point is which side you walk in from: this is 28.4 miles from Whiskey Bend up the Elwha, and 16 miles from the North Fork Quinault trailhead, so unless you are traversing the range you should be coming from the Quinault. Wasps have been a real problem on the lower forest sections in late summer, and stings there have put people out of action for days.
bivy.water: Reliable — a stream runs through the camp all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not itself a quota area, but it is a long way from any road and may not appear in an online search, so telephone the wilderness information centre if the site will not show. Bear canister mandatory. No fires at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: Around five sites, with a bear hang, a toilet and flat ground; small enough that a large party will fill it

wa_mount_christie_west.notes:
Low Divide is a divide, and the Elwha reaches it from the north just as the Quinault does from the south. Historically this meant the Elwha River Trail from the Whiskey Bend Trailhead. Since the November 2017 Olympic Hot Springs Road washout, Whiskey Bend has been closed to vehicles, which adds an extra 6.2 miles each way on foot or by bike from the Madison Falls parking area simply to reach the trailhead — check current road status before choosing this side, because that closure is what decides whether it is competitive with the Quinault.

From Low Divide the route is identical to the Quinault variant: the fisherman's path into Martins Park and the Martin Lakes basin, camp, and the north couloir.

No mileage is quoted for this side because published figures assume Whiskey Bend is drivable and most currently are not.
wa_mount_christie_west.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, on the same window as the Quinault side
hazards: Road closure at Olympic Hot Springs Road adds 6.2 miles each way and may change season to season
Everything above Low Divide is the same as the Quinault variant: the Class 4 step above the col, the Christie Glacier moat, and the entry couloir
A long Elwha valley walk with river crossings
No cell coverage and multi-day self-rescue exposure
wa_mount_christie_west.baseFinding:
Identical to the Quinault variant once you are at Low Divide, and that shared test is a good one: from lower Martins Park there is one broad snow-and-rock couloir and it runs south toward the peak. Walk to where the meadow ends and the snow begins. Up it about 2,100 ft, roughly three and a half hours, to a saddle on the north ridge near 5,600 ft; then down loose gravel to the Christie Glacier; then the moat at the glacier's top and the high col east of the summit.

The extra test this side needs is at Low Divide itself, because you arrive from the opposite direction. Low Divide is a trail junction and the site of the historic ranger station, and it is where the climbers' route leaves maintained trail for Martins Park. Coming up from the Elwha, that turn is on your right as you crest the divide and it is a rough fisherman's path, not a signed one. If you have started descending toward the Quinault, you have walked past it.

wa_mount_crowder_southwest_route.name: Hannegan Pass, Easy Ridge and Perfect Pass, then south along the west side of the range to the Phantom-Crowder col
camps: Easy Ridge bivouac ground below Easy Peak
Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
wa_mount_crowder_southwest_route.notes:
From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead the trail climbs about 4 miles to Hannegan Pass, then drops the far side to the Chilliwack River. Ford the river near Easy Creek and climb steeply onto Easy Ridge, then follow its crest over Easy Peak. The Imperfect Impasse, a notch guarded by snow moats and wet, down-sloping slabs, usually has to be passed by dropping several hundred feet and climbing back up exposed class 4 ground. Beyond it, carry on to Perfect Pass.

From Perfect Pass the line stays on the west side of the range and heads south: across the edge of the Challenger Glacier, below Crooked Thumb and Ghost Peak, and along under the west side of Phantom Peak. Keep going south to the col between Phantom and Crowder. It is several days of travel each way, with no shortcut and no easy way out once you are past Easy Ridge.
hazards: Fording the Chilliwack River
The Imperfect Impasse: snow moats, wet down-sloping slabs and an exposed class 4 climb back up
Crevasses wherever the line crosses glacier below Challenger and Crooked Thumb
Whiteout navigation on the open snowfields between the Impasse and Perfect Pass
No reasonable retreat once past Easy Ridge
wa_mount_crowder_southwest_route.baseFinding:
The climb starts at the col between Phantom Peak and Crowder, the low point, a little over 6,000 ft, of the ridge that runs south from Phantom. From the col, head southwest and up over a lesser summit of about 7,020 ft. The summit block is beyond it, not on it, and a rib of sound rock leads from its base to the top.

If the rock in front of you is a steep face dropping north toward Picket Creek, you are on the wrong side: Crowder's north side is the steep one, while its west and southwest slopes are moderate.

wa_mount_crowder_southwest_route.name: Baker River Trail and the Pioneer Ridge high route

road.name: Baker Lake Road / forest access
road.status: Per current USFS alert, closed to all vehicle and foot traffic at the Shannon Creek Bridge (~MP 23.8) through its terminus at the Baker River Trailhead, beginning approximately July 15, 2026, due to active construction — verify current status with the Mt. Baker Ranger District before driving.
road.driveNote: Access from the Baker Lake area; verify current road and trailhead status before driving.
road.seasonalGate: The road is also subject to normal winter snow closure; the 2026 mid-summer closure noted above is construction-related, not seasonal.

access.fees: $6 non-refundable lottery/reservation fee, plus a $10-per-person-per-night backcountry camping fee (free for ages 15 and under), under the park's current backcountry permit fees.
access.notes: 60% of sites are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: New fixed anchors (bolts) are prohibited park-wide under the wilderness climbing moratorium — clean, removable protection only. Practice Leave No Trace and pack out all waste in this cross-country zone.
access.permit: North Cascades NP wilderness/backcountry camping permit (required for any overnight stay; day climbs need none)
access.closures: No standing closures specific to Crowder, but check current park alerts for fire restrictions, wildlife closures, or trail/creek-crossing hazards before a trip.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park Service Complex (National Park Service)
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)
access.passRequired: A wilderness backcountry permit (not a highway pass) is required for any overnight stay; 60% of permits are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov, with the remaining 40% held for walk-up issue at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount. No permit is needed for a single-push day climb, but a Crowder trip is realistically multi-day.

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades NP backcountry permit (cross-country zone), fee per person, not free
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov, or get a walk-up permit in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Hannegan-side permits can also be picked up at the Glacier Public Service Center on its limited summer days.

approachLogistics.trailheadDirection: Drive Baker Lake Road (Forest Road 11) 25.5 miles north from WA-20 (milepost 82, near Concrete) to its end at the Baker River Trailhead (774 ft; Northwest Forest Pass required, vault toilet on site).

wa_mount_crowder_southwest_route.notes:
The seldom-used way in, from the west. From the Baker River Trailhead at the end of Baker Lake Road, take the Baker River Trail up the valley, then get up onto Pioneer Ridge and follow the high route along it to the southeast. Pioneer Ridge is a long, rough massif, walled by cliffs and slabs above the Baker River and Picket Creek, and its highest point is at the far southeast end, west of Goodell Creek. Crowder's southwest flank runs down at an easy angle to the foot of that ridge, so this line reaches the peak from below on the southwest rather than at the Phantom col.

Nothing about this line is recorded in detail: no mileage, no gain and no camps. Treat it as a serious cross-country route and plan it from the map. Baker Lake Road has been closed to vehicles and walkers from the Shannon Creek Bridge to the trailhead since mid-July 2026 for construction; check before going.
hazards: Long trailless travel on a rough ridge walled by cliff bands
No recorded water or camps along the ridge
Baker Lake Road construction closure from the Shannon Creek Bridge to the trailhead, in place since mid-July 2026
wa_mount_crowder_southwest_route.baseFinding: Coming off Pioneer Ridge, the peak is climbed by its easy southwest slope, which runs down to the ridge's foot. Head up it toward the summit block; the last part is the rib of sound rock that finishes the main line.

wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.name: Cathedral Pass and Peggy's Pond, then the east ridge and Lynch draw

bivy.name: Peggy's Pond, below Cathedral Rock
bivy.notes: The base for Mount Daniel and the eastern option for Mount Hinman, and by a distance the most convenient high camp on this side of the divide. Drive the Cle Elum River road north from Salmon la Sac roughly eleven to twelve miles of rough, narrow gravel to the Tucquala Meadows trailhead at the road end, take the Cathedral Pass trail — not the Deception Pass trail, which leaves the same lot — past Squaw Lake at about 4,800 ft and up to the pass near 5,600 ft, then the spur west to Peggy's Pond at about 5,560 ft directly under Cathedral Rock. That spur has a short exposed scrambly step that is a genuine obstacle for some parties under an overnight pack. From the pond the standard Daniel route takes the southeast ridge between Circle Lake and the permanent snowfield to the saddle below the east summit at about 7,899 ft and on to the true summit at 7,959 ft, the highest point in the Alpine Lakes; the Lynch Glacier on the north side is the historic line and has shrunk sharply in recent years, draining into Pea Soup Lake. Hinman from here is the less direct half of its two approaches — it means traversing the northeast slopes of Daniel at around 5,300 ft to Pea Soup Lake, crossing to its west end, dropping to about 5,500 ft and then climbing southwest to the summit — long, and much easier under continuous snow than on late-season talus. The Necklace Valley side is the shorter way to Hinman; come here when Daniel is the objective, or when you want both. The critical 2026 caveat: the Cle Elum River road and the Cathedral Pass trail have been inside a fire-area closure running from mid-August to the end of October, along with the campgrounds along that road, so the entire eastern approach has been shut for the back half of the season. Confirm the closure has lifted before driving out — it is a four-hour round trip from the Foss side to find out the hard way.
bivy.water: The pond itself and the snowmelt feeding it, reliable through the normal season. Squaw Lake, about 800 ft lower on the trail in, is the fallback and the overflow camp.
bivy.permit: This is the most restricted camp in the zone and the rules are the point. Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Campfires are prohibited outright — the pond is well above the fire-ban line, the basin is fragile and badly worn, and there is no wood. Party size is reduced here: plan on eight rather than the usual twelve, and midweek is the realistic window for a group that size. Camp only on the existing hardened pads; areas posted as closed for restoration are legally off limits and staying in one is a violation, not a discourtesy. Do not build wind blocks or fire rings — this is the single most common damage in the basin. Move on rock rather than heather. The spur trail is hiker-only, so no stock.
bivy.capacity: Small and strictly limited. Roughly four or five levelled bivouac pads plus a marginal sloping one, and several of the larger areas that used to be camped have been flagged for restoration and are closed. It fills, and there is no honest overflow inside the basin.

approachLogistics.trailhead: Cathedral Rock Trailhead (Cle Elum River Road)

wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.notes:
Hike the Cathedral Rock Trail to Nosh Nosh Wahtum (formerly Squaw Lake) at 2.5 miles, continue to Cathedral Pass at 5,550 ft, then turn left (west) onto the PCT. In less than half a mile turn right (northwest) onto Trail #1375 — do not follow the PCT down toward Deep Lake. Follow #1375 past Cathedral Rock to Peggy's Pond at about 5,560 ft and camp there. This is the shorter approach with the longer summit day, and it avoids the brush of the alternative.

From camp, climb to about 6,300 ft on the east ridge, then traverse below the Daniel Glacier at 6,100 to 6,300 ft toward Lynch draw.

Trailhead to camp is about 2.5 to 4 hours; camp to summit 5 to 7 hours.
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.season: Jun-mid Jul, while Pea Soup Lake is frozen and the moat closed; the lake crossing gets hard once it melts
hazards: Full-width crevasses opening late in the season across the Lynch Glacier
Loose, rotten rock on the ground used to gain and leave the ice — reported as the worst hazard on the route
A moat at the rock-to-ice transition that widens through the summer
Pea Soup Lake melting out and Lynch draw flooding from mid-July
Significant glacier recession, so old descriptions understate the rock and moat work
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.baseFinding:
The arrival test is a lake you walk across. Traversing below the Daniel Glacier you come to Lynch draw and, in season, to frozen Pea Soup Lake. Walk straight across it and get onto the ice above the low rocks on its far side. That is the base of the Lynch Glacier, and standing on the lake surface is an unambiguous confirmation you are in the right basin.

What to do when the lake has melted out, which is the common case from mid-July: do not try to force the draw, which can be flooded. Instead climb the ridge separating the Daniel and Lynch glaciers for a couple of hundred yards to the first minor notch at about 6,600 ft. Drop roughly 100 ft off it to a snowfield hugging the ridge, then work climbers' left via a second snowfield and rock benches onto the Lynch Glacier. First minor notch at 6,600 ft, then down 100 ft and left: that is a counted sequence rather than a described one, which is what you want in cloud.

Getting onto the ice, in either season: early, take the snow finger on climbers' right. Late, bypass on climbers' left by class 3 scrambling, and expect a moat at the transition. The loose rotten rock used to reach the ice is repeatedly reported as more dangerous than the glacier itself.

And the top tells you which summit is which: the glacier leads to the gap between the two highest summits. From the notch, the west summit — on your right — is the true high point. Late in the season expect a detour around crevasses about two thirds of the way up.

A scope note that matters to peak-list parties: reaching the upper Daniel Glacier from Peggy's Pond by the Southeast Ridge or the Hyas Creek Glacier is a scramble and is not this route.

wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.name: Deception Pass, Marmot and Jade Lakes, and Dip Top Gap from the east
camps: Hyas Lake and Upper Hyas Lake
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.notes:
From the Deception Pass trailhead, hike to Marmot and Jade Lakes and continue to Dip Top Gap. From the gap, traverse west to the shoulder overlooking the Foss River drainage, then descend to the outlet of Pea Soup Lake.

This is the longer, eastern line into the same basin. It reaches the Lynch Glacier at the same point the Peggy's Pond approach does, and everything about identifying the ice is identical from the lake outlet onward.
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.season: Early season, roughly June into July, before the moat opens
hazards: Crevasses across the full width of the glacier late in the season
The moat at the rock-to-ice transition
Loose rotten rock on the class 3 bypass
A long approach over Dip Top Gap with a descent to the lake that must be reversed on the way out
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.baseFinding:
You are aiming for the outlet of Pea Soup Lake, and the shoulder above the Foss River is the waypoint that gets you there. From Dip Top Gap the traverse is west until you are on the shoulder looking down into the Foss River drainage; the descent from that shoulder lands at the lake outlet. If you are looking down into a drainage that is not the Foss, you have not traversed far enough west.

From the outlet the finding is the same as from Peggy's Pond: get onto the ice above the low rocks at the head of the lake. Early season, take the snow finger on climbers' right; late season, bypass by class 3 on climbers' left and cross the moat. Then ascend the upper glacier toward the West Pyramid and the col between the Middle and True summits.

The negative test: this route is graded third class with only minor snow and ice difficulty. If you are on steep ice, you are not on the Lynch Glacier standard line.

wa_mount_ellinor_standard.name: Upper Trailhead on NFR 24, Trail #812 summer route
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.notes:
From the Upper Trailhead at about 3,500 ft, at the end of FS Road 2419-014 off FS 24 / FS 2419 — vault toilet, picnic table, Northwest Forest Pass required — Trail #812 climbs immediately. The first 0.3 mile is stacked stairstep switchbacks through forest, merging with the longer lower-trailhead trail at roughly 3,900 ft.

From the merge, continue up the south ridge through increasingly open forest to timberline at about 4,500 ft, roughly a mile in. In summer conditions the trail is snow-free and well cut essentially to the top, switchbacking across rock-strewn slopes and gravelly subalpine meadows, threading a narrow notch and crossing west-facing slopes to the 5,944 ft summit. Total gain from the Upper Trailhead is 2,444 ft over 1.6 miles one way. No water on the upper route; carry all you need.
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.season: Roughly Jul-Oct for the snow-free summer trail; outside that the chute fills and the upper switchbacks are buried
hazards: The southeast-facing chute is an avalanche funnel that becomes sun-soaked and prone to wet slides by early-mid afternoon — start early and check NWAC in spring
Chute-bordering rocks are extremely slick when wet or in fog
Losing the trail under snow leads onto steeper, looser ground
A very popular and crowded trail with kicked-loose rock from parties above
No water on route
Fragile subalpine vegetation on the open upper slopes
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.baseFinding:
The decision point on this mountain is a signed junction at timberline, roughly 4,500 ft, and a sign is the best fog marker there is because it does not depend on visibility beyond arm's length. At that junction the winter climbing route breaks right, straight up the prominent scree-and-snow chute, and the maintained summer trail switchbacks left across rock-strewn slopes and gravelly meadows. This variant is the left one.

If you find yourself climbing a single steep funnel-shaped gully rather than working a series of switchbacks, you have taken the right-hand branch and you are on the winter route.

Second test, higher: the summer trail threads a narrow notch and then crosses west-facing slopes before the final approach to the summit. Many of its switchbacks have stairstep risers built into them. Built steps are man-made and unambiguous underfoot. If you are on trackless scree you have left the trail.

Honest limit, and it is seasonal rather than navigational: outside roughly November to June, snow fills the chute and buries the upper switchbacks, and most parties then climb the chute directly because the summer trail is not there to be found. That is not a route-finding failure; it is a different route, and it demands an ice axe and traction. The rocks in and bordering the chute are notoriously slick when wet even outside full winter conditions — that is an official Forest Service warning, not a trip-report opinion.

wa_mount_ellinor_standard.name: Lower Trailhead, the long approach to the same trail

bivy.name: Big Creek Campground, Lake Cushman
bivy.notes: The obvious roadside base for Mount Ellinor and Mount Washington, sitting at the junction where the Lake Cushman road becomes FR 24, with FR 2419 climbing from there to the Ellinor lower trailhead at about 2,600 ft, the upper trailhead at about 3,500 ft, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the road end near 3,000 ft. Both peaks are genuine day objectives — Ellinor is a maintained trail and Washington a class 3 scramble through a basin and gully — so this is explicitly a contingency rather than the normal plan: it exists for the party that arrives the night before to get an early start on a hot day, or that comes down from the Washington gully later than intended and would rather not drive. It is also the sane base for anyone linking the Washington–Ellinor ridge traverse, which takes far longer than either peak alone. A trail from the campground connects up toward the Mount Ellinor system if you want to walk the whole thing from the tent, but that turns a half-day into a very long one.
bivy.water: Seasonal potable water is generally available in the campground, but do not count on it outside the main summer season. Big Creek runs alongside
bivy.permit: Per-night Forest Service fee. No wilderness permit — this is a developed campground on Forest Service land, outside the national park. Vault toilets, tables and fire rings, pack it in and pack it out. Note the separate parking rule up the hill: a Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Mount Ellinor upper trailhead but not at the lower one, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the end of FR 2419 follows the Forest Service pass regime as well
bivy.capacity: A large forested loop campground — published site counts vary between roughly two dozen and considerably more, so check current numbers rather than trusting a figure. Sites are well spaced in second growth

wa_mount_ellinor_standard.notes:
The Lower Trailhead sits at about 2,600 ft, 3.1 miles one way, and takes no fee. It welcomes you with an easy grade rather than the upper trailhead's near-immediate jolt, and it is the sensible choice when FS Road 2419-014 to the upper lot is snowed in or gated.

It climbs steadily through forest and joins the upper-trailhead trail at roughly 3,900 ft. Everything above the merge is identical.
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.season: Roughly Jun-Oct, and it is snow-free earlier than the upper road in some years
hazards: Same as the upper-trailhead variant, over a longer and gentler approach
The 3,900 ft merge is where parties descend to the wrong trailhead
No water on the upper route
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.baseFinding:
The first test is the merge at about 3,900 ft, where the lower trail joins the upper-trailhead trail. From below, that junction is the confirmation you are on the right path at all; from above it is the fork you take downhill to get back to the lower lot rather than the upper one. Parties have descended to the wrong car here.

The decision point is the same signed junction at timberline, roughly 4,500 ft, about 2.5 miles from the lower trailhead: the winter climbing route breaks right up the chute, the summer trail switchbacks left. Take the left.

And the same confirmations above it: stairstep risers built into the switchbacks, a narrow notch, and west-facing slopes before the summit.

wa_mount_ellinor_standard.name: The winter chute, direct from the timberline junction
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.notes:
Not a different trailhead but a genuinely different climb, and it is what most parties are on outside core summer because the summer switchbacks are buried. From either trailhead, follow Trail #812 to the signed timberline junction at about 4,500 ft and take the right-hand branch straight up the prominent scree-and-snow chute below the summit saddle.

This demands an ice axe and traction — crampons or microspikes — and it is steep, funnel-shaped slide-path terrain with real avalanche potential. Check avalanche conditions before going up.

It is also the fast descent when conditions allow: with an axe carried in self-arrest position, parties glissade roughly 1,000 ft in a couple of minutes. That is consequential terrain rather than a casual slide.
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.season: Roughly Nov-Jun, while the chute holds a firm continuous snowpack
hazards: A steep funnel-shaped slide path with real avalanche potential; check NWAC before going
Wet-slide danger by early-mid afternoon in spring on a sun-soaked southeast aspect
Exposed rocks and ice bulges lower in the chute as snow thins — glissading then becomes dangerous
An uncontrolled glissade or a fall on hard snow without self-arrest skill on genuinely consequential terrain
Slick chute-bordering rocks when wet or in fog
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.baseFinding:
The base is the signed timberline junction at about 4,500 ft and the right-hand branch out of it. That is the whole test and it is the same sign the summer parties turn left at. The chute is the prominent scree-and-snow funnel that runs straight up toward the summit saddle from there — there is one, it is obvious, and it is the reason the junction is signed at all.

The confirming test is that the ground stops switchbacking. The summer trail traverses; the chute goes up the fall line. If you are still zig-zagging you took the left branch.

The test for whether you should be there at all, which matters more on this route than finding it: the chute is south-east facing and sun-soaked, and by early-to-mid afternoon in spring it is prone to wet slides. Start early. Later in the season, as the snow thins and exposes talus, rock and ice bulges, the chute stops being the fast line and becomes the dangerous one — at that point the correct call is the summer switchbacks for the whole descent.

wa_mount_fernow_southeast_face.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin, over the col and across the Gloomy Glacier
wa_mount_fernow_southeast_face.notes:
Same walk in as for Seven Fingered Jack and Maude: Phelps Creek trail to the Leroy Creek crossing at about 4,140 ft, then the steep unmaintained climbers' trail on the north side of the creek into Leroy Basin at about 6,100 ft.

This is the common approach but not the elegant one. It exists because the alternative is the ferry up Lake Chelan to Holden and the Railroad Creek trail into Copper Basin, which gains the East Ridge — the standard route — much more directly. A third option starts at Cottonwood on the Entiat River and reaches the East Ridge by way of the Entiat Glacier. All three converge on the same south-east face finish.

From Leroy Basin, head north-west toward a waterfall and climb its left side to a small notch on the ridge of Seven Fingered Jack. Published descriptions of this saddle vary — one places it just west of an obvious 7,700 ft col with a couple of bivy sites at the low point, another gives it as a notch reached past a second creek crossing — and they may or may not be the same feature, so check it on a map rather than assuming.

From the saddle you must drop about a thousand feet into the moraine at the terminus of the Gloomy Glacier, and every foot of it has to be regained on the way out. Two published ways down: descend to the tarn below and go around a prominent rock formation that guards the basin, or descend to the right across sandy ledges and down large boulders.

Expect roughly nine hours round trip from Leroy Basin, and a very long day car to car — one party left the trailhead at three in the morning and got back at eleven at night.
wa_mount_fernow_southeast_face.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the Leroy-to-Gloomy crossing runs through avalanche terrain earlier than that
hazards: A thousand feet of descent into the Gloomy basin that must be regained on the way out
Avalanche terrain on the Leroy-to-Gloomy crossing
Icy forty-degree slopes near the top of the Gloomy Glacier, with crevasses below the usual line
Two thousand feet of exceptionally loose talus and scree above the basin
The narrow exposed ledge traverse off the col, which is avoidable and should be avoided
Route-finding is the crux — this is regarded as the most complex of the three Entiat nine-thousanders
wa_mount_fernow_southeast_face.baseFinding:
Fernow is not visible from Leroy basin, and this is confirmed rather than folklore. Parties climbing the basin under the cirque of Seven Fingered Jack report having real difficulty identifying the route because the peak simply is not in view. Do not stand in the basin trying to pick your line off the mountain; you cannot see it. Carry a track.

The arrival test is short and physical: cross the moraine below the Gloomy Glacier, go up the waterfall, and you are in the broad basin below Fernow. That is where the climbing starts.

Above that basin there are two decision points and both have a wrong answer that is on record.

First: descend the glacier to its terminal moraine at about 6,500 ft, then climb the right side of a stream to an upper snow-filled basin, and from there go south-west up a broad gully that turns eastward. That is Class 2-3 and gives you the luxury of knowing where you are. The alternative — dropping only to 7,000 ft and making a rising traverse through a succession of gullies, ribs and small cliffs — is Class 3-plus with snow and ice and the feeling of being lost somewhere in the Entiat Mountains.

Second, and this is the one that matters: from the broad gully, do not go all the way to the col and traverse the south-east face on the narrow ledges there. They are described as exposed enough to frighten a bird, with the honest observation that a fallen body would be unlikely to be found. Instead climb the broad gully to about 8,400 ft, then a loose gully to about 9,000 ft, and traverse the face at nine thousand on a wide ledge that is not exposed at all.

The 8,400 ft mark is a real landmark rather than a number on a map — two independent parties record the ground changing character there, one of them at a large bench holding permanent snow with water running off it. From 8,400 the line goes up loose talus to the ridge between Seven Fingered Jack and Fernow, where cairns pick up and weave around to the south-east ridge of the summit block. The cairns are reported by three separate parties, though one notes they stop near the summit itself.

The general principle behind all of it: climb as far as you can up the ridge separating Fernow's south-east and south-west faces. Once on the East Ridge, a couple of hundred feet of Class 3 on reasonably solid rock finishes it.

wa_mount_fernow_southeast_face.name: Holden Village and Copper Basin
wa_mount_fernow_southeast_face.notes: From Holden Village up to the Copper–Entiat divide and the east ridge. The most direct way to the standard east-side line, and climbable in a day from Holden, but it depends on the Lake Chelan boat.

wa_mount_fernow_southeast_face.name: Entiat River from Cottonwood

approachLogistics.trailhead: Entiat River Trailhead (Cottonwood, end of Entiat River Road)

wa_mount_fernow_southeast_face.notes: Up the Entiat River trail toward the Entiat Glacier and the east ridge. The longest way in, with less gain and little avalanche exposure.

wa_mount_hardy_snow_scramble.name: Rainy Pass, the crest trail to Methow Pass, and the east ridge
camps: Methow Pass and the PCT meadow camps below Snowy Lakes
wa_mount_hardy_snow_scramble.notes: The long way, and the one that suits a two-day trip. From the large paved lot on the north side of SR-20 at Rainy Pass, follow the crest trail north as it climbs steadily through subalpine forest and larch parkland past Porcupine Creek — fill up there, it is the last easy water before a long dry stretch of switchbacks — to Cutthroat Pass. From the pass the trail drops toward Granite Pass and a saddle beyond it, where a steep snowfield often lasts into August and has caused slide-for-life falls, so carry an axe if you are early in the season. Beyond, the trail contours across open, sparsely treed slopes to Snowy Creek Meadow, a common water and camp stop, with a short side trail west into the Snowy Lakes basin for a higher and more scenic bivy under Tower Mountain and Golden Horn. From the meadow, stay on the crest trail north to the open plateau at Methow Pass and leave it there: travel west and southwest off-trail through open heather and talus benches toward the peak's east ridge, gain the ridge, and follow moderate sand, scree and talus — loose in places, with real route-finding — up to the saddle between the true summit and its lower false summit.
wa_mount_hardy_snow_scramble.season: Late June through September, with July through September giving the driest scree. June ascents work but the final slopes and gully still hold snow and want an axe and crampons. The highway is shut for avalanche control through the winter, which closes both approaches outright.
hazards: loose scree, talus and blocky rock on the unmarked upper route, worst near the summit saddle and the final gully
a steep lingering snowfield just past Granite Pass that has caused slide-for-life falls into August
a long, mostly off-trail final leg with no marked line
afternoon thunderstorms and fast weather changes on exposed ridge crest and passes
wildfire smoke reducing visibility in late summer
seasonal closure of the highway cutting off road access entirely
wa_mount_hardy_snow_scramble.baseFinding: The saddle you are aiming for sits between the true summit and a lower knob to its east — do not stop on the knob. From Methow Pass, get up onto the east ridge as early as you can and keep close to its crest; the talus slopes below it are loose and slow, and parties who angle across them lose time. Moderate sand, scree and talus lead to the saddle between the summit and the eastern false summit. From the saddle, several hundred feet of blocky Class 2-3 scrambling on rock that takes hands reach the top. If the highest ground you can reach still has something higher a short distance to the west, you are on the knob, and the saddle below it is where you cross to the true summit.

wa_mount_hardy_snow_scramble.name: Swamp Creek pullout and the south ridge

approachLogistics.trailhead: Swamp Creek pullout (SR-20, about 2 miles west of Rainy Pass)

wa_mount_hardy_snow_scramble.notes: The short, steep alternative, and the way most day parties go. Start from the highway pullout at Swamp Creek and climb through brushy forest to the foot of the prominent ridge on the mountain's south side. Follow the ridge upward, staying on the crest where it lets you and moving climber's right to get around the cliff bands that block the crest around 5,200 ft — getting that traverse wrong is what turns parties back. Above the cliff bands the ridge opens out onto sand and scree and continues to the summit block. This side faces the sun and dries early, which is why it comes into condition before the crest-trail approach and why it turns into a loose, dusty grind by late summer; a snow finger on this flank can hold firm snow at a fairly steep angle into early summer, which speeds the ascent considerably for a party carrying an axe.
wa_mount_hardy_snow_scramble.season: Late June through September once the snow finger has stabilised or melted, with July and August driest. Earlier in the season the finger is a snow climb rather than a scramble.
hazards: cliff bands around 5,200 ft where the crest is blocked and the bypass is on climber's right — the main route-finding failure on this side
a steep snow finger on this flank into early summer, with wet-slide and sluff potential
brushy forest on the lower ridge with no maintained tread
loose scree and blocky rock on the upper route and in the final gully
an exposed ridge crest with no shelter from afternoon thunderstorms
seasonal closure of the highway cutting off road access entirely
wa_mount_hardy_snow_scramble.baseFinding: The notch is on the far side of the block from where you arrive, and you have to traverse to it. At about 7,200 ft the ridge you have been following runs into the summit block; leave the crest there and scramble loose scree and granite blocks across the east side — climber's right — until you reach a notch tucked under the summit block. Cross the notch, and the way on is a short, shallow gully leading up to the top. That gully is the marker: it is shallow and blocky rather than deep and cut, and it is the only break that goes at scrambling grade. If the block above you is unbroken wall, keep traversing right rather than starting up; if you have dropped far enough to be under steep cliff bands, you have gone too low and should regain height. The upper ground is several hundred feet of enjoyable blocky scrambling on rock that takes hands, and a lower false summit sits beside the true one — if the highest ground you can reach still has something higher a short distance away, you are on the false summit and the saddle between them is where you crossed.

wa_mount_hopper_standard.name: First Divide from the Duckabush and Marmot Lake

bivy.name: Upper Duckabush junction camp — the link between First Divide and the Duckabush head
bivy.notes: This is a connector rather than a destination, and it matters because of where it sits: the point where the trail down from First Divide and Home Sweet Home meets the Duckabush River trail coming up from the east and the O'Neil Pass trail heading west. If you are going for Mount Duckabush from Staircase, you come over First Divide, drop to this junction, and climb again toward Marmot Lake or O'Neil Pass — so the day involves losing about 1,600 ft off the divide and regaining it, which is the reason the peak feels harder than its distance suggests. Camping here is what makes that carry manageable. It is deep valley forest with no views, and it is a long way from anywhere in every direction; treat it as a place to sleep between two big days rather than a base for anything.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Duckabush River at the junction
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site; not a quota camp and usually available. Bear canisters are required. Below the fire line, so fires are allowed in the established rings outside seasonal bans.
bivy.capacity: A modest forested camp at the trail junction, a few sites; lightly used because almost everyone is passing through

wa_mount_hopper_standard.notes: The historic Skokomish approach is closed by fire damage, and so is this one where it leaves the Duckabush: the park lists the Home Sweet Home Trail, from the Duckabush River Trail junction over First Divide, closed for the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire with no reopening date (trail-conditions page updated September 14, 2026), so no open trail reaches First Divide while the closure stands. When it reopens, the way in is the long Duckabush valley over Big Hump to Marmot Lake, then back to the Home Sweet Home junction and over First Divide. Roughly double the old distance and firmly a multi-day trip with a camp at the lake or at Home Sweet Home.
hazards: Loose talus and steep meadow slopes on the upper mountain
Snow choking the summit gully well into summer
Rockfall in the gully system onto anyone below
Burn-scar hazard trees and rockfall along the closed Skokomish corridor
A very long, remote walk-out from anywhere on the route
wa_mount_hopper_standard.baseFinding: First Divide is a distinct saddle with Duckabush and Steel to the west and Hopper to the east, and the old climbers' way to the peak splits off here. Do not expect to find it — that tread has been under brush for more than a decade, so treat the saddle itself as the base of the off-trail travel and navigate rather than follow. From the divide, angle east through forest and brush and pop out into open summit meadow, then climb talus toward the rockwall below the top. The identification that actually matters is up there, not at the saddle: several gullies and ribs seam that wall and every one of them looks plausible from the bottom. The one that goes is the line that keeps laying back into short climbable steps; anything that walls up into a blank corner above you is the wrong one, and the honest expectation is that you may back off one and try another. Note a feature at the foot of whichever gully you commit to, because picking it out again from above is harder than finding it from below. The final crest narrows and is impassable in places, so choose your line early.

wa_mount_hopper_standard.name: Staircase and the North Fork Skokomish to First Divide
camps: Home Sweet Home — the meadow camp under First Divide for Steel and Hopper
wa_mount_hopper_standard.notes: The historic and shortest way in. From Staircase, follow the North Fork Skokomish trail up the valley to Home Sweet Home and on to First Divide, where the scramble leaves the trail. Fire damage has affected this corridor, so check the park's trail status before planning.

wa_mount_howard_south_slope.name: Merritt Lake Trailhead and Nason Ridge Trail to Crescent Lake
camps: Nason Creek Campground and the Lake Wenatchee drive-in camps
wa_mount_howard_south_slope.notes: The shorter and more direct way in. From the highway turn onto the rough forest road — high clearance is worth having — and drive to the Merritt Lake Trailhead. Climb the Merritt Lake trail to the lake, then join the Nason Ridge Trail and follow it east to Crescent Lake, which sits below the peak's south side. Water is available at Crescent Lake but is unreliable higher on the mountain, so fill there. The trail is well defined the whole way to the lake, and everything above it is your own route-finding.
wa_mount_howard_south_slope.season: July into October once the ridge clears; snow persists above about 5,000 ft into late spring.
hazards: Several little bowls look like the peak's south face and one of them is the wrong drainage entirely
A well-worn boot path leaves the ridge trail heading north — that is the climbers' route to the neighbouring summit, not this one
No established route above Crescent Lake, and the descent is the crux of the day
Loose, dirty Class 3 in whichever gully you pick through the cliff band
Slippery grass and dense alder low on the face when descending
Water unreliable above Crescent Lake
wa_mount_howard_south_slope.baseFinding: Make sure you are in the right drainage before you climb — several little bowls look like this face, and the one to your east is Royal Creek. That is the single mistake worth guarding against here, and it is made before you gain any height. From the northeast side of Crescent Lake, take the talus field at the head of the lake, directly below the obvious cliff band; a short thrash through woody brush leads to an upper talus field, and from there drift right to get around the cliff. Several gullies break the band and there is no single correct one — parties pick the easiest-looking line and find it loose, dirty Class 3 for about a hundred feet. That crux band is the confirmation you are on the face, not a sign to retreat, but it is unpleasant to reverse, so note your line. Above it the ground eases onto talus and dirt climbers' paths to the top.
