Note also that a well-worn boot path leaves the ridge trail heading north on the way in: that is the climbers' route to the neighbouring peak and not the way to this one.

wa_mount_howard_south_slope.name: Rock Mountain Trailhead via Rock Lake and the Rock–Crescent col

bivy.name: Crescent Lake
bivy.notes: The base camp for both Mount Howard and Mount Mastiff, and the natural halfway house on the crest traverse. It sits on the Nason Ridge trail one and three tenths miles beyond Rock Lake, reached by traversing a loose slope around the intervening ridge and dropping about five hundred feet, or from the other direction three and a half miles west of Merritt Lake. From the lake the south slope route on Howard goes around the northeast side and straight up, skirting trees and slide alder to a rock band that is passed by any of several easy scrambling gullies onto a large bench; from the bench you can go directly up the south flank to Howard's summit or traverse east onto the southeast ridge. Mastiff stands a mile east of Howard along the crest and almost everyone who camps here takes both in one day. This is a genuine overnight destination rather than pure contingency — the two summits together are a long push from any trailhead in a day, and sleeping at the lake turns a grim outing into a good one. Bugs are heavy through June and early July, and the approach from either end holds snow on the north-facing traverses well into summer.
bivy.water: The lake plus several small running streams in the immediate surroundings, which is unusually generous for this ridge and is exactly why parties fill their bottles here before going up. It is dependable through the season. Everything above the lake is dry, so the four quarts you want for a summit camp or a long crest day come from here.
bivy.permit: None — no wilderness, no permit, no quota. No pass is required at the Rock Mountain or Merritt Lake trailheads; Nason Ridge is the one fee trailhead on this crest, at $5 a day or $30 a year. No campfires above 5,000 feet, which includes this lake, and expect a total burn ban most of the summer.
bivy.capacity: Lakeside sites for a handful of tents, quieter than Merritt because it takes real effort to reach from either direction; use the existing spots rather than clearing new ground on the vegetation

bivy.name: Nason Creek Campground and the Lake Wenatchee drive-in camps
bivy.notes: The drive-in base for the whole ridge, and the honest recommendation for most parties climbing these peaks: all four summits are day objectives from the highway trailheads, and sleeping at a developed campground with water and driving fifteen or twenty minutes to a trailhead beats carrying an overnight load up two thousand feet of dry switchbacks. The season runs roughly May through mid-October. From here the Merritt Lake and Round Mountain trailheads are a short drive west and north along the highway and its spurs, with Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek further west toward the pass. It is also the sensible place to reorganise mid-trip: a party that has come off the crest at one end and needs to reposition to the other has this corridor to do it in. Note that the trailheads themselves have very limited parking — Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek in particular hold only a few cars — so an early start from a nearby campground is worth more here than the extra sleep of staying further out.
bivy.water: Piped potable water at the developed campgrounds through the operating season, and Nason Creek itself alongside. This is the one place where water is a non-issue, which is why every party working this ridge should fill everything here before driving up to a trailhead rather than counting on anything above.
bivy.permit: A per-night fee, currently around the high twenties at the forest campground, with advance reservations opening well ahead and closing a few days before arrival. The state park campgrounds have their own reservation system and their own fee. No wilderness permit is involved anywhere in this zone. Fire restrictions apply in the campgrounds through the summer and are commonly total bans in late season.
bivy.capacity: Nason Creek is the closest and largest, laid out over four loops on both sides of the highway near the southeastern end of Lake Wenatchee, taking vehicles up to about thirty-five feet. Roughly sixty percent of sites are reservable in advance and the remainder are first come, first served. The state park campgrounds around the lake add substantially more capacity, and there are further national forest campgrounds spread along the highway corridor.

bivy.name: Mount Howard summit-area bivouac
bivy.notes: Strictly a contingency and a preference, not a plan. Mount Howard is a day objective from a camp at Crescent Lake and there is no practical reason to haul water and a bag two thousand feet higher except to be on the crest at sunset and dawn, or to be positioned for a full ridge traverse taking in Mastiff to the east and Rock Mountain to the west in one push. It has been done and it works, but it commits you: there is no water, no shelter, no escape from wind, and the descent to the nearest water is a real drop. The route up from Crescent Lake goes around the lake's northeast side and directly up the slope, threading trees and slide alder to a rock band that is turned by easy scrambling gullies onto a broad bench, and the summit is straight up the south flank from there. In spring the upper slopes hold soft snow over a firm base and are booted rather than climbed, with crampons useful on the way down; that is the season a summit camp is most often chosen, and it is also when the exposure up here bites hardest.
bivy.water: None, and no prospect of any. Every drop comes up from Crescent Lake, roughly two thousand feet below, and a party planning to cook and sleep here has historically carried something like four quarts each. Late-lying snow patches on the north side can be melted in early season and are gone by midsummer.
bivy.permit: None — non-wilderness, no permit and no quota. No pass is required at the Rock Mountain or Merritt Lake trailheads; Nason Ridge is the one fee trailhead on this crest, at $5 a day or $30 a year. No campfires, and there is nothing up here to burn. Leave no constructed platform behind; the crest vegetation and thin soil do not recover.
bivy.capacity: One or two people on scraped benches just below the summit. There is no flat ground for a tent, no shelter of any kind, and nothing you would call a site — this is bare ridge crest and you are making a ledge, not finding one.

wa_mount_howard_south_slope.notes: The longer and more scenic way in, and the one commonly used by parties who want the neighbouring summit in the same outing. From the highway near the milepost, climb the Rock Mountain trail to Rock Lake — snow persists above about 5,000 ft into late spring on this side — then cross the col between the two peaks and descend roughly five hundred feet on the far side to Crescent Lake. From there the climb is the same as from the other trailhead. It costs a substantial descent that has to be regained on the return, which is the price of the extra ground it covers.
wa_mount_howard_south_slope.season: July into October. Snow lingers above about 5,000 ft into late spring and the col holds it longest.
hazards: A substantial descent to Crescent Lake that must be reclimbed on the way out
Snow persisting on the col into late spring
Several little bowls look like the peak's south face — confirm the drainage before climbing
The same cliff band and loose, dirty Class 3 gullies above the lake
A long day made longer by the added distance and the col crossing
wa_mount_howard_south_slope.baseFinding: Crescent Lake is the common starting point, and on this side you arrive at it from above. Cross the col between the two peaks and descend several hundred feet on the far side to the lake; the tell that you are on this variant rather than the direct one is that you reach the water losing height rather than gaining it. From the lake the climb is identical, and so is the mistake to guard against: several little bowls in this basin look like the peak's south face, and being sure of the drainage before you start upward matters more than anything higher on the route. Take the talus field at the head of the lake directly below the obvious cliff band, push through the woody brush to an upper talus field, then drift right to get round the cliff. Several gullies break the band, none of them the single correct one; expect about a hundred feet of loose, dirty Class 3 in whichever you choose. Above it, talus and dirt climbers' paths lead to the summit.

wa_mount_lago_south_slope_south_face.name: From Robinson Creek over Robinson Pass
camps: The high bench southwest of Shellrock Pass
The Berk Creek junction and the Middle Fork Pasayten river camps
wa_mount_lago_south_slope_south_face.notes: Lago is the highest peak in this group and the least loved underfoot, being a large pile of loose rock where the whole ascent asks for deliberate movement rather than any technique. Camp is normally Fred's Lake or Shellrock Basin, reached along the Middle Fork Pasayten, either over Robinson Pass from the low Robinson Creek trailhead or down the Whistler Cutoff from the high start at Slate Pass, with an awkward crossing of upper Eureka Creek when it is swollen with snowmelt. From camp the round trip is a half day. Many parties link straight over to Carru by the connecting col rather than descending and re-climbing, and the southwest slope is a common variation for coming down since it avoids some of the steeper upper rock ribs.
hazards: Notoriously loose, crumbly rock throughout the upper mountain
Rockfall onto a party stacked below on the face
An enormous cliff on the north side of the summit ridge
Difficult crossing of upper Eureka Creek during snowmelt
No shelter from thunderstorms on the open talus and crest
Grizzly and black bear country - proper food storage required
wa_mount_lago_south_slope_south_face.baseFinding: Everything about this climb is on the south side, and the base can be picked up from either of two places. Coming across from the Carru col at about 7,600 ft, the start is where the col's flattish talus stops being flat and tips up into the peak's southwest face, a mixed slope of scree, talus and occasional patches of solid rock with no path, no cairns and no single obvious line, which is itself the signature of this face. Coming up from Shellrock Basin, the start is the toe of the broad south slope above the last stunted trees, at the point where heather gives out and continuous rock begins. In both cases the confirming feature is what is not there: this side carries no cliff band across it. If you are looking up at a wall rather than a long, tedious, uniform slope, you have drifted round onto the wrong aspect and should traverse back south. The mountain's real hazard sits on the far side of the crest, so the top is where care is needed rather than the base. The north side of the summit ridge is an enormous cliff, and the moment you can see straight down you have gone too far north. Which of the crest's several rises is the true high point is not obvious from the face below, so gain the ridge first and judge from up there; a faint boot-worn line runs along the crest and following it is more reliable than picking a top from the slope.

wa_mount_lago_south_slope_south_face.name: From Slate Pass down the Middle Fork Pasayten

bivy.name: The high bench southwest of Shellrock Pass
bivy.notes: This is the staging camp that makes Mount Carru and Mount Lago short days instead of enormous ones, and it is deliberately not the same ground as the Shellrock Basin and Eureka Creek meadow camps lower down. It is a bench at around 7,500 ft immediately southwest of the pass, high enough that every summit in the group is within reach from it. For Carru the line runs west along the east fork of Eureka Creek, leaves the trail at a creek crossing and takes a red talus gully east of the Carru-Lago saddle for a few hundred feet — under two hours from camp to the 8,595 ft summit. Lago at 8,745 ft is the highest thing in this part of the wilderness and goes from the same saddle. What you pay for the position is water and weather. There is no tree cover, the pass funnels wind, and a party that has not carried enough will be walking back down for it. Snow holds on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the real constraint on when this is worth doing. Larches turn in the last days of September and the nights at this height are properly cold by then.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and a small tarn below the pass, both of them seasonal. By late summer there may be nothing at all up here and the passes on either side are reliably dry. Carry water up from the Eureka Creek meadows or the river; this is the single most common mistake made on these summits.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass to park. The bench is thin alpine ground that holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the turf alone. Assume no fires — there is nothing to burn at this elevation and the meadows below are fragile.
bivy.capacity: Roughly half an acre of usable bench, so realistically two or three small parties. No established sites, no facilities and no shelter of any kind.

bivy.name: The Berk Creek junction and the Middle Fork Pasayten river camps
bivy.notes: This is the hinge of the whole Middle Fork approach and it is where a party bound for Mount Carru, Mount Lago or Lost Peak actually sleeps on the first night. Two roads reach it: the high start from Slate Pass at nearly 6,900 ft with a short connector down to the Middle Fork trail, or the low start from the Robinson Creek trailhead at about 2,560 ft over Robinson Pass at 6,220 ft, which is nine and a half miles before the valley walking even begins. The high start is shorter by a long way and is what most parties use. From the junction the climb to Freds Pass and the crossing of the upper Eureka Creek country puts you in position for the summits; the whole approach from a road is around fifteen miles. Being on the river rather than up at the lakes costs you height on the second day and buys you shelter, running water and a warmer night — a real trade when the high camps are exposed and dry. The forest here is patchy burn in places and blowdown varies. This is remote country by any standard and there is no mobile service anywhere in the valley.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Middle Fork Pasayten and Berk Creek meet here and both run all season. This is the last easy water before the long climb to the passes, and the country above lives on tarns and snowmelt, so fill completely.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Slate Pass or Robinson Creek, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, though the valley is dry and bans are common by August.
bivy.capacity: A single established site at the junction where the trail up to Freds Lake and Doris Lake leaves the Middle Fork, plus scattered ground along the river flats above and below it. One or two parties each, nothing developed.

road.name: Harts Pass Road (FR 5400) and Slate Peak Road (FR 5400-600)
road.status: Narrow, steep gravel with few turnouts above the end of the pavement; no trailers. The 2026 Ptarmigan Fire burned into the Middle Fork Pasayten, and its closure shut the Buckskin Ridge and Eureka Creek trails this approach uses; check the Methow Valley Ranger District's alerts before you go, and expect burned forest and blowdown in the valley.
road.driveNote: From SR 20 at Mazama, follow Lost River Road to the end of the pavement and continue on the gravel Harts Pass Road (FR 5400) to Harts Pass. At the guard station turn right onto Slate Peak Road (FR 5400-600) and drive about 3.5 miles to the Slate Pass Trailhead at the second switchback beyond the horse loading area.
road.seasonalGate: Usually snow-free and open July to September

trip.approach: From the Slate Pass Trailhead (about 6,900 ft), take Buckskin Ridge Trail #498 a short way north to the Whistler Cutoff and drop to the Middle Fork Pasayten Trail #478 on the valley floor, about 3.1 miles and 5,280 ft. Follow it north about 4.8 miles to the Eureka Creek Trail and climb along Berk Creek to Fred's Lake (6,507 ft), a common camp. From the lake, cross the crest east into the upper Eureka Creek basin on the faint, unmaintained trail, where the creek can be hard to cross in snowmelt, and continue up into Shellrock Basin on the south side of the Lago-Carru ridge.
trip.itinerary: A common 3-day plan: Day 1 - hike in from the Robinson Creek or Slate Pass trailhead to Fred's Lake or Shellrock Basin. Day 2 - climb Mount Lago (often combined with Mount Carru via the connecting saddle) from a Shellrock Basin camp, roughly a half-day round trip. Day 3 - hike out. Many parties extend to 4-5 days to add Osceola Peak, Mount Rolo, or a full Pasayten ridge traverse (e.g. via Ptarmigan Peak and Dot Mountain).

waypoints.name: Slate Pass Trailhead
waypoints.directions: From SR 20 at Mazama, follow Lost River Road to the end of the pavement, then the narrow gravel Harts Pass Road (FR 5400) to Harts Pass; trailers are not allowed. At the guard station turn right onto Slate Peak Road (FR 5400-600) and climb about 3.5 miles to the Slate Pass Trailhead at the second switchback beyond the horse loading area, about 6,900 ft. Fill out the free self-issue Pasayten Wilderness permit at the kiosk.

waypoints.name: Middle Fork Pasayten Trail junction
waypoints.directions: Head north on Buckskin Ridge Trail #498 and take the Whistler Cutoff where it splits off, dropping steeply off the ridge to the Middle Fork Pasayten (Robinson Creek) Trail #478 on the valley floor. The slope just below the pass holds snow into summer, and the river here is crossed without a bridge.

waypoints.name: Fred's Lake
waypoints.directions: Turn north and follow the Middle Fork trail down the valley past the first Eureka Creek Trail junction. About 4.8 miles from the Whistler Cutoff, turn east on the Eureka Creek Trail and climb along Berk Creek to Fred's Lake.

waypoints.name: Shellrock Basin camp area
waypoints.directions: From Fred's Lake, climb to the pass on the crest above the lake and drop east into the upper Eureka Creek basin on the faint, unmaintained middle section of the Eureka Creek Trail; the crossing of upper Eureka Creek can be difficult in snowmelt. Continue east and up into Shellrock Basin on the south side of the Lago-Carru ridge.

waypoints.name: Mount Lago Summit
waypoints.directions: Climb north up Lago's broad south slope, leaving the heather for continuous scree, talus and loose rock ribs; there is no path and no single line. Gain the summit ridge and follow the faint boot path along the crest to the true high point, staying back from the north side, which drops off in a huge cliff.

wa_mount_lago_south_slope_south_face.notes: The high start most parties use. From Slate Pass the trail drops north into the Middle Fork Pasayten; follow it down-valley past the Berk Creek junction, then climb to Fred's Lake or Shellrock Basin to camp. Lago is usually combined with Carru and Osceola.

wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.name: Park Creek Pass and the heather traverse to the Fremont saddle and the hogsback
camps: Meadows north of Park Creek Pass
Valley camps on the walk in
wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.notes:
The standard start is the Colonial Creek Campground trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 130, about 1,060-1,200 ft, and the Thunder Creek trail south for roughly 16-18 miles to the Thunder Basin camp area around 6,000 ft and on to Park Creek Pass. A southern alternative reaches the same pass from Stehekin: the High Bridge guard station near 1,600 ft, the Stehekin River trail to the Park Creek trailhead, then the Park Creek trail past Buckner Camp — with a creek crossing on a less-than-substantial footlog that is genuinely nerve-wracking in the dark.

From Park Creek Pass leave the maintained trail and traverse gradually northward around a broad ridge through open heather and high alpine terrain, roughly a mile and a half to two miles, crossing a rib around 7,600 ft and a steep gully through cliff bands around 7,350 ft that can hold snow or ice. That brings you to the Fremont Glacier saddle around 8,000-8,250 ft, where rock-outcrop bivy sites with nearby running water make the standard high camp.

From camp it is about three and a half hours to the summit.
hazards: Crevasses on the Fremont Glacier, generally small but present — rope up
A bergschrund that opens below the summit ridge as the snow finger melts out late season, and a moat where the glacier meets the crest
Exposed, often unroped class 3-4 scrambling on the summit ridge
Long unmaintained cross-country route-finding above the moraine camp
Footlog crossings over Thunder and Park creeks that are hazardous at night or in high water
No fixed anchors anywhere on the route — a rappel off the summit block has to be built from a horn, a chockstone or a picket
wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.baseFinding:
The base is the Hogsback — the snow spine at the upper edge of the Fremont Glacier, on the peak's south ridge. You reach it by a gentle glacier crossing from the saddle camp, and there is a moat crossing to step from the snow onto the crest, which late in the season may have no bridge left at all. Snow spine plus a gap to step across is the confirmation you are at the start.

Then count three features in order, and the order is the whole route-finding problem: a class 3-4 rock pitch gains a left-slanting ramp — a fault-line weakness in the cliff bands — to the summit ridge; then exposed class 2-3 ledges on the east side of the ridge lead through a U-notch between the summit tower and the south horn; then a final class 3-4 pitch of about 100 ft on good holds and solid rock reaches the tiny summit.

The strongest negative test is the ramp: if you are trying to climb the summit tower directly from the glacier, you have missed it. The ramp is the way through the cliff bands and it slants left. Going straight at the tower puts you on ground the route deliberately avoids.

The U-notch is the second confirmation and it is a shape, not a height: a U-shaped gap between the summit tower and the south horn, reached by traversing ledges on the ridge's east flank. If you never dropped onto the east side, you did not take the ledges.

And know which side of the mountain you are on before you start: this is the southeast/southwest approach, from Park Creek Pass. The Douglas Glacier route comes from Easy Pass and the Douglas Creek alder on the northeast; the Banded Glacier route comes from Fisher Creek and gains the northeast ridge at about 8,800 ft. All three finish on the same summit block and share nothing below it.

wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.name: Stehekin and the Park Creek trail to Park Creek Pass

bivy.name: Moraine camp above the pass
bivy.notes: Roughly 6,350 ft, gained by turning east from the meadows and climbing about 500 ft into the moraine of the glacier remnant. Flat, sandy and better protected than the open meadows, and the usual high camp for the Fremont Glacier. From here the route traverses about two miles north around a broad ridge over heather and rock to reach the glacier near 8,000 ft.
bivy.water: Snowmelt off the glacier remnant beside the moraine
bivy.permit: Inside the park; covered by the same backcountry permit as the rest of the route
bivy.capacity: A sheltered flat big enough for a few tents

bivy.name: Meadows north of Park Creek Pass
bivy.notes: Broad sandy meadows a short way north of Park Creek Pass, which itself sits near 6,100 ft. This is where the long valley walk finally ends and the climbing terrain starts; parties either stop here or push the last 500 ft into the moraine above.
bivy.water: Creeks and snowmelt in the meadows below the pass
bivy.permit: Everything on this route is inside North Cascades National Park, so an overnight needs a park backcountry permit and the itinerary is built night by night from designated camps and cross-country zones
bivy.capacity: Open flat ground rather than built sites; a few parties at a time

bivy.name: Valley camps on the walk in
bivy.notes: The approach is long enough that most parties sleep at least one night in the forest before reaching climbing terrain — Thunder Basin in the upper Thunder Creek drainage from the Colonial Creek side, or Buckner Camp on Park Creek (named for the mountain, not on it) coming in from Stehekin. Park Creek has to be crossed near some of these camps and is worth doing in daylight.
bivy.water: Thunder Creek and Park Creek run beside these camps
bivy.permit: Designated North Cascades camps, reserved by name for specific nights on the backcountry permit; Stehekin-side parties can obtain the permit at the ranger station there
bivy.capacity: Established backcountry sites with a fixed number of parties each

wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.notes: From the Park Creek Trailhead on the Stehekin Valley Road, the Park Creek trail climbs to Park Creek Pass and joins the Thunder Creek line there. It needs the Lake Chelan boat and the Stehekin shuttle to reach the trailhead.

wa_mount_logan_r1.name: Fisher Creek to the lake camp, over the ridge onto the Banded Glacier
camps: Fisher Creek lake camp below the Banded Glacier
wa_mount_logan_r1.notes:
Two ways in, and which one you use depends on whether SR-20 is open. The always-open option is the Thunder Creek trail from Colonial Creek Campground near 1,200 ft for about nine miles to the Fisher Creek trail junction, then the Fisher Creek trail about three miles — past a good log bridge with a handrail — to a lake camp near 5,160 ft below the Banded Glacier. Roughly thirteen miles one way. The shorter option is Easy Pass from SR-20 near milepost 151, over the pass at 6,500 ft and down into Fisher Basin, about ten miles, but the trailhead is gated by the highway's seasonal closure.

From the lake camp, climb south-southeast to a low point on the ridge — sometimes called Christmas Tree Col — which may need a rope for steep snow or a short glacier section. Drop onto the Banded Glacier on the far side and ascend it to the Banded-Douglas Col.

The last two thirds of this route is sustained off-trail goat-path route-finding, and the scree below the glacier is described as moving like a Newtonian fluid: much easier to ascend than to descend. Party size in this NPS zone is capped at six.
hazards: A major crevasse crossed on a narrow snow bridge on the Banded Glacier
Talus lying on top of bullet-hard glacier ice, described as a pile of marbles — treacherous in a whiteout descent
Cliff bands above the lake camp
Loose chossy rock on the summit ridge and rockfall in the approach gullies
Heavy mosquitoes in the lake basin through June and July
wa_mount_logan_r1.baseFinding:
The critical transition is a negative test: gain the northeast ridge on solid rock at about 8,800 ft rather than attempting the summit block directly from the glacier. That is the base of the climbing and it is the single thing this route can get wrong. If you are trying to climb off the ice straight at the summit, you have skipped the transition — cross the glacier until you can step onto solid rock on the ridge, and only then start up.

Getting there is a sequence of two cols and they are different things. First, from the lake camp near 5,160 ft, climb south-southeast to a low point on the ridge — sometimes called Christmas Tree Col — and drop over it onto the Banded Glacier. Second, ascend the Banded to the Banded-Douglas Col, which is literally the saddle between the two named glaciers. A col you crossed to reach ice, and a col you reached by climbing ice, are not the same feature.

So the question that settles your position in fog is which glacier is under you: this route travels between two named glaciers, so if you can identify which one you are standing on, you know which stage you are at. The Banded is the one you drop onto from the ridge above camp; the Douglas is on the far side of the col above.

And all three Logan routes end on the same 300 ft of class 3-4 summit block, so the summit confirms nothing. What distinguishes them is entirely below: this one comes from Fisher Creek and a lake camp; the Douglas Glacier route comes from Easy Pass and the Douglas Creek alder; the Fremont Glacier route comes from Park Creek Pass on the other side of the mountain.

Watch the scree below the glacier on the way up with the descent in mind — it is unstable enough that parties note it climbs far better than it downclimbs.

wa_mount_logan_r1.name: Easy Pass and Fisher Basin

bivy.name: Fisher Creek lake camp below the Banded Glacier
bivy.notes: Reached via the Fisher Creek Trail fork off the Thunder Creek Trail (~9 miles in); the standard overnight camp below the Banded Glacier.
bivy.water: Lake at camp
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit — reserve via Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center
bivy.capacity: A few tent sites

wa_mount_logan_r1.notes: From the Easy Pass Trailhead on SR-20, over the 6,500 ft pass into Fisher Basin, then down the Fisher Creek trail to the lake outlet and the same camp as the Thunder Creek way.

wa_mount_maude_r1.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin to the Seven Fingered Jack / Maude col
wa_mount_maude_r1.notes: Drive the Chiwawa River Road, FR 62, roughly twenty-two miles and turn right onto the Phelps Creek road, FR 6211, to the trailhead at about 3,500 ft. The trail up the valley is the same tread hikers use for Spider Meadow. Walk the Phelps Creek trail, #1511, about three and a half flat miles to where it meets Leroy Creek near 4,120 to 4,140 ft. Cross on a large tree or by rock-hopping — awkward in early season with the creek up — and pick up the well-worn but unsigned climbers' trail, #1512, on the north side of the creek. It is sometimes called the Carne Mountain High Route, but the two are also treated as different paths, so do not assume the names are interchangeable. It climbs steeply, then eases into the Leroy Creek Basin meadow at about 6,100 ft, roughly five miles from the car and a little over two hours for a party moving well with light packs. Good camping and water. Above the basin, one party continued on the high-route path less than a quarter mile and then went directly into the upper basin below Maude by way of a gully with a small waterfall. Keep climbing cross-country over meadow, scrub, talus and probably snow to the Seven Fingered Jack / Maude col at about 8,150 ft, north-west of Maude's summit.
wa_mount_maude_r1.season: Best while the face still holds continuous snow and ice, roughly Jun into mid-Jul; it used to hold year round and no longer does
hazards: Cornice at the top of the face — parties have had pieces release across their tracks
Four hundred feet of exposed descending traverse from the col on snow, ice and very loose Class 3
Sixty-degree snow for the first moves off the traverse
Leroy Creek crossing running high in early season
Very poor rock quality throughout this group of peaks
Descending a west-side gully by mistake instead of continuing south toward Ice Lakes
wa_mount_maude_r1.baseFinding:
The col is not the route, and that is the thing to internalise before you get there. From the col you have to go down about four hundred feet, and not in one clean line — it comes in a series of forced descents alternating with traverses.

The recorded sequence: from the col, take the option toward the Entiat River valley side, downclimb roughly a hundred feet of face to a moderate bench, traverse a couple of hundred yards, be forced down again, traverse again, and eventually arrive at a steep snow slope beneath an overhang. That slope is the steepest ground of the day, around sixty degrees for the first moves, easing above.

The test is visual and it is unambiguous: you have descended far enough when the face comes into full view. Until it does, you are still traversing. One party took an hour and a half from the col to standing on continuous snow at the foot of the face.

Once on it, the lower face runs around thirty-five to forty degrees. A rib on the right side of the face is the line parties choose, not because it is named but because it keeps you out from under the cornice.

What not to expect: a bergschrund. The 1957 first ascent, coming from below on the Ice Lakes side, stood at a schrund between the glacier and the ice sheet above. Parties arriving by the col traverse enter partway up the face and bypass that ground entirely, and modern reports of this approach do not mention a schrund at all. The hazard people actually record here is the cornice at the top — one party had a piece of it come down and sweep across their tracks.

Honest gap worth knowing: nothing published tells you how to distinguish Maude's north face from Seven Fingered Jack's. The two, with Fernow, form one continuous headwall at the head of the Entiat, so the col is your positional anchor rather than the look of the wall.

On the way down, stay south and descend toward Ice Lakes. Parties regularly drop into one of the gullies cut into Maude's west side, either by mistake or thinking it a shortcut, and it is not.

wa_mount_maude_r1.name: Entiat River and Ice Lakes from the east — the first-ascent line

bivy.name: Upper Ice Lake
bivy.notes: The higher of two lakes in a pumice basin directly under the peak, about a mile and 400 ft above Lower Ice Lake, near the 6,900 ft high point of the Ice Creek trail. Parties climbing the north face camp on the snow-free ground at the lake's south end and start around four in the morning, dropping from the lake onto the slopes beside the face and climbing to the glacier; reckon on about four hours from the edge of the Entiat Glacier to the summit. It can be reached from Leroy Basin by the climbers' path heading south, or from the long Entiat River approach.
bivy.water: The lake, which can still be partly frozen early in the season
bivy.permit: Also in the Glacier Peak Wilderness, with the same free self-issued permit; the standard guidance is to pitch on the pumice and keep off the meadows
bivy.capacity: Open pumice flats with room for several parties, at the south end of the lake

approachLogistics.trailhead: Entiat River Trailhead (Cottonwood, end of Entiat River Road)

wa_mount_maude_r1.notes:
Drive the Entiat River Road and walk the Entiat River trail #1400 about eight and a quarter miles to the Ice Creek trail. The Entiat River has to be crossed on logs, and if there is no log at the trail there may be a large jam south of it.

The first-ascent party did not follow the river to the meadows at its head. They walked instead to the col between Spectacle Buttes and Maude's south-east side and dropped from Ice Lakes onto the slopes beside the face, judging it more direct and free of bushwhacking. That cost them nearly three thousand feet of climbing to reach Ice Lakes.
wa_mount_maude_r1.season: Same window; this side is a much longer walk and is mostly used by parties already camped at Ice Lakes or exiting that way
hazards: Unbridged crossing of the Entiat River on logs
Bergschrund at the foot of the face on this side
A very long walk in on a trail that has burned in the past
Cornice at the top of the face
wa_mount_maude_r1.baseFinding:
The base-finding here is one moment rather than a sequence: after the long grind up to Ice Lakes, you come over the crest and the face is right there in front of you. The first-ascent account says exactly that — the doubts about having picked the right way vanished on cresting the ridge.

Coming from this side you meet the face at its foot rather than partway up, which is the real difference from the col approach. That means descending steep snow slopes to a snowfield, then up to the glacier, and standing at the bergschrund between the glacier and the ice sheet above — around two thousand feet of it on the first ascent, averaging forty to forty-five degrees and over forty-five near the top.

So the test is which problem you are handed. If you are looking up at a schrund at the bottom of the whole face, you came from below. If you never saw one, you came across from the col.

wa_mount_noyes_standard.name: Low Divide and Seattle Basin to the Noyes–Meany col
camps: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
wa_mount_noyes_standard.notes: Low Divide is reached up the North Fork Quinault, or from the Elwha with a long road walk or ride added at the start. Almost nobody comes for this peak alone — it is normally tagged while linking Christie, Meany and Seattle from one camp near the divide or in Seattle Basin.
hazards: Steep snow fingers in the approach cols into early summer
Loose rock on the cliff bands below the summit cirque
Eroded, compacted sidehill gullies on the traverse beneath the peak
An Elwha ford at Chicago Camp that is hazardous at high water
Extreme remoteness — any rescue is a multi-day affair
wa_mount_noyes_standard.baseFinding: The base of this climb is a col rather than a face, and it is the same gateway parties heading for Meany use. From camp near Low Divide or in Seattle Basin, cross the head of Seattle Creek and work up talus and heather to the saddle between Noyes and Meany, gained by a loose rock couloir that tops out on a patch of snow. Standing in it, Meany's summit block is the abrupt tower on the north side and Noyes is the broader, lower ground opposite; the standard slopes leave the col directly and there is no gully mouth or rock step to identify, so the col itself is the landmark. The long sidehill traverse across eroded gullies that gets you there is the approach, not the climb, and the several similar-looking chutes cut into it do not go — resist the temptation to start up the first one that points at the summit. Above the col the ground is Class 2 to 3 along the summit ridge. If you find yourself over the far side and dropping toward the Elwha headwaters, you have crossed the divide instead of turning up it.

wa_mount_noyes_standard.name: Elwha River to Low Divide

bivy.name: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
bivy.notes: Low Divide is the saddle between Mount Seattle and Mount Christie and the obvious base for both, and by all accounts it is the most comfortable camp in the interior — flat, watered, with a toilet and a bear hang. Mount Seattle has three established scramble lines from here, by Noyes Basin, by Seattle Creek Basin and by the south slopes, and the upper meadows above camp are open walking. Mount Christie is usually taken by dropping to Martins Park, a boulder garden about three miles below the Christie Glacier, and climbing the north couloir from there. The honest planning point is which side you walk in from: this is 28.4 miles from Whiskey Bend up the Elwha, and 16 miles from the North Fork Quinault trailhead, so unless you are traversing the range you should be coming from the Quinault. Wasps have been a real problem on the lower forest sections in late summer, and stings there have put people out of action for days.
bivy.water: Reliable — a stream runs through the camp all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not itself a quota area, but it is a long way from any road and may not appear in an online search, so telephone the wilderness information centre if the site will not show. Bear canister mandatory. No fires at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: Around five sites, with a bear hang, a toilet and flat ground; small enough that a large party will fill it

bivy.name: Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
bivy.notes: The whole Elwha approach now begins with a road walk, and it is the single biggest change to planning in this valley. Vehicles stop at the Madison Falls parking area; the Olympic Hot Springs Road and then the Whiskey Bend Road are closed by a washout that has stood for years with no repair date, which puts the old Whiskey Bend trailhead about six to seven miles away on foot. The park's own figure is seven. Bicycles are allowed on the closed road and cut that leg to well under an hour each way, and most parties heading deep now ride it and stash a bike. Lillian River is around four and a half miles past Whiskey Bend and Mary's Falls a little further, so either one turns a brutal first day into a civilised one when you are carrying enough food for a week in the interior. Going higher on day one is possible but you gain nothing except a shorter second day; the elevation profile of the Elwha barely rises for the first fifteen miles.
bivy.water: Reliable at both — the Lillian River at one, the Elwha at the other; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance on the federal recreation site. These lower Elwha camps are not inside a quota area, so they are usually obtainable late, but no sites anywhere in this park are held back as same-day walk-ups. Bear canister mandatory. Fires are allowed at this elevation but the Elwha and every tributary are closed to fishing.
bivy.capacity: Lillian River has roughly six roomy riverside sites; Mary's Falls is smaller and set in maple and grass with the river some way off

bivy.name: Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
bivy.notes: Elkhorn sits about eleven miles up the Elwha from Whiskey Bend and Hayes River about sixteen, both on level ground and both far more pleasant than Canyon Camp between them, which has been badly hit by treefall and is worth walking past. Hayes River is the camp for Mount Norton: the peak's east side rises roughly 3,200 ft straight out of the Hayes River drainage in under a mile, and the ascent is a steep off-trail slog rather than a climb. It is also the last comfortable place to sleep before the valley narrows, so parties bound for Chicago Camp and the Elwha Basin peaks routinely take it as night two. Going further the same day is a real option in long daylight but the trail past Camp Wilder deteriorates and the camps beyond are rougher. Bugs are heavy in the meadows from late June into July.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha at Elkhorn, the Hayes River at Hayes; both run all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not a quota area, so these are among the easier permits in the park to obtain at short notice. Bear canister mandatory.
bivy.capacity: Both are spacious grassy flats with several sites each, alongside old guard stations that are usually empty; they are the least contested camps in the valley

bivy.name: Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
bivy.notes: Chicago Camp is where the trail effectively ends and the cross-country begins, roughly twenty-five miles from Whiskey Bend at the confluence of the Elwha and Delabarre Creek. It is the standard last-trail-camp for Mount Barnes, Mount Meany, Mount Noyes, Mount Queets and Mount Wilder, all of which are reached by pushing on into the Elwha Basin above. The ford at the camp can be genuinely hazardous in high water and is the crux of the walk in for many parties. A short way beyond, the upper Elwha has a cave-like recess under an overhanging wall that has served as emergency shelter for generations, but it is a bolthole and not a camp. Camping here rather than in the basin costs you three miles and a couple of thousand feet on summit day; the trade is a sheltered site with running water and a defined trail underfoot, which matters more than it sounds after four days of walking.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha and Delabarre Creek meet here
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. It is more than fifteen miles from any road, and the booking system does not always surface camps that far in, so ring the wilderness information centre rather than assuming it is unavailable. Bear canister mandatory. No fires above 3,500 ft, which applies once you climb out of here.
bivy.capacity: Small, and it has been battered by fallen timber — expect only a couple of usable sites near the river

wa_mount_noyes_standard.notes: The Elwha trail about 28 miles to Low Divide, plus the closed road walk at each end. Much longer, and used for traverses from the north.

wa_mount_rahm_south_side.name: Depot Creek from the Canadian side
wa_mount_rahm_south_side.notes: The unmaintained Depot Creek trail crosses the border to Ouzel Lake, then the bench leads east to the south side. The easiest and most used way, but it means crossing the border on foot away from a port of entry, so confirm the entry rules first, and the road needs high clearance.

wa_mount_rahm_south_side.name: Silver Creek from Ross Lake
wa_mount_rahm_south_side.notes: The all-US way: a water taxi up Ross Lake to the mouth of Silver Creek, then a long bushwhack up Silver Creek to Silver Lake and north to the upper terrace. Harder and much brushier.

wa_mount_rainier_kautz_glacier.name: Paradise, the Nisqually crossing and the Wilson bench
wa_mount_rainier_kautz_glacier.notes:
From Paradise (5,420 ft) follow the paved trail about a mile to Glacier Vista, then the Nisqually Moraine climbers' path to roughly 6,300 ft where boot paths drop onto the Nisqually Glacier. Rope up here — the crossing is through crevassed ground exposed to icefall from above and is dangerous in poor visibility.

From the east side of the glacier there are two ways onto the Wapowety Cleaver ground. One is a flat traverse to the base of a gully known as The Fan, climbed directly to a bench at about 7,300 ft; The Fan carries avalanche, rockfall and steep-snow hazard. The other climbs the Nisqually/Wilson margin at about 6,800 ft through an often-crevassed gully to the same 7,300–7,400 ft bench.

Above the bench, snow slopes lead to a string of established camps: Wilson Moraine (8,200–8,600 ft), Lower Castle (9,250 ft) and Upper Castle (9,400–9,500 ft), the most common base, with running water from about mid-June. Higher again, rock islands along the west edge of the Turtle snowfield between roughly 9,500 and 10,500 ft hold good bivouacs, and there is usually flowing water at the snowfield edges in warm weather.

Camp Hazard (about 10,800 ft) is the traditional high camp and is named for what sits above it: the Kautz Ice Cliff. Many parties deliberately camp lower and climb through Camp Hazard early rather than sleep under the cliff. On the Turtle, keep to the western, climber's-left side — the centre and east are raked by ice and rock off the cliff.

Rainier permits apply: a per-person climbing permit for glacier travel or ground above roughly 10,000 ft, and a wilderness permit for each overnight camp in the high-use season.
wa_mount_rainier_kautz_glacier.season: Mid-May into early August; the approach and glaciers deteriorate quickly after that
hazards: Serac fall from the Kautz Ice Cliff onto Camp Hazard and the traverse beneath it
Crevasses and icefall exposure on the Nisqually Glacier crossing
Avalanche, rockfall and steep snow in The Fan gully
Ice and rockfall raking the centre and east side of the Turtle snowfield
Thin or rotten ice in the chute late in the season
wa_mount_rainier_kautz_glacier.baseFinding:
The single most useful fact about this route is that the technical climbing starts below Camp Hazard, not above it. Parties who expect to walk out of camp and start climbing walk straight under the ice cliff.

From camp, pick up the climbers' path on the rock and follow it to a short rappel, which often has a fixed line on it. That rappel is the confirmation you are on the right line — it drops you about 150 ft into the drainage gully at the bottom of the ice cliff. You should be losing height before you gain any.

From the bottom of that gully, traverse west, underneath the ice cliff, until you can see an obvious snow-and-ice ramp running up on your left. That ramp is the Kautz ice chute, and it is the start of the route. The older description of the same ground is: down over the ridge, down the gully about 150 ft, then either cross the icefall into the broad chute or continue down and around the toe of the icefall to reach the bottom of the chute.

What you should find in the chute: two steps of alpine ice separated by lower-angle snow. The first is the easier, anything from a short pitch of steep snow to about 250 ft of ice; the second is the crux, from a short pitch to more than 300 ft, steeper, and where a second tool earns its place. Both change a great deal from year to year. In lean years the ice can be thin, rotten or frozen dirt rather than good ice; the angle, not the quality, is what identifies it.

Negative marker: if you are climbing directly up from Camp Hazard toward the ice cliff, stop. That is the serac fall line, and it is the reason the camp has its name.

wa_mount_rainier_kautz_glacier.name: Comet Falls and Van Trump Park

bivy.name: Upper Castle
bivy.notes: Where most parties camp, at about 9,400 to 9,500 ft, and where the Comet Falls way in joins. Wind-exposed.
bivy.water: Running water close by from about mid-June; otherwise melt snow
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier wilderness permit and climbing registration
bivy.capacity: Large rock rings behind old windbreaks

bivy.name: Camp Hazard
bivy.notes: On the climber's left of the Turtle Snowfield at about 10,800 ft: three large rock rings below the Kautz Ice Cliff, and the highest regular camp on the route. It shortens summit day. The original Camp Hazard, nearer 11,000 ft, sits in the fall line of ice from the cliff and is not used.

bivy.name: Rock Step bivy sites
bivy.notes: A few small sites by the notch above the Rock Step, right beside the morning rappel. Little room, and under the same ice cliff as Camp Hazard.
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier wilderness permit and climbing registration

wa_mount_rainier_kautz_glacier.notes:
Start at the Comet Falls trailhead (3,650 ft) on the Longmire–Paradise road. The maintained Comet Falls Trail climbs 2.2 miles and about 2,000 ft to a junction, then continues toward Van Trump Park for another 0.6 miles to the end of maintained tread. From there unmaintained social trails climb a steep moraine crest to about 6,500 ft and onto the permanent snow of the Van Trump Glacier remnant, which is followed to the Upper Castle at roughly 9,500 ft where this approach merges with the Paradise line.

The advantage is that it never crosses the Nisqually Glacier. The cost is a lower start, a steeper carry and a descent that is genuinely hard to reverse: the Park Service's own advice is to save a GPS track, because relocating the correct moraine and the treeline trail junction on the way down is difficult even in clear weather. Several parties a season lose that junction and end up bushwhacking.
wa_mount_rainier_kautz_glacier.season: Same window; avoids the Nisqually Glacier crossing entirely
hazards: Losing the moraine crest and the treeline trail junction on descent — carry a saved track
Steep unmaintained moraine travel above the end of maintained trail
Same serac and ice-cliff exposure above the Castle and at Camp Hazard
wa_mount_rainier_kautz_glacier.baseFinding:
This variant's finding problem is the reverse of most: the hard recognition is on the way down, not the way up. On the way up, the sequence is trail to a junction, more trail to the end of maintained tread, then a steep moraine crest — if you are still on graded tread above about 6,500 ft you have followed the wrong branch toward Van Trump Park's meadows rather than the climbers' line.

The merge point is the Upper Castle at about 9,400–9,500 ft, a rock rib with established camp sites and, from mid-June, running water. Once you are there the route ahead is the same as the Paradise approach: up the Turtle keeping to its western edge, to Camp Hazard, and then down a short rappel into the gully beneath the ice cliff to reach the chute.

wa_mount_rainier_kautz_headwall.name: Paradise and Glacier Vista, across the Nisqually to the Turtle and Camp Hazard
wa_mount_rainier_kautz_headwall.notes:
From Paradise at 5,400 ft, the common approach follows the Skyline Trail to Glacier Vista and the Nisqually Moraine, then drops west onto the glacier. The route crosses the lower Nisqually, gains the Wilson Glacier and climbs to the Turtle Snowfield, with camps at The Castle around 9,200-9,500 ft and Camp Hazard at 10,800 ft at the top of the snowfield.

Roped travel and crevasse-rescue readiness are needed from the moment you leave the Nisqually. Water is available from snowmelt lower down on the Comet Falls and Van Trump side but not once you are on glacier ice.

Rockfall and icefall off the Wapowety Cleaver and the Kautz Icefall are the approach-zone hazards; move through the exposed ground early and efficiently.
wa_mount_rainier_kautz_headwall.season: Roughly mid-May to early Aug; the ice holds into summer but the approach and glacier conditions degrade quickly after the start of August
hazards: Two steep ice steps beneath serac and rockfall from the Wapowety Cleaver and the Kautz Icefall
Brittle or hard ice on the upper step, with screws the only protection
Genuinely complex crevassed glacier travel on the Kautz approach
A short rappel or fixed-line downclimb off the Camp Hazard bivy rock to reach the base
Descent rappels are on ice anchors you build yourself; old ascent-placed threads must not be reused
wa_mount_rainier_kautz_headwall.baseFinding:
The headwall and the standard Kautz Chute are two different lines off the same camp, and the test is how many steep steps you meet.

Count two. This route presents as two ice steps separated by a band of lower-angle snow: the lower step around 35-40 degrees, the upper around 45-50. Step, bench, step. If you climb one sustained runnel and the angle then eases the whole way to the summit plateau, you were in the standard Kautz ice chute, not on the headwall.

The upper step is the one that settles it — noticeably steeper and more sustained than the lower, needing two tools and screws in ice that is often harder or more brittle. The lower step is broad and stepped out and rarely steeper than about 35-40 degrees, and most parties get up it with a single tool and a couple of screws. If the harder ground came first, you are not on this.

Where you rope up is part of the finding: on the Turtle or Wilson Glacier below the headwall, often after a short rappel or a fixed-line downclimb off the bivy rock at Camp Hazard. Descending off camp before you climb is correct and is a good sign you are on the right line rather than walking out along the chute.

The approach has two starts and they land in the same place, so do not let the difference unsettle you: Paradise via Glacier Vista and the Nisqually Moraine, or the Comet Falls and Van Trump Park trail from a lower trailhead. Both cross the Nisqually onto the Wilson and climb the Turtle. If you find yourself on maintained trail beside a waterfall you are on the second of those, not lost.

What being too late looks like: seracs and rockfall off the Wapowety Cleaver and the Kautz Icefall hang over the steep ground. The upper step must be climbed efficiently and early. The honest reading of arriving at it warm and in the sun is to go down.

wa_mount_rainier_kautz_headwall.name: Comet Falls and Van Trump Park

bivy.name: Castle camps on Wapowety Cleaver
bivy.notes: Two camp areas on the ridge below Wapowety Cleaver at the edge of the Wilson Glacier. Lower Castle, about 9,250 ft, has a few closely spaced rock rings for small parties; Upper Castle, 9,400 to 9,500 ft, has large rock rings and is where most parties camp. Wind-exposed.
bivy.water: Melt snow
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier wilderness permit and climbing registration
bivy.capacity: Several small tent sites behind old rock windbreaks

bivy.name: Camp Hazard
bivy.notes: On the climber's left of the Turtle Snowfield at about 10,800 ft: three large rock rings below the Kautz Ice Cliff, and the highest regular camp on the route. It shortens summit day. The original Camp Hazard, nearer 11,000 ft, sits in the fall line of ice from the cliff and is not used.
bivy.water: Melt snow
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier wilderness permit and climbing registration
bivy.capacity: A handful of tent sites on rock and snow

wa_mount_rainier_kautz_headwall.notes: Climbs from the Comet Falls trailhead past Van Trump Park and up the moraine beside the remnant Van Trump Glacier, joining the Paradise line around the Castle and the base of the Turtle. Preferred late in the season: it never crosses the Nisqually and has running water low down, but it starts about 1,700 ft lower and the descent is easy to lose in the trees.

wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.name: Mowich Lake and Spray Park

bivy.name: Ptarmigan Ridge high camp
bivy.notes: Planned high camp and the one the route is built around. Comfortable bivy ground on the ridge crest, deliberately sited just outside the serac fall line off the Liberty Wall — that icefall is the single largest objective hazard on the climb, so the exact spot matters more than the comfort. Fully exposed to wind. Parties who want an acceptable risk margin wait for an overnight freezing level at or below about 12,000 ft.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.permit: climbing permit required above 10,000 ft in addition to the camping permit
bivy.capacity: one to two tents on dug snow platforms

bivy.name: Camp Schurman
bivy.notes: Descent camp, not an ascent camp — most parties come off Ptarmigan Ridge down the Emmons-Winthrop and use this. Has a ranger hut and a solar toilet, but both can be buried in snow well into the season, so plan to be self-sufficient and pack out waste. Reserve early; this is one of the first camps on the mountain to fill.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.permit: wilderness camping permit required; separate climbing permit for glacier travel
bivy.capacity: limited designated tent sites; fills early in season

wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.notes:
From Mowich Lake, follow the trail roughly 3 miles to Spray Park, then climb the lower slopes of Ptarmigan Ridge. The ridge narrows above Observation Rock; continue along it until you find bivouac sites. High camp is normally somewhere between about 9,500 and 10,300 ft, at the point where Ptarmigan Ridge runs into the main cone below the Liberty Cap icefall. Higher camps are worth the extra carry because they let you look at the bergschrund and pick a line the evening before.

This is the shorter of the two approaches, and it is the one most parties would choose if the road cooperated. Since April 2025 the Mowich Lake road has had no public access, because the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge was closed permanently to cars, bikes and walkers; this start is unavailable until that changes. Even before that, the summer-only road usually opened after the route came into condition.

The approach to high camp is normally split over two days.
wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.season: May-Jul; the road to Mowich Lake has had no public access since the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge closed permanently on April 22, 2025, so this start cannot be reached by car
hazards: Bergschrund crossing off the Mowich Glacier, conditions-dependent
Loose rock descending from high camp onto the glacier
Icefall exposure below the Liberty Cap icefall near high camp
Verglassed rock and water ice on the upper mixed ground
Committing position with a descent by a different route — plan the carry-over
wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.baseFinding:
High camp is not the start of the climbing — and the mistake this route invites is treating the ridge you camped on as the ridge you climb.

From camp at around 10,000–10,300 ft you descend, on loose rock or steep snow, onto the Mowich Glacier. If you are gaining height straight out of the tents along a rocky crest, you are still on the approach ridge.

The first real feature is the bergschrund, usually crossed by a bridge just left of a rock outcropping near the centre. Above it the climbing is 40–45 degree snow for about 1,000 ft, and it ends in an obvious way: you run up under large rock cliffs. That is the signal to traverse left into an hourglass-shaped snow face rather than to keep going up.

The next decision point is a rock buttress at about 11,500 ft, where the route splits — left and around toward Liberty Cap between the buttress and the icefall, or right through mixed ground, a minor rock rib and the left margin of the Mowich Face to a second rock gully. Either way there is a short section of real rock or mixed climbing above 12,000 ft; if you have got that high on pure snow, you have probably drifted onto the Liberty Cap glacier ground.

Descent is normally the Emmons, not this route.

wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.name: White River, St Elmo Pass and Curtis Ridge
wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.notes:
Follow the Glacier Basin trail from White River Campground and leave it for St Elmo Pass (7,400 ft), about 4 miles in. Descend onto the Winthrop Glacier and traverse west toward Curtis Ridge, holding elevation. Cross Curtis Ridge, cross the Carbon Glacier, then climb moderate snow slopes onto Ptarmigan Ridge below its 10,200 ft high point, where there are good bivouac sites.

This is the long way around the north side of the mountain and it shares its first half with the Liberty Ridge approach. It usually implies a car shuttle or, more often, a carry-over with descent by the Emmons–Winthrop back to White River — which conveniently is also the standard descent from the route itself.
wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.season: Available earlier in the season than the Mowich Lake road, at the cost of a much longer approach
hazards: Serac discharge from Willis Wall on the traverse between Curtis Ridge and the Carbon
Crevasse fields on the Winthrop and Carbon glaciers
Long committing traverse with no quick exit
Same bergschrund and upper mixed-ground hazards as the Mowich approach
wa_mount_rainier_ptarmigan_ridge.baseFinding:
Up to the Carbon Glacier this is the Liberty Ridge approach, and the same negative markers apply: leave the Glacier Basin trail rather than walking into Glacier Basin, lose height off St Elmo Pass rather than gaining it, and treat the ground under Willis Wall as a crossing rather than a place to stand.

Where it diverges: instead of turning up the Carbon toward the toe of Liberty Ridge, you continue west across the Carbon and climb snow onto Ptarmigan Ridge below its 10,200 ft high point. If you find yourself gaining a defined rib immediately above the Carbon with Willis Wall right behind you, you have stopped at Liberty Ridge — Ptarmigan is further round to the west.

Once camped on Ptarmigan Ridge the start of the climbing is the same as from the Mowich side: down off the ridge onto the Mowich Glacier, then the bergschrund, then 40–45 degree snow to the base of the rock cliffs.

wa_mount_seattle_south.name: Low Divide and Seattle Meadows
camps: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
wa_mount_seattle_south.notes: Reached up the North Fork Quinault or by the higher, rougher Skyline Ridge primitive route past Three Lakes and Kimta Peak, or from the Elwha side. Two other lines come in through Noyes Basin and directly up Seattle Creek Basin. Whichever you pick, plan on a multi-day backpack just to reach a base camp.
hazards: Loose scree and talus on both flanks with rockfall onto parties below
Steep, brushy bushwhacking where the Seattle Creek drainage steepens
Unbridged fords on the Elwha and North Fork Quinault approaches
A northeast aspect dropping thousands of feet — stay off that side
Extreme remoteness with emergency contact frequently impossible
wa_mount_seattle_south.baseFinding: The staging point is Seattle Meadows, the high camp in upper Seattle Basin about a thousand feet above Seattle Creek. There is no gully mouth to find here: from camp the climb starts on scree on the mountain's western side, and the base is simply where meadow gives way to loose scree and the slope steepens. What identifies the route is the sequence, so hold it in mind — climb the west-side scree, cross over a connecting ridge, then continue up scree and talus on the eastern side, and finish with Class 2 to 3 scrambling on the east ridge to a craggy top. If you are still high on the west side and the ground is cliffing out above you, you have failed to make the crossing and need to traverse. The summit is confirmed by an unusually large plastic tube jammed into a crack holding the register. Coming instead up Seattle Creek Basin, follow the creek's waterfalls until the drainage steepens, then take the steep brushy bushwhack onto the Noyes–Seattle ridge; that brush low down is the crux of that variant, not the scrambling above.

wa_mount_seattle_south.name: Up the Elwha to Low Divide

bivy.name: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
bivy.notes: Low Divide is the saddle between Mount Seattle and Mount Christie and the obvious base for both, and by all accounts it is the most comfortable camp in the interior — flat, watered, with a toilet and a bear hang. Mount Seattle has three established scramble lines from here, by Noyes Basin, by Seattle Creek Basin and by the south slopes, and the upper meadows above camp are open walking. Mount Christie is usually taken by dropping to Martins Park, a boulder garden about three miles below the Christie Glacier, and climbing the north couloir from there. The honest planning point is which side you walk in from: this is 28.4 miles from Whiskey Bend up the Elwha, and 16 miles from the North Fork Quinault trailhead, so unless you are traversing the range you should be coming from the Quinault. Wasps have been a real problem on the lower forest sections in late summer, and stings there have put people out of action for days.
bivy.water: Reliable — a stream runs through the camp all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not itself a quota area, but it is a long way from any road and may not appear in an online search, so telephone the wilderness information centre if the site will not show. Bear canister mandatory. No fires at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: Around five sites, with a bear hang, a toilet and flat ground; small enough that a large party will fill it

bivy.name: Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
bivy.notes: The whole Elwha approach now begins with a road walk, and it is the single biggest change to planning in this valley. Vehicles stop at the Madison Falls parking area; the Olympic Hot Springs Road and then the Whiskey Bend Road are closed by a washout that has stood for years with no repair date, which puts the old Whiskey Bend trailhead about six to seven miles away on foot. The park's own figure is seven. Bicycles are allowed on the closed road and cut that leg to well under an hour each way, and most parties heading deep now ride it and stash a bike. Lillian River is around four and a half miles past Whiskey Bend and Mary's Falls a little further, so either one turns a brutal first day into a civilised one when you are carrying enough food for a week in the interior. Going higher on day one is possible but you gain nothing except a shorter second day; the elevation profile of the Elwha barely rises for the first fifteen miles.
bivy.water: Reliable at both — the Lillian River at one, the Elwha at the other; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance on the federal recreation site. These lower Elwha camps are not inside a quota area, so they are usually obtainable late, but no sites anywhere in this park are held back as same-day walk-ups. Bear canister mandatory. Fires are allowed at this elevation but the Elwha and every tributary are closed to fishing.
bivy.capacity: Lillian River has roughly six roomy riverside sites; Mary's Falls is smaller and set in maple and grass with the river some way off

bivy.name: Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
bivy.notes: Elkhorn sits about eleven miles up the Elwha from Whiskey Bend and Hayes River about sixteen, both on level ground and both far more pleasant than Canyon Camp between them, which has been badly hit by treefall and is worth walking past. Hayes River is the camp for Mount Norton: the peak's east side rises roughly 3,200 ft straight out of the Hayes River drainage in under a mile, and the ascent is a steep off-trail slog rather than a climb. It is also the last comfortable place to sleep before the valley narrows, so parties bound for Chicago Camp and the Elwha Basin peaks routinely take it as night two. Going further the same day is a real option in long daylight but the trail past Camp Wilder deteriorates and the camps beyond are rougher. Bugs are heavy in the meadows from late June into July.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha at Elkhorn, the Hayes River at Hayes; both run all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not a quota area, so these are among the easier permits in the park to obtain at short notice. Bear canister mandatory.
bivy.capacity: Both are spacious grassy flats with several sites each, alongside old guard stations that are usually empty; they are the least contested camps in the valley

bivy.name: Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
bivy.notes: Chicago Camp is where the trail effectively ends and the cross-country begins, roughly twenty-five miles from Whiskey Bend at the confluence of the Elwha and Delabarre Creek. It is the standard last-trail-camp for Mount Barnes, Mount Meany, Mount Noyes, Mount Queets and Mount Wilder, all of which are reached by pushing on into the Elwha Basin above. The ford at the camp can be genuinely hazardous in high water and is the crux of the walk in for many parties. A short way beyond, the upper Elwha has a cave-like recess under an overhanging wall that has served as emergency shelter for generations, but it is a bolthole and not a camp. Camping here rather than in the basin costs you three miles and a couple of thousand feet on summit day; the trade is a sheltered site with running water and a defined trail underfoot, which matters more than it sounds after four days of walking.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha and Delabarre Creek meet here
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. It is more than fifteen miles from any road, and the booking system does not always surface camps that far in, so ring the wilderness information centre rather than assuming it is unavailable. Bear canister mandatory. No fires above 3,500 ft, which applies once you climb out of here.
bivy.capacity: Small, and it has been battered by fallen timber — expect only a couple of usable sites near the river

wa_mount_seattle_south.notes: The long northern way: follow the Elwha River trail up the whole valley past Hayes River and Chicago Camp, then climb to Low Divide. It takes several days, and a road walk or bike ride may be needed to reach the trailhead.

wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.name: White Salmon Creek from the old lodge site, up the White Salmon Glacier to the dividing shoulder
camps: North Face bivy, where the rib meets the face
wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.notes: Get the backcountry permit at the Glacier Public Service Center on the way in — it is required, not advisory. Then continue up the Mount Baker Highway to the pull-off at the old White Salmon Lodge site, walk round the gate, and follow the old roadbed roughly a mile to where it ends at an old clearcut. From the road-end, with adequate snow cover, drop northeast off-trail to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley up toward the toe of the White Salmon Glacier. Roped travel usually begins at the toe, and the crevasse hazard grows through the season. Ascend glacier and moraine to a bivy below the first rock and ice barrier. Published bivy elevations for this route disagree by around a thousand feet — so the honest instruction is to camp at the rock outcrops on the eastern edge of the White Salmon, where the ridge meets the face, rather than at a number. The Hanging Glacier and North Face approach is in the White Salmon Creek drainage, one valley west of Price Lake — not on the Nooksack and Ruth Creek side of the mountain.
wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.season: Roughly Jul-Aug. Earlier the valley is snow-covered and simpler but the true North Face above you sheds avalanches; later the crevasses on the White Salmon are open and the lower valley is alder
hazards: Frequent avalanches off the true North Face onto the traverse, worst in early season
Serac fall from the hanging glacier itself, which is described as very active
Open crevasses on the White Salmon Glacier that grow through the season
Brush and alder in the lower White Salmon valley once the snowline recedes
A traverse with no easy retreat once committed, and a bivy on the mountain
wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.baseFinding:
Price Lake must stay below you and to your north-east, and that is the test. From the bivy the day is a traverse climber's left, above and across the hanging glacier that sits over Price Lake and beneath the upper hanging glacier tucked under the first rock barrier. In cloud you will not see the summit and you do not need to: the lake is the reference and it belongs on your left-hand side, downhill.

Arrival: you are at the base of the technical climbing when you reach the shoulder — the snow-and-ice rib that divides the White Salmon cirque from the Price Glacier cirque. It is the only place on this traverse where the ground stops being a sidehill and becomes a defined rib with a cirque falling away on each side. Stand on it and you should be able to look down into two separate basins.

The error that kills people here is drifting left, and it is worth stating as a hard rule: stay right during the traverse. Going further left puts you onto the true North Face, which sheds avalanches frequently, especially early season. Left feels like progress toward the mountain and is the wrong direction.

After 500 ft of traverse the line goes up, on a firn-and-ice finger west of the upper hanging glacier. If you are still traversing horizontally after a long way, you have gone past the finger and are running out under the face.

wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.name: Fisher Chimneys and Winnie's Slide, then down the White Salmon Glacier to the base

bivy.name: Fisher Chimneys camps, White Salmon and above Winnie's Slide
bivy.notes: Camping above the chimneys is what makes Fisher Chimneys a comfortable two- or three-day climb rather than a very long push, and it puts the party above the loose, route-finding-heavy section for summit day. The lower site near the top of the White Salmon is the more common choice and the more scenic; the higher one above Winnie's Slide costs you a steep snow or ice pitch with a full pack. Which is preferable depends on the party and on conditions in the chimneys, and reasonable people disagree. Both are small and exposed, so a party arriving to find them occupied needs a plan.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only in practice. Runoff sometimes appears on the rock below the glaciers in warm conditions, but neither site should be planned around finding liquid water.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required — these camps are inside the park, past the signed boundary above Lake Ann. Reserve through Recreation.gov or take a walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center within 24 hours; fees apply and the zone carries a small daily party quota. A Northwest Forest Pass covers only the parking at the Lake Ann trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Small platforms for one or two parties at each of two levels — around 6,800 ft where the chimneys top out near the White Salmon, and higher near 7,300 ft above Winnie's Slide

wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.notes:
The alternative used by parties who would rather start from the standard trailhead than from the White Salmon roadbed: from the Lake Ann Trailhead on SR-542, climb the Fisher Chimneys and Winnie's Slide to a bivy near the Upper Curtis Glacier, then descend about 1,000 ft down the White Salmon Glacier and traverse the northwest rib to reach the foot of the Hanging Glacier.

It is longer in vertical terms because it climbs to a camp and then gives back a thousand feet, and it commits you to regaining that thousand feet on the way out if you return the same way. Its advantage is a maintained trail to a known camp instead of a valley bushwhack, and it does not require the White Salmon roadbed to be walkable.

No trailhead-to-base time is given for this variant; published figures for it vary too much to quote one.
wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.season: Roughly Jul-Aug, once the Lake Ann trail is out from under snow
hazards: A 1,000 ft descent that must be re-climbed on the return if you reverse this variant
Winnie's Slide, which is sometimes rappelled rather than downclimbed when icy
Crevasses on both the Lower Curtis and the White Salmon
Avalanche exposure from the true North Face during the traverse
Committing to a route whose descent normally exits a different valley from the one you started in
wa_mount_shuksan_hanging_glacier.baseFinding:
You arrive from above, so the test is inverted — you are looking for the bottom of a descent, not the top of a climb. From the Upper Curtis bivy you drop roughly 1,000 ft down the White Salmon Glacier. Stop descending when the ground lets you traverse northeast onto the northwest rib; if you keep going down the White Salmon you end up in the valley the other variant walked up, and you will have thrown away the whole approach.

The rib is the marker. The northwest rib is a defined feature between the White Salmon and the Hanging Glacier, and once you are on it the foot of the Hanging Glacier is the next thing you meet.

Confirm with the same test the other variant uses: from the base of the climbing, Price Lake should be below you and to the north-east, and you should be standing on the shoulder that separates the White Salmon cirque from the Price cirque, with a basin on each side of you.

And the same hard rule applies: do not drift left onto the true North Face. It avalanches, and arriving from this side does not change that.

wa_mount_shuksan_northeast_ridge.name: Up the North Face to the summit pyramid
camps: North Face bivy, where the rib meets the face
Fisher Chimneys camps, White Salmon and above Winnie's Slide
wa_mount_shuksan_northeast_ridge.notes: Most parties meet this ridge as the finish of a longer climb. Climb the North Face (or the Hanging Glacier or the Northwest Rib) to the upper mountain, then continue up the northeast ridge of the summit pyramid. A common way to the foot of the North Face is over Fisher Chimneys and down the White Salmon Glacier to a bivy at its base.

wa_mount_shuksan_northeast_ridge.name: From the Sulphide Glacier, across the Crystal Glacier
wa_mount_shuksan_northeast_ridge.notes: Climb the Sulphide Glacier to the base of the summit pyramid, then descend a short way east onto the Crystal Glacier and cross it to the foot of the ridge, avoiding a few small crevasses. The ridge is very loose fourth class until the last 200 ft, which is a solid, clean face of low fifth class leading almost to the summit.

wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.name: From Ross Lake by boat and up Silver Creek to the lake basin camp
