wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.notes: Book a water taxi for the long run up Ross Lake and get dropped at the mouth of Silver Creek at about 1,600 ft. A trail climbs the north side of the creek roughly two and a half miles to an old cabin at about 2,900 ft; above that the route is cross-country with occasional blazes, across slide alder and forest slopes, to the camp in the Silver Lake basin at about 6,763 ft. This is the shorter side for this particular route and it keeps the whole trip inside the United States, at the cost of depending on a boat.
hazards: a booked boat on a lake with no road out
slide alder and unmarked cross-country above the old cabin
crevasses on the glacier above its toe
loose moraine between the lake and the glacier toe
a high camp with a long committing retreat
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.baseFinding:
From the Silver Lake camp the route does not go near a col. Walk round the north side of the lake to its far, south-west end, then head south across moraine and snow, skirting a small rock buttress, to the toe of the glacier at about 7,400 ft. Allow an hour to an hour and a half from camp.

You should be able to see at least the lower glacier from camp, so pick your line onto it before you leave. The ice comes down toward the lake from the north side of the peak; you rope up at its toe and climb it, with no saddle or gully on the way.

The wide gully and the col at about 7,380 ft between this peak and its neighbour to the north-west belong to the other approach, from the lake on the Depot Creek side. If you are climbing a gully toward a gap, you have left this line.

And the negative marker that matters most: the south-west route on this peak starts at the toe of a different glacier on the other flank, reached by traversing round a rock buttress into heather and moraine basins rather than by gaining any col. If you are roping up at the foot of an icefall with no saddle in sight, you have started the other route.

wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border, over the col between the two peaks
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.notes: The other way in starts on the Canadian side: a rough spur off the lake road to a washout at about 2,600 ft, an overgrown roadbed to the boundary obelisk and register, and then the climbers' path up the creek through old growth to the falls, whose wet slabs and old fixed hand-line are the crux of the walk-in. Above them the path leads to the lake camp at about 5,700 ft. From that camp the way to this route climbs toward and over the col between the two peaks rather than onto the south-west side.
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.season: Late July through September, and only with passports
hazards: an international border crossing on foot
wet slabs and an old fixed hand-line at the falls
an overgrown approach road that washes out
crevasses on the ice above the col
two routes leaving one camp, with the wrong turn costing a day
wa_mount_spickard_silver_glacier.baseFinding:
From the Depot Creek camp, climb north-east from the lake's north side up the obvious wide gully that leads to the col.

The fixed point is the same: the col at about 7,380 ft between this peak and its neighbour to the north-west. It is a gap with a summit on either hand and the glacier beyond. The wide gully you came up is the way back to camp; the glacier lies on the far side.

The test that you are at the right gap is that both summits are identifiable from it, and that the ice you are about to climb runs away from the col rather than up to it. A notch with only one summit beside it, or with no glacier beyond, is a different gap on the same ridge.

Do not confuse this start with the south-west route, which leaves the same camp. That route turns right around the toe of a rock buttress well before any saddle and ropes up at the toe of a glacier on the other flank. If you have not gained a col, you are not on this route.

wa_mount_spickard_southwest.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border to the lake camp
wa_mount_spickard_southwest.notes:
From the road washout at about 2,600 ft, reached by a rough spur off the lake road on the Canadian side, walk the old roadbed about nine minutes to an inconspicuous spur on the left, follow that spur four minutes to a T-junction, and bear right onto an extremely overgrown and sporadically muddy road for about thirty-five minutes. That brings you to the boundary obelisk, where there is a register - carry a passport, because this approach crosses the international border on foot.

Above the boundary the way becomes a crude but discernible climbers' path along the creek through old growth, easy where deadfall has been cut and full of uncut logs where it has not. About three miles in it reaches the falls, which are the real crux of the approach: wet slick boulders and slabs at their base, with steep steps rigged with an old fixed hand-line. Treat the line as an aid rather than as protection, and back it up with a heavy pack on.

Above the falls the path continues through meadow and upper valley to the lake at roughly 5,700 ft - flat sandy mostly treeless benches at the toe of the talus, the standard base camp for this peak and its neighbour, with reliable water.
wa_mount_spickard_southwest.season: Late July through September, for a crossable glacier and a passable creek
hazards: an international border crossing on foot, with a register at the obelisk
a road that washes out and lengthens the walk without warning
wet slick boulders and slabs at the base of the falls, with an old fixed hand-line of unknown condition
crevasses on the south-west glacier and one marginal snow bridge on the standard line
a short steep loose gully at the head of the glacier
thirty-five to forty degree snow near the summit ridge
wa_mount_spickard_southwest.baseFinding:
The critical instruction is that you leave the drainage before the pass, not at it. From camp, ascend the broad talus couloir and stream drainage north to north-east toward the saddle at roughly 7,200 ft - but well before reaching that saddle, cut right around the toe of a steep rocky buttress into open heather and moraine basins.

The negative marker is exact and easy to use: if you have arrived at the saddle and are looking down into the cirque on the far side, you have gone too far. Go back down and find the buttress toe.

The buttress toe is the feature - a steep rock nose that the couloir runs past on its left. Turning its foot puts you into open heather and moraine, which is different ground from the couloir you have been climbing, and that change underfoot is the confirmation.

The base is the toe of the south-west glacier, reached by traversing those basins. Rope up and put crampons on there rather than part-way across. The line up the ice is its climber's-right margin, which holds hard snow and ice at thirty to forty degrees and relatively few crevasses; about half-way up, one poor-looking crevasse has to be crossed on a marginal bridge, so probe it and expect it to be worse late in the season.

Confirm at the top of the ice: a short steep loose rock gully at the glacier's head tops out on a low col on the south-west ridge, above the cirque. That col is where the summit scramble starts. If the ice runs you out onto a broad snow shoulder with no gully and no col, you have taken the glacier's centre or its left side instead of its right margin.

wa_mount_spickard_southwest.name: From Ross Lake by boat and up Silver Creek to the lake basin
wa_mount_spickard_southwest.notes:
The other side of the mountain is reached without leaving the United States. A booked water taxi runs a long way up Ross Lake to a drop at the mouth of Silver Creek at about 1,600 ft. A trail climbs the north side of the creek for roughly two and a half miles to an old cabin at about 2,900 ft, above which the way is cross-country with occasional blazes across slide alder and forest slopes to the camp in the Silver Lake basin at about 6,763 ft.

This puts you on the opposite side of the peak from the Depot Creek camp, so it changes which col you reach and in what order - plan the climb from this camp rather than translating a description written from the other one.
wa_mount_spickard_southwest.season: Late July through September, once the boat is running and the cross-country is clear of snow
hazards: a booked boat on a lake with no road out, fixing both ends of the trip
slide alder and unmarked cross-country above the cabin
a long carry to a high camp
crevasses on the glaciers either side of the divide
a camp position that makes descriptions written from the other approach misleading
wa_mount_spickard_southwest.baseFinding:
The old cabin at about 2,900 ft is the proof you are on the right side of the creek. The trail climbs the north side; if you have not passed a cabin by the time the trail gives out, you are on the wrong bank and should cross before the cross-country starts, not after.

Above the cabin the markers are occasional blazes on trees rather than tread. Blazes that stop appearing mean you have drifted; the slide alder will let you keep going anyway, which is why this is worth checking rather than assuming.

The camp is the lake basin at about 6,763 ft, and from it the route to this peak's south-west side goes up and over toward the col between it and its neighbour to the north-west.

Be clear which route you are on when you arrive. From this side the natural line gains the col at about 7,380 ft between the two peaks, which is where the glacier route on the north side starts. The south-west route instead wants the toe of the south-west glacier, which is reached by traversing into open heather and moraine basins round the toe of a rock buttress, not by gaining a col. If you find yourself standing in a saddle between two summits, you are on the other route's start.

wa_mount_steel_standard.name: Duckabush River Trail to the unmarked creek turnoff
camps: Marmot Lake — the Duckabush-side high camp for Steel and Duckabush
Upper Duckabush junction camp — the link between First Divide and the Duckabush head
wa_mount_steel_standard.notes: Twenty-odd miles up the Duckabush over Big Hump, with a wide ford of the river above Duckabush Camp that runs thigh-deep and swift in early season. The climbers' line leaves the maintained trail roughly three miles below Marmot Lake. A multi-day backpack with a high camp at the lake or in the basin, never a car-to-car day.
hazards: Cornices and unconsolidated snow on the summit ridge into late June
Avalanche potential on east-facing slopes below the summit early season
An unmarked turnoff and unmapped off-trail travel above the amphitheater
A wide river ford, worse in the afternoon than at dawn
Fallen timber through the burned sections of the lower valley
wa_mount_steel_standard.baseFinding: The turnoff is unmarked — no sign, cairns at best — and getting it right is the whole navigation problem on this route. Above Duckabush Camp, watch for a small feeder creek coming in from climber's-left and follow it up out of the valley. It leads into a rocky amphitheater on the west side of the summit, and that amphitheater is the base: once you are standing in it the climbing is easy Class 2 heather and talus straight up to the summit ridge, so the hard part is behind you. The maintained trail runs on past the turnoff toward the pass, so if you find yourself gaining the pass or arriving at Marmot Lake you have walked past the creek and should drop back down the trail. Snow fills the amphitheater and the slopes above into summer and cornices build on the summit ridge into late June, so carry an axe and treat the crest as possibly unsupported. Water is dependable at the creek and scarce once you leave it — fill up before you start climbing.

wa_mount_steel_standard.name: First Divide and the unnamed lake basin

approachLogistics.trailhead: Staircase Trailhead (North Fork Skokomish, Olympic NP)

wa_mount_steel_standard.notes: Parties generally find this the easier of the two lines and it is much shorter, but the corridor on that side has been closed by fire damage — confirm before planning around it. From the divide the route runs west into a basin, then over a col and north along the crest.
hazards: Cornices and unconsolidated snow on the summit ridge into late June
Avalanche potential on east-facing slopes below the summit early season
Burn-scar hazard trees and rockfall on the closed valley corridor
Open ground above the basin that is easy to lose in fog
Loose talus on the connecting slopes either side of the col
wa_mount_steel_standard.baseFinding: From First Divide, follow the ridge west into a basin holding an unnamed lake. That lake is the marker for this whole variant — it is the only standing water in the basin and it sits directly below the two summit humps of Steel, so if you are in an open basin with no lake in it you are in the wrong one. From the lake, drop southwest to the saddle between those humps; the saddle is the base of the climb, and from it you turn north along the summit ridge for the final easy Class 2 stretch to the high point. The direction of that turn is the thing to get right. Duckabush lies beyond the same col to the southwest and reads as the higher, more striking mountain from below, so a party that turns the wrong way off the saddle ends up committed to a different peak. The early-summer cornice and unconsolidated-snow caution applies just as strongly on this side: the crest holds snow late and it is not always attached to the rock beneath it, so stay back from the eastern lip.

wa_mount_stone_lake_of_angels.name: Putvin Trail from Hamma Hamma Road to Lake of the Angels
camps: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
wa_mount_stone_lake_of_angels.notes:
From the Putvin Trailhead on Hamma Hamma River Road (FS 25) at about 1,565-1,600 ft — an unmarked roadside pullout, roughly 4.5 miles past the Lena Lake Trailhead — the Putvin Trail is an unmaintained, primitive user trail that climbs steeply and directly from the first steps. Expect root-staircase steps and boot-track tread through forest for the first mile. In recent years a slide near road mile 10.5 has at times blocked the last 1.2 miles of road, adding a road-walk; check Forest Service status.

About halfway up the trail meets a rock headwall requiring hand-over-hand climbing, with a large tree root as the key handhold and, historically, a fixed handline on the steepest pitch. Above it the trail eases into subalpine forest and heather meadows, passing near Whitehorse Basin and the Pond of the False Prophet, and reaches Lake of the Angels at roughly 4,850-4,920 ft in a cirque below Mount Stone's south face — about 3 to 3.5 miles and 3,000 ft of gain. Little to no reliable water on the lower trail; carry enough to reach the lake.
wa_mount_stone_lake_of_angels.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Snow lingers in the basin above the lake well into summer
hazards: Trail-less, route-finding-dependent terrain above Lake of the Angels
Near-vertical root and rock steps on the lower Putvin Trail, genuinely exposed when wet, and worse descending on tired legs
Loose rock on the headwall and summit block with rockfall onto parties below
An ambiguous Class 3/4 crux near the summit
Fog is common here and multiple parties have lost the route on the upper mountain
wa_mount_stone_lake_of_angels.baseFinding: The base of the climb is a notch in Mount Stone's west ridge, and the test for it is a turn you make before a gate. From Lake of the Angels contour and climb toward St. Peter's Gate — the obvious notch above the basin. Just before the gate, turn sharply left and traverse along the base of the cliffs to a notch in the west ridge. If you walk through St. Peter's Gate, you have gone too far; the Gate is the marker you turn short of, not the one you pass through. That works in cloud because the cliff base is a tactile handrail: once you have made the turn, you keep rock on one side of you the whole traverse. Lose contact with the cliff and you have drifted downhill. Second test, at the notch: turn right and climb toward a first sub-summit rock, then up a short low class 3 chimney to its top. A chimney is a shape you can feel with both hands. If the first difficulty above the notch is a face or a slab rather than a chimney you can bridge, you are not on the line. Third test, on the summit spire: from the sub-summit cross a brief, somewhat exposed ridge to the base of the true summit spire, then follow a groove on the left side that bends right, where a faint climbers' path leads the last steps to the top. Left then right — a groove that runs straight up is not it. What the route's own timing says: about 2.5 hours up from the Lake of the Angels camp and about 1.5 hours back down. If you have been on the ground above the lake far longer than that without finding the notch, you have most likely missed the turn short of the Gate. Fog warning specific to this mountain: Mount Stone has more than one summit, and parties have confused the true south summit with the Middle and North summits in cloud. Count your ridges.

wa_mount_stone_lake_of_angels.name: Lena Lake and Upper Lena Lake, the St. Peter's traverse from the east

bivy.name: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging option for everything on the Hamma Hamma side: Lena Lake and The Brothers, the Putvin trail to Lake of the Angels for Mount Skokomish and Mount Stone, and the Jefferson Creek spur for Mount Pershing. Lena Creek is the more useful of the two because it sits essentially at the Lena Lake trailhead, so a party arriving late can sleep at the car and start walking at first light instead of driving the gravel in the dark. This is a contingency and staging site rather than the normal plan for anyone climbing here — the objectives are all hours above it — but it is the right answer for a party that arrives after dark, gets weathered off, or comes out late and does not want to drive home tired. Being at 700 ft it is usable long before the high camps melt out, which makes it the practical base for an early-season Brothers attempt.
bivy.water: No potable water at either campground — this catches people out. The Hamma Hamma River runs alongside both and can be filtered, but bring drinking water from Hoodsport
bivy.permit: Modest per-night Forest Service fee with an extra vehicle charge, paid at the fee machine, which is cashless. No reservation system and no wilderness permit — this is developed Forest Service camping. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site, vault toilets, no hookups. Typically open from mid-May into late October and gated the rest of the year
bivy.capacity: Lena Creek has around thirteen well-spaced sites at the Lena Lake trailhead junction; Hamma Hamma has around fifteen a couple of miles further down the river. Both first come, first served, no reservations

approachLogistics.trailhead: Lena Lake Trailhead (Hamma Hamma Road, FR-25)

wa_mount_stone_lake_of_angels.notes:
The other side of the same notch. From the Lena Lake Trailhead on FS 25 at roughly 600-750 ft, take the well-graded Lena Lake Trail #810 about 3 miles to Lena Lake at about 1,800 ft, then the steep primitive tread up the West Fork Lena Creek drainage roughly 3.5 more miles to Upper Lena Lake at about 4,550 ft, some 6.5 miles and 4,000 ft from the trailhead. Upper Lena Lake is the last maintained-trail camp and the last reliable water before the traverse goes cross-country; wilderness permit and bear canister required.

From Upper Lena Lake, leave the trail and head west on the Scout Lake way-trail across meadows and heather past Lena Tarn to Scout Pass at about 5,200 ft, down slightly to Upper Scout Lake, round it into Scout Basin, and up to Ullin's Pass at about 5,000 ft above the tarns known as Ullin's Bathtubs. From there a rising traverse above the small lakes leads to a snow ramp across a steep hillside below Mount Stone that ends at a loose moraine, and then exposed dirt-and-mud slopes to St. Peter's Gate at about 5,950 ft.

This is a two- or three-day trip and it is chosen for the country it crosses, not because it is quicker.
wa_mount_stone_lake_of_angels.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the off-trail benches and passes are largely clear
hazards: Extensive off-trail way-trail route-finding over multiple passes and basins with faint tread
Loose glacial moraine of all sizes near St. Peter's Gate and exposed dirt-and-mud slopes on the final ramp
Fog on the upper mountain — multiple parties have lost the route here and ended up in harder terrain
No dependable water between Upper Lena Lake and the tarns near Ullin's Pass
A very long approach with limited bail options partway through
wa_mount_stone_lake_of_angels.baseFinding: Coming from the east you arrive at St. Peter's Gate itself, which is the high point of the traverse at about 5,950 ft and an obvious rocky notch in Mount Stone's southeast ridge. That is the arrival test and it is unmistakable in any weather: the ground stops rising, the notch pinches, and the Lake of the Angels basin opens on the far side. From the gate there are two ways onto the peak and they are different climbs. The one this route describes is the west-ridge notch: go through the Gate and drop toward the Lake of the Angels basin, then work back up and turn the corner onto the cliff-base traverse to the notch in the west ridge — the same notch the Putvin parties reach by turning sharply left just short of the Gate. The other is the south-face gully, which starts by descending about 300 ft from the Gate to the base of a basalt cliff; that is the Lena Lake traverse route's line, not this one. So the fog test for this variant is which side of the gate you end up on: this route goes over to the Lake of the Angels side and approaches the west ridge from the south-west, keeping the cliff base at your shoulder. Above the notch the tests are identical to the Putvin variant: turn right, low Class 3 chimney to a sub-summit, a brief exposed ridge, then a groove on the left that bends right to the true south summit.

wa_mount_stuart_north_ridge.name: North side — Stuart Lake TH via Mountaineer Creek
camps: Mountaineer Creek basin (beneath the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers)
The 8,200 ft notch on the North Ridge
wa_mount_stuart_north_ridge.notes:
Park at the Stuart Lake Trailhead at the end of FR 7601 (Eightmile Road) out of Leavenworth and walk the Stuart Lake Trail up Mountaineer Creek. At the signed split roughly two miles along, ignore the Colchuck Lake branch on the right and carry straight on. A short distance further you leave maintained tread altogether, well before Stuart Lake, ford Mountaineer Creek and follow its south fork upstream cross-country. Late in the season there is a cairned climbers' path through much of this; early in the season there is not, and the creek runs hard.

Above the streamside travel a steep, unstable talus and boulder slope lifts you into the hanging basin under Sherpa Peak and the Sherpa Glacier. This basin holds the usual bivies. From it you angle up onto the glacier bench beneath the ridge.

This is the shorter, lower-gain way in and it puts you at the toe with the most in the tank, but it commits you to a car shuttle: the standard descent is the Cascadian Couloir, which spills out on the far side of the range at Ingalls Creek. Parties report the shuttle drive between the two trailheads costing several hours round trip. In June and early July the Sherpa Glacier is a reasonable way back down to this side and removes the shuttle problem — later in the summer it is not.

There is running snowmelt near the toe of the ridge (reported around 47.48095, -120.89454); above the 8,200 ft notch there is no reliable water once the last snow patch there melts out.
wa_mount_stuart_north_ridge.season: Jun to mid-Jul is the sweet spot; workable through Sep
hazards: Mountaineer Creek and its south fork run high and fast in early-season melt
Loose talus and boulder slope below the Sherpa Glacier basin — poor footing, rockfall onto parties below
Serac and icefall exposure if you drift east under the Ice Cliff Glacier
No reliable water above the 8,200 ft notch once its snow patch is gone
Committing: standard descent exits on the opposite side of the range, so a shuttle or a very long walk-around is required
wa_mount_stuart_north_ridge.baseFinding:
You are climbing the complete North Ridge, which begins at about 6,600 ft — roughly 1,500 ft of roped ground below the point where most people who say 'North Ridge' actually start. The toe is the lowest rock of the rib that separates the two glaciers: Stuart Glacier on its west side, Ice Cliff Glacier on its east. Standing at the base with the Ice Cliff Glacier and its seracs on your left and the Stuart Glacier hidden around the corner to your right, you are in the right place. If you are underneath hanging ice you have drifted too far east onto the Ice Cliff side and need to come back west to the rib's lowest rock.

The feature to not mistake for the start is the notch at 8,200 ft. That notch is obvious — a saddle in the crest with a scatter of bivy platforms and, usually, a small lingering snowfield for water — and it is where the Upper (original) North Ridge begins. It is reached by a rock gully climbed from the edge of the Stuart Glacier at about 7,700 ft, on the ridge's west flank. If you find yourself scrambling a gully up from snow toward a bivy saddle, you have skipped the lower 1,500 ft and are on the Upper route, not the Complete.

In cloud, use the glaciers rather than the rock: the toe is where the moraine/snow of the basin runs out against the first continuous rock, and the ice above and left of you belongs to the Ice Cliff Glacier. The 8,200 ft notch is above and right of that, reached only after the ridge has already risen well above the ice.

wa_mount_stuart_north_ridge.name: South side — Esmeralda TH over Longs Pass and Goat Pass

bivy.name: Goat Pass
bivy.notes: The camp for the southern approach over Longs Pass and up Ingalls Creek — a longer, higher-gain walk in, but it sets up a much shorter car-to-car loop because the Cascadian Couloir descent drops back the same way. A planned camp with plenty of flat ground, though water becomes a carry once the snow patches are gone.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small tarns early to mid season; Ingalls Creek is the reliable source, below the pass
bivy.capacity: Numerous good bivy sites on the pass

bivy.name: The 8,200 ft notch on the North Ridge
bivy.notes: The classic place to split the complete ridge, reached by the snow-filled gully (usually climbed on 4th-class rock at its edge) above the Stuart Glacier. This is a planned bivy, not an emergency ledge, but only two spots are actually comfortable and a party of three or more will be spread out. Wind-scoured and fully exposed, with no water above it, so the summit day starts with everything you carried.
bivy.water: None reliable — seasonal snow patches only, and nothing at all once they melt out
bivy.capacity: Two genuinely good bivy spots, plus a number of mediocre ones nearby

wa_mount_stuart_north_ridge.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737), take the trail over Longs Pass and up Ingalls Creek to Goat Pass, then traverse east beneath the Stuart Glacier, staying above the large moraine mound, and aim for the toe of the ridge.

About 2,000 ft of the day is descent, so the round trip is more work than the raw gain suggests, and parties consistently report it taking longer than planned — budget eight hours and expect route-finding on the traverse rather than tread.

The reason to accept the longer, higher approach is that it removes the shuttle entirely. The Cascadian Couloir descent drops to Ingalls Creek on this side, so a party that walked in from Esmeralda walks out to its own car. Parties who came in from the north do not.

How much snow remains on the Goat Pass traverse is the recurring gear question here: sections have been reported at around 40 degrees, and whether you need an axe and traction changes week to week through the summer. Recent photos and current reports are worth more than any fixed answer.
wa_mount_stuart_north_ridge.season: Jul-Sep, once the traverse under the Stuart Glacier has melted or consolidated
hazards: Snow slopes on the Goat Pass traverse reported near 40 degrees; conditions change through the summer
~2,000 ft of descent on the way in, all of which must be regained on the way out
Long day with no bail-out once past Goat Pass
Approach consistently underestimated; parties arrive at the toe late and tired
wa_mount_stuart_north_ridge.baseFinding:
Coming from Goat Pass you arrive at the ridge from below and to the west, which is the opposite side from the northern approach — so the Ice Cliff Glacier is not your handrail here, the Stuart Glacier is. Keep the Stuart Glacier snow on your left as you traverse east and stay above the big moraine mound; the toe of the Complete ridge is the first continuous rock the traverse runs into, at about 6,600 ft.

The decision point is unmissable once you know to look for it: from the edge of the Stuart Glacier at roughly 7,700 ft a rock gully leads up the ridge's west side to the notch at 8,200 ft. Taking that gully puts you on the Upper North Ridge and skips the lower 1,500 ft. Continuing the traverse past and below it, down to the lowest rock, is what starts the Complete route. In poor visibility: if the snow you are standing on is still rising to your right toward a saddle, you are too high; the toe is below, where the snow ends.

wa_mount_stuart_stuart_glacier_couloir.name: Mountaineer Creek to the basin, then west onto the Stuart Glacier
wa_mount_stuart_stuart_glacier_couloir.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road, follow the trail about three miles to the Colchuck Lake turnoff and continue past it for roughly another mile. Where the Stuart Lake trail switchbacks up and to the right, veer left to stay in the main valley — the same leaving point every north-side route on this mountain uses.

Follow the valley about a mile and a half to where it steepens, then turn right and work up the steep slope into the small hanging valley above, the flat basin under the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers at roughly 5,400 ft. Standard camp is here.

From the basin the route continues west, round the far side of the North Ridge, onto the Stuart Glacier. Entry to the couloir is at about 7,800 ft.

The couloir itself runs 40-50 degree snow, narrows to a short steep step whose character depends entirely on the season, then a second shorter step, then opens into a wider snowfield leading to a notch in the West Ridge. Six pitches of mixed ground follow from that notch to the summit.
wa_mount_stuart_stuart_glacier_couloir.season: Best while the couloir holds continuous snow and the steps take ice, roughly late spring into early summer; later the steps go rocky and the climbing turns mixed
hazards: Crevasses on the Stuart Glacier below the couloir
Rockfall and wet-snow avalanche in the couloir as the day warms
The steep steps turning to bare ice or dry-tooling ground later in the season
Six pitches of mixed climbing above the notch, on the far side of the mountain from camp
An unmarked, often snow-covered off-trail turn out of the Mountaineer Creek valley
wa_mount_stuart_stuart_glacier_couloir.baseFinding: The north ridge rock rib decides it, and the side it is on is the answer. From the basin you are looking at four things in a row: the Sherpa Glacier, the Ice Cliff Glacier, the enormous rock rib of the North Ridge, and beyond it the Stuart Glacier. You want to be past the rib. So: if the North Ridge rib is on your left (east) you are on the Stuart Glacier and correct. If it is still on your right you have not gone far enough west and are on the Ice Cliff side. That is the same test the Ice Cliff Glacier route uses, read in the opposite direction, and it is the reliable one in cloud because it does not depend on seeing the summit. Second test — what the couloir leads to. This couloir does not go to the summit. It goes to a notch in the west ridge, which is on the far side of the mountain from where you camped. If the line you are looking up appears to head for the top of the peak, you are looking at the wrong feature. Third, the shape. Entry is at about 7,800 ft and the couloir narrows above you before it widens again — moderate snow, then a short steep step, then a second shorter one, then an open snowfield. A line that is uniformly wide with no steps is not this one. And the negative test: no hanging ice cliff or serac band should be above you anywhere. If there is one, you are back on the Ice Cliff Glacier, on the wrong side of the rib.

wa_mount_stuart_stuart_glacier_couloir.name: Esmeralda, Ingalls Lake and Stuart Pass to Goat Pass

bivy.name: Goat Pass bivies
bivy.notes: The high camp of choice for the upper North Ridge and the Stuart Glacier Couloir when approaching from the Ingalls side, putting the traverse under the glacier and the entry gully within an easy morning. Bivy ground is plentiful and reasonably flat, but the position is exposed and windy, so bring a shelter rather than counting on a sheltered nook. From here the standard line traverses east below the Stuart Glacier above the moraine, with snow crossings well into summer. The water situation is the binding constraint late in the season — treat it as a dry camp unless you have seen recent conditions.
bivy.water: No dependable running water. Snowmelt trickles and lingering patches are usually workable into midsummer, but by late season the pass is dry and you must carry water up or melt snow off the glacier below
bivy.permit: Reached from the Esmeralda Basin trailhead over Ingalls Pass and Stuart Pass, so approached on Alpine Lakes Wilderness ground under the Cle Elum Ranger District — free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass to park, no Enchantment lottery permit. The pass sits on the divide, however: a party that continues down into the Mountaineer Creek drainage and camps there is entering the Stuart Zone and needs that overnight permit between May 15 and Oct 31.
bivy.capacity: Numerous small rock-and-gravel platforms along the pass; several independent parties can spread out without crowding each other

wa_mount_stuart_stuart_glacier_couloir.notes: From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead, hike over Ingalls Pass to Ingalls Lake, then traverse toward Stuart Pass. Near 7,000 ft cross the scree gully north to Goat Pass at about 7,600 ft, where there is plenty of bivy ground. From the pass descend a short way onto the Stuart Glacier and traverse under the North Ridge to the couloir; the glacier passes above some large crevasses.

wa_mount_torment_south_ridge.name: Boston Basin, rising traverse to the Taboo Glacier
camps: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
wa_mount_torment_south_ridge.hours: 2.5-4 to high camp, about 1-2 more to the notch
wa_mount_torment_south_ridge.notes:
From the unsigned Boston Basin pullout on Cascade River Road at roughly 3,300 ft (about 21.7 miles from Marblemount, directly opposite Johannesburg), take the old Diamond Mine roadbed about three quarters of a mile to a mile, then the sharp right turn onto the steep climbers' trail. Four small creek crossings, treeline about 5,300 ft, low camp 5,300-5,500 ft, high camp about 6,200-6,400 ft.

From high camp leave any semblance of trail and make a rising traverse to the northwest, holding roughly the 6,200 ft contour across talus, tundra and slab steps. You pass beneath the south spur of Forbidden Peak and cross a prominent rock rib below the cliffs, with the Taboo Glacier coming into view above.

Gain the Taboo Glacier on its climber's-left side and follow it up. Some parties skip the summit-day traverse entirely by carrying up the Taboo and camping at about 7,100 ft directly beneath Torment's southeast face at the foot of the couloir.

This traverse is the part that gets people lost in cloud. It is open, uniform ground with no trail, and in early season the creek channels are buried and there is avalanche exposure across it.
hazards: Bergschrund or moat at the base of the couloir — fatal accident on record
Loose class 3-4 rock in the gully with parties above
Featureless traverse from Boston Basin, easy to lose in whiteout
Early-season avalanche exposure on the traverse; buried creek channels
Couloir can be entirely melted out late season
wa_mount_torment_south_ridge.baseFinding:
The climbing starts at a prominent notch in the South Ridge, at the top of the east couloir that comes off the Taboo Glacier — and the couloir, not the notch, is what you are hunting for from the glacier.

Follow the Taboo up until a deep gully or couloir breaks through the rock band on your left. It is a definite break, not a weakness in a face. A bergschrund or moat guards its bottom; this crossing is the standard place parties stop, put the sharp end on, and it has been the site of a fatal accident, so it is not a formality. Early season it is snow-bridged; late season it is wide open and the couloir above it may be completely melted out to rock.

From the schrund, scramble roughly a hundred feet of loose class 3-4 up the gully to the notch. You are at the base of the route when you are standing in a notch on the ridge crest with Torment Basin dropping away on the west side and the Taboo Glacier below you to the east. If you have gained rock but there is no crest and no view down the far side, you have gone up a break in the rock band rather than the couloir.

The late-season workaround is worth knowing, because it removes the moat problem entirely: instead of crossing onto the ridge at the notch, cross the South Ridge at about 6,600 ft and gain the ridge from the Torment Basin side. Adjacent scrambling variations that avoid the snow couloir and reach the same notch are also described.

Be aware this gully is a queue on a busy weekend — parties commonly wait below the schrund for the group above to clear the loose class 3-4 rather than climb underneath them.

wa_mount_torment_south_ridge.name: Torment Basin climbers' path

bivy.name: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
bivy.notes: Parties attempting the Torment-Forbidden traverse, a long day on Boston Peak, or a late finish on the Forbidden North Ridge sometimes end up bivouacking on snow or rock above the established camps, in the Sharkfin Col area, or in a notch on route. Treat these as unplanned or emergency shelter rather than as an itinerary: they are exposed, they have no water once the snow goes, and the surrounding terrain is glaciated. Human waste must be packed out, and food still needs bear-resistant storage.
bivy.water: Entirely snowmelt and therefore seasonal. Early in the summer there is running water almost everywhere; by late season the high ground can be bare rock with nothing running, so plan to carry water up or melt snow.
bivy.permit: Still requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, from Marblemount. Whether an unestablished high bivouac is acceptable in Boston Basin is genuinely contested — the general zone regulation allows camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while the site-specific guidance for Boston Basin says to use the two designated camps. Ask when you collect the permit rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Party-sized ledges and snow platforms only; no facilities, no toilet, and no reliable flat ground once the snow has melted out.

approachLogistics.trailhead: Cascade River Road at the river bridge, about a mile past the Eldorado Creek trailhead

wa_mount_torment_south_ridge.notes:
A separate and much less-used way in that skips Boston Basin altogether. Drive Cascade River Road only about 20 miles — roughly a mile past the Eldorado Creek trailhead — and look for the climbers' path starting about fifty feet upstream of the bridge over the Cascade River.

It is a steep, hard climb on a boot path that is mostly easy to follow up into Torment Basin, but despite decades of traffic some sections stay genuinely brushy. It puts you on the west side of the South Ridge rather than the east.

The reason to use it is the moat: from the Torment Basin side the South Ridge can be gained at about 6,600 ft without crossing the moat at the top of the Taboo Glacier, which is the late-season crux of the standard approach. It is also the shorter drive.
hazards: Brushy sections on a steep unmaintained boot path
Less-travelled approach — fewer parties, less current beta on conditions
wa_mount_torment_south_ridge.baseFinding: Coming from Torment Basin you meet the South Ridge from the west, so you do not arrive at the notch from below — you gain the crest at about 6,600 ft and follow it. The confirmation is the crest itself and the Taboo Glacier appearing below on the east side once you are on it. This is the same ridge the standard approach reaches at the notch above the couloir, entered lower down.

wa_mount_townsend_standard.name: Mount Townsend Trail #839 from the Upper Trailhead
wa_mount_townsend_standard.notes: Three sets of switchbacks, the last fully sun-exposed and the hottest, most water-hungry part of the day — there is no dependable creek on the trail itself. Camp Windy and an unmarked spur to Windy Lake sit at about 5,300 ft. The Lower Trailhead adds roughly two round-trip miles and five hundred feet. The small upper lot fills early on summer weekends.
hazards: Snow and ice on the upper trail and summit ridge into June in heavy years
A wind-scoured, lightning-exposed summit ridge in summer storms
Loose pea gravel over hardpack on the lowest switchback set
A steep open slope below the summit ridge that holds consolidated snow
Route-finding confusion at the Silver Lakes junction in fog
wa_mount_townsend_standard.baseFinding: There is no scramble on this route, so the questions that matter are which fork and which top. Above Camp Windy, at about 5,500 ft and roughly three miles in, the trail meets the Silver Lakes Trail: stay right and uphill. The left fork drops toward Silver Lakes on loose, unmaintained ground and is not the route. You have taken the right branch when the forest opens into subalpine meadow and the grade eases markedly for the final stretch, with the last quarter mile crossing open, low-angle grassy and rocky tundra rather than anything steep. The high ground is a broad, flat ridge with more than one apparent top. The south summit is the true high point; the popular viewpoint where most people stop and turn round sits a short, easy walk below the actual crown, and the north summit further along the crest is lower still. Rock outcrops on the south top give the only wind shelter up there. Early season, snow on the upper meadow and on the steep open slope gaining the ridge is where the tread is easiest to lose in flat light.

wa_mount_townsend_standard.name: Little Quilcene Trail over Little River Summit
wa_mount_townsend_standard.notes: The shortest way to the top, with the least gain. The trail climbs steadily through forest to Little River Summit, then follows an open, exposed ridge for the last mile to meet the main trail near the summit. Carry water, as the ridge is dry and sunny.

wa_ne_ridge.name: Upper Cathedral Lake camp, then the grassy south-east slope onto the ridge
camps: Cathedral Pass benches and the tarn slabs
wa_ne_ridge.notes:
Reach Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft by any of the long trails — Andrews Creek #504 is the shortest drive, the Cathedral Driveway #510A the shortest walk, Thirtymile via the Chewuch #510 the middle option. All are multi-day and all put you in the same basin.

From the Boundary Trail below the peak, this route does not go into the Cathedral–Monk gully at all. Scramble up the grassy south-east slope directly from the main trail to gain the ridge.
hazards: Continuing north along the ridge toward The Pope and the Canadian border
Loose rock on a long broken ridge
Very long walk out from a remote basin if anything goes wrong
A no-fall step-across on the standard walk-off descent
wa_ne_ridge.baseFinding:
You are aiming for the long broken ridge that runs between Cathedral Peak and The Pope, a separate small peak further north along the same crest, sitting right on the Canada–United States border.

That relationship is the base-finding and it is also the warning. The ridge has a peak at each end. If you keep working north along the crest past the point where the ground starts descending away from Cathedral, you are heading for The Pope and, shortly after that, for an international border it is illegal to cross here.

The route itself confirms as you go rather than at a single spot: each pitch has a move or two of old-school 5.3 with scrambling between, so seven pitches of mostly-easy ground with occasional short difficulties is correct here and is not a sign you have wandered onto the walk-up. The real crux announces itself — about 400 feet below the summit you cross a dike, and the two short pitches immediately above that dike are the hardest climbing on the route. A final airy fourth-class scramble finishes it.

Negative marker for the start: if you find yourself entering a deep gully with a detached tower on your right, you have walked to the SE Buttress start. The NE Ridge is gained from open grassy slope off the main trail, with no gully involved.

Descent is the ordinary walk-up route to the west, and a short rappel may be wanted to get off the summit ridge.

wa_ne_ridge.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee

bivy.name: Upper Cathedral Lake basin
bivy.notes: The working climbers' camp for both the Southeast Buttress and Amphitheater's ridges, sitting directly under the peaks with short walks to either. The basin has taken heavy use for decades and the Forest Service has posted revegetation closures on damaged ground here in the past, so treat the shoreline as off limits and camp on rock or bare dirt well back from the water. Check the posted signs on arrival rather than assuming last year's layout still applies — which sites are open has changed between seasons. Nights are cold and exposed at this elevation even in August.
bivy.water: The most dependable water anywhere on this approach — the lake holds through the season and needs no rationing. The one place on the route where you can plan on filling without checking a report first.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten Wilderness permit at the trailhead you start from. No quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. Some trailheads also require a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites on slabs and benches back from the water; realistically three or four small parties before it feels crowded, and it does fill on midsummer weekends and during larch season

wa_ne_ridge.notes: From the Cathedral Driveway Trailhead on the Toats Coulee road out of Loomis, the trail drops to join the Chewuch trail and then climbs the valley to the Cathedral Lakes basin. The eastern way in, with less climbing than Andrews Creek.

wa_ne_ridge.name: Thirtymile Trailhead and the Chewuch River trail toward Remmel Lake

bivy.name: Upper Cathedral Lake basin
bivy.notes: The working climbers' camp for both the Southeast Buttress and Amphitheater's ridges, sitting directly under the peaks with short walks to either. The basin has taken heavy use for decades and the Forest Service has posted revegetation closures on damaged ground here in the past, so treat the shoreline as off limits and camp on rock or bare dirt well back from the water. Check the posted signs on arrival rather than assuming last year's layout still applies — which sites are open has changed between seasons. Nights are cold and exposed at this elevation even in August.
bivy.water: The most dependable water anywhere on this approach — the lake holds through the season and needs no rationing. The one place on the route where you can plan on filling without checking a report first.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten Wilderness permit at the trailhead you start from. No quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. Some trailheads also require a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites on slabs and benches back from the water; realistically three or four small parties before it feels crowded, and it does fill on midsummer weekends and during larch season

approachLogistics.trailhead: Thirtymile Trailhead (end of the Chewuch River Road)

wa_ne_ridge.notes: Follow the Chewuch River trail north from the Thirtymile Trailhead nearly to Remmel Lake, then climb to the Cathedral Lakes basin. A longer way round than Andrews Creek, used when combining the Remmel Lake country with the climb.

wa_north_face_left_buttress.name: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail to the north-face glacier
wa_north_face_left_buttress.notes:
The approach that stays inside the United States, and much the longer of the two.

From the highway pullout above the dam, a spur trail drops to the lake shore; cross by water taxi or by a boat portaged down it, and land near the head of the lake. Follow the Lightning Creek trail, then the abandoned and increasingly brushy Freezeout Creek trail. The steep rock-and-alder diagonal immediately above the trail junction is the hardest navigation on the whole walk; look for intermittent orange flagging. The cabin at about 3,600 ft is a waypoint and an emergency shelter, and tread mostly disappears around 4,200 ft.

Camping in the lower corridor needs a park backcountry permit; the upper part is wilderness with a free self-issue permit.

From the upper basin, work round to the north side and onto the glacier at the foot of the wall, which is mellow enough for easy travel.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.season: Summer; the documented ascent was made in early August
hazards: At least four unmarked lines on one wall, two of them starting close together on the same buttress
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the base of the climbing
Roughly half the pitches are at the upper end of the grade, with the crux on a corner low down
Descent by the east ridge and a snow finger, not by reversing the climb
Multi-day approach and a retreat measured in days
wa_north_face_left_buttress.baseFinding:
The face is about fourteen hundred feet of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs above a glacier and it carries several routes with nothing marked. Do not identify by name; identify by feature.

First, place the central buttress. Stand back on the glacier and find the summit, then look at the buttress directly beneath it — that is the neighbouring route, and this line is not on it. This route takes the left margin of that buttress system, so you want to be off to the left of the plumb line from the summit.

Second, find the gully or chimney at the buttress's left edge. The start is in the blocky line of face holds just left of it. Blocky face holds, immediately left of a gully or chimney, at the left edge of the buttress: that is the whole identification at the ground. The first pitch is long, mostly low fifth class, with a wide crack near its end.

Third, and this is the confirmation higher up that nothing else on the face gives you: this route follows a distinctive yellow quartz dyke up the wall to avoid the dirtier rock either side of it. A yellow band running up the granite is not a subtle feature. If you never meet one, you are on a different climb.

Watch for an awkward bergschrund or moat where the glacier meets the rock.

Negative markers, and they matter because two of the neighbours are hard: if the summit is directly overhead from your belay and your second pitch is desperate face climbing wanting an aid move, you are on the central buttress line. And the face's original route and at least two others also exist here, so the honest rule is that anything without the yellow dyke above it is not this.

Descent is not the route reversed and not a rappel: take the east ridge from the top to an obvious col, then a snow finger back down toward the approach glacier and basin.

wa_north_face_left_buttress.name: Provincial park approach from the north over Frosty Mountain to Crow Creek

bivy.name: Castle Peak north-side glacier bivy
bivy.notes: Camp below the glacier under the north face, at the end of the approach and at the foot of the glacier crossing to the route.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and glacier runoff.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten Wilderness permit.
bivy.capacity: A few tent spots on rock and moraine; no established sites.

approachLogistics.trailhead: Lightning Lake, E.C. Manning Provincial Park (British Columbia)

wa_north_face_left_buttress.notes:
Read the legal point first. This approach walks in from the provincial park on the northern side and crosses the international boundary cross-country. That is not a lawful crossing. Away from a port of entry it needs prior arrangement with the border authority, the corridor is patrolled, and casual parties cannot simply walk over. It is recorded because it is the commonly published line and the shorter of the two, not as a recommendation.

As described, it follows the marked trail from Lightning Lake up the Frosty Mountain area to a pass near 8,000 ft, then leaves the trail and travels cross-country south over the boundary, descending through the next creek basin and over the divide into the drainage below the peak's north face, finishing at the toe of the glacier.

The lawful alternatives are the boat crossing and abandoned creek trail from the east, or the crest trail from the west, both of which are considerably longer.
wa_north_face_left_buttress.season: Summer, once the divide traverse is clear enough to travel
hazards: The described approach crosses the international boundary cross-country and is not a lawful crossing
Cross-country travel over a mountain and a drainage divide to reach the glacier
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the base of the wall
Several unmarked routes on one face, two of them on the same buttress
Descent by the east ridge and a snow finger rather than the way you came up
wa_north_face_left_buttress.baseFinding:
Whichever way you arrive, the glacier is the same and so is the identification, and this side has one advantage worth using: you come down toward the wall, which gives you the whole face in one view before you are under it. Take that view rather than sorting the routes out from the bergschrund.

From back on the glacier, find the summit and note the buttress directly under it — that is the neighbouring line and it is not this one. This route is on the left margin of the same buttress system.

The ground marker is a gully or chimney at the buttress's left edge, with the route starting in the blocky line of face holds just left of it. The confirmation above is a yellow quartz dyke, which the line follows deliberately to stay on clean rock and away from the dirtier granite either side. Yellow band, left margin, blocky start beside a chimney: those three together are the route.

Expect an awkward bergschrund or moat at the transition from ice to rock.

Negative markers. Directly under the summit with a very hard second pitch means the central buttress line. No yellow dyke anywhere above you means one of the other lines on this face, of which there are several and none is marked.

Second negative marker and it is not about climbing: the boundary clearing is a visible cut line across this ground. It is not a route and it is not a shortcut.

Descent is the east ridge to an obvious col and then a snow finger back to the glacier and basin.

wa_north_face_left_buttress.name: Pacific Crest Trail north from Harts Pass

bivy.name: Castle Peak north-side glacier bivy
bivy.notes: Camp below the glacier under the north face, at the end of the approach and at the foot of the glacier crossing to the route.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and glacier runoff.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten Wilderness permit.
bivy.capacity: A few tent spots on rock and moraine; no established sites.

bivy.name: Harts Pass and Meadows campgrounds
bivy.notes: This is the staging ground for almost everything in the zone and the road to it is a substantial fact in its own right. Forest Road 5400 climbs roughly twenty miles of unpaved single lane from Mazama with pullouts rather than passing room, a rock wall on one side and an unguarded drop on the other, and grades approaching seventeen percent on the upper ramps. Trailers are prohibited outright and motorhomes and wide vehicles are strongly discouraged. The road opens with the snowmelt, typically early to mid July and occasionally not until later, and closes with the first serious autumn storms. Above the pass it continues to the gate below Slate Peak at about 7,440 feet, the highest driveable point in the state, which puts you at a trailhead where the walking starts near 7,000 feet instead of 2,500. Four trails leave from here — the Pacific Crest Trail, the West Fork Pasayten, the Middle Fork Pasayten and Buckskin Ridge — so this one pass is the door to Osceola, Blackcap, Dot, Ptarmigan, Castle and Blizzard. Nights are cold and wind at the pass is relentless; pitch behind timber rather than in the open meadow. Wildfires close this road and parts of the northern wilderness in some summers, so confirm the road is actually open before committing to a long drive.
bivy.water: None. Neither campground has potable water and there is no piped supply anywhere on the pass, so haul everything up from the valley or plan on filtering from creeks well below. This is the single most common mistake parties make staging here.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or an Interagency pass to park at the trailheads; the campgrounds themselves are free but carry no services and no trash collection, so everything you bring comes back out. The free self-issue Pasayten wilderness permit is filled out at the trailhead kiosk before you walk in, not here. Campfires are legal in the existing rings when no burn ban is in effect, but the ground is thin alpine meadow and firewood is scarce, so most parties do without.
bivy.capacity: Two small Forest Service campgrounds a mile apart, five or six sites at the pass itself and roughly twice that at Meadows, first come first served with no reservations. They fill on summer weekends and in larch season, and there is no overflow up here.

bivy.name: Windy Pass and the crest camps north of Harts Pass
bivy.notes: This is the first day of every trip toward Castle and Blizzard and the natural stop for anyone who wants a night high on the crest without a valley grind. The trail leaves Harts Pass at about 6,200 feet, tops out just under 7,000 a little over two miles north, and never drops below 5,000 the whole way to the border, so this is sustained high open country with long views and no shelter. Snow lingers on the north-facing traverses well into the summer and those crossings are the reason most parties wait until mid August in a heavy year. Wind is the standing complaint at Windy Pass and it earns the name; camping a little below the crest costs nothing and buys a great deal. There is no mobile service anywhere along here. As pure staging these camps do nothing for the Robinson Creek or Middle Fork peaks, which go the other direction from the pass.
bivy.water: Sparse and the defining planning problem of this stretch. There is nothing at the pass itself; the nearest campsites with water sit most of a mile further on and a couple of hundred feet higher. Carry enough for at least six miles at a time, and treat the basin between Foggy Pass and Windy Pass, the Shaw Creek crossing and the spring near Holman Peak as the fixed points to plan around rather than assuming you will find something in between.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Harts Pass, no quota and nothing to reserve. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Party size limits and any seasonal campfire ban are posted at the trailhead and change year to year, so read the board rather than assuming. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of any lake shoreline, and stock parties must carry certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight.
bivy.capacity: A string of small established sites in the meadows and basins along the crest, most taking one or two tents. The Pacific Crest Trail hiking season overlaps the climbing season, so expect company at the obvious ones and be ready to walk on to the next.

bivy.name: Hopkins Lake and Castle Pass
bivy.notes: These are the camps that make Castle Peak and Blizzard Peak possible at all from the American side. Hopkins Lake sits about twenty-four trail miles north of Harts Pass, six hundred feet below the trail, and Castle Pass is roughly twenty-seven miles out at about 5,450 feet. Castle Peak rises directly north and east of the pass and is a scramble from a camp here; Blizzard Peak lies further east toward Frosty Pass and the Chuchuwanteen country and is more often reached by dropping down the West Fork Pasayten from Harts Pass instead, which is a different but comparably long line. Either way this is a three to five day trip for a fit party and there is no shortcut — the loss of the Canadian exit removed the only short approach that ever existed for these two summits. Plan food and water for the full round trip, expect snow on the north slopes into August, and understand that a weather change up here leaves you a very long way from the car.
bivy.water: Hopkins Lake is the reliable one and is worth the descent for that reason alone — it is the best water for many miles in either direction. Castle Pass is drier and the sources near it are seasonal, so fill at the lake before continuing north.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Harts Pass. The international boundary matters here in a way it does not elsewhere in the zone: crossing north into Canada from the backcountry is not lawful and the long-standing arrangement that let northbound trail hikers walk out to the highway in British Columbia was ended in 2025, so there is no exit that way and no legal entry southbound either. Everything in this corner is now an out-and-back from Harts Pass. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of the lake shoreline; pull back into the trees.
bivy.capacity: Hopkins Lake holds several small established sites in the trees around the shore and is the most comfortable camp in the far north of the wilderness. Castle Pass itself has room for a couple of parties in the timber. Neither is large and both see through-hiker traffic.

wa_north_face_left_buttress.notes: Follow the Pacific Crest Trail north from Harts Pass along the crest, about 27 miles to Castle Pass, then go cross-country onto the peak and around to the north side. It needs no boat and stays in the United States, but it is a very long high walk and the Harts Pass road usually opens only in July.

wa_north_ridge_2.name: From the west: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack River Trail and Brush Creek to Whatcom Pass
camps: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
wa_north_ridge_2.notes:
About 16-17 miles one-way. Start at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of Hannegan Pass Road, FS-32, at about 3,100 ft, and follow Trail #674 about 4 miles and 2,000 ft to Hannegan Pass, then descend the far side to Boundary Camp in the Chilliwack River valley.

Continue down-valley on the Chilliwack River Trail, unmaintained and rough in sections with stretches obliterated by avalanche debris, past Copper Creek Camp and US Cabin Camp, cross the Chilliwack by the hand-operated cable car just beyond US Cabin (or ford it), then turn up the Brush Creek Trail at its junction near mile 12 and climb past Graybeal Camp and Whatcom Camp to Whatcom Pass. Typically split over two days with a valley-bottom camp.
hazards: Loose, exposed 3rd to low-4th-class choss in the final several hundred feet below the summit
Downclimbing that ground with an overnight pack, which reports rate as the riskier option
An unmaintained Chilliwack River Trail with stretches obliterated by avalanche debris
No fixed anchors anywhere on the ridge
wa_north_ridge_2.baseFinding:
The base is the broad toe of the ridge, and you find it by walking south off the pass until the path dies. From Whatcom Pass a faint, informal climbers' trail leaves the maintained trail and heads directly south, gaining the broad toe of Whatcom Peak's north ridge. The path quickly gives way to snow patches and broken rock, and from there the route-finding rule is stay on the crest rather than follow any marked line.

So the fog test is a handrail test, and it is the best kind: once you are on the crest, keep it under your feet. Any time you find yourself sidehilling with the crest above you, you have come off it. There is nothing to identify on this ridge except the ridge.

Arrival at the start: you are on the route as soon as the informal path stops being a path and the ground becomes broken rock rising to a crest. That transition happens within a few hundred feet of the pass; this is not a route with a long walk to its base.

What the upper ridge is like, because it decides whether you come back this way: the final several hundred feet below the summit are described bluntly by climber reports as a chossy nightmare of loose, exposed 3rd to low-4th-class terrain, and downclimbing it with a heavy overnight pack is considered the harder, riskier option even though it is shorter. Many parties instead go over the summit and down the South Spur side.

And the other thing this ridge is: it is the direct line from Whatcom Pass to Perfect Pass that Challenger parties are told not to take. It is loose, extremely exposed and called a formidable obstacle. If you are on it as a shortcut rather than as your objective, you have chosen the wrong tool.

wa_north_ridge_2.name: From the east: Ross Lake water taxi to Little Beaver, then 16 miles up-valley to Whatcom Pass

bivy.name: Twin Rocks and Stillwell Camps, Little Beaver
bivy.notes: These two sit at the hinge between the Little Beaver and Big Beaver trails and are what make the water-taxi loop practical: get dropped at the Little Beaver landing, walk up to Whatcom Pass for Whatcom Peak and Challenger, and exit over Beaver Pass and down Big Beaver, or run it the other way. For the Northern Pickets they are through-camps on a long walk rather than climbing bases. The Ross Lake water taxi is chartered by the boat rather than per head, takes about six people, needs a reservation, and only runs during the resort's summer season — outside it, plan on walking in from Ross Dam and adding a day at each end.
bivy.water: Little Beaver Creek at both — reliable
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camps, reservable or walk-up. Both closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure, which covers Little Beaver from Ross Lake to Whatcom Pass.
bivy.capacity: Twin Rocks: two 6-person sites, party limit 6. Stillwell: four 4-person sites, party limit 4

wa_north_ridge_2.notes: Comparable in mileage to the western line. Hire a water taxi from Ross Lake Resort, near Diablo off SR-20, to the Little Beaver Creek trailhead at about 1,600 ft on Ross Lake, then follow the Little Beaver Trail roughly 16 miles up-valley, passing Perry Creek Camp at 4.6 miles and Twin Rocks Camp around mile 8, then the Big Beaver Trail junction at 10.5 miles, before the final steep switchback climb through big-fir forest up to Whatcom Pass.
hazards: A 16-mile valley walk that depends on a water-taxi booking at both ends
The same loose upper ridge as the western approach
Returning over the summit strands you on the wrong side of the peak from this trailhead
wa_north_ridge_2.baseFinding:
Whichever way you arrive at Whatcom Pass, the base test is identical: leave the maintained trail, head directly south on the faint climbers' path, and stay on the crest once the path dies. The two approaches differ only in how you get to the pass.

The one thing this side changes, and it is a logistics fact rather than a navigation one: your car is at Ross Lake, not at Hannegan. That rules out the common descent option of crossing the summit and coming down the South Spur side to Perfect Pass, unless you are prepared to loop back around the peak's east side or across the Whatcom Glacier to regain Whatcom Pass.

How you know you are at the pass and not at a camp below it: the last stretch from the Big Beaver junction is a steep switchbacking climb through big fir. The pass is where that climb stops.

wa_north_ridge_3.name: The SR-20 South Buttress pullout, then bear right into the basin beneath the North Ridge Notch
camps: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby
Cutthroat basin climbers' bivy, south side
wa_north_ridge_3.notes:
The standard approach uses the same SR-20 pullout as the South Buttress, on the north side of the highway about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass. Follow the South Buttress approach: creek crossing, brushy climbers' path into the meadow, up into the boulder field.

Eight pitches at 5.7. It sees far less traffic than the South Buttress, the peak's classic line.
hazards: A loose, runout 5.7 PG13 pitch with marginal protection simply to reach the base of the ridge
A descent that leaves the ridge at the notch and continues down a different route's rappel line
Loose rock and brush on the lower approach
A more direct West Ridge descent from higher on the North Ridge exists but is considered worse for rockfall
wa_north_ridge_3.baseFinding:
At the boulder field, bear right and north into the basin beneath the north ridge notch, rather than left toward the south buttress gully. That is the fork, and left versus right is the whole difference between two of this peak's routes.

The route's real base is the notch, and getting to it is itself a pitch: from the basin, A loose, runout 5.7 PG13 pitch gains the north ridge notch. Protection is marginal, one or two small cams and narrow-head-width pieces help, and this pitch should be treated as the technical and psychological crux of the approach, not of the ridge above it.

So the test is blunt: if the hardest, scariest thing you have done is the pitch that got you to the notch, you are on the right route. If you got to a notch by walking, you are somewhere else.

Arrival: a notch, a gap on the crest with the ridge running above it. Everything above is the North Ridge.

The northern alternative, which arrives at the same notch from the other side: from Rainy Pass, follow the Pacific Crest Trail into the Porcupine Creek drainage, then climb two or three short pitches of low fifth class to gain the North Ridge Notch from that side. That is a legitimate option for parties camping near Rainy Pass, and it adds significant approach time. Two or three easy pitches versus one hard runout one is how you tell which side you came up.

Descent does not reverse the approach pitch all the way: from the summit, reverse the North Ridge with several short rappels through the steeper fifth-class steps, then one longer rappel back into the North Ridge Notch. From the notch, descend via the standard South Buttress and West Ridge line, downclimbing to the first set of bolted chain rappel anchors and continuing down the same four-rappel West Ridge sequence, a single 60 m rope sufficient for each, before the final scramble through the scree bowl and boulder field back to the meadow and creek crossing.

wa_north_ridge_3.name: Rainy Pass and Porcupine Creek into the basin northwest of the peak

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground
bivy.notes: The closest developed campground to Washington Pass, on SR 20 along Early Winters Creek six or seven miles east of the pass, just past the turn for the Cutthroat Creek road. Because nothing here can be booked, arriving Friday evening in July or August is a gamble and the fallback is dispersed camping on a spur road. The season runs roughly May or June through September or October, entirely dependent on when the highway opens and when snow returns.
bivy.water: No drinking water at Lone Fir. Early Winters Creek runs through the campground and needs filtering; Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds, farther east, have drinking water in season.
bivy.permit: No reservations and no permit — first-come, first-served with a nightly fee. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to camp, only to park at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: 27 sites, tents and small RVs

bivy.name: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby
bivy.notes: Klipchuck sits about a quarter mile off SR 20 in fir and pine down-valley toward Mazama, low enough to be warm and dry when the passes are still wet. Early Winters Campground is further east, smaller at around a dozen tent sites, split by the highway near the Methow River, and fills quickly. Both are a longer drive to the trailhead than Lone Fir, which is the tradeoff for a better chance of finding a site on a busy weekend.
bivy.water: Drinking water spigots in season; vault toilets. Water is turned off at the end of the season while the sites stay usable.
bivy.permit: First-come, first-served, nightly fee, no reservation and no permit required.
bivy.capacity: 46 sites, the largest campground on this stretch of highway

wa_north_ridge_3.notes: From Rainy Pass, follow the PCT north for about twenty minutes and leave it before the Porcupine Creek bridge, climbing through timber into the basin northwest of the peak. Two or three short low-fifth pitches reach the North Ridge notch. Longer than the south-side basin, but on cleaner rock to the notch; parties camped near Rainy Pass or combining objectives use it.

wa_north_ridge_west_side.name: Rainy Pass, the PCT north and the ridge above Porcupine Creek
wa_north_ridge_west_side.notes: Follow the PCT north from Rainy Pass about a mile and a half, to just before the Porcupine Creek bridge, then climb the ridge northeast for about two miles to the base. The shorter way, with the cleaner gully to the base.

wa_north_ridge_west_side.name: Cutthroat Lake and Cutthroat Pass

bivy.name: Cutthroat Creek trailhead
bivy.notes: The lot sits a mile up the forest road from SR 20 and has a vault toilet but no water. It is the start for Cutthroat Wall and for the Cutthroat Lake trail toward Cutthroat Pass, and some parties sleep here or in a pullout on the road in before a pre-dawn start, though the lot itself is signed for day use and how strictly that is read varies; dispersed camping in the trees along the forest road below is the uncontroversial option. Access is entirely gated by the SR 20 winter closure, and the road has been shut for construction windows in recent seasons, so confirm before driving out.
bivy.water: None — no potable water at the trailhead. Cutthroat Creek runs below the lot and needs filtering.
bivy.permit: No camping permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day pass covers parking. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, NOT the national park, so there is no backcountry permit system here at all.
bivy.capacity: Large gravel lot, roughly 20-30 vehicles; fills on summer weekends with larch-season hikers

bivy.name: Cutthroat Lake basin, outside the quarter-mile closure
bivy.notes: The lake sits about 1.8 miles in with roughly 500 ft of gain, in the basin below Cutthroat Peak. It is a pleasant place to stage, but the quarter-mile closure exists because the shoreline was being loved to death and it is enforced rather than advisory. On this approach the lake is on the way: the trail continues past it and climbs to Cutthroat Pass, from where the crest leads south about a mile to the base of the North Ridge. From the Rainy Pass side it is off the route entirely.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet stream are dependable all season. Treat or filter.
bivy.permit: No permit needed, but a hard rule applies: NO overnight camping within a quarter mile of Cutthroat Lake. Camp outside that radius and you are legal with no paperwork.
bivy.capacity: Limited and regulated — the usable ground is set back from the water, so realistically a handful of small parties

wa_north_ridge_west_side.notes: The eastern way: on trail most of the way, to Cutthroat Lake and up to Cutthroat Pass, then south along the crest for about a mile.

wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.name: Lyman Lakes basin to the south flank
wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.notes: Access is the hard part and it has changed. The classic way in is by passenger ferry up Lake Chelan and a village shuttle to the Railroad Creek trail, then a long valley walk to the Lyman Lakes basin — but that corridor has been shut by flood and landslide damage with no near-term reopening, so plan instead on the longer route in from the Phelps Creek side over Spider Gap, which is eleven or twelve miles one way and involves glacier travel with an axe. Either way this is a camp-in-the-basin objective, not a day out. Maintained tread effectively ends at the lakes; everything above is picked by eye with no path and no cairns. It is commonly paired with the lower summit less than a mile to its south from the same camp.
wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.season: Late July to September; axe early
hazards: Unconsolidated talus and scree with no path, releasing rock easily onto anyone below
A snowfield at the foot of the flank persists through late summer in most years
The lower southwest ridge is cliffed and drops off — it is not an ascent line from the basin
Extremely remote with access itself uncertain; confirm the corridor is open before committing
Glacier travel with moats and crevasses if you come over Spider Gap
wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.baseFinding: From the Lyman Lakes basin the mountain shows as a broad talus flank above open meadow, and the base is a specific, findable thing rather than a general slope: a snowfield lying at roughly 7,000 ft at the foot of that flank, which survives into late summer most years and is visible as a white patch from the camps when you look up from the lake. Cross the meadow, round onto the south and southeast side, and climb to it. Above the snow a broad ledge leads rightward into the main gully, and the gully takes you to a notch on the crest from which the ridge runs to the top. Do not try to gain the crest lower down on the southwest side — that ridge is cliffed below the notch and the drop-offs are the reason parties are warned off it. The other thing to keep straight is which summit you are under: a lower, closer peak sits under a mile to the south, and if the ground ahead is easing toward a rounded top rather than steepening into a gully, you are on that one.

wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.name: Phelps Creek over Spider Gap

bivy.name: Lyman Lakes and Cloudy Pass
bivy.notes: This basin is the reason North Star Mountain, Cloudy Peak and Chiwawa Mountain sit in the same zone as Bonanza — it is reachable from both sides and belongs to neither. From the west it is roughly two miles and 1,700 ft above Spider Meadow over Spider Gap, crossing the permanent snowfield below the gap and dropping onto the Lyman Glacier, which puts an ice axe and traction on the packing list even in August. From the east it is a long valley walk up Railroad Creek from Holden, with intermediate camps at Hart Lake and at Rebel Camp about a mile beyond it that break the approach in two. North Star and Cloudy are scrambles off the Cloudy Pass trail from here; Chiwawa is reached by traversing the Lyman Glacier to its east ridge, which is a roped glacier objective rather than a walk.
