Cloudy Pass itself is scenic and thoroughly exposed to wind and lightning. With the Holden road closed and the Chiwawa road under its own closures, both ends of this corridor have been unreachable at times through 2026.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lakes, the Lyman Glacier outflow and creeks all through the basin
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. Camping and campfires are prohibited within 200 feet of Lyman Lake's shoreline, so pitch back from the water; carry a stove rather than planning on a fire. Reached from the west, no recreation pass is needed at the Phelps Creek trailhead, which the Forest Service lists as a no-fee site; reached from the east it needs the ferry and bus booking instead.
bivy.capacity: Established sites at Lower Lyman Lake, more scattered ground toward the upper lakes, and a small number of exposed camps at Cloudy Pass; a popular corridor, so plan on sharing

bivy.name: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds
bivy.notes: These are staging camps, not climbing camps: the point of them is that the drive up the Chiwawa River road is around twenty-three miles from the Lake Wenatchee end, the last twelve are rough gravel and dirt genuinely unsuited to low clearance vehicles, and doing that at the end of a long drive from the west side is how parties end up starting the walk in tired and late. Phelps Creek Campground sits near the confluence of Phelps Creek and the Chiwawa a short distance below the Phelps Creek trailhead, and the Trinity trailhead at about 2,800 ft — the start of the Buck Creek trail toward Buck Creek Pass and Fortress Mountain — is a mile or so away, so one night here stages either objective. The road is the fragile part of this whole side of the zone. Storm damage has closed it above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year order, and a 2026 fire closure covered the Chiwawa River road and the Phelps Creek spur on top of that, so check whether you can drive to the trailhead at all before planning around it. When the road is shut above Atkinson Flat the lower campgrounds are still a reasonable base but the trailhead becomes a long walk or ride further on.
bivy.water: The Chiwawa River is right there but these are primitive campgrounds — treat water and expect no potable supply or trash service
bivy.permit: Small nightly fee at the developed sites, first come first served with no reservations, so arrive early on a summer Friday. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers trailhead parking the next morning, and the free self-issue wilderness permit is picked up at the trailhead itself. Fire restrictions bite here in late summer and often ban all open flame including in the fire rings.
bivy.capacity: Phelps Creek Campground has roughly seven tent sites plus half a dozen equestrian sites; Atkinson Flat, Schaefer Creek, Rock Creek and the other small forest campgrounds strung along the road below it each hold a handful more

bivy.name: Spider Meadow and Phelps Basin
bivy.notes: About five and a half miles and 1,250 ft from the Phelps Creek trailhead at roughly 3,500 ft, this is the standard first night for almost everything on the Chiwawa side. It stages the Spider Gap crossing to Lyman Lakes and so serves North Star, Cloudy and Chiwawa; Phelps Basin half a mile above the head of the meadow is the base for Dumbell Mountain, whose route climbs northwest out of the upper basin, steepens around 6,100 ft and works up talus and a weakness to the notch west of the summit. Higher bivouac ground exists at Larch Knob, about 1,600 ft above the meadow on the switchbacks toward Spider Gap, with a few platforms partly sheltered from the wind pouring through the gap. The same trailhead also serves the Carne Mountain trail, whose basin at about 6,100 ft holds several camps with good water and is the link to the saddle above Ice Lakes and across to Leroy — those saddle camps have no water other than snowmelt. Road access is the weak point here: the Chiwawa River road is long, the final twelve miles are rough gravel unfriendly to low clearance, and the last two miles of the Phelps Creek spur are rougher still.
bivy.water: Reliable — Phelps Creek runs the length of the meadow and the basin above holds snowmelt streams well into the season
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead, which is entered about two and a half miles up. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers parking at Phelps Creek. Camp on established bare sites rather than in the meadow itself, and expect fire restrictions from midsummer onward on top of the usual high-elevation limits.
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites through a mile-long meadow, plus quieter ground in Phelps Basin above it — the meadow absorbs a lot of parties but is genuinely busy on summer weekends

wa_north_star_mountain_east_route.notes: The Phelps Creek trail to Spider Meadow, over Spider Gap and down to Lyman Lakes, then the same basin to the south flank. No boat needed.

wa_phantom_peak_south_route.name: Hannegan Pass, Whatcom Pass and Perfect Pass to a camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine
camps: Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine high camp
Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.notes: The northern option, favoured by several recent parties. From the Hannegan Trailhead at 3,100 ft, the Hannegan Pass Trail leads over the pass to the Chilliwack River Trail, which includes a cable-car crossing, then up the Brush Creek Trail to Whatcom Pass. From there the route leaves trail and goes off-trail via the Whatcom Glacier and Perfect Pass to a base camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine. Expect 2-3 days of travel each way.
hazards: A bergschrund on the summit snow finger, crossed via a slabby rock step
Somewhat rotten rock on the summit tower and gully section, with natural anchors only
Rockfall off the buttress walls onto the snow finger
A 1,000 ft descending traverse that has to be regained on the return
The Chilliwack cable-car crossing and the Whatcom Glacier traverse on the way in
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.baseFinding:
The start of the climbing is a saddle inside the buttress, at about 6,100 ft, and you get there by losing height first. From the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine camp, the way to Phantom is a roughly 1,000 ft descending traverse east across snow and talus to the base of Phantom's broad southwest buttress, then up a snowfield to a saddle around 6,100 ft within the buttress. That saddle is effectively the start of the technical climbing.

So the test in cloud is the shape of the ground, not the view: you go down and east for a thousand feet, then up a snowfield, and you stop when the snowfield delivers you into a gap in a rock rib rather than onto open mountainside. A saddle inside a buttress has rock rising on both sides of you; open snow does not.

What going too far looks like: continuing the descending traverse east past the buttress toe drops you toward Luna Cirque and the ground the peak's other route uses, which is a different climb from a different camp.

Confirm on the climb: above the saddle the route takes a pocket glacier and snowfield to a bergschrund crossed by a slabby rock step, then a snow finger, then broken class 2-3 rock to a false summit and a short exposed step to the true summit. One bergschrund, one snow finger, one false summit. If you have crossed two schrunds you are not on this line.

wa_phantom_peak_south_route.name: Big Beaver Trail to Luna Camp, then the Luna Creek bushwhack up Phantom's south side

bivy.name: Luna Cirque floor
bivy.notes: The floor of the great bowl beneath Luna Peak, walled on three sides, and the low point of the traverse that enters by Access Creek and Luna Pass and leaves over Challenger Gap onto Wiley Ridge. It sits directly under the eastern side of the crest that carries Spectre Peak, and parties coming off Challenger sometimes drop southeast into it rather than reversing the glacier. As a bed it is a long way below Luna Col, which remains the right camp for climbing Luna Peak itself; the value of the cirque is that it links the Access Creek and Wiley Ridge sides without going back over the top. Getting in and out is trackless in both directions and the brush low in Access Creek, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
bivy.water: Meltwater running off the cirque walls, and a shallow seasonal lake on the floor that becomes warm sand as the summer dries it out. Early season is wet and late season is a search.
bivy.permit: Luna cross-country zone, walk-up only — it cannot be reserved, and a party that has already driven, boated and walked in can still be turned away if the night's slots are taken. Carry a fallback itinerary. Camp on sand, rock or snow, 100 ft from water, no fires.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on sand, gravel and slab; party limit 6

bivy.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
bivy.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
bivy.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. Closed after the Luna Fire; check the park's fire-closure list for current status before building a trip around it.
bivy.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

wa_phantom_peak_south_route.notes: From Ross Lake Resort, take the water taxi across Ross Lake, roughly $35 and saving about 6 miles, to the Big Beaver trailhead. From there it is about 9 to 10 miles of maintained, mostly flat, forested trail up the Big Beaver Creek drainage through old-growth cedar and past beaver ponds to Luna Camp, an established backcountry site where a wilderness permit is required. From Luna Camp the trail effectively ends. Climbers leave the tread and push cross-country up the Luna Creek drainage toward Phantom's south side, gaining roughly 4,000 ft over a few miles through some of the worst brush in the Cascades. Modern parties report huckleberry, devil's club, vine maple and slide alder dense enough that half a mile an hour is a good pace, with heavy insect pressure.
hazards: Some of the worst brush in the Cascades, at roughly half a mile an hour, with devil's club and slide alder
Fords of Luna Creek that get harder the lower you are
High risk of falling into a hole hidden by brush, and of separating from a partner
Heavy mosquito and fly pressure in summer
No trail, no cairns and real disorientation on the way back down
wa_phantom_peak_south_route.baseFinding:
In this drainage the navigation rule is about height, not direction, and it is the one thing that makes the day work. The creek must be forded in places, and fords get harder the lower and farther downstream you are. Gain elevation out of the valley bottom as early as you can rather than fighting the brush along the creek. If you are still beside running water after a couple of hours, you are on the losing line.

Arrival, which is unambiguous even with no visibility: above the brush line the drainage opens into subalpine meadow and talus below Phantom's south aspect. The brush stopping is the signal. Nothing else in this valley changes character that completely.

From there the base test is the same one the northern approach uses: find the snowfield that leads up into a saddle at about 6,100 ft within the southwest buttress. That gap is where the technical climbing starts.

A real risk peculiar to this approach, recorded because it has happened: in brush this thick, parties have become separated from each other. Agree a regrouping rule before entering it, not during.

wa_pinnacle_mountain_entiat_scramble.name: North Fork Entiat over Saska Pass and Snow Brushy Creek
camps: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
Fox Camp, North Fork Entiat trail
wa_pinnacle_mountain_entiat_scramble.notes: A long, largely off-trail approach through burned country for a summit that is barely a scramble. From the North Fork Entiat road end the tread runs up-valley past the Fern Lake spur to the Pyramid Mountain junction, which is the usual last camp with water; fill there, because the drainages between it and the pass are seasonal and often dry. Gain Saska Pass by climbing the drainage directly rather than following the sidehill traverse, which is slower and more tiring across scree. From the pass you lose about 1,500 ft into the Snow Brushy burn, where the tread is gone entirely and ash-covered slopes and fallen snags erase any line, then regain nineteen hundred feet or so out of the creek — that descent and reclimb are what make the day long, not the peak. A separate approach exists up the Entiat River trail and the sheep driveway from the south, also through heavy fire blowdown.
hazards: Loose scree on the headwall below the pass, and worse for anyone climbing beneath you
Burn-zone deadfall and standing snags with no surviving tread, so a cairn line cannot be relied on
Scarce water above the last creek crossings
A steep, loose couloir on the final approach to the crest saddle
Long remote off-trail travel with little or no cell coverage
wa_pinnacle_mountain_entiat_scramble.baseFinding: The base is the saddle on the Chelan Mountains crest immediately south of the peak, reached by a steep couloir of loose rock, and the thing to know before you get there is that the true summit is hidden from it. Standing on the saddle you see a rocky bump close by to the south — a point just over 7,760 ft — and a broad, easy-angled slope running north. The bump is not the mountain and is only a short side trip for the view; the slope is your line. Turn north and climb the south-facing talus, keeping to the west side of the crest where the scrambling stays easiest, and the top only reveals itself in the last few hundred feet. The rock underfoot changes noticeably as you go: poor scree low down where the burn ends, then firmer blocks on the crest that make a hands-on class 3 finish rather than a walk. If the ground ahead drops away toward the Emerald Peak basin instead of rising, you have crossed the crest too far east.

wa_pinnacle_mountain_entiat_scramble.name: Entiat River trail and Snow Brushy Creek to Borealis Pass

bivy.name: Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
bivy.notes: This is the road head for the whole eastern side of the Chelan Mountains crest and the standard place to sleep the night before a long walk in. The drive is the thing people underestimate — it is roughly 38 miles of valley road from the Columbia, most of it paved, and getting here from the west side of the state is the better part of four hours. Cottonwood sits at the end, just short of where the Entiat River trail begins. Camp here and you can be walking at first light with the entire day for the eleven miles to Entiat Meadows or the eight to Fox Camp. Recognise what has happened to this valley: successive fires have run through it and the lower trail corridor is open, burned, dusty and hot, with young growth and standing snags rather than shade. That makes the river the only dependable water for the first several miles and it makes an early start a safety measure rather than a preference. A landslide near the river trailhead currently blocks the normal approach; a temporary high-clearance route has been pushed through the slide, trailers are turned back, and the campground short of it is being used as the turnaround. Confirm before committing to the drive, because there is nothing at the end of this road.
bivy.water: The Entiat River runs beside every one of these campgrounds and is the most reliable water anywhere in the zone. Treat it. Some of the smaller road campgrounds have a hand pump but several have none at all and nothing should be assumed potable.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent recreation pass for the trailhead lot. No permit to camp. Forest-wide Stage 2 fire restrictions have prohibited campfires on all national forest land since early July 2026, including in established rings, and the county has a total outdoor burn ban. All of these campgrounds are inside the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026, and Cottonwood is written off for the remainder of the season.
bivy.capacity: Cottonwood has around two dozen sites; the string of small campgrounds down-valley adds a similar number again

wa_pinnacle_mountain_entiat_scramble.notes: From the Entiat River trailhead just past Cottonwood Campground, walk the Entiat River trail about six and a half miles to the Snow Brushy Creek trail, then follow it up-valley about five miles; the creek crossing there is a reliable place for water. A faint, sometimes hard-to-follow trail branches north and climbs to Borealis Pass in about a mile, below the easy south slopes of the peak. Much of the valley is burned, so expect downed timber.

wa_point_success_south_side.name: Longmire, the Wonderland Trail and Indian Henry's Hunting Ground
camps: Point 6631 (base camp north of Pyramid Peak)
Dug platform on the lower-mid cleaver
wa_point_success_south_side.notes:
Longmire (2,762 ft) is the start, on the Wonderland Trail toward Indian Henry's Hunting Ground. About 3 miles out the trail drops steeply to cross Kautz Creek — a braided glacial outwash channel whose crossing is periodically wrecked by debris flows off the Kautz Glacier. Ask at the Longmire wilderness desk before you leave, because a failed crossing means a long reroute rather than a wet foot.

Beyond Kautz Creek the trail switchbacks through old growth, fords Fisher's Hornpipe Creek and passes Devil's Dream camp (about 5 miles, reliable water) before opening into the meadows of Indian Henry's Hunting Ground at roughly 6.3–7 miles and 5,300 ft, marked by the 1915 patrol cabin.

At Indian Henry's leave the Wonderland for the Mirror Lakes spur — plank walkways over marshy meadow, then the end of maintained tread. The path fades into a boot track at about 5,600 ft in the basin between Copper Peak and Pyramid Peak. From there it is cross-country on the southwest and west slopes of Pyramid Peak, between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft, to Point 6631 just north of the peak. Snowmelt water is often available here into early summer, and the rock-slab camp below Pyramid Peak at about 6,300 ft is a common first night.

This is one of only two routes on Rainier that avoids significant glacier travel, which is its whole appeal; the cost is that it is long, loose and unfrequented, with about 12–13 miles and roughly 11,500 ft of gain to Point Success. Most parties take two days, often with a second camp dug into the cleaver crest around 10,700 ft.
wa_point_success_south_side.season: May through September; the lower cleaver is best while it still holds snow, since it becomes loose scree once bare
hazards: Kautz Creek crossing washed out by glacial debris flows
Rockfall from parties above on the loose lower cleaver
Sustained loose choss and scree with no established line
Knife-edge crest section, exposed once melted out
Very long approach with no bail-out — a retreat is the full walk back to Longmire
wa_point_success_south_side.baseFinding:
The climbing starts at the col north of Pyramid Peak, at about 6,400 ft, and getting into that col is where people go wrong.

From Point 6631 you drop north-northeast a short way to a saddle. It is a scree and loose-boulder col, and it is ugly — that is the correct place. There is an easier descent line into it than the obvious one, and trip reports record missing it and taking the worst ground; look for the line before you commit, and note it for the way back.

From the col the cleaver rises continuously in front of you and does not stop. There is no single track and no cairned line: the lower cleaver is loose choss and scree with short bursts of class 3 scrambling, and the route-finding is yours.

The test that you are on the cleaver and not off it is what is on either side. You should be on a broad rubbly crest with the South Tahoma Glacier falling away to your north (climber's left) and the Pyramid and Success glaciers to your south (climber's right). If a glacier is underfoot you have left the cleaver — this route is defined by not being on one.

An easy, clean start is the wrong sign. If the ground out of the col is pleasant walking on solid rock, you are probably contouring around the peak rather than gaining the cleaver. Travel only improves higher, above about 7,000 ft, where the rock firms up and, early in the season, continuous snow and goat tracks take over.

Higher still the crest includes a knife-edge section that needs genuine scrambling once the snow melts off it, and the route then angles climber's right up snow gullies onto the Kautz Cleaver at roughly 12,200–12,600 ft.

wa_point_success_south_side.name: Kautz Creek Trail to Indian Henry's

bivy.name: Point 6631 (base camp north of Pyramid Peak)
Cleaver crest col
bivy.notes: Planned high camp and the best ground on the route: a broad saddle on the cleaver crest that is generally out of the rockfall lines, which very little else on this cleaver can claim. No water. Above it the crest includes a knife-edge that has to be scrambled once the snow melts off it, so leaving from here in the dark is easier early season when it is still snow-covered. Some parties instead stop around 10,200 ft, which is also comfortable but leaves more of the crest for summit day.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.permit: climbing permit required above 10,000 ft in addition to the camping permit
bivy.capacity: one to two tents; platforms stomped or dug into snow

bivy.name: Dug platform on the lower-mid cleaver
bivy.notes: Planned alternative for parties who run out of daylight low on the cleaver. Reports describe digging in here specifically because the spot felt protected from the rockfall lines running down either side — the lower cleaver is loose choss with real exposure to anything a party above knocks down, so on this route the shelter of the platform is the point rather than the view.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.capacity: one tent on a dug platform

wa_point_success_south_side.notes: From the Kautz Creek trailhead on the Longmire-Paradise road, follow Kautz Creek about a mile to a log-bridge crossing, then climb steeply through old growth and along the flank of Mount Ararat into the meadows of Indian Henry's Hunting Ground, about 5.75 miles and 3,000 ft. Shorter than the Longmire route but uphill nearly the whole way; from Indian Henry's the climb continues as from Longmire. The Kautz Creek crossing is periodically damaged by debris flows, so ask about its status before you go.

wa_prusik_peak_der_sportsman.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, fifty feet left of the standard south-face line
camps: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
wa_prusik_peak_der_sportsman.notes:
The Core Enchantments approach: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail 2.5 miles to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. From the boulder field at the lake's south end, Aasgard Pass — 1.25 miles gaining about 2,000 ft of steep loose scree and dirt, the physical crux of the approach, with a hidden creek and moat under lingering snow into early July.

From the pass at 7,841 ft, continue cross-country through the upper Core past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Prusik Pass and Gnome Tarn. Parties commonly bivy at the tarn, about twenty minutes from the base. There is no maintained trail for the last stretch.

The Snow Lakes trail is the longer alternative when Aasgard or the trailhead is closed: past Nada and Snow Lakes to Lake Viviane, then up and right toward Temple Lake and up climbers' paths through boulders to the base of the south face.
wa_prusik_peak_der_sportsman.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the route is a hard rock climb and wants dry, warm granite
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose steep scree with a hidden creek and moat under early-season snow, and a fatal history
A 5.11+ crux on the first pitch, so retreat decisions come early
A loose block in the finishing chimney
Mixed rappel anchors on the north side — one bolted station near the top, gear and slung naturals below
Unmarked cross-country approach over slabs and talus
Core Zone camping needs a permit
wa_prusik_peak_der_sportsman.baseFinding:
Fifty feet left of the standard South Face route. That is the published position and it is a pace count, not a description — find the classic line at the middle of the base of the face, then walk left about fifty feet.

The first pitch is the check, and it is a brutal one. This route's opening pitch is 5.11+. The line fifty feet to your right opens at 5.6 or 5.7 in a chimney. There is no ambiguity between those two pieces of climbing: if you are cruising your first pitch, you are on the wrong route, and if you are fighting a tipsy crux entering a stembox, you are on this one.

What the first pitch looks like from the ground, so you can commit before you leave the deck: an easy, unappealing left-slanting crack system leading up to a stance below an obvious stembox. The unremarkable start is deceptive and is exactly why the fifty-foot offset matters — the interesting rock is not visible from the base.

Belay confirmation: pitch one ends at a two-bolt anchor after liebacking and stemming up the right of twin cracks. Most of this face is natural gear; arriving at bolts is strong evidence you are on this line rather than on a neighbour.

And the named pitch higher up: an undercling flake pitch that parties call the money pitch, then a committing corner where the route switches cracks. If you never leave one crack for another, you have wandered onto adjoining ground.

Descent note that affects the approach decision: this one rappels the north side in five, then needs one more rappel from the balanced-rock landmark at the base of the West Ridge to get back down to your packs.

wa_prusik_peak_der_sportsman.name: Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments

bivy.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
bivy.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.
bivy.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
bivy.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

bivy.name: Gnome Tarn
bivy.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. Getting there means leaving the main basin route and scrambling up from around Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass on a faint, easily lost path over granite. It is exposed and high, so a night here can be considerably colder and windier than the lakes below. The camping is on rock, which is both the right surface to use and the reason a level spot takes some hunting.
bivy.water: The tarn itself, though it is small and can drop low or silty late in a dry season; the lakes below are the fallback
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded

wa_prusik_peak_der_sportsman.notes: The longer, more gradual way in from Icicle Creek Road: the Snow Lakes trail climbs past Nada and Snow lakes to Lake Vivianne, about ten miles with well over 5,000 ft of gain, looking straight at Prusik's south face. From Vivianne continue past the upper lakes to the base of the south face. It avoids the loose grind of Aasgard Pass at the cost of roughly two more miles and a thousand more feet.

wa_prusik_peak_sail_away.name: Colchuck Lake and Aasgard Pass
wa_prusik_peak_sail_away.notes: The usual way in. From the Stuart Lake trailhead walk the Colchuck Lake trail to Colchuck Lake, then climb the loose boulders and scree of Aasgard Pass into the Core Enchantments. Walk down through the basin past Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass and scramble up to the base of the south face; Aasgard is steep and can hold snow into early summer.

wa_prusik_peak_sail_away.name: Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments
wa_prusik_peak_sail_away.notes: The longer, more gradual way in from Icicle Creek Road: the Snow Lakes trail climbs past Nada and Snow lakes to Lake Vivianne, about ten miles with well over 5,000 ft of gain, looking straight at Prusik's south face. From Vivianne continue past the upper lakes to the base of the south face. It avoids the loose grind of Aasgard Pass at the cost of roughly two more miles and a thousand more feet.

wa_prusik_peak_solid_gold.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core to the left flank of the south face
wa_prusik_peak_solid_gold.notes:
As for the rest of the face: Stuart Lake trailhead at about 3,400 ft, Stuart Lake Trail two and a half miles to the signed Colchuck Lake Trail junction, left and across Mountaineer Creek — a rock-hop or log crossing, and the last easy water for a while — then 1.6 miles of switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft.

Boulder-hop the east shore to the boulder field at the south end, then Aasgard Pass: 2,000 ft in 1.25 miles of steep loose dirt and scree, cairned when snow-free. In early season, and often into July, snow bridges a hidden creek and moat on the left side of the gully; people have been badly hurt and killed there postholing or glissading into it.

From the pass at 7,841 ft, drop into the upper Core past Isolation and Tranquil Lake and continue cross-country a mile or so north over slabs and heather benches toward Prusik Pass and Gnome Tarn. The start is fifteen to twenty minutes from a Gnome Tarn camp.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose steep scree, and a hidden creek and moat under snow into early July with a fatal history
Avalanche on the pass in shoulder season
Loose rock past the chimney at mid-height
Natural, non-bolted rappel anchors on the north side shared with several routes; inspect and back up old tat
Cross-country navigation over slabs with no tread for the last mile
Core Zone camping requires a permit that most parties do not have
wa_prusik_peak_solid_gold.baseFinding:
Go to the outside corner and start just right of it. The left flank of the south face ends in an outside corner — the arête where the south face turns the corner onto the west side — and this route begins just to the right of it, on a right-leaning crack system leading to a stembox.

That corner is the anchor for the whole left end of the face, and the three routes here are placed off it:
  - Left of the corner, on the west face proper: a line with a large roof at its base, sometimes called the Elephant Ear.
  - Just right of the corner: this route.
  - About 100 ft further right: another four-pitch line to the West Ridge.
So if you are under a roof, you have gone one route too far left; if you have walked a hundred feet right of the corner, one too far right.

The honest warning about where this route ends, because it is the best single check that you are on the left flank at all: this line and its immediate neighbours top out on the west ridge, not on the summit. Only the classic line at the middle of the face reaches the true summit. If you have come for the summit and started here, you have an extra scramble at the top and you started on the wrong route.

Sequence check: right-leaning cracks to a stembox, then a roof and hand-crack pitch, then slabby and wide ground past a chimney with loose rock, then a final splitter corner. Five pitches, about 450 ft. A seven-pitch line with two big V-features low down is Beckey-Davis, well to your right.

wa_prusik_peak_solid_gold.name: Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments
wa_prusik_peak_solid_gold.notes: The longer, more gradual way in from Icicle Creek Road: the Snow Lakes trail climbs past Nada and Snow lakes to Lake Vivianne, about ten miles with well over 5,000 ft of gain, looking straight at Prusik's south face. From Vivianne continue past the upper lakes to the base of the south face. It avoids the loose grind of Aasgard Pass at the cost of roughly two more miles and a thousand more feet.

wa_prusik_peak_south_face_burgner_stanle.name: Aasgard Pass to Gnome Tarn
camps: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
wa_prusik_peak_south_face_burgner_stanle.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead, Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A across Mountaineer Creek and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft — about four miles and 2,000-2,200 ft.

From the boulder field at the lake's south end, climb Aasgard Pass: roughly 2,000 ft in a little over a mile of loose scree and dirt, and the crux of the day. Stay climber's left of the cliff bands; the terrain to climber's right, toward the waterfalls on Colchuck Peak's flank, cliffs out and has killed people. Snow lingering into early July hides a creek running beneath the talus.

From the pass at 7,841 ft travel cross-country through the Core, dropping from Talisman Lake toward Rune Lake, then ascending to the gentle ridge east of Rune's upper basin to reach Gnome Tarn. Gnome Tarn is the standard camp for this face and sits close under it.

A longer approach on the Snow Lakes Trail exists and is the fallback when Aasgard or the Stuart Lake trailhead is closed; some parties deliberately go in over Aasgard and out via Snow Lakes, about 21 miles, to spare their knees a second descent of the pass.

The last stretch to the wall is unmarked cross-country over slabs and talus.
wa_prusik_peak_south_face_burgner_stanle.season: Jul-Sep; earlier the pass is a snow climb and the Core travel is on snow
hazards: Aasgard Pass: cliffed-out terrain to climber's right, loose rock, fatalities on record
Hidden creek beneath the talus on the pass under early-season snow
Avalanche exposure on the pass in shoulder season
Unmarked cross-country slab and talus travel from Gnome Tarn to the base
Rappel descent on the north side is shared by several south-face routes and backs up when busy
wa_prusik_peak_south_face_burgner_stanle.baseFinding:
From Gnome Tarn, traverse northeast to the south face. The base of the Stanley-Burgner sits at about 7,350 ft.

The defining feature is a pair of deep chimneys on the face. The route starts to the left of those two chimneys, in a crack system on steep white granite — the base is immediately beside a left-slanting chimney. Two deep chimneys with the route just left of them is the pattern to hold in your head; if you have walked past the chimneys and are still looking, you are right of the start.

The second confirmation is vegetation. The first pitch is 5.8 up the crack system and finishes at a belay just below some shrubby pines. From the talus, a photograph-worthy way to say it is that the route starts at the trees on the left and goes up. Pitch 2 then works up through those pines at 5.7. So: white granite, left of the two deep chimneys, aiming for a small stand of scrubby pines about a pitch up.

This face carries several routes that share the same base area and the same north-side rappel descent, so being one crack system over is easy and consequential. If your first pitch is harder than 5.8 or has no pines above it, you are on a neighbour.

Note that the West Ridge starts somewhere else entirely — around at Prusik Pass on the far side of the peak — so the two are not confusable at the base, only on the map.

wa_prusik_peak_south_face_burgner_stanle.name: Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments

From Vivianne continue past the upper lakes to Gnome Tarn and the base of the south face. It avoids the loose grind of Aasgard Pass at the cost of roughly two more miles and a thousand more feet.

wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge.name: Aasgard Pass to the Core, dry conditions
wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead, left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail at the signed junction, and about four miles and 2,200 ft to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. Filter here; there is nothing simple above until the Core.

Skirt the east and south shore to the boulder field at the lake's south end and start up Aasgard Pass: roughly 2,000-2,200 ft in under a mile, on what regulars fairly describe as a jenga pile. Follow the outlet drainage and stay climber's left (east) of the first band of cliffs. Veering climber's right toward the waterfall complex on Colchuck Peak's flank is the classic and repeatedly fatal error here — people have died on that side and it cliffs out easily. Near the top the path passes in front of a small waterfall and climbs steeply beside a much larger one; missing the turn there puts you on vertical rock.

Cairns are everywhere on Aasgard and they mark more than one line. Trust the worn tread over the cairn.

Top out around 7,800-7,841 ft, then lose 600-700 ft east through the Core's tarns and slabs, then climb north to Prusik Pass. In the Core there are a couple of places where it is easy to add distance without adding progress, but the navigation is not hard in clear weather.

Most parties do this car-to-car, and a fit team should expect a 20-21 hour day; the Enchantments overnight permit lottery is competitive enough that camping is not a plan you can rely on.
wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge.season: late Jul-Sep, once Aasgard Pass is bare talus
hazards: Aasgard Pass: veering climber's right into the cliffed waterfall terrain has killed people
Loose talus and rockfall the full length of Aasgard, worse in the afternoon heat
Misleading and multiplying cairns on the pass and in the Core
No water between Colchuck Lake and the Core tarns
Very long day; parties routinely finish the descent of Aasgard in the dark
Descent from Prusik is rappels, not a walk-off — do not arrive without the gear
wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge.baseFinding:
From the highest point of Prusik Pass, do not go over the first bump in front of you — go around it. Parties who climb straight over it lose time and, more importantly, lose the path.

Past the bump the climbing line drops out of sight. Keep scrambling easy blocky class 2 ground and it reappears. The landmark you are heading for first is a huge balanced, dish-shaped rock — that is the right place to stash packs and put on shoes, and it is not yet the start of the climbing.

One more knob of scrambling past that brings you to the actual base: an overhanging rock at the foot of the route, which is the natural sheltered spot to leave big bags.

The first pitch is the final confirmation and it is unmistakable even in cloud: a long pitch up a wide crack, about 5.6, in a conspicuously white section of rock. The white band is the marker — the surrounding stone is not that colour. A distinct crack of roughly 5.6 leading up through blocky ground to the ridge is what you want; if you are staring at clean, hard, featureless granite you are on one of the south-face routes instead.

Belay at a slingable block; the 5.7 slab crux with an old piton comes above that.

wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge.name: Aasgard Pass with snow, early season
wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge.notes:
Same line, different problem. With snow on it, Aasgard is an axe-and-sometimes-crampons proposition rather than a talus grind, and it is avalanche terrain in shoulder season.

Early-season snow softens through the day into deep, punchy stuff that hides ice underneath, and the hidden creek running beneath the talus is a real hazard where snow bridges it. The consolidated dawn snow that makes the ascent quick is also the surface that makes an uncontrolled slide easy.

On the plus side the route-finding is simpler with the talus buried, and the Core beyond the pass travels fast on snow.

On the north side of Prusik itself, snow adds both hazard and time to the rappel descent — budget for it.
wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge.season: May-early Jul, while the pass holds continuous snow
hazards: Avalanche terrain on Aasgard Pass in shoulder season
Hidden creek running beneath the talus under snow bridges
Punchy afternoon snow concealing ice
Uncontrolled slide on the pass, ascending or descending
Snow on Prusik's north side lengthens and complicates the rappel descent
wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge.baseFinding:
The Prusik Pass landmarks survive the snow, because they are large rock features: go around the first bump rather than over it, find the huge balanced dish-shaped rock to gear up at, then one more knob to the overhanging rock at the base.

The first pitch's white rock band and wide 5.6 crack still identify the start. What changes early season is the ground below the base — snow can cover the scrambling approach entirely, so the sequence of bump, dish rock, knob, overhang is what you navigate by rather than any boot path.

wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge.name: Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments to Prusik Pass

bivy.name: Inspiration and Perfection Lakes
bivy.notes: The most used camping ground in the basin, on the benches and the bluff between the two lakes, and the closest general camp to the peak — the signed path toward Prusik Pass leaves the western shore of Perfection Lake. Open granite and heather, thoroughly worn in, and shared with mountain goats that come in for salt. The exposed benches right at Isolation and Tranquil Lakes are above treeline and windy by comparison.
bivy.water: The lakes.
bivy.permit: An Enchantment Permit Area overnight permit is required from 15 May to 31 October, and Prusik's camps lie in the Core Enchantment Zone, which is allocated by lottery. Maximum group size is eight. Camp only on ground already worn bare — do not clear vegetation, move rocks or build walls. Fires are prohibited anywhere above 5,000 ft or within half a mile of a lake, which rules them out at every camp in this basin; solid-fuel and wood-burning stoves are also prohibited above 5,000 ft, but liquid and canister gas stoves are allowed. Dogs are not permitted anywhere in the Enchantment Permit Area, and no stock is allowed in the Core Zone. Maximum stay is fourteen consecutive days. Two traps worth knowing: a Snow Zone permit lets you climb here for the day but you must camp at or below Upper Snow Lake, and a Colchuck Zone permit does not allow camping above the 6,500 ft contour below Aasgard Pass. A Core Zone permit, by contrast, allows camping in any of the five zones on the way in or out.
bivy.capacity: No published tent count for any site in the basin. The permit is the real constraint: the Core Zone quota counts people entering per day rather than groups, and the whole of a permitted group must camp together at one site.

wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge.notes: From the Snow Lakes Trailhead, climb past Snow Lakes and Lake Viviane to the Gnome Tarn and Prusik Pass area below the peak. More gain than Aasgard Pass but no steep snow or talus headwall.

wa_ptarmigan_peak_pasayten_scramble.name: Shellrock Pass camp and the south side
camps: Doris Lake and Freds Lake basins
Shellrock Pass, Shellrock Basin and the Eureka Creek meadows
wa_ptarmigan_peak_pasayten_scramble.notes: Ptarmigan is one of the most isolated summits in this wilderness, sitting less than a mile from the most remote point in it, and the whole difficulty is getting underneath it. From the Slate Pass road end the standard line drops through larch and avalanche-lily meadows to the Middle Fork Pasayten trail, runs down-valley through a stretch with a long-standing reputation for blowdown, then climbs by Fred's Lake and over the pass at the head of Eureka Creek to Shellrock Pass. A broad bench just southwest of the pass is the standard high camp for this peak and its neighbours. From the south the mountain is a rounded, tundra-covered massif and the walking is genuinely easy; its north side is another matter entirely.
hazards: Sheer, seldom-seen north face immediately off the summit
Loose talus and a steep waterfall drainage on off-route descent lines
Short exposed scrambling on the connecting ridge to the south
Brush-choked valley approaches and heavy blowdown
Faint or obscured tread near the Eureka Creek turn
Extreme remoteness with no fast rescue
wa_ptarmigan_peak_pasayten_scramble.baseFinding: There are two ways onto this peak and each has its own recognisable base. From the south, the base is the Ptarmigan-Dot saddle at about 7,800 ft, a genuine meadow holding a small tarn, unmistakable ground after miles of talus and the last water on the day. From that saddle the south slopes rise as open alpine tundra, scree and easy talus and there is nothing to find; you simply walk up. Getting to the saddle from the Shellrock Pass camp means gaining the crest north of camp and travelling over or around the shoulder of Mount Lago, with a short exposed step or two on the connecting ridge near the two rock points south of Dot. From the north and west the base is a saddle at about 7,250 ft overlooking Ptarmigan Lake, and the marker there is better still: a well-trodden boot path leaves the maintained trail at the Tatoosh Buttes junction around 6,950 ft and heads due south across the hillside and over a low rise on Tamarack Ridge, and following it to the saddle puts you at the foot of the north ridge, which is broad and easy. Whichever side you come from, the same rule identifies the route: the ground under you should stay rounded, open and tundra-covered. Ptarmigan's north face is sheer and seldom seen, so any point where the slope stops falling away gently and starts breaking off is the signal that you have wandered onto the wrong aspect and should move back south.

wa_ptarmigan_peak_pasayten_scramble.name: Eightmile Creek, Eightmile Pass and the Hidden Lakes

approachLogistics.trailhead: Billy Goat Trailhead (end of Eightmile Creek Road)

wa_ptarmigan_peak_pasayten_scramble.notes: The shortest line on the map, but it starts below 3,500 ft instead of high on the Slate Pass road. From the trailhead at the end of Eightmile Creek Road, cross Eightmile Pass and follow the trail past the Hidden Lakes to Ptarmigan Creek, northeast of the peak, then go a further two or three miles to the base. Expect a long day of trail before any climbing.

wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.name: Andrews Creek to Remmel Lake
wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.notes: The shortest line to the peak. Walk the Andrews Creek trail up the valley past the Meadow Lake and Peepsight junctions, then continue to Remmel Lake at the foot of the northwest ridge. The lower valley is burned and can hold a lot of blowdown.

wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.name: Chewuch River trail to Remmel Lake

bivy.name: The lower Chewuch River camps out of Thirtymile
bivy.notes: These exist to break the walk rather than to serve a summit, and on an approach this long that is worth more than it sounds. The Chewuch trail is gentle enough that a party can cover a lot of it quickly, but thirteen miles to the Four Point junction with a full pack is a poor first day after the drive from the west side, and the river ford above is better met in the morning with fresh legs and lower water. Stopping around the falls at six or seven miles makes the second day short and puts you at Four Point Lake by early afternoon with the summit still available. It is also the piece of this zone most likely to be open. When the fires shut Iron Gate, Andrews Creek and the Harts Pass road, this corridor stayed passable and volunteers kept clearing it, which is why it is written up separately rather than folded into the Four Point entry. Expect burned forest for long stretches, little shade, and a trail whose blowdown situation changes with every windstorm. Ask the ranger district before building a schedule on it.
bivy.water: Good, and unusually so for this wilderness. The Chewuch runs beside the trail for the whole of the lower valley and every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. Water only becomes a problem once you leave the river for the climb to Four Point Lake.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park at Thirtymile. Weed-free feed for stock; animals may not be tied to trees overnight or highlined close to them. Fires in existing rings outside a burn ban, and this is dry east-side country where bans are the norm from midsummer.
bivy.capacity: Dispersed sites scattered along the first several miles of the valley, including good ground near Chewuch Falls. Most take one or two tents and they are seldom occupied — this is a corridor rather than a destination.

wa_remmel_mountain_nw_ridge.notes: A longer but gentler and generally better-kept trail. From the Thirtymile trailhead at the end of the Chewuch road, follow the Chewuch River trail north toward Four Point Lake and on to Remmel Lake. Most parties break the walk with a night along the river.

wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.name: Reynolds Creek Trail and the South Fork drainage
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.notes: The short way in, and short is relative. From the road end off the Twisp River an unmaintained primitive trail climbs through forest alongside the creek for roughly three miles. Above the confluence the tread gives out and about two miles of intermittent bushwhacking through slide alder, downed timber and a boot path that comes and goes is the real crux of the day — several parties lose more time here than on the mountain. The basin above holds snow well into summer, so an axe is worth carrying even when the valley looks dry. A longer alternative comes in over War Creek Ridge from the Williams Creek side and can be strung into a loop with a neighbouring summit, but it joins the same finish. Mark the point where you leave the tread; it is easy to miss coming down.
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.season: Mid-July to September; axe for snow
hazards: Avalanche terrain on the approach slopes and the summit gully whenever they hold snow
Loose rock and real exposure on the summit block
Deadfall and heavy brush on the lower trail, which sees little maintenance
Breakable crust and postholing on spring ascents
Afternoon thunderstorms on this dry east-side peak
wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.baseFinding: Follow the creek trail to about 4,800 ft, where the forest opens at the confluence of the South Fork with the main creek — a real, obvious junction of two running streams, usually crossed on a downed log. That confluence is where you leave the maintained tread. Follow the South Fork drainage upward staying roughly fifty feet above the water, which keeps you out of the worst alder and log-hopping in the streambed itself. Timber thins around 5,600 ft and the drainage narrows into a ravine that opens into a broad talus and scree basin directly beneath the peak's southeast face; that basin, at roughly 5,500 to 6,700 ft depending where you stop, is the base of the climbing. From it, a gully that often holds snow well into summer leads up to a notch on the ridge above. The decoy is at the top rather than the bottom: two horns stand across a short notch, the northern one is reached first and is lower, and the true summit is the southern horn.

wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.name: Williams Lake and War Creek Ridge

approachLogistics.trailhead: Williams Creek Trailhead (West Twisp River Road)

wa_reynolds_peak_scramble.notes: Longer, but on good trail at first and far more scenic. From the Williams Creek trailhead on the West Twisp River road at about 2,800 ft, follow the well-marked trail to Williams Lake at about 6,500 ft, then climb over Williams Butte and follow War Creek Ridge toward Camel's Hump. Drop through a boulder break in the cliffs into the upper South Fork Reynolds Creek basin and climb heather and scree to the summit pyramid.

wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.name: Climb East Fury first; the traverse starts on its summit
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.notes:
This route has no approach of its own in the ordinary sense. It is the connecting ridge between the two summits of Mount Fury, and the only way to arrive at its start is to have climbed East Fury, which is reached from the Ross Dam Trailhead by water taxi to Big Beaver Landing, the Big Beaver Creek Trail, the Access Creek bushwhack, Access Col, Luna Col and the Southeast Glacier.

Budget the East Fury ascent as a full day in its own right before this one begins, and note that the traverse is about half a kilometre of ridge, which says nothing useful about how long it takes.
hazards: Poor-quality anchors on chossy rock, with each rappel making retreat harder
A committing position on a ridge between two of the most remote summits in the range
Loose class 2-3 talus on the descent of East Fury's east side
The whole outing sits behind a full day's climb of East Fury and a multi-day approach
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury.baseFinding:
The base of this route is a summit, which is the one thing on a mountain you cannot walk past. You are at the start when you are standing on the top of East Fury with the ridge running west toward the West Peak. There is no gully to find, no bench to identify and no chance of starting the wrong line: if you are not on East Fury's summit, you have not started.

What that means in practice, and it is a decision rather than a landmark: the commitment happens at the first rappel, not at the summit. Getting off each tower on the traverse means rappelling off poor-quality anchors on chossy rock, and each rappel down makes retreat progressively harder. The place to decide whether the weather and the hour justify the traverse is on East Fury's summit, before the first pull.

What going too far looks like, on the other end: once off the traverse, the way home is back over East Fury and down its east side to the saddle on loose class 2-3 talus, then down the Southeast Glacier to Luna Col. Descending anywhere off the north side of the connecting ridge drops you into Luna Cirque, 2,400 ft below the col you camped at.

wa_rock_mountain_west_route.name: Trail #1587 from US-2 to the Nason Ridge crest
wa_rock_mountain_west_route.notes: One of the steepest maintained trails near Stevens Pass, and it starts working immediately. From the dirt pullout on the north side of the highway the tread climbs on an old service road beneath powerlines, leaves the roadbed at a signed bend about a third of a mile up, and then runs into ninety-odd tight switchbacks on an open south-facing slope with no shade at all. Schilling Creek near the bottom is the only accessible water on the climb and it drops away quickly, so fill everything at the car and carry three litres or more. The grade eases into heather meadows around 2.8 miles and the tread tops out on the crest at about 6,000 ft. An alternate approach comes up the Snowy Creek trail from the Smithbrook road and joins the ridge higher.
wa_rock_mountain_west_route.season: Late June to October; snow lingers
hazards: No reliable water on route above the creek low down
Fully exposed south-facing switchbacks with real heat and sun load
Loose rock and jumbled talus on the upper ridge
A north-facing snow patch below the summit ridge can persist into fall and goes slick by afternoon
A cornice or residual snow on the narrow connecting ridge into early summer
Afternoon thunderstorms on a wholly exposed crest
Habituated mountain goats near the summit — keep your distance
wa_rock_mountain_west_route.baseFinding: Two signed junctions bracket the start of the scrambling and neither is the base by itself. The first is where the trail tops out on the crest at roughly 6,000 ft and meets the Nason Ridge trail; turn left along the ridge here, since the right-hand branch drops away toward a lake overlook. The second, about half a mile on, is where the Snowy Creek trail joins from the south — that is the alternate approach, not your line, and past it the constructed tread stops being tread and thins into a path over loose jumbled talus. That change underfoot is the base. From there the crest runs over a false south summit first; it carries no structure on it. The true summit beyond is identified by the stone foundation of the old fire lookout, and the short connecting ridge between the two is narrow enough to want care and can hold a cornice or old snow into early summer. If you are standing on a high point with nothing built on it and the ridge carries on, keep going.

wa_rock_mountain_west_route.name: Snowy Creek trail from Smith Brook road

bivy.name: Nason Creek Campground and the Lake Wenatchee drive-in camps
bivy.notes: The drive-in base for the whole ridge, and the honest recommendation for most parties climbing these peaks: all four summits are day objectives from the highway trailheads, and sleeping at a developed campground with water and driving fifteen or twenty minutes to a trailhead beats carrying an overnight load up two thousand feet of dry switchbacks. The season runs roughly May through mid-October. From here the Merritt Lake and Round Mountain trailheads are a short drive west and north along the highway and its spurs, with Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek further west toward the pass. It is also the sensible place to reorganise mid-trip: a party that has come off the crest at one end and needs to reposition to the other has this corridor to do it in. Note that the trailheads themselves have very limited parking — Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek in particular hold only a few cars — so an early start from a nearby campground is worth more here than the extra sleep of staying further out.
bivy.water: Piped potable water at the developed campgrounds through the operating season, and Nason Creek itself alongside. This is the one place where water is a non-issue, which is why every party working this ridge should fill everything here before driving up to a trailhead rather than counting on anything above.
bivy.permit: A per-night fee, currently around the high twenties at the forest campground, with advance reservations opening well ahead and closing a few days before arrival. The state park campgrounds have their own reservation system and their own fee. No wilderness permit is involved anywhere in this zone. Fire restrictions apply in the campgrounds through the summer and are commonly total bans in late season.
bivy.capacity: Nason Creek is the closest and largest, laid out over four loops on both sides of the highway near the southeastern end of Lake Wenatchee, taking vehicles up to about thirty-five feet. Roughly sixty percent of sites are reservable in advance and the remainder are first come, first served. The state park campgrounds around the lake add substantially more capacity, and there are further national forest campgrounds spread along the highway corridor.

bivy.name: Rock Lake
bivy.notes: The camp for Rock Mountain and the western anchor of the whole crest. The Rock Mountain trail leaves US 2 at about 2,650 feet and is relentless — roughly 3,400 feet in four miles of endless switchbacks on a hot, open, south-facing slope with no water and very little shade, which is the single most quoted complaint about this peak. The lake sits in a basin below the summit ridge, so a party that has ground up the trail can drop packs, camp, and take the northeast ridge and the summit unencumbered. Most people do Rock Mountain in a day; camping here is what you do when the heat has beaten you, when you are starting the Nason Ridge traverse rather than finishing it, or when you want the summit at first light. The alternative approach by the Snowy Creek trail from the forest road on the north side starts higher and climbs less, and it is the kinder line in warm weather, though the road is brushy. Snow lingers on the upper slopes into early summer and the basin holds it later than the trail below. West of the lake, the crest trail toward Crescent Lake has badly eroded steep sidehill sections with little tread left, and that stretch is the crux of moving along this ridge with a pack.
bivy.water: The lake, and it is the first water of any kind on the Rock Mountain trail — the entire climb from the highway is dry. It holds all season. Treat it, because the shoreline is well used and the basin is small. Fill here for everything you intend to do on the crest, since the next dependable source westward or eastward is Crescent Lake, and the ridge between the two carries nothing.
bivy.permit: None. Nason Ridge sits outside the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, so there is no wilderness permit, no self-issue slip, no quota and no lottery anywhere. The Rock Mountain trailhead has very limited parking, though no fee is charged there and the Merritt Lake end requires no pass either; of the trailheads serving this crest only Nason Ridge is a fee site, at $5 a day or $30 a year. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet in this national forest, which covers this camp and every other high site here, and summer burn bans are routine on this dry east-side ground.
bivy.capacity: Several pleasant established sites around the lake, enough for two or three parties; small and it feels small, with no facilities

wa_rock_mountain_west_route.notes: Drive Smith Brook road six miles and the narrow, brushy Snowy Creek road a further three and a half to a small trailhead with very limited parking. The trail follows Snowy Creek through old growth, then climbs to the crest and joins the main route about half a mile short of the summit. It is shorter and far less steep than the highway trail. The Snowy Creek road has been closed by storm damage since June 2026, so check before driving it.

wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.name: North Fork Entiat and the primitive Pyramid Creek Trail to the Emerald-Saska basin
camps: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
Fox Camp, North Fork Entiat trail
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.notes: From the North Fork Entiat Trailhead at about 3,940 ft at the end of FR-5606, the first four miles of Trail #1437 climb gently up the valley through old burn, where blowdown and washed-out sections make the going slower than the grade suggests. There is little shade and the valley bottom runs hot and dry — carry water. Continue up-valley another four miles, gaining roughly 3,000 ft from the trailhead, to the Pyramid Creek / Fern Lake junction. That junction is anywhere from seven to nine miles in depending on how far up the road you were able to start. Fox Camp sits about a quarter mile north of it. From the junction take the primitive, unmaintained Pyramid Creek Trail west and climb about 1,000 ft over a mile to a mile and a half into the upper basin between Emerald and Saska, around 7,100 ft. The tread is intermittent. Pushing to that camp rather than stopping at the junction costs an extra hour on the approach day and returns about the same on summit day. This is reported as the easiest and shortest of the Saska / Emerald / Cardinal trio's summit scrambles.
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.season: Mid-Jul-Sep once the col and summit gullies clear. October adds larch colour and early-snow risk; before mid-July carry an axe for lingering snow and ice
hazards: Loose rock and rockfall throughout the Emerald-Saska col basin and along the summit ridge
Cliff bands below the south-west face that have caught descending parties in icy or snow-covered conditions
A narrow, sometimes knife-edged connecting crest that has to be avoided rather than followed
Lingering snow and ice in the col and summit gullies into early-to-mid July in heavy years
Heavy blowdown and washed-out sections on the lower North Fork Entiat Trail from past wildfires and storm damage
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.baseFinding:
The base is the col and the direction off it is west. From the basin camp, about 600 ft of gain on talus, scree or lingering snow reaches the Emerald-Saska Col at roughly 7,700 ft — a notch on the south ridge with a peak on either side. From the col, head west toward Saska. Emerald is the other way. If you leave the col climbing east you are on the neighbouring peak's ground.

The positive test is that you do not stay on the crest. The connecting ridge is narrow and knife-edged in places with steep drop-offs on both sides, so the usual line drops slightly onto its west flank to pick up an obvious scree-and-rock gully, then follows a cairned rising traverse back toward the crest. West flank, gully, cairned rising traverse. A party grimly balancing along the crest itself has missed the line rather than found the hard way.

The finish is counted in feet, not features: roughly 300 ft of final Class 3 on loose blocks gains the top. Test every hold — nothing here is fixed and no rope is standard, although the last exposed moves are steep enough that some parties carry a short handline for them.

The descent marker is a warning with a documented consequence: cliff bands sit below the south-west face. Stay well clear of them when the ground is snow-covered or icy. A winter party misjudging that descent line in icy conditions lost a ski over those cliffs. In early-to-mid season the continuous snow below the col gives a glissade or boot-ski; by August and September the same ground is loose scree and dirt that has to be walked slowly.

Loose rock is the theme of the whole cirque. Helmet, and do not stack the party directly above one another, from the moment you leave the basin.

wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.name: Lake Chelan: Lucerne and Emerald Park to Milham Pass

bivy.name: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
bivy.notes: The high camp for the crest traverse, about a mile and a half beyond Fox Camp on the Pyramid trail, in the basin that separates Emerald Peak from Saska Peak. This is where a party stages to link Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain in a single push over Milham Pass at about 6,663 ft, which is the classic way to do these four and much the most efficient. From the basin you climb to the upper shelf just below the ridge between Emerald and Saska and pick up the broad gully to the summit. Cardinal is the highest of the group and the furthest, and it is the one that turns a two-day plan into three. The setting is superb and the ground is loose — expect scree and blocky scrambling rather than clean rock, and expect the descents to take longer than the ascents. Season is short at this height in a heavy year, realistically mid-July to early October, and the reason to come late is the larch and the reason not to is the water. Weigh that honestly: an August party that finds the tarns dry has a long, hot walk back down to fix it. Weather moves in from the west with little warning here and the basin is fully exposed.
bivy.water: Snowmelt tarns and rivulets in the basin, and these are the crux of the whole plan. They are dependable in early and mid summer, unreliable by mid-August, and in a dry year they are gone entirely by late August, at which point the nearest certain water is back down at Fox Camp. Do not commit to a high camp here in late season without either confirming water or carrying it up. Milham Pass itself has none.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue, party limit of twelve. Camp on durable ground and well back from the tarns. No campfires — forest-wide restrictions aside, there is no fuel at this elevation and the ground is fragile. The approach trails, including the Emerald Park, Domke Lake, North Fork Entiat and Pyramid Creek trails, have been closed under the Little Giant Fire closure; check its status with the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest before you go.
bivy.capacity: A small number of tent-sized spots on benches and moraine in the upper basin; two or three parties at most, and less if you want flat ground

wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.notes: Take the boat up Lake Chelan to Lucerne, then climb the trail past the Domke Lake junction and up Emerald Park Creek to Emerald Park, about 6.5 miles, and on another two miles to Milham Pass. Drop from the pass into the basin between Emerald and Saska and pick up the south-slopes route there. A long, remote approach that suits parties already on the Lake Chelan side.

wa_sentinel_peak_standard.name: Le Conte-Sentinel col from Yang Yang Lakes
camps: Cache Col and the Cache Glacier shoulder
wa_sentinel_peak_standard.notes: This peak is reached from a camp on the Ptarmigan Traverse rather than from a road end. From Cascade Pass go over Cache Col to Kool-Aid Lake, take the Red Ledge beneath Art's Knoll through the cliff band, cross to Yang Yang Lakes, then climb the broad Le Conte Glacier to the notch north of the peak. The notch carries dry bivy platforms and most parties leave overnight gear there and climb on light packs.
wa_sentinel_peak_standard.season: Late July to mid-September, and climbed in the morning — the basin snow takes crampons cleanly at dawn and goes soft by afternoon
hazards: The Le Conte Glacier is actively crevassed — rope up and carry a rescue kit
The Red Ledge is genuinely serious when banked with snow, which is common into early July
Snow in the west basin reaches 35-40 degrees near its top and softens through the day
wa_sentinel_peak_standard.baseFinding: The Le Conte-Sentinel col is the reference: a flat notch at the top of the glacier carrying dry gravel bivy platforms, the only level dry ground for a long way in any direction. From the notch the peak's west side presents one continuous basin of snow running up to a rock face, and that snow is the route. Its top is the only place on the face where a broad, walkable ledge cuts leftward, to the north, beneath a short cliff band. Those two features together are the proof: continuous snow steepening as it rises, and an obvious ledge running left off the top of it. If the snow you have chosen tops out against blank rock with no ledge leading off it, you are too far south in the basin. If you are on bare rock with no snow beneath you at all, you have wandered onto the east side, which degrades into rotten rock and steep snow — that is the side parties get wrong on the descent, and it is not the route.

wa_sentinel_peak_standard.name: Downey Creek and the south end of the traverse

bivy.name: Sentinel Pass and Lizard Col
bivy.notes: The two saddles either side of Sentinel Peak, crossed one after the other on the way from the Le Conte Glacier to the South Cascade Glacier. These are the highest useful sleeping spots on this part of the crest and the direct bases for Sentinel Peak and for Lizard Mountain, which stands just east of the col that carries the route across to the far side. accounts disagree on the elevations of both saddles by several hundred feet, with Lizard quoted anywhere from the high 6,000s to the mid 7,000s, so no numbers are recorded. A camp here is a fair-weather decision and nothing else: there is no shelter, no water, and the ground on both sides is glaciated, so retreating in cloud means downclimbing snow you only saw once in daylight. Most parties cross both in a day and sleep at a lake; the ones who stop are the ones who came to climb the peaks rather than pass them.
bivy.water: None running. Melt snow, or carry from the lakes below on whichever side you came from. In a late, thin season the snow at the saddles can be gone and then there is nothing at all.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or ice only. Pack out human waste, which matters here because the meltwater below feeds the lakes people are drinking from.
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms and small rock benches at each of the two saddles, one party at a time at either. Nothing built, no toilet, nothing sheltered.

bivy.name: White Rock Lakes
bivy.notes: The camp at the south end of the high traverse, under the Dana and Chickamin glaciers. Sentinel and Old Guard are climbed from here or from the col above.
bivy.water: The lakes and snowmelt
bivy.permit: No permit required (Glacier Peak Wilderness)
bivy.capacity: Several sites on slabs and heather near the lakes

bivy.name: Crest bivouacs above the South Cascade and Chickamin glaciers
bivy.notes: Say it plainly: these are not sites, they are wherever a party gets to. Elephant Head is the southernmost peak, standing on the divide above the lakes at the south end of the crest with big cliffs dropping east into the head of the west fork of Agnes Creek, between the ice on either side. It gets a handful of ascents in a decade and there is no established camp for it, so parties climbing it either work out from the lake basin below or level a spot on the divide and accept a dry, exposed night. The same is true of anyone caught out on the South Cascade side by weather or by a slower day than planned. The season is short and matters more here than anywhere else: July into August has the glaciers covered and the bivouac snow usable, while September brings open crevasses, bare ice and no water at all. Anyone planning a night on this ground should carry the fuel to melt snow and treat the whole thing as an unplanned shelter that happens to be foreseeable.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and unreliable after midsummer. The last certain water on this stretch is the lakes below, and everything east of the divide is snow, ice and bare rock.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or ice, never on the heather benches. Pack out human waste. No fires; there is nothing to burn and nothing that would recover.
bivy.capacity: Whatever the party can level. Rock rings, gravel benches and snow platforms for one party at a time, scattered along the divide. No toilet and no established sites of any kind.

approachLogistics.trailhead: Downey Creek Trailhead (Trail #768, Suiattle River Road)

wa_sentinel_peak_standard.notes: From the Downey Creek trailhead on the Suiattle River Road, walk the Downey Creek trail and the brushy Bachelor Creek path to Cub Lake and Itswoot Ridge, then cross the Dana Glacier country to White Rock Lakes. From the lakes, work back up onto the South Cascade Glacier to reach the peak. Plan on several days of off-trail and glacier travel.

wa_silver_star_ne_ridge.name: SR-20 pullout, Burgundy Creek climbers' trail, the Bench, Burgundy Col
camps: Burgundy Creek bench camp — west side
Burgundy Col high camp — west side, the Wine Spires
Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — west side
wa_silver_star_ne_ridge.notes:
Park at the broad pullout and overlook on SR-20 near milepost 165-166, about four miles east of Washington Pass, where a sign points toward Silver Star Mountain.

Drop down the embankment roughly 150 to 200 ft to Early Winters Creek and cross on a log. Logjams shift year to year, so scout up and down for the best crossing and be prepared to ford in high water or early season when the creek runs cold and fast with snowmelt. Treat this crossing as your last reliable water until camp.

On the far bank pick up the unofficial but well-defined climbers' trail that climbs the timbered rib on the west (left) side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. From there it climbs relentlessly and steeply through forest and brush for roughly 2,500-3,000 ft with almost no switchbacks and only fleeting water access early on. The tread erodes and is easy to lose in the timber.
hazards: Early Winters Creek crossing — log can be wet, mossy or washed out; ford in high water
Steep eroding brushy tread that is easy to lose in the timber
Loose microwave-sized blocks in the gully bed above the bench
Loose kitty-litter slabs on the final traverse into the col
No water between the creek and the bench
wa_silver_star_ne_ridge.baseFinding:
The unmistakable break on this approach is the bench, at roughly 6,400-6,700 ft: the grade suddenly eases onto an open larch-and-heather shelf with several established campsites and usually a seasonal trickle or snowmelt nearby. That is the standard overnight camp and the natural turnaround check for a day trip.

Above the bench there is a gully running obviously and directly to Burgundy Col. That gully is the wrong one — it is loose and exposed. Instead stay left and follow the trail up the gully directly above camp. Within it, stay climber's left of the gully proper: the bed holds loose microwave-sized blocks, while the left side is unpleasant kitty-litter-covered slab but far less dangerous. Near the head of the gully make an ascending traverse to the right, under the cliffs, over heather-covered slabs into the col at roughly 7,800 ft. This gully and traverse is where parties describe the real crux of route-finding, both up and down. The col — not the glacier — is where the route proper begins; from there trend toward the northeast side of the west summit.

wa_silver_star_ne_ridge.name: Silver Star Creek from the north

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
bivy.notes: A roadside vehicle campground rather than a site on any approach — it is for sleeping the night before, not for the climb. It opens around May and closes with the first serious snow, tracking the same window as everything else here. The whole area is gated by the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts in late November or early December and reopens in spring, with the date driven by avalanche work and storm damage rather than the calendar. In closed months the pullout is inside the gated section and the approach becomes a long ski or snowmobile trip.
bivy.water: No drinking water at the campground. Early Winters Creek runs alongside and needs filtering; Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds, farther east, have drinking water in season.
bivy.permit: Per-night campground fee; no wilderness permit involved. The unmarked Silver Star Creek pullout that starts the west approach is not itself a signed fee site — check current signage rather than assuming either way.
bivy.capacity: 27 developed first-come, first-served sites for tents and small vehicles

wa_silver_star_ne_ridge.notes: Park where SR-20 crosses Silver Star Creek and follow the trail up the east side of the creek for about two miles. Where it fades near 4,850 ft, trend west across the valley and climb open talus toward Burgundy Spire and onto the glacier. Best on continuous spring snow, when it makes a good ski or snowshoe approach; once the valley melts out it turns brushy and swampy and Burgundy Col is the better choice.

wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.name: Tunnel Creek trail to the crest trail at the lake, then south to the pass
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.notes:
