From the forest road east of Skykomish, the Tunnel Creek trail climbs about eleven hundred and seventy feet in under a mile and a half from roughly 3,100 ft to a small lake on the crest, where it meets the long-distance crest trail. Turn south and follow that trail several miles to the pass at roughly 5,800 ft.

This is the option with the least climbing and the easiest tread. It is a little longer along the crest than the other trailhead, and the walking is straightforward the whole way, which makes it the better choice with heavy loads or a late start.
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.season: July through September, once the crest trail is clear
hazards: an unmaintained ridge path beyond the pass with no signage
a long enough round trip that many parties camp, so a day attempt commits to a late finish
loose rock on the tower and on the ridge approach to it
a two-pitch face that still needs a rope, a rack and a plan to get back down
no water on the ridge between the pass and the tower
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.baseFinding:
The pass is the gate and the climbers' path leaves directly from the top of it. Do not look for it below the pass or beyond it: an unmaintained path runs south along the ridge from the pass itself. If you are casting about on the trail below the pass for a junction, you have not got high enough.

The tower is a distinct rock tower on that crest and it is the first one. The face you want looks back toward the pass on the north-east side, so from the path it presents itself as you approach rather than after you have passed it.

The critical negative marker is the mountain further along the same ridge. If you have walked past the tower and are looking at a broad peak with a lake basin below it, you have continued to the mountain and gone past the tower. Turn round; the tower is a slender formation and the mountain is not.

The route confirms itself on the second pitch: two pitches of easy fifth class, with the upper one diagonalling left into a gully and finishing at a large boulder near the top. A line that runs straight up with no leftward gully, or that takes more than a couple of pitches, is not this face.

One more caution about names: there are several mountains called Thunder in this state and more than one formation of this sort on crest trails. The identifying combination here is a pass on the long-distance crest trail with an unmaintained path leaving its top southward, and a tower standing before the mountain on the same ridge.

wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.name: Surprise Creek trail past the two lakes, then the switchbacks to the pass

bivy.name: Trap Lake
bivy.notes: The closest camp to Slippery Slab Tower and the best base for Thunder Mountain. Two trailheads reach it: Tunnel Creek, which climbs about a mile and a half to Hope Lake on the Pacific Crest Trail and then runs south a couple of miles over meadowy ground before the switchbacks up to Trap Pass; or Surprise Creek at Scenic, which climbs to Surprise Lake and joins the Pacific Crest Trail heading north. Trap Lake sits a little below Trap Pass on the east side. From the pass a faint but obvious climbers' track branches south along the ridge crest, follows it to a boulder field, and works up that to the base of the tower — the whole point of camping here rather than at the Scenic lakes is that it puts a party at the pass within half an hour of leaving the tent. Slippery Slab Tower is two short pitches of pleasant lower fifth class on an arete whose flakes are not to be trusted for protection, so it is a short climb with a long walk attached, and an overnight makes the arithmetic work. Thunder Mountain itself is a scramble from the same ground. The Thunder Mountain Lakes further south are a delicate basin where camping is discouraged; use this lake instead. Season is roughly July to October, with snow on the Trap Pass switchbacks well into summer.
bivy.water: The lake, and the inlet above it. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is required for day and overnight use, taken at the trailhead register from mid-May to the end of October. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Surprise Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 feet west of the crest, and a stove is the right answer here in any case.
bivy.capacity: Several small informal sites in the trees at the lake, below the pass on the east side of the crest. Quiet, and rarely more than a party or two.

bivy.name: Surprise Lake and Glacier Lake
bivy.notes: The other half of the Thunder Mountain approach, and the one most parties use because the trailhead is simple to find and the walk is pleasant. From US 2 turn south into Scenic, ten miles east of Skykomish, cross the railway tracks and follow gravel a third of a mile to the trailhead at about 2,200 feet. It is four and a half miles to Surprise Lake and a further mile to Glacier Lake, climbing steadily through forest with the creek alongside. From either lake the Pacific Crest Trail runs north to Trap Pass, from where the climbers' track along the ridge reaches Thunder Mountain and Slippery Slab Tower. Camping here rather than at Trap Lake adds an hour or more to the summit morning but gives a better camp and a shorter, easier walk in with heavy loads, so it suits a party carrying a rope and rack. Both lakes are subalpine and hold snow into July in a normal year. The lower trail is steep enough in places to be slow with overnight packs, and the railway line at the trailhead is active and noisy at night, which is worth knowing before you pitch near the car.
bivy.water: Both lakes and the creek between them. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness self-issue permit at the trailhead, free, required for day and overnight use from mid-May to the end of October. Northwest Forest Pass or the daily fee at the Surprise Creek trailhead. No campfires above 4,000 feet west of the crest, which includes both of these lakes. Camp only at the established sites on the west shores.
bivy.capacity: Established sites along the west shores of both lakes. Surprise is the larger and busier; Glacier, about a mile further and three hundred feet higher, is quieter and holds fewer parties.

wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.notes:
The other trailhead climbs the Surprise Creek trail past the first lake at about 4,500 ft and its neighbour, then switchbacks up to the same pass. It is roughly a mile shorter to the pass than the crest-trail option and costs several hundred feet more climbing, and it is in the trees for essentially the whole way, so it gives less to look at and less warning of the weather ahead.

Both trailheads meet at the pass and nothing above it differs.
hazards: more climbing than the other trailhead for a slightly shorter distance
forested trail the whole way, with little view of conditions ahead
an unmaintained ridge path beyond the pass
loose rock on the tower
no water on the ridge beyond the pass
wa_slippery_slab_tower_ne_face.baseFinding:
From the pass the approach is identical to the other trailhead's: an unmaintained climbers' path leaves the top of the pass and runs south along the ridge.

The tower is the first distinct rock formation on that crest, and its north-east face looks back toward the pass. Because this approach arrives at the pass from below and in trees, take a moment on the pass itself to pick the tower out along the crest before starting the path - it is much harder to identify from underneath.

The negative marker is the same and it is the one that matters: the mountain lies further along the same ridge, above a lake basin. A broad peak with lakes below it is not the tower. If you are walking under a mountainside rather than under a slender formation, you have gone too far.

Confirm on the climb itself: two pitches of easy fifth class with the second diagonalling left into a gully to a large boulder near the top. If your first pitch is hard or your route runs straight up a face for several rope lengths, you are not on it.

wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.name: Bedal Creek Trail #705 (FR 4096)

bivy.name: Ridge above the Sloan Glacier
bivy.notes: The preferred high camp, on the crest overlooking the glacier with a long view. From here it is about half a mile of traverse east-southeast to the saddle near 5,900 ft and then up to gain the glacier around 6,800 ft, which makes for a short summit morning. Expect to camp on snow through June; the route's window is squeezed at both ends, with routefinding through the heather benches hard when they are still buried and the glacier growing impassable late in the season.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams below camp; the last running water is around 6,000 ft, and above that you are melting snow.
bivy.capacity: Several pleasant spots, with one dry site big enough for about four tents — more if you are willing to pitch on snow.

bivy.name: Bedal-Sloan saddle
bivy.notes: The first camp on the ridge, reached by traversing open and partly brushy slopes past a small lake. Usable, but the ridge above is the better camp and most parties who carry a camp go the extra distance. Elevation is given as either 5,330 or 5,380 ft depending on the account.
bivy.water: A tarn at the saddle, and it is the weak point — it is stagnant, and parties have found frog and mosquito larvae in it. Better water is a short way above, around 5,500 ft, where small streams cascade down; fill there rather than at the pond.
bivy.capacity: Four to six tents, so leave room for another party.

bivy.name: Bedal Creek roadhead
bivy.notes: Worth recording because it is the overnight most Sloan parties actually use. The Corkscrew from Bedal Creek is a reasonable single day of thirteen or fourteen hours for a fit party, and successful ascents in under twelve hours are common, so the usual pattern is to sleep at the trailhead and start around four in the morning rather than carry a camp to the ridge.
bivy.water: Carry it, or take it from Bedal Creek on the way in.
bivy.permit: A Northwest Forest Pass is usually reported as the required parking permit, though not universally; carry one.
bivy.capacity: Roadside parking, not a designated site.

wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.notes:
From the Mountain Loop Highway take FR 4096, a rough narrow spur where high clearance genuinely helps, to the Bedal Creek trailhead at about 2,790 ft. Distance and gain above are the full round trip by this line.

Walk the old Bedal Creek trail roughly 1.5 miles and 700 ft. It is overgrown in stretches but stays followable. The critical junction is around 3,500 ft, where a climbers' path turns off to the left near 48.0560, -121.3631; it has carried pink flagging tape in recent years. Missing that turn is the standard error here — the old tread continues and dies in a brushy washout below the basin.

The climbers' path gains about 1,400 ft steeply through forest. At roughly 4,900 ft it breaks out into talus, then bends southeast through meadow and scattered timber to the Bedal-Sloan saddle at 5,300 ft, where a shallow, somewhat stagnant pond marks the usual camp. This is the last easy water; cascading streams just below the saddle are the alternative.

Southeast from the saddle the ground opens into scramble terrain. At about 5,800 ft you cross a minor rock ridge and get your first view of the glacier. Snow from here is often firm in the morning and may want axe and crampons.
wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.season: Jul-Sep, once the forest band below 4,900 ft is clear of snow
hazards: Losing the 3,500 ft climbers'-path junction and ending in the brushy washout
Firm early-morning snow on the open slopes above 5,800 ft
Crevasses on the Sloan Glacier, normally bridged but open in lean years
Rough, narrow FR 4096 access spur
wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.baseFinding: The Corkscrew does not begin at the glacier — it begins after you are off it. Cross the Sloan Glacier and keep going until you are standing on bare rock at the southeast edge of the summit block, around 7,300 ft; that bare-rock arrival is where parties cache rope, axe and crampons, and it is the single most reliable confirmation on the route. From there a boot track runs along heather ledges for ten to fifteen minutes. Watch to your right for a gully of pale, near-white rock and take that. Two negatives to check yourself against: if you are still on snow or ice you have not reached the start, and if you have walked the heather for much more than a quarter hour with no white-rock gully on the right, you are contouring too low — climb.

wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.name: North Fork Sauk / Cougar Creek (FR 49)
wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.notes:
The start is an unsigned climbers' pullout on FR 49 (Sloan Creek Road) at roughly 1,900 ft, on the north side of the North Fork Sauk. It is not the maintained North Fork Sauk River Trail #649 — that is a different trailhead a short distance back along the road, and taking it is the common mistake.

The path runs flat and brushy through stinging nettle and then devil's club for a few tenths of a mile before dropping to the river. The river must be forded or crossed on a log jam; jams are usually adequate around half a mile in but shift from year to year and are a poor bet in high water. The path then crosses river braids two or three times over the next mile before turning up Cougar Creek on a faint, intermittently cairned and flagged track through sandy streambed and forest.

Around 3,000-3,200 ft the path crosses Cougar Creek itself; lower crossings can be impassable, so hold out for the 3.2K-ish one. Steep forest switchbacks follow, passing a waterfall on Cougar Creek near 5,000 ft — roughly two to two and a half hours from the car and the last reliable water before the basin. Above the falls the track leaves the trees onto scree and slabs and angles up to the 5,800 ft basin on Sloan's northeast side, where there is a small stream and the standard bivy. This line converges with the Bedal Creek approach around 5,000-5,500 ft.
wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.season: Jul-Aug, after the North Fork Sauk drops from snowmelt flow
hazards: Fording or log-crossing the North Fork Sauk — deep, cold and fast in early season
Log jams that move year to year and cannot be relied on
Devil's club and nettle on the lower path
Faint, easily lost tread up the Cougar Creek streambed
wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew.baseFinding: Same as the Bedal line: from the basin, ledges and slabs lead to the toe of the Sloan Glacier — rope and gear up there, not earlier. The climbing begins only once you are back on bare rock at the southeast edge of the summit block near 7,300 ft, and the entry is the gully of pale rock on your right, ten to fifteen minutes along the heather ledges from where you leave the ice.

wa_south_face_10.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 from the Chewuch River road
camps: Cathedral Pass benches and the tarn slabs
wa_south_face_10.notes:
The drive is the easy part — paved the whole way from Winthrop up the Chewuch River valley to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,050 ft. The walk is one of the longest wilderness approaches in the state.

Trail #504 climbs the drainage for roughly twelve miles to Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, crossing an old burn for much of that: hot, rocky, buggy, and no shade. From the pass the trail drops into the next drainage before the Cathedral Lakes side trail climbs to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft, below the peak's south-west side.

Treat this as a two-to-four day backpack with a summit push from camp in the basin. A free self-issue wilderness permit is taken at the trailhead along with a parking pass. There is no cell coverage anywhere on this trip.
wa_south_face_10.season: Roughly July through the first snow of October
hazards: Three separate routes share this face and the lower ground accepts almost any line
The tower in front of the wall carries its own routes under a colliding name
Loose rock and rockfall from parties above on a wall this size
Walk-off descent to the west whose crux is a no-fall step across a gap
No cell coverage and a multi-day walk out
wa_south_face_10.baseFinding:
From camp, follow the trail toward Cathedral Pass and then climb scree and talus to the foot of the main wall. Thirty to sixty minutes.

First, rule out the tower. A semi-detached tower leans against the lower right side of the wall, and a deep gully separates it from the mountain. If that tower is between you and the rock, you are under the buttress route, which climbs the ridge behind it. This route is on the open wall, and specifically on its centre. Nothing should be standing in front of you.

Start low and central, near the bottom of the wall rather than off to one side. The line then confirms itself by a run of features in a fixed order, and this is the identification that actually works, because the lower face accepts many lines:

Low down there is a boxed-in feature the first ascent called a confession box. At mid-height there is a spectacular curving chimney — this is the single best confirmation on the route and it is visible from the ground if you look for it. High up you cross a pulpit ledge and then a belfry ledge before easier ground runs to the top.

Negative marker, and it matters because the two lines converge: if instead of a curving chimney you find yourself pushed rightward along a long ramp toward a steep thin crack in a headwall, you have drifted onto the harder line that takes the right-hand third of the face. That one is several number grades above this and it takes very thin protection. Come back left and look for the chimney.

Second negative marker: the tower in front of the wall has its own small south face carrying several short routes. Beta written about the tower will also be headed South Face. The tower's routes are two to five pitches; this wall is about a thousand feet.

wa_south_face_10.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee

bivy.name: Upper Cathedral Lake basin
bivy.notes: The working climbers' camp for both the Southeast Buttress and Amphitheater's ridges, sitting directly under the peaks with short walks to either. The basin has taken heavy use for decades and the Forest Service has posted revegetation closures on damaged ground here in the past, so treat the shoreline as off limits and camp on rock or bare dirt well back from the water. Check the posted signs on arrival rather than assuming last year's layout still applies — which sites are open has changed between seasons. Nights are cold and exposed at this elevation even in August.
bivy.water: The most dependable water anywhere on this approach — the lake holds through the season and needs no rationing. The one place on the route where you can plan on filling without checking a report first.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at the Andrews Creek trailhead. No quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day fee to park.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites on slabs and benches back from the water; realistically three or four small parties before it feels crowded, and it does fill on midsummer weekends and during larch season

wa_south_face_10.notes:
The high trailhead above Loomis, reached by Toats Coulee Road and the forest roads beyond it, sits at about 5,570 ft. This is a trail and not a four-wheel-drive road, whatever you may have read; the high-clearance warning in circulation belongs to a different spur.

The trail drops from the trailhead to meet the valley trail lower down, then follows the valley up to the Cathedral Lakes basin. It is the shortest walk and the least total climbing of the ways in.

Both ends carry a penalty. The drive is about two hours longer than from Winthrop, and because the trailhead is high and the trail loses height to reach the valley, the trip finishes with roughly 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out.
wa_south_face_10.season: Roughly July through the first snow of October
hazards: 1,300 ft of climbing at the very end of the trip on the way out
A trailhead published under several different names
The wall foreshortens badly from directly below, so the mid-height chimney is hard to relocate at the base
Same walk-off descent with a no-fall gap crossing near the summit
wa_south_face_10.baseFinding:
The base is the same and reached the same way from camp. What changes is where you first see the wall, and on a face this size that is worth more than any description.

Coming up the valley you enter the basin from below rather than over the pass, so the whole south side stands up in front of you at once. Stop at the lake and sort out three things before walking up: the small detached tower at the lower right of the wall; the deep gully between that tower and the mountain; and the open centre of the wall to the left of both. This route is the open centre.

While you are looking, find the curving chimney at mid-height in that centre panel. It is the feature that proves the line and it is far easier to pick out from across the water than from underneath, where the wall foreshortens and everything reads as featured granite. Fix it against the skyline above it so you can re-find it at the base.

Negative marker from the lake: if the panel you are looking at has a long ramp cutting rightward across it toward a steep headwall crack, that is the right-hand line, not this one. And if the wall you are looking at is only a few pitches tall and stands clear of the mountain, you are looking at the tower.

wa_south_face_10.name: Thirtymile Trailhead and the Chewuch River trail toward Remmel Lake

bivy.name: Upper Cathedral Lake basin
bivy.notes: The working climbers' camp for both the Southeast Buttress and Amphitheater's ridges, sitting directly under the peaks with short walks to either. The basin has taken heavy use for decades and the Forest Service has posted revegetation closures on damaged ground here in the past, so treat the shoreline as off limits and camp on rock or bare dirt well back from the water. Check the posted signs on arrival rather than assuming last year's layout still applies — which sites are open has changed between seasons. Nights are cold and exposed at this elevation even in August.
bivy.water: The most dependable water anywhere on this approach — the lake holds through the season and needs no rationing. The one place on the route where you can plan on filling without checking a report first.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at the Andrews Creek trailhead. No quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day fee to park.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites on slabs and benches back from the water; realistically three or four small parties before it feels crowded, and it does fill on midsummer weekends and during larch season

approachLogistics.trailhead: Thirtymile Trailhead (end of the Chewuch River Road)

wa_south_face_10.notes: Follow the Chewuch River trail north from the Thirtymile Trailhead nearly to Remmel Lake, then climb to the Cathedral Lakes basin. A longer way round than Andrews Creek, used when combining the Remmel Lake country with the climb.

wa_south_gully_south_spur.name: Winter and spring: Commonwealth Basin from Summit West, straight at the gully

bivy.name: Denny Creek Campground, I-90 exit 47
bivy.notes: The nearest developed campground to the Alpental trailhead, roughly a twenty-minute drive back down I-90 and then three miles up the Denny Creek road. The sensible answer for a party arriving late the night before a Tooth or Chair Peak day, since it needs no wilderness permit and no early-morning decisions. Sites go quickly on summer weekends; book ahead rather than driving up hoping. In winter this option disappears entirely and you are back to sleeping in the valley towns or driving up in the dark.
bivy.water: Potable water provided during the operating season.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, reserved through recreation.gov up to six months ahead; a small number of first-come sites. No wilderness permit needed, and no trailhead pass required to sleep here. Seasonal — closed outside the summer months, so it is not an option for a winter climb.
bivy.capacity: About 33 sites, most reservable, including electric and double sites plus one group site

bivy.name: Tinkham Campground, I-90 exit 42
bivy.notes: Further down the valley than Denny Creek, about 1.5 miles in on Forest Road 55 from exit 42, and the usual fallback when Denny Creek is booked out. The extra driving costs perhaps fifteen minutes on the approach next morning, which matters little against a ten-hour climbing day. Like every developed site on this stretch of I-90 it is a summer-only option. It sits well below the pass, low in the South Fork valley.
bivy.water: Water availability here varies by year and is not guaranteed — confirm before relying on it and carry enough for the night otherwise.
bivy.permit: Campground fee via recreation.gov; seasonal operation only, closed outside the summer months. No wilderness permit or trailhead pass involved.
bivy.capacity: Small forested Forest Service campground, reservable sites

wa_south_gully_south_spur.notes:
The fast winter line does not start at Alpental. Park at Summit West and walk the short distance to the start of the winter Commonwealth ski and snowshoe trail, which is usually well compacted. Cross the log and head directly at the route.

Where the ground steepens, trend far left until you come up against huge cliffs, then go about 100 ft further left again and climb to the start of the gully. The whole approach is about a mile and takes roughly an hour on firm snow.

The adjacent Summit at Snoqualmie ski area does avalanche control on nearby slopes in season; check with the resort before a winter attempt.
wa_south_gully_south_spur.season: Roughly December to April, once the gully has filled and consolidated — that is also exactly when the avalanche problem is live, so the NWAC Snoqualmie Pass forecast is a mandatory read
hazards: Avalanche: a confined south-facing gully below cliffs, adjacent to controlled ski terrain
Ski-area avalanche blasting on neighbouring slopes in season
Highly fractured, crumbly rhyolite with a documented fatal history from rockfall and breaking holds
Poor, deep slush and hidden moats at snow-to-rock transitions on the South Spur
Large overhanging cornices along the summit ridge and above the north summit
wa_south_gully_south_spur.baseFinding:
The cliffs are the marker, and the instruction is to overshoot them by 100 ft. Climbing the steepening slope you trend far left until you are stopped by huge cliffs. Those cliffs are not a wrong turn — they are the landmark. Go 100 ft further left past them and then up, and you are at the mouth of the South Gully. A published fix for the start is roughly 47.4395, -121.4070.

What confirms it once you are in: the gully begins at the cliffs that form it just above treeline, and after roughly 300 to 400 ft — about three 60 m pitches — you reach the first chockstone, sitting at a constriction in the canyon. That chockstone is the crux except in deep snow, and it can be passed either left or right. A second chockstone follows about 50 ft beyond. First chockstone at a constriction, second one 50 ft above: no other gully on this side gives you that pair.

The exit test for later: continue about 30 m past an ice or rock step of no more than 8 ft until you can see the end of the gully. It is possible to turn left before the gully ends — look for two large trees and follow the ramp up climbers' left around the cliff to the South Spur.

And one descent warning that parties get wrong: do not rappel from the south summit. Traverse the ridge to the middle summit first, until you are looking directly at the north summit, and rappel from the tree there. Rappelling early has tempted more than one party.

wa_south_gully_south_spur.name: Summer and autumn: the south side of the peak from Alpental, as a dry scramble
wa_south_gully_south_spur.notes:
From I-90 exit 52, follow Alpental Road up to the ski area. Guye Peak's rock rises directly above the parking area, so there is essentially no approach walk to the south-side routes. Respect the posted no-parking signs on the private sections of road; access on foot through the Alpental Community Club's private ground has been closed to climbers, so plan a line from public ground.

Once below the peak, find the obvious gully on the south side and scramble it.

The summer version of this line is not well loved: discontinuous rock, vegetation, deep pine needles and general gully looseness are what a dry ascent actually delivers.
wa_south_gully_south_spur.season: Roughly June to October as an easy-fifth-class rock scramble — a completely different and lower-consequence outing from the winter climb
hazards: Highly fractured, crumbly rhyolite; climber-triggered rockfall is very likely and the peak has a documented history of fatalities from rockfall and breaking holds
Rockfall multiplies with parties stacked in the gully — helmet on from the talus upward
Wet or mossy chockstone sections in shoulder-season conditions
Discontinuous rock, deep pine needles and vegetation make the dry version loose and unpleasant rather than technical
Access: private property on the walking approach, closed to climbers
wa_south_gully_south_spur.baseFinding:
The gully is the obvious one on the south side, and the test is that it forces you out left. Walk round the south side until you are under the single obvious gully cleaving it. That is the whole identification at ground level; there is no second candidate on this aspect.

The confirmation is the chockstone, and it comes early. Scramble the gully until one or two chockstones jammed in it stop you and force you climbers' left out onto the adjacent face for a short section before you regain the gully and follow the South Spur. If you can walk the gully to its top without ever being pushed onto the face, you are not in the right one.

What the rock should feel like: easy fifth class at most, protected by a small rack and slung trees, with parties sometimes rigging a hand line over the exposed ground above the chockstones. Anything sustained or steep is not this route.

And the negative test against its neighbours: the big west face and the South Rib are separate features on other aspects. If you are looking at a large clean wall rather than into a vegetated cleft, you are round on the west side.

wa_southeast_ridge_se_corner.name: Shannon Ridge and the Sulphide Glacier to the notch on the southeast ridge
wa_southeast_ridge_se_corner.notes:
From the Shannon Ridge Trailhead, climb east-northeast up Shannon Ridge and onto the Sulphide Glacier — the standard Shuksan approach, and the same one the Sulphide Glacier route uses. Most parties camp on the large flat plateau around 6,400 ft, which is the usual staging point for summit day.

The snow between roughly 5,400 and 6,400 ft is where visibility bites: it is featureless open ground and parties report it as the tricky stretch in reduced visibility. Above camp the upper Sulphide is mellow, with a few small crevasses that are generally stepped over.

This route then leaves the standard finish. Where the Sulphide Glacier route walks to the foot of the summit pyramid and takes its Class 3-4 gully, this one gains the ridge at a notch further east and climbs about six pitches of well-featured 5.3 rock to the top.
wa_southeast_ridge_se_corner.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the Sulphide is walkable and the rock is out from under snow
hazards: Featureless snow between 5,400 and 6,400 ft that is genuinely hard to navigate in reduced visibility
Limited protection on well-featured but sparsely protectable 5.3 rock
Severe exposure on both sides of the crest on the final steps
Crevasses on the Sulphide, small but present
A descent that rappels a gully shared with the standard route, so parties above you are a rockfall source
wa_southeast_ridge_se_corner.baseFinding:
The notch is the route, and you can feel it rather than see it. Gaining the southeast ridge happens at a prominent notch at the top of the upper Sulphide. In cloud, work up the glacier until the snow stops rising and you can step onto rock at a low point in the ridgeline with ground falling away on the far side. A notch you can stand in with air behind you is the arrival; a rock wall in front of you with snow still under your feet is not.

The discriminator against the standard route, and it is the mistake to avoid: the Sulphide Glacier route's finish is a fourth-class gully up the summit pyramid, and it is the line almost everyone on the mountain is walking toward. If you find yourself queueing at the bottom of a gully with a bootpack into it, you are at the standard finish, not at this route's start. This route gains a ridge crest, not a gully.

Second test, on the rope: the climbing here is six pitches of extremely well-featured rock that parties describe as easy in boots, with limited protection and severe exposure on both sides of the crest. If your first pitch is a gully with walls either side of you rather than a crest with air either side of you, you have started in the wrong place. Exposure on both sides is the confirmation.

What walking past it looks like: continuing up the Sulphide beyond the notch brings you under the summit pyramid's south side, where the standard gully is. That is the descent for this route — the same gully is rappelled on the way down — so recognising it does not mean you are lost, but it does mean you have gone past the start.

wa_southeast_ridge_se_corner.name: Lake Ann and the Fisher Chimneys to the summit pyramid
wa_southeast_ridge_se_corner.notes:
From the Lake Ann Trailhead on SR 542, follow the whole Fisher Chimneys route to the foot of the summit pyramid: Lake Ann Trail #600 to the saddle, the climbers' path east to the chimneys, about 1,000 ft of class 3–4 scrambling through them, Winnie's Slide onto the Upper Curtis Glacier, then Hell's Highway onto the upper Sulphide Glacier.

Longer, steeper and more technical than the Shannon Ridge approach, and most parties take two or three days, camping at Lake Ann or above the chimneys. Where the Fisher Chimneys route finishes up the central gully, this one trends right off the glacier and takes the southeast ridge instead.
hazards: rockfall inside the Fisher Chimneys, especially with parties above
steep snow or ice on Winnie's Slide, firm before the sun reaches it
crevasses on the Upper Curtis Glacier
Hell's Highway crosses exposed slopes below the Upper Curtis icefall
wa_southeast_ridge_se_corner.baseFinding: You arrive on the upper Sulphide from Hell's Highway, so the summit pyramid is ahead of you and the southeast ridge is its right-hand skyline. Do not head for the central gully, the line with the fixed rappel anchors, which is the standard finish. Work right across the top of the glacier to the notch where the ridge meets the snow. This is the same arrival the Shannon Ridge approach makes.

wa_storm_king_southwest_scramble.name: The shared Goode approach to 7,400 ft, then the talus cirque and the right-most notch
camps: Rib camp below Storm King/Goode basin
Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail
wa_storm_king_southwest_scramble.notes:
Storm King sits at the head of Thunder Creek and is one of the range's most remote summits — a three-day car-to-car trip is the norm, and three separate trailhead approaches converge on the same high basin below Goode's south side.

The most common is Thunder Creek: from Colonial Creek Campground on SR-20, the Thunder Creek trail roughly 13 miles with little gain to the McAllister Creek confluence, past Junction, Skagit Queen and Thunder Basin camps, then the Park Creek Pass trail junction and the switchbacks to Park Creek Pass. Alternatives are McAlester Pass and Rainbow Creek from SR-20, or a boat or shuttle to Stehekin and High Bridge Camp then the Park Creek trail from the south. From Stehekin the boot path starts on the north side of a large whitish-rock washout about two miles above the Two Mile camp, near 4,100 ft, five minutes further into the woods.

Every approach joins that trail: from Thunder Creek, cross Park Creek Pass and descend its south side to the washout. Leave the trail at the small cairn, climb the burned ridge beside the washout ravine, trend climber's left through heather and game trails, and follow cairns above about 6,500 ft to the basin below Goode at about 7,400 ft. From there, traverse snow and talus, favouring climber's left, roughly a mile to the cirque below Storm King's east and west towers. A rib camp around 7,450 ft with nearby water is the usual base.

From the cirque, a long and very loose talus and scree slope leads up toward the southwest gully system. Helmet on and space out — that slope is the approach's main hazard.
wa_storm_king_southwest_scramble.season: Late July through September; snow often lingers in the basin above about 7,400 ft into early August, so carry an axe and consider crampons even for a nominally dry climb
hazards: Loose blocky rock on the talus approach and the summit ridge, with rockfall onto parties below
Lingering snow and ice in the basin and the summit gully into early August, and bullet-hard patches
An exposed class 4 ledge traverse just below the summit with real fall consequences
In-situ slings at the crux that are aging tat and need backing up before they are weighted
Extreme remoteness — assume a multi-day evacuation or a helicopter for any serious injury
wa_storm_king_southwest_scramble.baseFinding:
The most important thing to know about this approach is that below 7,400 ft it is indistinguishable from Goode Mountain's. The same trail, the same basin, the same cairned climber's path. A party in fog below that elevation cannot tell from the ground which peak's route it is on. The split happens above it, where this route trends toward the towers while Goode's continue toward the glacier or Black Tooth Notch.

The counting test is the notch, and the word is right-most. There are several notches in the summit rocks; the route crosses at the right-most one. Most of the way up to it is loose scree and talus, which is what makes the notch worth confirming rather than guessing.

Cross to the north side of that notch and the ground changes character completely: a fun ledge traverse on the backside of the tower, roughly 70 ft, with two or three class 4 moves and full exposure. If you have not crossed to the north side, you have not found the ledge traverse, and there is no version of this route that goes up the front.

Confirm on the ledge: it includes a squeeze under a slight overhang, and there are in-situ slings at the crux left by earlier parties. A squeeze move plus old tat is the strongest positive confirmation on the climb — though the tat is aging and is not to be trusted with body weight without backup.

The last move is a choice, not a crux: a 15-ft solid class 4 face crack, or a wrap around its left side on class 3 blocks. Both reach the register and the rappel slings.

And know which top you want: two 8,520-ft-plus points sit east of a triangulated 8,515 ft subsummit, and the easternmost is the true high point.

wa_storm_king_southwest_scramble.name: Stehekin and the Park Creek trail

bivy.name: Rib camp below Storm King/Goode basin
bivy.notes: Flat, grassy camp on a small NE/SW-trending rib just south of Storm King, with a nearby water source. It is reached by a mostly level traverse from the basin below Goode.

bivy.name: Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail
bivy.notes: The eastern counterpart to Thunder Basin: the last practical night before crossing Park Creek Pass from the Stehekin side, and the staging point for Buckner and Booker approached from the east. The trail above climbs through hanging meadows to the pass with good views of Goode, Buckner and Booker on the way. Coming in from Stehekin turns a very long one-way walk into a shorter approach than the roughly nineteen miles from Colonial Creek, at the cost of a lake crossing and road transport. Which side is faster depends entirely on whether the shuttle is running to the upper valley that season.
bivy.water: Park Creek is immediately adjacent and reliable.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required, covering Lake Chelan National Recreation Area as well as the park proper. Permits for an approach started from Stehekin still come through the same park system. Plan around Lake Chelan boat and shuttle schedules, since a missed connection can put you a day off your permitted itinerary.
bivy.capacity: Creekside stock camp on the Park Creek trail. Small; the neighbouring Two Mile camp downvalley was reduced to a single site by past flooding, so do not count on it as overflow.

wa_storm_king_southwest_scramble.notes: Take the boat up the lake to Stehekin and the shuttle to High Bridge, then walk up the valley past Bridge Creek to the Park Creek trail and climb it past Two Mile Camp. About a mile before Five Mile Camp, look for cairns marking a class 2-3 climbers' path up to the basin below Goode at about 7,400 ft. The least climbing of the three ways if the boat and shuttle schedule suits.

wa_storm_king_southwest_scramble.name: Cascade Pass and the upper Stehekin valley

bivy.name: Rib camp below Storm King/Goode basin
bivy.notes: Flat, grassy camp on a small NE/SW-trending rib just south of Storm King, with a nearby water source. It is reached by a mostly level traverse from the basin below Goode.

bivy.name: Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail
bivy.notes: The eastern counterpart to Thunder Basin: the last practical night before crossing Park Creek Pass from the Stehekin side, and the staging point for Buckner and Booker approached from the east. The trail above climbs through hanging meadows to the pass with good views of Goode, Buckner and Booker on the way. Coming in from Stehekin turns a very long one-way walk into a shorter approach than the roughly nineteen miles from Colonial Creek, at the cost of a lake crossing and road transport. Which side is faster depends entirely on whether the shuttle is running to the upper valley that season.
bivy.water: Park Creek is immediately adjacent and reliable.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required, covering Lake Chelan National Recreation Area as well as the park proper. Permits for an approach started from Stehekin still come through the same park system. Plan around Lake Chelan boat and shuttle schedules, since a missed connection can put you a day off your permitted itinerary.
bivy.capacity: Creekside stock camp on the Park Creek trail. Small; the neighbouring Two Mile camp downvalley was reduced to a single site by past flooding, so do not count on it as overflow.

wa_storm_king_southwest_scramble.notes: A drive-to start from the west side when the boat is impractical. Cross Cascade Pass and descend into the Stehekin valley, follow it down to the Park Creek trail, then climb Park Creek to the same cairned climbers' path up to the basin below Goode.

wa_sw_ridge.name: Agnes Creek from High Bridge, into the Blue Glacier basin
camps: High camp above the Blue Glacier
wa_sw_ridge.notes: From High Bridge, follow the Pacific Crest Trail and the Agnes Creek trail about nine to ten miles, cross Agnes Creek on a log and bushwhack steeply into the upper Blue basin, gaining about 5,000 ft. Camp on the exposed rock ridge above the Blue Glacier, directly below the east side of the Gunsight peaks.

wa_sw_ridge.name: Downey Creek and the Chickamin Glacier
wa_sw_ridge.notes: From the Downey Creek trailhead on the Suiattle River Road at about 1,400 ft, follow the Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek trails to Bachelor Meadows and Cub Pass, then go past Cub Lake, over Itswoot Pass and across the Dome Glacier to the Chickamin-Dome col. From the col, descend onto the heavily crevassed Chickamin Glacier and traverse it to the west side of the Gunsight peaks. This is a long, fully glaciated approach with a rope, crevasse gear and route-finding needed throughout.

wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.name: The northern line: Access Creek and Luna Col, then the high traverse over Luna, East Fury and West Fury to the Swiss-Fury saddle
camps: Luna Col bivy, Luna cross-country zone
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.notes:
From the Ross Dam Trailhead at milepost 134 on WA-20, about a mile of trail and service road drops to Ross Lake, crossed by the resort water taxi or by paddling or walking round. Pick up the Big Beaver Trail north along the lake and follow it roughly 10 miles to Luna Camp, then about 1.5 miles further to the Access Creek drainage.

Leave the trail and climb the brushy, moderately steep Access Creek valley, staying on its north side, to the open basin east of Luna Peak at about 4,300 ft. This is described as the easiest and least brushy approach on the east side of the Pickets. From there, gain Access Col and traverse cross-country and glaciated terrain over Luna Peak, East Fury and West Fury to reach the Swiss-Fury saddle.
hazards: A full traverse of both Fury summits simply to reach the saddle
Glaciated terrain between Luna Col and the Fury summits
One of the most remote positions in the range, with no independent descent
No marked features on the face; expect to find the line yourself
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.baseFinding: The base is a saddle between two named summits and you reach it by having crossed both summits of Fury. That is a hard test to fail and a hard one to pass: there is no way to arrive at the Swiss-Fury saddle by this line without having traversed West Fury, so if you have not climbed Fury, you are not there. Arrival: a saddle is the low point between two rises. From it, this route climbs the southwest face, and the descent runs back down near the northwest ridge toward the same saddle. If the ground above you steepens into a face rather than a ridge, that is the route. Nothing marks the foot of the southwest face; what you navigate by is the saddle and the ridge. Do not expect a cairn, a gully or a flake to confirm you; expect the shape of the col. What going too far looks like: continuing northwest along the crest past Swiss takes you toward the ground the Northern Pickets traverse uses, with no easier way down on that side.

wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.name: The southern line: Bacon Creek Road, Porkbelly and Mystery Ridges, Jasper Pass and Crowder's northeast ridge to Pickell Pass

approachLogistics.trailhead: Bacon Creek Road (off SR-20 near Marblemount)

wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.notes:
The alternate, and the shorter of the two in spirit if not in effort. It reaches Swiss from the south via Bacon Creek Road, Porkbelly Ridge, Mystery Ridge, Jasper Pass, Pioneer Ridge and Mount Crowder's northeast ridge, down to a camp at Pickell Pass.

This line is off-trail for most of its length, so treat the ridge sequence as the route rather than any particular tread.
hazards: A long off-trail ridge sequence with no maintained tread
No independent descent; exiting the range means committing to one of the long approach drainages
No tread or markers on either approach; the navigation is all your own
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route.baseFinding:
From Pickell Pass the south side of Swiss is climbed directly, and the test is that you are going up rather than along. Camp is a heather bench at the pass; the climbing starts on the class 3 south side immediately above it. Parties on this line downclimb the same class 3 south side back to the bench, so the ascent and descent are the same ground, and a party that has to traverse to find its line has left the route.

How to know you are at Pickell Pass rather than another saddle on the same ridge system: it is reached by descending Mount Crowder's northeast ridge. The last named summit before the pass is Crowder. If you have not been on Crowder, you have not arrived by this line.

Why this side may be the better choice, as a planning fact rather than a landmark: the northern line requires traversing Luna, East Fury and West Fury. This one does not require crossing Fury at all. The cost is a long ridge sequence with no trail and no bailout.

wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.name: Foggy Dew Creek and Merchants Basin to Cooney Lake
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.notes: Most parties backpack in and camp at one of the lakes rather than push the whole eighteen to twenty mile round trip in a day. From the Foggy Dew road end the trail climbs the North Fork past a two-tiered cascade — the last easy water before the country opens — and tops out of the timber into a wildflower basin below the ridge, where a spur trail branches toward the lake. An alternative comes in on the Crater Creek and Eagle Lake trail, taking a signed cutoff south past a second set of lakes to reach the same lake basin. Above the lake the ground is dry, so fill there. Larches turn gold around the basin in late September, which is a fine but colder window with a real chance of early snow icing the summit blocks.
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.season: Mid-July to early October; larch Sep
hazards: Lightning exposure on an open ridge and summit with nowhere to shelter — be off it by early afternoon
Loose rock and talus on the ridge crest
A long, essentially waterless final push above the lake
Off-trail route-finding from the pass to the summit
Iced blocks in shoulder season, which turn an easy scramble into something considerably more serious
Mosquitoes in the lake basins through mid-July
wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.baseFinding: From the lake the trail keeps climbing for roughly another mile, crossing a saddle at about 7,900 ft on the peak's southeast side, and then runs into the broad southeast ridge of the mountain. The point where the tread meets that crest is the base — everything to there is walking on a path, and everything above it is off it. The ridge itself is easy and broad, so the confirmation is the last few hundred feet rather than the first: the crest steepens into a field of large, mostly stable blocks that wants hands only occasionally, with a few more exposed steps possible right at the top. The neighbour to watch for is the similar summit under a mile north along the same crest, which is a comparable height, a comparable walk and shares a lake name with this one in places — parties do link the two, but if you have walked north along easy open ridge for the better part of a mile you are on the other peak.

wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.name: Crater Creek and the Eagle Lakes side

bivy.name: Upper Eagle Lake and Horsehead Pass
bivy.notes: The hub of the southern Sawtooth and the practical base for Switchback Mountain, with Hoodoo and Raven Ridge also within reach along the crest. Access is the Gold Creek side, not the Twisp River: turn off the highway onto the North Fork Gold Creek road, then a signed spur for several miles to the Eagle Lakes trailhead at about 4,760 ft. It is roughly 12.5 miles round trip to Upper Eagle Lake at 7,110 ft with only about 2,350 ft of gain, so it is a gentle carry by the standards of this range. Lower Eagle Lake at about 6,490 ft is the quieter option. Horsehead Pass at roughly 7,540 ft sits just above camp and is the gateway both to Boiling Lake on the far side and to the ridge walking that reaches Switchback. Linking on to Martin Lakes and Cooney Lake makes a longer circuit that takes in more of the southern summits. Season is roughly July into October; the pass holds snow on its north side later than the approach suggests. Be aware that Upper Eagle can be crowded and noisy on a fine weekend - if you want quiet, camp at Lower Eagle or push over the pass.
bivy.water: Both Eagle Lakes, and Eagle Creek is bridged on the way up. Above the lakes, on the pass and along the crest, there is nothing; carry water for any traverse day.
bivy.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit needed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Eagle Lakes / Crater Creek trailhead. This trail is open to motorcycles and stock as well as walkers, which surprises people. Fires are restricted most summers and firewood at 7,000 ft is not a renewable resource here.
bivy.capacity: Many sites - almost every level spot around Upper Eagle Lake gets used, plus a large horse camp just below it and further sites at Lower Eagle Lake about a mile off the main trail. This is the busiest backcountry camping in the range.

wa_switchback_mountain_scramble.notes: A higher start at about 4,760 ft and a gentler grade, with a creek ford. From the Crater Creek trailhead follow the Eagle Lakes trail a little over two miles, then the Martin Creek trail to the Cooney Lake trail; parties can also base at Upper Eagle Lake and cross Horsehead Pass. Often used to make a loop with the Foggy Dew side.

wa_thunder_mountain_north_face.name: Surprise Creek past Surprise and Glacier lakes
wa_thunder_mountain_north_face.notes: The more popular way in, from a trailhead that is easy to find near Scenic on US 2. Climb the Surprise Creek trail to Surprise Lake, join the Pacific Crest Trail and follow it north to Trap Pass, then take the unofficial path south from the pass to the Thunder Mountain lakes basin under the north face.

wa_thunder_mountain_north_face.name: Tunnel Creek, Hope Lake and the PCT

bivy.name: Trap Lake
bivy.notes: The closest camp to Slippery Slab Tower and the best base for Thunder Mountain. Two trailheads reach it: Tunnel Creek, which climbs about a mile and a half to Hope Lake on the Pacific Crest Trail and then runs south a couple of miles over meadowy ground before the switchbacks up to Trap Pass; or Surprise Creek at Scenic, which climbs to Surprise Lake and joins the Pacific Crest Trail heading north. Trap Lake sits a little below Trap Pass on the east side. From the pass a faint but obvious climbers' track branches south along the ridge crest, follows it to a boulder field, and works up that to the base of the tower — the whole point of camping here rather than at the Scenic lakes is that it puts a party at the pass within half an hour of leaving the tent. Slippery Slab Tower is a single pitch of pleasant lower fifth class on an arete whose flakes are not to be trusted for protection, so it is a short climb with a long walk attached, and an overnight makes the arithmetic work. Thunder Mountain itself is a scramble from the same ground. The Thunder Mountain Lakes further south are a delicate basin where camping is discouraged; use this lake instead. Season is roughly July to October, with snow on the Trap Pass switchbacks well into summer.
bivy.water: The lake, and the inlet above it. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is required for day and overnight use, taken at the trailhead register from mid-May to the end of October. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Surprise Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 feet west of the crest, and a stove is the right answer here in any case.
bivy.capacity: Several small informal sites in the trees at the lake, below the pass on the east side of the crest. Quiet, and rarely more than a party or two.

bivy.name: Thunder Mountain Lakes
bivy.notes: Lake basin under the granite of Slippery Slab Tower and Thunder Mountain, reached by the unofficial trail south from Trap Pass. The closest camp to the north face. Fragile ground; camp only on rock or bare sites.
bivy.water: The lakes
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit
bivy.capacity: A few small sites on durable ground

wa_thunder_mountain_north_face.notes: From the Tunnel Creek trailhead off US 2, climb about a mile and a half to Hope Lake on the Pacific Crest Trail. Follow the PCT south a couple of miles over meadowy ground and up the switchbacks to Trap Pass, then take the unofficial path south to the Thunder Mountain lakes basin.

wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.name: Goat Pass and the Stuart Glacier to the fourth-class gully and the notch
camps: Upper Ingalls Creek meadows, below Stuart Pass
Ingalls Creek basin camp, below Longs Pass
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, take the Ingalls Way trail over Ingalls Pass, past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, then the climbers' path onto the talus shoulder under Stuart's West Ridge and northwest to Goat Pass at about 7,600 ft.

From Goat Pass, traverse onto and across the Stuart Glacier rather than along beneath it, aiming for a fourth-class gully that runs up to the obvious notch in the North Ridge. This is the difference between this route and the complete ridge in one sentence: the complete-ridge party traverses east below the glacier to the toe, this party crosses the glacier and goes up.

The notch is a bivy: there are two good sites in it, which is why parties who intend to climb the upper ridge in a day from a high camp use it.

Published descriptions of this route are frank that the last of the navigation is yours — one of them says outright to take a topographic map and work it out. Treat that as a real warning rather than as rhetoric.
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; earlier the gully to the notch holds snow and the glacier crossing is simpler, later it is bare and looser
hazards: Crevasses on the Stuart Glacier crossing
Loose rock in the fourth-class gully, with parties above you in it
Knife-edge exposure on the ridge above the notch
The Great Gendarme's offwidth high on the route, with retreat from there awkward
Cold wind on an exposed crest; parties routinely carry bivy kit
wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.baseFinding:
The notch is a place you can sit down, and that is the test. There are two good bivy sites in it. If you have arrived somewhere on the crest with no flat ground, you are not at the notch — you have gained the ridge somewhere else along its length.

The approach to it is a fourth-class gully off the Stuart Glacier, not a scramble up the ridge flank. If the ground you are climbing is open face rather than a defined gully, you are not in the right line.

Orientation at the notch, which settles it: standing in the notch, the whole lower ridge falls away below you to the north and the Ice Cliff Glacier is on the far side of it. Everything above you is the upper ridge, and the Great Gendarme is roughly eight or nine pitches up from here. If the big tower is already below you, you have joined the crest above the notch and above two of the route's three named features.

What you have deliberately given up: about 1,200 ft of climbing, including the sustained lieback crack that is the hardest pitch on the complete ridge. So the notch is not a shortcut to be found by accident — a party that meant to climb the complete ridge and ends up here has walked past its own route. Confirm which climb you are on before you start up.

wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.name: Mountaineer Creek and the Stuart Glacier from the north

bivy.name: North Ridge notch bivy
bivy.notes: The ridge is gained at roughly 8,200 ft from the upper Stuart Glacier at about 7,800 ft via a snow-filled gully usually climbed on fourth-class rock along its edge, and the notch just above is the last genuinely comfortable bivy before the climbing proper. A second cluster of usable ledges sits several pitches higher, above the junction with the lower west variation, which suits parties splitting the Complete North Ridge over two days. Everything here is an emergency-grade perch rather than a campsite: no water, no shelter, and no easy retreat once committed. Whether to bivy at all is a live disagreement — many parties climb the route in a single push from Goat Pass, and which is better depends on your speed and the descent you have chosen.
bivy.water: None on the ridge. Fill from snowmelt streams on the traverse below the Stuart Glacier before committing, or melt snow from the glacier; there is nothing above.
bivy.permit: No separate climbing permit exists for the ridge itself, and the wilderness permit requirement is driven by which drainage you camped in. Parties staging from Ingalls and the Esmeralda side need only the free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit; parties who camped in Mountaineer Creek below are in the Stuart Zone and need that overnight permit May 15 to Oct 31. The boundary in the upper basin is not clearly drawn — confirm with the Wenatchee River Ranger District if you intend to bivy low on the north side.
bivy.capacity: Around four or five people at the notch itself, with a scattering of poorer spots higher on the ridge; the good ledges are few and far between once you are on the route

wa_upper_north_ridge_w_great_gendarme.notes: From the Stuart Lake trailhead, follow the trail up Mountaineer Creek, then leave it for the climbers' path into the basin below the Stuart and Sherpa glaciers. Climb the Stuart Glacier to the notch where the upper ridge begins. This suits parties camping in the north-side basin, but leaves the car on the opposite side from the Cascadian Couloir descent.

wa_whistler_mountain_scramble.name: Rainy Pass PCT lot, then cross-country east into the meadow basin and the col toward Cutthroat's southwest peak
wa_whistler_mountain_scramble.notes:
Park at the marked Pacific Crest Trail North trailhead lot on the north side of Rainy Pass at about 4,850 ft, next to the Road 600 turnoff. Leave the PCT almost immediately and strike out cross-country east into open forest, gaining steeply through timber and over downed logs. There is no maintained tread once you leave the PCT.

This is Whistler Mountain above Rainy Pass in Chelan County, not the Whistler Canyon trailhead area near Oroville, which is about 100 miles away and unrelated.

Round trip runs roughly 3.7 miles with about 3,000 ft of gain.
hazards: No maintained tread above the PCT; route-finding the whole way
Downed logs in the lower forest
Loose talus and scree in the gullies, with class 3-4 moves and real exposure near the ridge crest
Downsloping slabs and loose gravel in the summit gully
No reliable water above the lower forest
Early-season snow lingering in the forest and basin, firming the gullies
wa_whistler_mountain_scramble.baseFinding:
Climb until the forest opens. At about 6,100 ft the timber gives way to A meadow basin below the west ridge and gully complex, and that transition is the first reliable confirmation on a trail-less approach. Trees stopping is something you notice in any visibility.

From the basin, trend south and southeast on a rising traverse to gain the col and basin between Whistler and the southwest peak of Cutthroat. That col is the aiming point, and it is named by the two peaks either side of it.

Then work up the broad west ridge, or the shallow gully just north of it, to the summit shoulder.

The last section is the one that confirms you are on the summit line rather than a neighbouring gully: a rock gully with a visible ramp along the headwall, over downsloping slabs and loose gravel. A ramp cutting the headwall is the way through; helmet on here for rockfall from parties above.

wa_whistler_mountain_scramble.name: The unmarked SR-20 turnout, then a boot path onto the true south ridge at 6,180 ft

approachLogistics.trailhead: Unmarked SR-20 pullout about 3.1 miles east of Rainy Pass

wa_whistler_mountain_scramble.notes:
The second option, and the one that reaches the true south ridge. From the unmarked pullout on SR-20 about 3.1 miles east of Rainy Pass, 0.7 mile before the Blue Lake trailhead, at about 5,000 ft, walk back down and along the road shoulder to a boot path that starts at the west edge of a stand of trees.

About 4 miles round trip with roughly 3,000 ft of gain, the same as the PCT option.
hazards: An unmarked trailhead identified only by its distance from the Blue Lake trailhead
Trail-less above the first stretch of forest
Class 2-3 with occasional class 3-4 moves and real exposure near the ridge crest
Loose talus and scree in the connecting gullies
No reliable water on the route
wa_whistler_mountain_scramble.baseFinding:
The trailhead is unmarked and the path start is a tree-line edge, so the find is at the road rather than on the mountain. The pullout is 0.7 mile before the Blue Lake Trailhead coming from Rainy Pass. If you have reached the Blue Lake Trailhead, you have driven 0.7 mile too far. From the pullout, walk the shoulder to where a stand of trees begins, and the boot path leaves from its west edge.

Follow the boot path up through a meadow, then rising-traverse to intersect the level portion of Whistler's south ridge at about 6,180 ft. A level section of ridge is the arrival, and a level stretch on a ridge is something you can feel underfoot without seeing anything.

From there, scramble up the ridge and connecting gullies to the summit. The alternative, which is also correct: leave the ridge around 6,800 ft, cross a couple of gullies left, west, onto gentler southwest-facing slopes, and finish that way.

So the decision at 6,800 ft is a real fork and both branches work: stay on the crest for more exposure and directness, or cross two gullies west for easier ground.

The negative test against the other approach, which matters because both start within three miles of each other on the same highway: the PCT option leaves from the marked PCT North lot at Rainy Pass and gains a meadow basin at 6,100 ft below the west ridge. This one leaves from an unmarked turnout and gains the south ridge at 6,180 ft. Marked lot and west ridge, or unmarked turnout and south ridge.

wa_windy_peak_trail.name: Trail 342 from Long Swamp
wa_windy_peak_trail.notes: This is the easternmost of the high peaks here and by far the least technical, being a trail walk with a very short scramble stapled on the end, so the real work is the drive. Long gravel forest roads out of Loomis reach Long Swamp Campground, where Trail 342 starts and climbs steadily through burned lodgepole and recovering meadow to a camp with water partway up and then out onto open, treeless ridge. A shorter trail comes in from the Cathedral Driveway trailhead a few miles further west but is overgrown in stretches from lack of use, and a third start at Iron Gate involves the roughest driving of the three. Water on the upper trail is limited and seasonal, so carry enough for a long day.
hazards: Long trail mileage with limited seasonal water on the upper half
Fully exposed, treeless summit ridge in wind and lightning
Faint, braided cross-country tread over talus for the final stretch
Standing fire-killed snags along the burned lower trail in wind
Long gravel road driving far from any town
wa_windy_peak_trail.baseFinding: The trail does not go to the top, which is the single most useful thing to know here. Tread climbs to a junction and high point below and south of the summit at roughly 8,100 ft and then begins contouring and descending onward toward Horseshoe Basin and the Boundary Trail. The base of the scramble is exactly where the trail stops climbing. Standing on the plateau at that point, the summit rocks are obvious: they stand up as a small blocky pyramid of about three hundred feet, and there is nothing else nearby that looks like it. Leave the constructed tread and take the cairned, braided path up open talus on the south side of that pyramid; it is easy blocky scrambling and takes only a few minutes. The confirmations at the top are physical and worth checking, because the plateau carries other rises. Benchmark nails are set in the summit rock at the site of the old lookout, and remnants of the lookout's telephone line still run down the northwest slope toward the saddle, so if you can find the wire you are on the right high point. The way to know you have overshot is comfort: if you are walking downhill on good graded tread with the summit rocks behind your shoulder, you have passed the turn and should come back to the trail's high point.

wa_windy_peak_trail.name: Windy Creek trail from Cathedral Driveway
wa_windy_peak_trail.notes: The shortest way up. From the Cathedral Driveway trailhead, a few miles west of Long Swamp on the same road, climb the Windy Creek trail about five miles to its junction with the Windy Peak trail, then go a short distance more to the summit. Some maps wrongly show the trail starting from the Cathedral Driveway trail about half a mile west of the trailhead.

wa_windy_peak_trail.name: Boundary Trail from Iron Gate

bivy.name: Horseshoe Basin — Sunny Pass, Louden Lake and the Smith Lake meadows
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Windy Peak and the reason the trip is worth doing at all — the basin is one of very few places in the lower states carrying genuine alpine tundra, open rolling meadow at seven thousand feet with bighorn sheep on it. From the Iron Gate trailhead the trail is nearly flat for a mile and then climbs steadily to Sunny Pass at about 7,200 ft at roughly four and a half to five miles, drops slightly to Horseshoe Pass at around 7,000 and opens into the basin; Louden Lake is a little beyond, and the usual round trip to the basin and back is around twelve miles. Windy Peak itself is taken off the basin trails on open ground and is a walk-up rather than a climb, which makes this a rare Pasayten summit a party can reach without route-finding. Expect burn. Every approach into Horseshoe Basin passes through fire-killed forest, standing dead timber comes down in wind, and blowdown volume changes year to year. The last six miles of the Toats Coulee road to Iron Gate are rough enough to want high clearance. Late July through September; the tundra is exposed and there is nothing to shelter behind when weather comes over the border.
bivy.water: The limiting factor and it gets worse through the season. The climb from the trailhead is essentially dry after a tributary about a mile and a half up, and the basin itself is high rolling tundra rather than wet ground — Louden Lake and the small meadow ponds are the dependable supply and everything else is a gamble by August. Fill low and carry it up rather than counting on finding something at the pass.
bivy.permit: Pasayten Wilderness, national forest ground, and the permit expectation is the opposite of the Olympic files: a free self-issued permit filled out at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed to park at Iron Gate. Camp at least a hundred feet back from any lake shoreline. Stock parties need certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight. Campfires are legal in existing rings outside a burn ban, but bans run most of the summer here and firewood in the basin is scarce enough that most parties do without.
bivy.capacity: Dispersed rather than designated. There is room for several parties spread widely through the basin, with the usual spots at Louden Lake and around the Smith Lake meadows; horse parties use this country heavily and the good ground near water goes first.

wa_windy_peak_trail.notes: The roughest drive of the three. From FR-39, turn onto FR-3900-500 and follow it about six miles to the Iron Gate trailhead; a high-clearance vehicle is recommended and passenger cars are not advised. Hike north on the Boundary Trail toward Sunny Pass and Horseshoe Basin, then take the Windy Peak trail west to the summit scramble.
